docs.text: DEIStools ¶ Impedance estimation for electrochemical systems that change while you measure them. Classical EIS assumes the cell is the same at the end of the sweep as at the start. A cell that is charging, ageing or relaxing is not, and what comes back is a plausible-looking spectrum that belongs to no single instant. DEIStools collects the published methods for recovering \(Z(f, t)\) from a single multi-frequency record, so that they can be compared rather than chosen on faith. The package is deliberately several methods and not one. Each rests on a different assumption, and which is best depends on the system in front of you — a question this package is built to let you answer for yourself. Status of each method ¶ Research software is only as useful as it is honest about its own maturity. method status validated against STFT usable analytic ground truth on four simulated systems BLA per burst usable predicted noise within 0.3% of the observed scatter over three noise decades; no false distortion alarm on a linear cell DMFA :warning: provisional definition and filter now verified against the source papers; an end-to-end check against an independent implementation is still open BLTVA usable the source papers' algorithms, plus exact-recovery tests on a prescribed Legendre system Lock-in usable agrees with STFT to 9e-14 at the window centres Goertzel usable reproduces numpy's DFT and the STFT estimator to 1e-10 Detrending usable four strategies, each measured against the others; only differencing is accepted by BLTVA Uncertainty estimation exists for BLTVA only. STFT and DMFA return an estimate with no error bars, because the corresponding theory has not been settled here yet. See the roadmap . DMFA Treat DMFA results as provisional. The definition, the filter and the variance have now been checked against Koster 2017, Battistel 2016/2019 and Chukwu 2022, and three bugs were fixed in the process; what remains open is an end-to-end comparison against an independent implementation. See the roadmap and the implementation notes . Install ¶ pip install -e . A first estimation ¶ import numpy as np from deistools.processing.bltva import bltva, legendre_basis # a record of P whole periods of a multisine on these odd harmonics harmonics = np.array([1, 3, 5, 9, 13, 17, 27, 39, 59, 89, 133, 201, 301]) result = bltva( voltage, current, fs, P, harmonics, Np=8, # order of the Legendre expansion of Z(f,t) Nq=2, # order of the trend polynomial Na=None, # transient order: chosen for you harmonics="excited", band_halfwidth=50, ) # bltva returns model coefficients, not an impedance per instant Z = result.H_p @ legendre_basis(len(voltage), 8).T # (n_freq, n_samples) sigma = result.std_H_p # and an uncertainty Where to go next ¶ Getting started — the shortest path to a result on your own data, and which example scripts to read. Concepts — the signal model, the notation, and when "the impedance at time \(t\) " is a meaningful thing to ask for. Methods — one page per estimator: what it assumes, what its parameters do, how it fails. Implementation notes — where the source papers are ambiguous and what this code chose, with the evidence. Sources ¶ The methods implemented here come from: Hallemans et al. , IEEE TIM 70 (2021) 6503814 — the BLTVA model, Algorithms 1 and 2, the nonlinear-distortion and uncertainty expressions of Sections V and VI, eq. (49) and (55). Hallemans et al. , IEEE TIM 71 (2022) 6501711 — trend removal by differencing, the weighting of eq. (26), the rule for \(N_a\) in eq. (22). Breugelmans et al. , Electrochim. Acta 76 (2012) 375 - the short-time Fourier approach, and the transistor circuit of Fig. 7. For the per-burst BLA: Lataire, Louarroudi and Pintelon, IEEE TIM 61 (2012) 2132 — the best linear time-invariant approximation of a time-varying system, and the frequency-correlation test that tells noise from time variation. Pintelon, Louarroudi and Lataire, IEEE TIM 61 (2012) 3387 — the multiple-input time-invariant equivalent of a slowly varying system. Pintelon, Louarroudi and Lataire, IEEE TIM 62 (2013) 3361 — the periodic-excitation procedure: which bins carry noise, which carry distortion, and why two periods per burst are the minimum. Pintelon and Schoukens, System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach , 2nd ed., Wiley-IEEE Press (2012) — the underlying framework. For DMFA: Battistel, Du and La Mantia, Electroanalysis 28 (2016) 2346 - the first statement of DMFA, with the first-order expansion of eq. (11) that the later papers replace. Koster, Du, Battistel and La Mantia, Electrochim. Acta 246 (2017) 553 - the quadrature-filter definition, eq. (9), which is what this package implements, and the bandwidth ceiling set by the multisine spacing. Battistel and La Mantia, Electrochim. Acta 304 (2019) 513 - the physical definition via a Volterra series, the FFT-EIS/DMFA comparison, and the Fermi-Dirac filter of eq. (12). Chukwu, Mugisa, Brogioli and La Mantia, ChemElectroChem 9 (2022) e202200109 - the variance of the error on the admittance, eq. (19), and the correlation between neighbouring instants. For Goertzel: Goertzel, Am. Math. Monthly 65 (1958) 34 — the original recurrence. Sysel and Rajmic, EURASIP J. Adv. Signal Process. (2012) 56 — the generalisation to non-integer bins, which is the form implemented here. The lock-in has no source listed because it is the textbook demodulator; what is specific to a multisine is the integrator design, derived in Lock-in amplifier .

docs.text: Getting started ¶ Install ¶ git clone https://github.com/federicoscarpioni/DEIStools cd DEIStools pip install -e . The package needs only numpy and matplotlib . What you need from a measurement ¶ Three things, and one constraint. voltage , current the two channels, as 1-D arrays of equal length fs the sampling rate in Hz the excitation which frequencies were applied, and with what amplitudes The constraint: the record must contain a whole number of multisine periods . A rectangular window over a fractional period leaks, and the leakage is indistinguishable from time variation — the very thing you are trying to measure. bltva refuses a record that is not an integer number of periods rather than returning something plausible and wrong; STFT and DMFA will not complain, so trim the record yourself before using them. Check the record before you estimate anything ¶ N , the number of periods P , the period Tp and the rate fs are tied together by N = P * Tp * fs . When one of them is wrong the estimators do not stop; they return an impedance that moves in time because the arithmetic is wrong, not because the cell is. One call says whether the four agree with each other and with the signals, and when they do not, which one the tones disagree with: from deistools.processing.consistency import check_consistency, visualize_consistency report = check_consistency(voltage, current, frequencies, 1 / fs, period=Tp, n_periods=P) print(report) if not report.ok: visualize_consistency(report) It separates the two faults that look the same in the arithmetic: a record cut mid-period leaves the lines where they are, while a wrong sampling rate or period moves every line in proportion to its harmonic number — and the size of that movement gives the rate the record was really taken at. It also says whether every listed tone is present, whether anything is present that is not listed, and whether the channels are clipping. The shortest path to a result ¶ Each estimator is called differently, because each works in a different domain. The five "first run" examples show one estimation each, at settings that work, on the same simulated measurement: 04_stft_first_run.py STFT one function call, four arrays back 05_dmfa_first_run.py DMFA four steps: transform, locate, filter, extract 06_bltva_first_run.py BLTVA one call, returning model coefficients and an uncertainty 07_goertzel_first_run.py Goertzel a recurrence per bin, and a streaming filter 08_lock_in_first_run.py lock-in mix, low-pass, divide — the familiar instrument They are self-contained: each builds its own simulated measurement at the top, so you can replace that block with your own data and the rest still runs. A reading path ¶ If you are new to the package: 00_synth_stationary.py and 01_synth_transistor.py — how a measurement is simulated, and what a time-varying one looks like. 04–08 — one estimation with each method. 09_detrending.py — if your cells drift, which they do. Concepts — what the methods are actually doing, and the notation they are written in. 10–15 — what each parameter does, measured against known truth. 20–23 — the three main methods side by side on one system each. That is roughly an hour of reading and five minutes of running. Running the examples ¶ python examples/04_stft_first_run.py # figures in windows python examples/04_stft_first_run.py --save # figures to examples/figures/ python examples/05_dmfa_first_run.py --no-widgets # skip interactive sliders Every seed is fixed, so the numbers you get are the numbers in the commentary. The full set of twenty scripts takes about five minutes and produces 57 figures. Which method should I use? ¶ Short answer: try them — that is what the package is for. First, a simplification. There are five estimators but three ideas : Goertzel and the lock-in both compute the same thing as STFT , verified to 1e-10 and 9e-14 respectively. Choose between those three on what they offer — Goertzel runs on a stream, the lock-in gives a continuous output and a drift-corrected demodulator — not on accuracy, where they coincide. The real choice is between STFT, DMFA and BLTVA . Longer answer, from the comparisons in examples 20–23: Your system is roughly stationary. All three agree to within a factor of a few. Use whichever is convenient. BLTVA will tell you the system is stationary, by pruning its time-varying coefficient to exactly zero. Your system varies smoothly — charging, slow ageing, a temperature ramp. BLTVA is the most accurate and the only one that reports an uncertainty. DMFA decouples the time resolution from the multisine period and is a good cross-check. Your system changes abruptly , or in a way no low-order polynomial describes. BLTVA's assumption fails and no setting rescues it. Use STFT, which assumes nothing about the form of the variation. You do not know. Run BLTVA and compare its reported uncertainty with the error you actually see. A large gap means the model, not the measurement, is your limit — see BLTVA . My cell drifts ¶ Almost all of them do, and the handling is not symmetric between the methods, so it is worth reading Detrending before reaching for a filter. The short version: With BLTVA , raise Nq and do not detrend at all. It models the trend jointly with the impedance, which neither distorts the signal nor needs the trend to be guessed in advance. With DMFA or STFT , use PolynomialFit at the lowest degree that works, and know that it removes some signal along with the trend. Never pass Differencing to DMFA or STFT. It is built for BLTVA, which divides its attenuation back out; without that step it annihilates the lowest tones outright. 09_detrending.py shows all four strategies on one drifting record — the signals, the spectra, and what each costs.

docs.text: Roadmap ¶ DEIStools exists to collect the published methods for estimating impedance from multi-frequency signals of slowly time-varying systems, so that they can be compared and each one's limitations studied. That makes the list of methods not yet implemented part of the specification rather than a backlog. Done ¶ item outcome 2 BLA-style short-time Fourier method per-burst BLA : noise level calibrated to 0.3% against the observed scatter, odd/even distortion with no false alarm on a linear cell, and a frequency-correlation test that separates noise from time variation (9–19 against 0.73). The varying-cell case is item 2b. 1 Lock-in amplifier and Goertzel filter both implemented, with examples 07 and 08 and 15 tests. Both turned out to be the STFT by another route — Goertzel to 1e-10, the lock-in to 9e-14 — which makes them independent checks on it rather than fourth and fifth methods 4 Variance estimation for DMFA extract_impedance_with_error , following Chukwu 2022 eq. (19)–(20). Predicted/observed = 0.997 across three noise configurations. The comparison against traditional band filtering is still open. 6 Other detrending strategies moving average, Butterworth low-pass removal and polynomial fit, measured against differencing, with example 09 . Conclusion: only differencing can be a BLTVA weighting factor, and only the polynomial fit helps DMFA — and differencing buys columns rather than accuracy. See detrending Planned ¶ item why 2b The three-step estimator of Pintelon 2013 §V-B the per-burst BLA reports noise and distortion on a cell that is steady inside a burst, but on a varying one the time-variation skirt swamps both. Modelling the variation first — fitting the \(H_p\) branches at the non-harmonic bins — would lift that. Its step 3 cannot be transcribed as published -- the central differences it uses need equispaced harmonics, and on this grid they cost 156x on the first derivative while the second-difference formula diverges under refinement. The implementation note measures that and gives the replacement, so this is specified rather than blocked 3 End-to-end check of DMFA against an independent implementation the definition, filter and variance are now verified against Koster 2017, Battistel 2016/2019 and Chukwu 2022, and three bugs were fixed; what is left is a comparison against code that is not this code — see the notes 4b Slepian-basis DMFA the Fourier basis forces a periodicity that band-limitedness does not require; a DPSS basis is 5× better at the leading edge for the same cost 5 BLTVA with the Gaussian method for automatic \(N_q\) and \(N_p\) selection would remove the two parameters that currently need judgement — and the \(N_q\) result makes this more valuable than it looked, since \(N_q\) matters more than the detrending choice 6b Joint trend + envelope solve for DMFA a filter cannot separate a trend from the signal when both are in the same bins; putting the trend in the design matrix returns every affected tone to its trend-free accuracy. The normal equations are block-arrow and can be formed by FFT 6c Trend-aware demodulation for the lock-in method='ls' already carries a local slope and is 11× better than mixing on a drifting cell. Extending it to a local quadratic, and to STFT's windows, is cheap and untested Also open: uncertainty estimation for STFT and DMFA, deferred until the literature on it has been worked through. BLTVA has it because Hallemans et al. derive it; offering error bars for the other two without that grounding would be worse than offering none. Known gaps ¶ Loading measured data. deistools.processing.data_loader opens a Tkinter file dialog and takes no path argument, so it cannot be called from a script, a test or a headless session. cut_signal_extemes in data_preparation is an unimplemented stub, and its name is misspelled. Record trimming is left to the user. The examples all generate whole numbers of periods. bltva refuses a record that is not one; STFT and DMFA do not check. No diffusion model. All four simulated systems are RC-like. There is no Warburg or finite-length diffusion element, which is what most electrochemists would want to validate against. How a new estimator should arrive ¶ To keep comparisons honest, a new method should come with: a first-run example — one estimation at good settings, showing the call and what comes back; a parameter example — each parameter swept against a known ground truth; an all-systems example — the method on all four simulated systems; entries in the four comparison scripts; a row in the status table on the home page , stating honestly what it has been validated against. The existing examples 04–06, 10–15 and 20–23 follow exactly this pattern.

docs.text: deistools.processing ¶ Signal processing and impedance estimation. BLTVA ¶ bltva ¶ BLTVA — Band-Limited Time-Varying Analysis estimator. Estimates the time-varying transfer function H(w,t) between an excitation signal and a response signal measured under (odd random phase) multisine excitation, following Hallemans et al., Electrochim. Acta 466 (2023) 142939, eq. (71)-(81) Hallemans et al., IEEE TIM 70 (2021) 6503814, eq. (55), (58), Algorithm 2 Breugelmans et al., Electrochim. Acta 76 (2012) 375, eq. (1)-(14) [LTV-only variant] Model, per excited bin k_e, over a local band K_w: V(k) = sum_p theta_p(k_e) B_p(k - k_e) # target skirt + sum_{k'} sum_p theta_p(k') B_p(k - k') # other harmonics in band + sum_q theta_q B_q(k) # drift skirt at DC + sum_r alpha_r L_r(xi(k)) # transients + out-of-band H_p(w_ke) = theta_p(k_e) / U(k_e) H(w_ke, t) = sum_p H_p(w_ke) b_p(t) with the scaled DFT X(k) = (1/N) sum_n x(n) exp(-j2 pi k n / N) and Legendre basis b_p(t) = L_p(2t/T - 1). Naming is deliberately excitation/response rather than current/voltage: in galvanostatic mode pass (excitation=i, response=v) and read the result as an impedance; in potentiostatic mode pass (excitation=v, response=i) and read it as an admittance. Included: the band-limited least-squares estimate (TIM 2021 eq. 55-58), noise variance estimation (Algorithm 1), regressor selection (Algorithm 2), nonlinear distortion variances (Section V), uncertainty from both noise and distortion (Section VI), and trend removal by differencing (TIM 2022), via :mod: deistools.processing.detrending . Distortion estimation needs harmonics="all_nl" and an excitation that leaves harmonics unexcited -- an odd random phase multisine. With harmonics="excited" there are no regressors away from the excited bins, so the distortion is unobservable and cov_H_p falls back to the noise term alone. The excitation must also carry uniformly random phases, which no inspection of the data can confirm; see the precondition note on :class: BLTVAResult . Designing such an excitation is out of scope here -- this module takes H_exc as given, whatever produced it. The companion multisine package has Multisine.generate_orp for it, but nothing in DEIStools depends on that, by design: a user with their own waveform designer should not be shut out. Still outstanding: the local band is narrower than eq. (55) prescribes; see _band_bins . Dependencies: numpy, matplotlib. BLTVAResult dataclass ¶ Output of :func: bltva . The classical instrument, implemented offline. For each excited frequency the record is multiplied ("mixed") with a cosine and a sine at that frequency and the product low-pass filtered, which leaves the slowly varying complex amplitude of that tone. The ratio of the voltage and current amplitudes is Z(f, t). Mathematics Write the response near the k -th tone as a carrier with a slowly varying phasor:: v(t) = A_v(t) * cos(w_k * t + phi_v(t)), w_k = 2*pi*f_k Mixing with the in-phase and quadrature references gives v(t) * cos(w_k t) = (A_v/2) * cos(phi_v) + (A_v/2) * cos(2 w_k t + phi_v) v(t) * sin(w_k t) = -(A_v/2) * sin(phi_v) + (A_v/2) * sin(2 w_k t + phi_v) so a low-pass filter that rejects 2*w_k and every other excited tone leaves X = (A_v/2) cos(phi_v) and Y = -(A_v/2) sin(phi_v) . Twice the complex combination is the phasor:: V(t) = 2 * (X - 1j*Y) = A_v(t) * exp(1j * phi_v(t)) The same is done for the current, and Z(f_k, t) = V(t) / I(t) Choosing the integrator The low-pass filter is the whole method, because it must reject the image at 2*f_k produced by the mixing, and every other tone of the multisine , which after mixing appears at the difference frequency |f_j - f_k| . The second requirement is the binding one. For a multisine whose tones are all harmonics of a base frequency f_b , a boxcar average over exactly an integer number of periods of f_b has spectral nulls at every multiple of f_b -- that is, at every difference frequency that can occur. It rejects all of them exactly. A Hann (or any tapered) window has its nulls in the same places but a mainlobe twice as wide, so with a one-period window the nearest harmonic sits inside the mainlobe and is not rejected. A Hann integrator therefore needs at least two base periods. :func: integrator_length enforces this, and :func: tone_rejection measures it. The integrator length is also the time resolution: a window of m periods of f_b cannot follow anything faster than m / f_b seconds, which is the same trade STFT makes with its window and DMFA with its bandwidth. Edges The output within half an integrator length of either end of the record is computed from a window that extends past the data. This module reflects the signal at the boundaries, which is exact for an envelope with zero slope there and good otherwise, and :func: valid_mask marks the affected samples so they can be excluded from a fit. integrator_length ¶ integrator_length(sampling_time, base_frequency, n_periods=1, window='boxcar') Samples in the lock-in integrator, as a whole number of base periods. The Goertzel algorithm evaluates a single DFT bin with a second-order recurrence instead of a transform, costing O(N) per bin rather than O(N log N) for all of them. It is the standard way to detect a handful of known tones -- DTMF decoding is the textbook case -- and it is attractive here because a multisine measurement wants exactly a handful of known tones. Mathematics For a block of N samples and a bin k (the frequency in units of the block's own resolution, k = f * N * dt ), define w = 2*pi*k/N coeff = 2*cos(w) and run, from s1 = s2 = 0 , s[n] = x[n] + coeff*s[n-1] - s[n-2], n = 0 .. N-1 After the last sample the DFT value is recovered from the final two states:: X[k] = (exp(1j*w) * s[N-1] - s[N-2]) * exp(-1j*2*pi*k) That combination is asymmetric, and the symmetric-looking rearrangement is wrong:: X[k] = (s[N-1] - exp(-1j*w) * s[N-2]) * exp(-1j*2*pi*k) # WRONG It has the right magnitude and is out by exactly exp(-1j*w) in phase. The error cancels in any ratio -- including V/I -- so an impedance test will not catch it; only a comparison against the DFT itself will, which is what test_output_formula_is_not_the_tempting_rearrangement does. The correct form is what one further iteration with a zero input would give, s[N] - exp(-1j*w)*s[N-1] , written closed-form. The trailing factor is unity whenever k is an integer, which is the usual presentation. Keeping it is the generalised Goertzel of Sysel and Rajmic, and it makes the result correct for a non-integer k as well -- useful when a tone does not fall exactly on a bin of the block you chose. References Goertzel, Am. Math. Monthly 65 (1958) 34 -- the original recurrence. Sysel and Rajmic, EURASIP J. Adv. Signal Process. (2012) 56 -- the generalisation to non-integer bins, which is the form implemented here. Only two state variables are carried, so nothing but the recurrence has to be stored. That is what makes the filter usable on a stream, one sample at a time, with no buffer: see :class: GoertzelFilter . What it is, and is not, good for Offline, on the records this package deals with, Goertzel is slower than an FFT. The crossover is at roughly n_bins ~ log2(N) : below that Goertzel wins, above it the FFT does. A 13-tone multisine over a 20 000-sample block has log2(N) = 14.3 , so the two are a wash, and the FFT is better optimised. It is included because: it is a standard estimator and the package exists to collect them; it computes exactly the same quantity as a rectangular-window STFT, which makes it a useful independent check on that path; its per-sample recurrence is the natural route to online processing, where no FFT is possible because the record has not finished. The offline functions above exist because this package analyses recorded files, but the recurrence itself needs no record: it carries two numbers. This class is the streaming form, for an acquisition that has not finished. >>> filt = GoertzelFilter(frequency=0.05, sampling_time=1e-3, block=20000) >>> for sample in stream: # doctest: +SKIP ... value = filt.push(sample) ... if value is not None: ... ... # one block completed ``push`` returns ``None`` until a block is complete, then the complex DFT value for that block, and resets itself for the next one. """ def __init__(self, frequency, sampling_time, block): self.block = int(block) self.k = float(frequency) * self.block * float(sampling_time) self.omega = 2 * np.pi * self.k / self.block self.coeff = 2 * np.cos(self.omega) self.reset() def reset(self): self._s1 = 0.0 self._s2 = 0.0 self._n = 0 def push(self, sample): """Feed one sample; returns the block's DFT value when it completes.""" s = float(sample) + self.coeff * self._s1 - self._s2 self._s2, self._s1 = self._s1, s self._n += 1 if self._n < self.block: return None value = (np.exp(1j * self.omega) * self._s1 - self._s2) * \ np.exp(-1j * 2 * np.pi * self.k) self.reset() return value push ¶ push(sample) Feed one sample; returns the block's DFT value when it completes. The short-time Fourier estimator in :mod: ~deistools.processing.stft_functions reads the excited bins of each window and divides. That is enough to get an impedance and nothing else: a single window gives no way to say whether the number it produced is limited by measurement noise, by nonlinearity, or by the cell changing while the window was open. This module adds that. It keeps STFT's assumption -- the system is whatever it is inside one window, with no model of how it varies -- and uses the bins STFT throws away to classify the error. The one structural fact Cut a record into windows of P whole multisine periods. The DFT of a window has fundamental 1/(P*Tp) , so a tone at harmonic h of the multisine lands on bin P*h and only every P-th bin is a harmonic of the multisine at all . A nonlinear system of the PISPO class (period in, same period out) answers a periodic input with a periodic output, so its distortion is harmonically related to the input and can land only on those bins. That splits the spectrum of one burst into four classes: ======================== ==================================== bins what is there ======================== ==================================== ``k = P*h``, h excited signal (+ everything below) ``k = P*m``, m odd odd-order distortion + noise + drift ``k = P*m``, m even even-order distortion + noise + drift ``k`` not a multiple of P noise + drift ======================== ==================================== This requires P >= 2 . At P = 1 the window fundamental is the multisine fundamental, every bin is a harmonic, and the fourth class is empty. On the package's 13-tone grid, in band, :func: classify_bins counts === ======= ===== ====== ======== P noise odd even excited === ======= ===== ====== ======== 1 0 168 180 13 2 301 138 150 13 4 903 138 150 13 8 2107 138 150 13 === ======= ===== ====== ======== so the noise class appears only at P >= 2 and then grows with the burst, while the detection lines stay put. Since one period is exactly the window the plain STFT prefers, the uncertainty is bought with time resolution and there is no way around that. What the noise class actually contains On a time-varying cell the non-harmonic bins are not noise alone. The time variation convolves each excited line into its neighbours (Lataire 2012 eq. 48: a linear-in-time variation has B_1(k) ~ 1/k ), so every tone grows a skirt, and with a dozen tones the skirts cover the band. Measured on the transistor system, a 40 s burst cut from the usual 400 s record, as a ratio to the pure-noise floor at the same bins: ================ ======= distance to the ratio to nearest tone noise floor ================ ======= 1-2 bins 7656 6-10 bins 463 21-50 bins 71 51-100 bins 44 ================ ======= It decays, and it never arrives. So a noise level read off these bins is an upper bound , and on a strongly varying cell a loose one. That is not a defect of the implementation; separating the two needs a model of the variation, which is what :mod: ~deistools.processing.bltva is for and what this module deliberately does not assume. :func: ratio_noise_to_time_variation says which case you are in, so the bound can be read correctly rather than trusted blindly. Why this is not a preprocessing step A trend cannot simply be subtracted before estimation. Whatever filter removes it also shapes the signal of interest and the noise, and the estimator has to know about that shaping or it will report a biased transfer function with wrong uncertainties. Removing a trend therefore changes four things at once (2022 paper, eq. 18-27): every skirt regressor is multiplied by the filter response F(k) (eq. 21) the cost function is weighted by W = (F F^H)^-1 (eq. 26) the filter's boundary effects add their own regressors (eq. 21) the transient order Na shrinks by the order of the filter (eq. 22) A strategy here is consequently not "a function that returns a cleaned signal". It is the bundle of those four things, which is what the protocol below encodes. A strategy that cannot report its frequency_response cannot be used safely, because step 2 would be impossible. The weighting is what makes differencing free: it attenuates low frequencies and amplifies high ones, but it does the same to the signal and the noise, so the signal-to-noise ratio at every bin is unchanged (eq. 20). A naive low-pass-and-subtract has no such guarantee -- it would destroy exactly the low-frequency impedance information the measurement is for -- which is why frequency_response is mandatory rather than optional. Why only differencing works here Of the strategies in this module, only differencing may be passed to BLTVA . That is not an implementation gap; it follows from what the weighting does, and the reason is worth stating because it is easy to assume the opposite. (Differencing is also not usually the best option -- plain Nq , with no detrending at all, beats it unless eq. (49) caps Nq too low. See :class: Differencing .) A filter applied by circular convolution is diagonal in frequency: it multiplies bin k by F(k) and nothing else. Trend and signal that share a bin are scaled by the same number, so |T(k)| / |S(k)| is unchanged, for every k and every diagonal filter -- measured here as bit-identical before and after. The filter cannot separate them, because at a single bin there is nothing to separate them with. Step 2 then undoes even the attenuation: for a real, zero-phase response F/|F| = 1 , so the weighted system is identical to the one built from the raw record (verified to 5.6e-17 on the skirt regressors). What survives is only the damage: the trend block of eq. (58) has been deleted, the trend is still in the data, and nothing models it. Measured on the 2022 paper's own trend, with F(k) = 1 exactly -- a filter that does nothing at all, which the protocol happily accepts: ========================================== ========== configuration error at the lowest tone ========================================== ========== no trend, Nq = 5 2.2e-04 trend, Nq = 5, no detrending 1.6e-02 trend, ``F(k) = 1`` "detrending" 2.6e+00 ========================================== ========== A moving average does score well in that test (1.8e-04), which looks like a refutation until one varies the averaging length: L = 101 , 401 and 1601 all return 1.8e-04. An answer that does not depend on the averaging length is not coming from the averaging. It comes from the 1/|F(k)| weighting applied to the transient block, which eq. (21) does not multiply by F : since F ~ k^2 near DC for any boxcar, the weighting hands the transient polynomial a k^-2 envelope, and that reshaped basis absorbs the trend skirt. The trend removal is an accident of the reparametrisation, and a Butterworth low-pass -- same protocol, different 1/|F| shape -- scores 2.6e-02, worse than no detrending at all. Differencing escapes all of this because it is not diagonal. The zero-prepend of eq. (12) makes Delta^d annihilate a degree- d-1 polynomial identically in the time domain , which no multiplication in frequency can do, and leaves a boundary term that step 3 models exactly. Its F(k) = (1 - z_k^-1)^d is also complex, so F/|F| is a phase ramp that the magnitude weighting does not cancel. The non-circular route is closed for the others by eq. (49) rather than by principle: a causal length- L moving average with a zero-padded history would annihilate a constant exactly, but its boundary term needs L-1 regressors -- 400 columns for L = 401 , against the 2P-1 = 39 a band can support. So the other three strategies are provided for the estimators that have no weighting to undo, and for studying what naive detrending costs. They refuse to be used as a BLTVA weighting factor, and :func: check_response is the test that decides which category a new strategy falls into. Which strategy for which estimator Detrending is an argument to the BLTVA call rather than state on :class: ~deistools.processing.mfa.MultiFrequencyAnalysis , because only BLTVA can compensate for the shaping. The other estimators have no weighting at all, so for them whatever a filter removes is simply gone, and the choice inverts: ======================= ===================== ===================== strategy BLTVA DMFA / STFT ======================= ===================== ===================== :class:`Differencing` the only one that **destroys the works signal** :class:`MovingAverage` refused at best 1.7x, and not consistently :class:`LowPassRemoval` refused no help on an overlapping trend :class:`PolynomialFit` refused; use ``Nq`` the only one that reliably helps ======================= ===================== ===================== The two columns are exact complements, and one fact explains both. A diagonal filter cannot separate trend from signal inside a shared bin, so neither diagonal strategy helps anywhere. What remains is whether the estimator can undo an attenuation: BLTVA can, which is what lets differencing trade the whole low-frequency band away and get it back, so only differencing works there. DMFA and STFT cannot, so only the non-diagonal strategy -- the polynomial fit -- is any use, and it pays in distortion instead. Never pass differencing to DMFA or STFT. Differencing(1) attenuates the lowest excited bin of a 160000-sample record to |F| = 3e-04 ; the measured DMFA error at that tone is 1.00e+00, i.e. the tone is gone. In BLTVA the same attenuation costs nothing, because step 2 divides it back out. This is the single most dangerous thing in this module, and the reason frequency_response is mandatory: it is the only way to see the 3e-04 coming. Record consistency check ¶ consistency ¶ Does the record agree with the numbers that describe it? Every estimator here is handed a sampling time, a list of excited frequencies and -- for the windowed ones -- a multisine period, and every one of them assumes those numbers describe the record they were given. Four quantities are tied together by one equation, .. math:: N = P \, T_p \, f_s the samples in the record, the multisine periods it holds, the period and the sampling rate. Get one wrong and almost nothing refuses to run. The excited tones stop landing on DFT bin centres, the leakage that a periodic record was designed to avoid comes back, and every estimator in the package reports it as impedance: STFT sees a window that is not a whole number of periods and calls the leakage time variation, BLA's bin classes point at the wrong bins, BLTVA fits its Legendre polynomials to a record whose period it has wrong. The three error modes, and what separates them The arithmetic alone cannot say which number is wrong -- only that they disagree. The signal can, because a wrong fs or Tp moves the spectral lines while a wrong N only smears them: ========================= =========================================== what is wrong what the spectrum does ========================= =========================================== ``N`` (record truncated the lines stay where they are and the mid-period) *nominal* bin positions slide off the grid instead, in proportion to the harmonic number. Measured and nominal still agree with each other; each tone grows a leakage skirt because its bin is no longer a bin. ``fs`` (card clock, or a every line moves, by an amount typo) *proportional to its harmonic number*, away from a nominal position that is off the grid as well ``Tp`` (generator period the same as a wrong ``fs``: of the two only is not the one designed) the product ``T_p f_s`` is observable from one record, so the report gives both readings and you choose ``P`` (miscounted) nothing -- the record is what it is. The count is checked against the other three, and against how many whole periods the signal turns out to hold ========================= =========================================== So the measurement to make is the fractional bin position of each tone, :math: k_i , against its nominal position :math: h_i N T_s / T_p . Fitting .. math:: k_i^{\rm meas} = (1 + e) \, k_i^{\rm nom} gives one number, the relative timebase error :math: e , and the three readings of it are .. math:: f_s^{\rm true} = f_s / (1+e), \quad T_p^{\rm true} = T_p / (1+e), \quad P^{\rm true} = (1+e) P A record whose only fault is a truncated tail gives :math: e \ne 0 as well, and is told apart by :math: P^{\rm true} landing on a whole number while :math: f_s^{\rm true} comes out at an implausible value -- which is why the report prints all three and leaves the choice to the person who knows what the instrument was set to. :math: e is measured twice, by two routes that fail differently: from the whole-record spectrum, by sub-bin interpolation of each peak (Jacobsen's estimator). Precise, and blind to nothing except a tone buried in noise. from the phase of each tone period by period. If the period is right the phase is constant across periods; if it is off by a fraction of a sample the phase advances linearly, at a rate proportional to the harmonic number. This one also responds to the cell genuinely drifting -- but drift is not proportional to the harmonic number, and that is the discriminant. They agree on a timing error and part company on a drifting cell, so the pair says more than either alone. What else this looks at The same pass over the spectrum answers the neighbouring questions cheaply: whether every listed tone is actually present (a tone with no line above the local noise floor was not excited, or is not at the frequency it is listed at), whether anything not on the list is comparable to the tones (mains pickup, a forgotten harmonic, strong distortion), whether the harmonic numbers are integers at all -- :meth: ~deistools.processing.mfa.MultiFrequencyAnalysis.run_bla , run_bltva and run_lia all round f / f.min() and will quietly use the rounded value -- and whether the lowest listed tone really is the fundamental, which those same three functions assume. Nothing here raises on a bad record; reporting is the whole job. The one exception is a sampling time that is not a positive number, which leaves nothing to report on. References Jacobsen and Kootsookos, IEEE Signal Processing Magazine 24 (2007) 123 -- the sub-bin frequency estimator used for the peak positions. Pintelon and Schoukens, System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach , 2nd ed., Wiley-IEEE Press (2012), ch. 2 -- leakage, and why periodic excitation is measured over a whole number of periods. 'ls' fits a cosine, a sine, an offset and a local slope in a sliding window instead, which is insensitive to drift within the window but far slower. decimate ( int , default: None ) – Report every n-th sample ( 'mix' only). The result is smooth on the scale of the integrator, and the full-rate array is large. stride ( int , default: None ) – Spacing of the reported instants for method='ls' . Returns: (impedance, time) : ndarray, ndarray – impedance has shape (n_frequencies, n_instants) . Notes A boxcar integrator spanning exactly one base period makes this identical to :meth: run_stft_eis with a one-period window -- verified to 1e-13 -- evaluated at every sample instead of once per window. Use :meth: lia_valid_mask to drop the instants whose window ran past the end of the record. Each tone is mixed down with a cosine and a sine at its own frequency and the product low-pass filtered, leaving that tone's slowly varying phasor. The ratio of the voltage and current phasors is Z(f,t). Parameters ---------- n_periods : int Integrator length, in periods of ``base_frequency``. This is the time resolution: ``n_periods / base_frequency`` seconds. base_frequency : float, optional The frequency every tone is a harmonic of, in Hz. Defaults to the lowest excited frequency, which is correct for a multisine built on harmonics of ``1/Tp``. The integrator has to span whole periods of *this* frequency, not of the tone being demodulated, because that is what puts the other tones in its nulls. window : {'boxcar', 'hann'} ``'boxcar'`` nulls every harmonic exactly and is the default. ``'hann'`` rolls off faster but needs ``n_periods >= 2``. method : {'mix', 'ls'} ``'mix'`` demodulates and filters. ``'ls'`` fits a cosine, a sine, an offset and a local slope in a sliding window instead, which is insensitive to drift within the window but far slower. decimate : int, optional Report every n-th sample (``'mix'`` only). Notes ----- A boxcar integrator spanning exactly one base period makes this identical to :meth:`run_stft_eis` with a one-period window -- verified to 1e-13 -- evaluated at every sample instead of once per window. After mixing at one frequency, every other tone of the multisine lands at the difference frequency. This reports the integrator's response there -- one row per demodulated tone. A boxcar over whole base periods nulls them all, so the numbers are limited only by arithmetic. docs.text: BLTVA — Band-Limited Time-Varying Analysis estimator. Estimates the time-varying transfer function H(w,t) between an excitation signal and a response signal measured under (odd random phase) multisine excitation, following Hallemans et al., Electrochim. Acta 466 (2023) 142939, eq. (71)-(81) Hallemans et al., IEEE TIM 70 (2021) 6503814, eq. (55), (58), Algorithm 2 Breugelmans et al., Electrochim. Acta 76 (2012) 375, eq. (1)-(14) [LTV-only variant] Model, per excited bin k_e, over a local band K_w: V(k) = sum_p theta_p(k_e) B_p(k - k_e) # target skirt + sum_{k'} sum_p theta_p(k') B_p(k - k') # other harmonics in band + sum_q theta_q B_q(k) # drift skirt at DC + sum_r alpha_r L_r(xi(k)) # transients + out-of-band H_p(w_ke) = theta_p(k_e) / U(k_e) H(w_ke, t) = sum_p H_p(w_ke) b_p(t) with the scaled DFT X(k) = (1/N) sum_n x(n) exp(-j2 pi k n / N) and Legendre basis b_p(t) = L_p(2t/T - 1). Naming is deliberately excitation/response rather than current/voltage: in galvanostatic mode pass (excitation=i, response=v) and read the result as an impedance; in potentiostatic mode pass (excitation=v, response=i) and read it as an admittance. Included: the band-limited least-squares estimate (TIM 2021 eq. 55-58), noise variance estimation (Algorithm 1), regressor selection (Algorithm 2), nonlinear distortion variances (Section V), uncertainty from both noise and distortion (Section VI), and trend removal by differencing (TIM 2022), via :mod: deistools.processing.detrending . Distortion estimation needs harmonics="all_nl" and an excitation that leaves harmonics unexcited -- an odd random phase multisine. With harmonics="excited" there are no regressors away from the excited bins, so the distortion is unobservable and cov_H_p falls back to the noise term alone. The excitation must also carry uniformly random phases, which no inspection of the data can confirm; see the precondition note on :class: BLTVAResult . Designing such an excitation is out of scope here -- this module takes H_exc as given, whatever produced it. The companion multisine package has Multisine.generate_orp for it, but nothing in DEIStools depends on that, by design: a user with their own waveform designer should not be shut out. Still outstanding: the local band is narrower than eq. (55) prescribes; see _band_bins . Dependencies: numpy, matplotlib.

docs.text: Output of :func: bltva . Attributes: f_exc ( (M,) float ) – Excited frequencies in Hz. t ( (N,) float ) – Time axis in s. H_p ( (M, Np+1) complex ) – Basis coefficients of the transfer function at each excited frequency. H_p[:, 0] is the best stationary (time-averaged) transfer function. H_wt ( (M, N) complex ) – Time-varying transfer function, reconstructed on the full time axis. diagnostics ( list of dict ) – One entry per excited frequency: band width, unknowns before and after pruning, how many regressors each pruning step removed, the noise variance used as threshold, condition number, rank, relative residual. Notes Precondition on the distortion results. var_distortion_even , var_distortion_odd , cov_H_p_distortion and :meth: sndr_db are only meaningful for an odd random phase excitation. That means three things at once: only odd harmonics excited, so even-order distortion lands on empty even harmonics; some odd harmonics left unexcited, so odd-order distortion has somewhere to appear; phases drawn uniformly at random, which is what makes E{exp(j*phi)} = 0 and the best linear approximation well defined. The first two are visible in H_exc and are enforced: a grid with no unexcited odd harmonic in band yields None and :meth: sndr_db raises. The third cannot be checked from a single record and is the caller's responsibility. Phases chosen for a low crest factor -- Schroeder, or a best-of-N random search -- violate it, and the distortion variances then come out wrong rather than absent , with nothing to indicate it. If you optimised the crest factor, do not read these attributes. The drift is deliberately not reported. In Hallemans TIM 2021 theta_q is a nuisance parameter: eq. (58) carries the trend so that it does not bias theta_p(k_e) , and eq. (68) extracts only G_p . Within a single band the trend's 1/k tail is nearly collinear with the transient polynomial, so theta_q is not individually identifiable there. An earlier version of this module returned it anyway, reconstructed from the lowest band alone, and it was wrong by ~50% of the drift range with a 26% imaginary part. Recovering the trend belongs to a detrending step, which knows what it removed. Source code in src/deistools/processing/bltva.py @dataclass class BLTVAResult: """Output of :func:`bltva`. Attributes ---------- f_exc : (M,) float Excited frequencies in Hz. t : (N,) float Time axis in s. H_p : (M, Np+1) complex Basis coefficients of the transfer function at each excited frequency. ``H_p[:, 0]`` is the best stationary (time-averaged) transfer function. H_wt : (M, N) complex Time-varying transfer function, reconstructed on the full time axis. diagnostics : list of dict One entry per excited frequency: band width, unknowns before and after pruning, how many regressors each pruning step removed, the noise variance used as threshold, condition number, rank, relative residual. Notes ----- **Precondition on the distortion results.** ``var_distortion_even``, ``var_distortion_odd``, ``cov_H_p_distortion`` and :meth:`sndr_db` are only meaningful for an odd random phase excitation. That means three things at once: 1. only odd harmonics excited, so even-order distortion lands on empty even harmonics; 2. some odd harmonics left unexcited, so odd-order distortion has somewhere to appear; 3. phases drawn uniformly at random, which is what makes ``E{exp(j*phi)} = 0`` and the best linear approximation well defined. The first two are visible in ``H_exc`` and are enforced: a grid with no unexcited odd harmonic in band yields ``None`` and :meth:`sndr_db` raises. **The third cannot be checked from a single record and is the caller's responsibility.** Phases chosen for a low crest factor -- Schroeder, or a best-of-N random search -- violate it, and the distortion variances then come out *wrong rather than absent*, with nothing to indicate it. If you optimised the crest factor, do not read these attributes. The drift is deliberately not reported. In Hallemans TIM 2021 ``theta_q`` is a nuisance parameter: eq. (58) carries the trend so that it does not bias ``theta_p(k_e)``, and eq. (68) extracts only ``G_p``. Within a single band the trend's 1/k tail is nearly collinear with the transient polynomial, so ``theta_q`` is not individually identifiable there. An earlier version of this module returned it anyway, reconstructed from the lowest band alone, and it was wrong by ~50% of the drift range with a 26% imaginary part. Recovering the trend belongs to a detrending step, which knows what it removed. """ f_exc: np.ndarray t: np.ndarray H_p: np.ndarray H_wt: np.ndarray cov_H_p_noise: np.ndarray | None = None cov_H_p_distortion: np.ndarray | None = None var_distortion_even: np.ndarray | None = None var_distortion_odd: np.ndarray | None = None response_power: np.ndarray | None = None diagnostics: list = field(default_factory=list) _basis: np.ndarray | None = field(default=None, repr=False) def worst_condition(self) -> float: return max(d["cond"] for d in self.diagnostics) def worst_residual(self) -> float: return max(d["rel_residual"] for d in self.diagnostics) @property def cov_H_p(self) -> np.ndarray: """Total covariance of ``H_p``, eq. (76): noise plus odd distortion. Falls back to the noise term alone when distortion was not estimated, i.e. when ``harmonics="excited"`` left no unexcited harmonic to read it from. """ if self.cov_H_p_noise is None: raise ValueError( "no uncertainty available: bltva was called with prune=False " "and no noise estimate, so C_V is unknown") if self.cov_H_p_distortion is None: return self.cov_H_p_noise return self.cov_H_p_noise + self.cov_H_p_distortion @property def std_H_p(self) -> np.ndarray: """Total standard deviation of each ``H_p``, shape ``(M, Np+1)``.""" diag = np.einsum("mpp->mp", self.cov_H_p).real return np.sqrt(np.maximum(diag, 0.0)) def sndr_db(self) -> np.ndarray: """Signal-to-nonlinear-distortion ratio at each excited frequency, dB. ``|Y(k_e)|^2`` against the total distortion variance, which is what Section V says to compare in order to "decide whether the linear approximation of the system is acceptable". Large is good: the measurement examples in the paper report a minimum around 30 dB and treat a linear model as justified there. Requires an odd random phase excitation -- see the precondition on :attr:`var_distortion_odd`. """ if self.var_distortion_odd is None: raise ValueError( 'no distortion estimate: run with harmonics="all_nl" and an ' "excitation that leaves harmonics unexcited") total = np.nansum(self.var_distortion_even, axis=1) + \ np.nansum(self.var_distortion_odd, axis=1) with np.errstate(divide="ignore"): return 10.0 * np.log10(self.response_power / total) def variance_over_time(self, t_index=None) -> np.ndarray: """eq. (87): sigma^2(jw_k, t) = b(t) C_G(jw_k) b(t)^T. The uncertainty of the time-varying transfer function, shape ``(M, len(t_index))`` -- by default ``(M, N)`` over the whole record. Pass ``t_index`` to evaluate on a subset, since the full array is ``M x N``. The variance is time-dependent even though ``C_G`` is not: the Legendre basis weights the coefficients differently at each instant, and the higher orders grow towards the edges of the window. That is why estimates are least certain at the start and end of a record. """ cov = self.cov_H_p # raises when unavailable b = self._basis if t_index is None else self._basis[t_index] # real by construction: b is real and C_G is Hermitian var = np.einsum("tp,mpq,tq->mt", b, cov, b).real return np.maximum(var, 0.0) def std_over_time(self, t_index=None) -> np.ndarray: """Standard deviation of H(w, t); the square root of eq. (87).""" return np.sqrt(self.variance_over_time(t_index))

(39). dof : int Target degrees of freedom left after the fit. m : (K,) int Number of singular directions projected out in each band. Returns a real array of shape ``(N, order+1)``. The sample mean is removed from every p >= 1. On a finite sampled window the continuous property (1/T) int b_p dt = 0 does not hold exactly, so without this every time-varying regressor leaks into the DC bin. """ x = 2.0 * np.arange(N) / N - 1.0 b = legvander(x, order) # (N, order+1) b[:, 1:] -= b[:, 1:].mean(axis=0, keepdims=True) return b

docs.text: legendre_spectra(b: ndarray) -> np.ndarray Scaled DFT of the basis functions: B_p(k) = FFT(b_p)/N. Kept at full length N. The skirts are two-sided about their own centre, so a column centred at harmonic k' is indexed as B[(K_w - k') % N, p] . Source code in src/deistools/processing/bltva.py def legendre_spectra(b: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """Scaled DFT of the basis functions: B_p(k) = FFT(b_p)/N. Kept at full length N. The skirts are two-sided about their own centre, so a column centred at harmonic k' is indexed as ``B[(K_w - k') % N, p]``. """ return np.fft.fft(b, axis=0) / b.shape[0]

docs.text: build_regressors(K_w, k_e, centres, B, Np, Nq, Na, detrend=None) TIM 2021 eq. (58), or TIM 2022 eq. (21) when detrending is in use. Without detrending: target skirt, other harmonics in band, trend block at DC, transient polynomial. The trend block is present in every band, as the paper prescribes; bands where it carries nothing are handled by the pruning of Algorithm 2 step 6 on statistical grounds, not by excluding it up front. With detrending, two things change (2022 eq. 21). The skirts are multiplied by the filter response F(k) , because the data they model has been through that filter. And the trend block disappears -- the trend was removed rather than modelled, which is the entire point -- replaced by the filter's own boundary regressors. Source code in src/deistools/processing/bltva.py def build_regressors(K_w, k_e, centres, B, Np, Nq, Na, detrend=None): """TIM 2021 eq. (58), or TIM 2022 eq. (21) when detrending is in use. Without detrending: target skirt, other harmonics in band, trend block at DC, transient polynomial. The trend block is present in every band, as the paper prescribes; bands where it carries nothing are handled by the pruning of Algorithm 2 step 6 on statistical grounds, not by excluding it up front. With detrending, two things change (2022 eq. 21). The skirts are multiplied by the filter response ``F(k)``, because the data they model has been through that filter. And the trend block disappears -- the trend was removed rather than modelled, which is the entire point -- replaced by the filter's own boundary regressors. """ N = B.shape[0] blocks, cmap, j = [], {}, 0 def add(name, block): nonlocal j cmap[name] = slice(j, j + block.shape[1]) blocks.append(block) j += block.shape[1] F = detrend.frequency_response(K_w, N)[:, None] if detrend is not None else 1.0 add("target", F * B[(K_w - k_e) % N, : Np + 1]) for kp in centres: add(f"h{kp}", F * B[(K_w - kp) % N, : Np + 1]) if detrend is None: # q = 0 is identically zero off DC; its coefficient is the mean, V[0]. if Nq >= 1: add("drift", B[K_w, 1 : Nq + 1]) elif detrend.n_extra_params: add("boundary", detrend.extra_regressors(K_w, N)) xi = 2.0 * (K_w - K_w[0]) / (K_w[-1] - K_w[0]) - 1.0 add("transient", legvander(xi, Na).astype(complex)) return np.hstack(blocks), cmap

docs.text: estimate_noise_variance(response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, *, Np=6, Nq=5, Na=None, dof=5, safety=10.0, k_max=None, step=None, detrend=None) Estimate the noise variance spectrum (Hallemans TIM 2021, Algorithm 1). Parameters: response – As for :func: bltva . excitation – As for :func: bltva . fs – As for :func: bltva . P – As for :func: bltva . H_exc – As for :func: bltva . Np ( int , default: 6 ) – Upper bounds on the model orders, used to size the sliding band. Nq ( int , default: 6 ) – Upper bounds on the model orders, used to size the sliding band. Na ( int , default: 6 ) – Upper bounds on the model orders, used to size the sliding band. dof ( int , default: 5 ) – Degrees of freedom left after the fit in each band, eq. (39). Larger means a wider band, so a smoother but less local estimate. safety ( float , default: 10.0 ) – Safety factor a in the rank threshold, eq. (53). k_max ( int or None , default: None ) – Highest bin to cover. Defaults to a margin past the top excited bin, which is enough for every band BLTVA will use. step ( int or None , default: None ) – Spacing of band centres. Defaults to the band half-width n , so consecutive bands abut. The paper sweeps every bin; because the variance is smooth in frequency this subsamples and interpolates, which is far cheaper and indistinguishable in practice. Returns: NoiseEstimate – Source code in src/deistools/processing/bltva.py def estimate_noise_variance(response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, *, Np=6, Nq=5, Na=None, dof=5, safety=10.0, k_max=None, step=None, detrend=None): """Estimate the noise variance spectrum (Hallemans TIM 2021, Algorithm 1). Parameters ---------- response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc As for :func:`bltva`. Np, Nq, Na : int Upper bounds on the model orders, used to size the sliding band. dof : int Degrees of freedom left after the fit in each band, eq. (39). Larger means a wider band, so a smoother but less local estimate. safety : float Safety factor ``a`` in the rank threshold, eq. (53). k_max : int or None Highest bin to cover. Defaults to a margin past the top excited bin, which is enough for every band BLTVA will use. step : int or None Spacing of band centres. Defaults to the band half-width ``n``, so consecutive bands abut. The paper sweeps every bin; because the variance is smooth in frequency this subsamples and interpolates, which is far cheaper and indistinguishable in practice. Returns ------- NoiseEstimate """ if Na is None: Na = select_na(P, Np, d=getattr(detrend, 'order', 0)) N, _T, _t, k_exc, _c, _b, B, V, _U = _prepare( response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, Np, Nq, Na, "all_nl", detrend) n_theta_max = Nq + 3 * Np + Na + 1 n = min(int(np.ceil((dof + n_theta_max + 2) / 2)), P) if 2 * n + 1 <= n_theta_max: raise ValueError( f"P={P} is too small for Np={Np}, Nq={Nq}, Na={Na}: the noise band " f"({2 * n + 1} bins) cannot support {n_theta_max} regressors. " "Measure more periods or lower the model orders.") if k_max is None: k_max = min(N // 2 - 1, int(k_exc.max()) + 2 * P + n) if step is None: step = max(1, n) centres = np.arange(max(1, n), k_max + 1, step) sigma2 = np.empty(centres.size) m_used = np.empty(centres.size, dtype=int) for i, k_c in enumerate(centres): sigma2[i], m_used[i] = _noise_variance_in_band( V, int(k_c), n, N, P, B, Np, Nq, Na, safety, detrend) return NoiseEstimate(k=centres, sigma2=sigma2, n=n, dof=dof, m=m_used)

docs.text: select_na(P, Np, d=0) Transient polynomial order, Hallemans TIM 2022 eq. (22). Na = floor(3P/4) - Np - d + 1 d is the differencing order used for trend removal; it is 0 while no detrending is applied, which reduces the rule to floor(3P/4) - Np + 1 . Verified against the 2022 simulation example: P = 20, Np = 4, d = 3 gives Na = 9, as the paper states. The order is an upper bound. Algorithm 2 step 3 prunes transient columns that the skirts already span, so choosing generously costs little. Source code in src/deistools/processing/bltva.py def select_na(P, Np, d=0): """Transient polynomial order, Hallemans TIM 2022 eq. (22). Na = floor(3P/4) - Np - d + 1 ``d`` is the differencing order used for trend removal; it is 0 while no detrending is applied, which reduces the rule to ``floor(3P/4) - Np + 1``. Verified against the 2022 simulation example: P = 20, Np = 4, d = 3 gives Na = 9, as the paper states. The order is an upper bound. Algorithm 2 step 3 prunes transient columns that the skirts already span, so choosing generously costs little. """ Na = int(np.floor(3 * P / 4)) - Np - d + 1 if Na < 0: raise ValueError( f"eq. (22) gives Na={Na} for P={P}, Np={Np}, d={d}. Measure more " "periods or lower Np.") return Na

docs.text: check_identifiability(P, Np, Nq, Na) Hallemans TIM 2021 eq. (49): Nq + 3*Np + Na + 1 < 2P - 1. A band holds at most three harmonics of K_nl, so the largest number of parameters any band has to support is n_theta_max = Nq + 3*Np + Na + 1 . The band itself spans at most 2P+1 bins, of which up to three are removed, so there must be fewer parameters than that for the fit to be determined. Returns n_theta_max . Raises when the condition fails -- as the paper puts it, at that point one should redo the measurement with more periods. Source code in src/deistools/processing/bltva.py def check_identifiability(P, Np, Nq, Na): """Hallemans TIM 2021 eq. (49): Nq + 3*Np + Na + 1 < 2P - 1. A band holds at most three harmonics of K_nl, so the largest number of parameters any band has to support is ``n_theta_max = Nq + 3*Np + Na + 1``. The band itself spans at most 2P+1 bins, of which up to three are removed, so there must be fewer parameters than that for the fit to be determined. Returns ``n_theta_max``. Raises when the condition fails -- as the paper puts it, at that point one should redo the measurement with more periods. """ n_theta_max = Nq + 3 * Np + Na + 1 if n_theta_max >= 2 * P - 1: raise ValueError( f"eq. (49) violated: Nq + 3*Np + Na + 1 = {n_theta_max} is not " f"below 2P - 1 = {2 * P - 1} for P={P}, Np={Np}, Nq={Nq}, Na={Na}. " "There are more parameters than a band can support. Measure more " "periods, or lower the model orders.") return n_theta_max

docs.text: bltva(response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, *, Np=6, Nq=5, Na=None, harmonics='all_nl', band_halfwidth=None, rcond=None, noise=None, prune=True, detrend=None) Estimate the time-varying transfer function H(w_k, t). Parameters: response ( (N,) real ) – Measured time series. Galvanostatic: response=voltage, excitation=current. excitation ( (N,) real ) – Measured time series. Galvanostatic: response=voltage, excitation=current. fs ( float ) – Sampling frequency [Hz]. P ( int ) – Number of measured multisine periods. Must divide N exactly. H_exc ( sequence of int ) – Excited harmonic numbers of the multisine (h_m, so f_m = h_m/T_p). Np ( int , default: 6 ) – Order of the Legendre expansion of the transfer function. Controls time resolution: the variation is resolved on a scale of about T/Np. Nq ( int , default: 5 ) – Order of the Legendre expansion of the drift. Na ( int or None , default: None ) – Order of the transient / out-of-band polynomial. None selects it from eq. (22) via :func: select_na . All three orders are jointly bounded by eq. (49), which :func: check_identifiability enforces. harmonics ( ('all_nl', 'excited') , default: "all_nl" ) – "all_nl" -> regressors at every harmonic {0, P, 2P, ...} in band. This is the BLTVA of Hallemans TIM 2021; needed when odd nonlinear distortion is present, since its skirts sit on non-excited harmonics. "excited" -> regressors only at excited bins. The LTV estimator of Breugelmans 2012 eq. (11). Far fewer unknowns; correct when the response is linear. band_halfwidth ( int or None , default: None ) – Band half-width in DFT bins. None uses the half-distance-to-neighbours rule. For sparse log-spaced multisines, a few multiples of P (e.g. 5*P) is better. rcond ( float or None , default: None ) – Singular-value truncation passed to np.linalg.lstsq . noise ( NoiseEstimate or None , default: None ) – Noise variance spectrum driving the pruning threshold of Algorithm 2 step 6. Computed internally when prune is true and none is given; pass one to reuse it across calls, since it is the expensive part. prune ( bool , default: True ) – Run the statistical regressor selection of Algorithm 2 step 6. With it off the result is a plain least-squares fit of the full eq. (58) model, which overfits noise into the high Legendre orders. Returns: BLTVAResult – Source code in src/deistools/processing/bltva.py def bltva(response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, *, Np=6, Nq=5, Na=None, harmonics="all_nl", band_halfwidth=None, rcond=None, noise=None, prune=True, detrend=None): """Estimate the time-varying transfer function H(w_k, t). Parameters ---------- response, excitation : (N,) real Measured time series. Galvanostatic: response=voltage, excitation=current. fs : float Sampling frequency [Hz]. P : int Number of measured multisine periods. Must divide N exactly. H_exc : sequence of int Excited harmonic numbers of the multisine (h_m, so f_m = h_m/T_p). Np : int Order of the Legendre expansion of the transfer function. Controls time resolution: the variation is resolved on a scale of about T/Np. Nq : int Order of the Legendre expansion of the drift. Na : int or None Order of the transient / out-of-band polynomial. None selects it from eq. (22) via :func:`select_na`. All three orders are jointly bounded by eq. (49), which :func:`check_identifiability` enforces. harmonics : {"all_nl", "excited"} "all_nl" -> regressors at every harmonic {0, P, 2P, ...} in band. This is the BLTVA of Hallemans TIM 2021; needed when odd nonlinear distortion is present, since its skirts sit on non-excited harmonics. "excited" -> regressors only at excited bins. The LTV estimator of Breugelmans 2012 eq. (11). Far fewer unknowns; correct when the response is linear. band_halfwidth : int or None Band half-width in DFT bins. None uses the half-distance-to-neighbours rule. For sparse log-spaced multisines, a few multiples of P (e.g. 5*P) is better. rcond : float or None Singular-value truncation passed to ``np.linalg.lstsq``. noise : NoiseEstimate or None Noise variance spectrum driving the pruning threshold of Algorithm 2 step 6. Computed internally when ``prune`` is true and none is given; pass one to reuse it across calls, since it is the expensive part. prune : bool Run the statistical regressor selection of Algorithm 2 step 6. With it off the result is a plain least-squares fit of the full eq. (58) model, which overfits noise into the high Legendre orders. Returns ------- BLTVAResult """ if Na is None: Na = select_na(P, Np, d=getattr(detrend, 'order', 0)) N, T, t, k_exc, all_centres, b, B, V, U = _prepare( response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, Np, Nq, Na, harmonics, detrend) _warn_if_bands_are_huge(k_exc, N, band_halfwidth, P) if prune and noise is None: noise = estimate_noise_variance(response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, Np=Np, Nq=Nq, Na=Na, detrend=detrend) # --- sweep the excited frequencies ------------------------------------- M = k_exc.size H_p = np.zeros((M, Np + 1), dtype=complex) has_cov = noise is not None cov_noise = np.zeros((M, Np + 1, Np + 1), dtype=complex) if has_cov else None cov_dist = np.zeros((M, Np + 1, Np + 1), dtype=complex) if has_cov else None var_even = np.full((M, Np + 1), np.nan) var_odd = np.full((M, Np + 1), np.nan) Y_exc = np.zeros(M) any_distortion = False k_exc_set = {int(k) for k in k_exc} diagnostics = [] for e in range(M): fit = _fit_band(e, k_exc, N, band_halfwidth, all_centres, B, Np, Nq, Na, V, rcond, noise, detrend, prune) cmap, theta, K_w = fit["cmap"], fit["theta"], fit["K_w"] gain = np.abs(U[fit["k_e"]]) ** 2 H_p[e] = theta[cmap["target"]] / U[fit["k_e"]] Y_exc[e] = np.abs(V[fit["k_e"]]) ** 2 if has_cov: # eq. (84): dividing theta by U(k_e) divides the covariance by # |U(k_e)|^2. tgt = cmap["target"] cov_noise[e] = fit["cov"][tgt, tgt] / gain # Section V needs regressors at the unexcited harmonics, which only # harmonics="all_nl" provides. if harmonics == "all_nl": even, odd, odd_free = _distortion_variances( fit, P, k_exc_set, fit["sigma2_n"], Np) var_even[e], var_odd[e] = even, odd if odd_free: any_distortion = True if has_cov: C = _distortion_covariance( fit, B, N, Np, odd_free, fit["sigma2_bins"]) if C is not None: cov_dist[e] = C / gain diagnostics.append({ "k_e": fit["k_e"], "f_exc": fit["k_e"] / T, "N_w": int(K_w.size), "n_theta": fit["n_theta"], "n_theta_full": fit["n_theta_full"], "n_centres": len(fit["centres"]), "n_transient_dropped": fit["n_transient_dropped"], "n_unsupported_dropped": fit["n_unsupported_dropped"], "sigma2_n": fit["sigma2_n"], "cond": fit["cond"], "rank": fit["rank"], "rel_residual": float(np.linalg.norm(fit["residual"]) / np.linalg.norm(fit["V_w"])), }) # --- reconstruct over time --------------------------------------------- H_wt = H_p @ b[:, : Np + 1].T # (M, N) if not any_distortion: var_even = var_odd = None cov_dist = None return BLTVAResult( f_exc=k_exc / T, t=t, H_p=H_p, H_wt=H_wt, cov_H_p_noise=cov_noise, cov_H_p_distortion=cov_dist, var_distortion_even=var_even, var_distortion_odd=var_odd, response_power=Y_exc, diagnostics=diagnostics, _basis=b[:, : Np + 1], )

docs.text: visualize_bltva_fit(response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, *, Np=6, Nq=5, Na=None, harmonics='all_nl', band_halfwidth=None, rcond=None, noise=None, prune=True, detrend=None) Slider-based visual check of the band-limited least-squares fit. For each excited frequency (selected with a slider, as in :func: deistools.processing.dmfa_functions.visualize_dmfa_filtering ), shows: top: the local DFT band data |V(k)| against the least-squares model |K @ theta| , restricted to the band actually used for that frequency. bottom: the fitted target-block Legendre coefficients |theta_p| (the ones that become H_p ), which exposes overfitting or ill-conditioning as unreasonably large high-order coefficients. Parameters are identical to :func: bltva , so the same call used to produce a result can be reused here to inspect it. Returns: ( fig , axs ) – Source code in src/deistools/processing/bltva.py def visualize_bltva_fit(response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, *, Np=6, Nq=5, Na=None, harmonics="all_nl", band_halfwidth=None, rcond=None, noise=None, prune=True, detrend=None): """Slider-based visual check of the band-limited least-squares fit. For each excited frequency (selected with a slider, as in :func:`deistools.processing.dmfa_functions.visualize_dmfa_filtering`), shows: - top: the local DFT band data ``|V(k)|`` against the least-squares model ``|K @ theta|``, restricted to the band actually used for that frequency. - bottom: the fitted target-block Legendre coefficients ``|theta_p|`` (the ones that become ``H_p``), which exposes overfitting or ill-conditioning as unreasonably large high-order coefficients. Parameters are identical to :func:`bltva`, so the same call used to produce a result can be reused here to inspect it. Returns ------- fig, axs """ if Na is None: Na = select_na(P, Np, d=getattr(detrend, 'order', 0)) N, T, _t, k_exc, all_centres, _b, B, V, U = _prepare( response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, Np, Nq, Na, harmonics, detrend) _warn_if_bands_are_huge(k_exc, N, band_halfwidth, P) M = k_exc.size if prune and noise is None: noise = estimate_noise_variance(response, excitation, fs, P, H_exc, Np=Np, Nq=Nq, Na=Na, detrend=detrend) def plot_band(e): fit = _fit_band(e, k_exc, N, band_halfwidth, all_centres, B, Np, Nq, Na, V, rcond, noise, detrend, prune) f_band = fit["K_w"] / T f_exc = fit["k_e"] / T theta_p = fit["theta"][fit["cmap"]["target"]] axs[0].plot(f_band, np.abs(fit["V_w"]), '-o', color='C0', label='Data') axs[0].plot(f_band, np.abs(fit["fit"]), 'x', color='C1', label='Fit') axs[0].axvline(f_exc, color='green', linestyle='--') axs[0].set_xlabel('Frequency / Hz') axs[0].set_ylabel('|V(k)|') axs[0].set_title( f'Excited frequency {f_exc:.4g} Hz ' f'cond={fit["cond"]:.2e} ' f'rel. residual={np.linalg.norm(fit["residual"]) / np.linalg.norm(fit["V_w"]):.2e} ' f'kept {fit["n_theta"]}/{fit["n_theta_full"]} regressors' ) axs[0].legend() axs[1].bar(np.arange(theta_p.size), np.abs(theta_p), color='C0') axs[1].set_yscale('log') axs[1].set_xlabel('Legendre order p') axs[1].set_ylabel(r'$|\theta_p|$ (target block)') def update(val): for ax in axs: ax.clear() plot_band(val) fig.canvas.draw_idle() fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 8)) fig.subplots_adjust(bottom=0.25) sliders_freq_ax = fig.add_axes([0.20, 0.15, 0.60, 0.03]) slider_frequency = Slider( ax=sliders_freq_ax, label="Excited freq. index", valmin=0, valmax=M - 1, valinit=0, valstep=1, ) plot_band(slider_frequency.val) slider_frequency.on_changed(update) plt.show() return fig, axs

The band is Npts_elab DFT bins wide and the bins are 1/T apart, so it spans Npts_elab / T Hz -- not the sampling rate. Build the passband filter on this axis, or its bandwidth is scaled wrongly by fs*T/Npts_elab . The band is ``Npts_elab`` DFT bins wide and the bins are ``1/T`` apart, so it spans ``Npts_elab / T`` Hz -- *not* the sampling rate. Build the passband filter on this axis, or its bandwidth is scaled wrongly by ``fs*T/Npts_elab``. """ return (np.arange(Npts_elab) - Npts_elab // 2) / float(measurement_time)

The inverse transform of Npts_elab bins of width 1/T returns Npts_elab samples covering the whole record, so the step is T / Npts_elab -- coarser than the acquisition, and the resolution at which DMFA can follow a change. The inverse transform of ``Npts_elab`` bins of width ``1/T`` returns ``Npts_elab`` samples covering the whole record, so the step is ``T / Npts_elab`` -- coarser than the acquisition, and the resolution at which DMFA can follow a change. docs.text: max_elaboration_points(indexes_multisine_freq, n_samples) Largest Npts_elab whose band fits inside the spectrum at every frequency. Each frequency is extracted from a window of Npts_elab bins centred on its peak, so the window must not run past either end of the spectrum. The binding constraint is the frequency closest to an edge -- in practice the highest one, since its bin sits max(index) from the top. Source code in src/deistools/processing/dmfa_functions.py def max_elaboration_points(indexes_multisine_freq, n_samples): """Largest ``Npts_elab`` whose band fits inside the spectrum at every frequency. Each frequency is extracted from a window of ``Npts_elab`` bins centred on its peak, so the window must not run past either end of the spectrum. The binding constraint is the frequency closest to an edge -- in practice the highest one, since its bin sits ``max(index)`` from the top. """ lowest = min(indexes_multisine_freq) highest = max(indexes_multisine_freq) return 2 * min(lowest, n_samples - highest)

docs.text: extract_impedance_with_error(ft_voltage, ft_current, variance_voltage, variance_current, indexes_multisine_freq: list, filter, Npts_elab) Impedance and the variance of its error, per frequency and instant. DMFA is a linear estimator of the envelope -- band selection, a diagonal weighting by the filter, and an inverse transform are all linear -- so the variance of its output is the covariance of a linear map applied to the measurement noise. That is the same route BLTVA takes, and it gives the expression of Chukwu et al. (2022) eq. (19)-(20): var(Re Z) = [ var_v + |Z|^2 * var_i ] / ( 2 * N' * |I_filtered|^2 ) N' = N / sum(|g|^2) with N the length of the whole record -- not of the extracted band -- and N' the usual equivalent noise bandwidth. The real and imaginary parts have the same variance, which is why the factor of two appears. Verified against the scatter of 200 noise realisations on a stationary cell: predicted and observed agree to better than 1%. Parameters: variance_voltage ( float ) – Variances ( not standard deviations) of the noise on the two channels. They can be measured from the instrument, or -- better -- taken from bins the excitation never reaches, as :func: deistools.processing.bltva.estimate_noise_variance does, which also captures the noise colour. variance_current ( float ) – Variances ( not standard deviations) of the noise on the two channels. They can be measured from the instrument, or -- better -- taken from bins the excitation never reaches, as :func: deistools.processing.bltva.estimate_noise_variance does, which also captures the noise colour. Returns: (impedance, variance) : ndarray, ndarray – Both (n_frequencies, Npts_elab) . variance is that of either the real or the imaginary part. Notes This covers noise only . Nothing here knows about the band-limited model being wrong, which near the record edges it badly is; compare the prediction with the error you actually see, exactly as for BLTVA. Source code in src/deistools/processing/dmfa_functions.py def extract_impedance_with_error( ft_voltage, ft_current, variance_voltage, variance_current, indexes_multisine_freq: list, filter, Npts_elab, ): """Impedance and the variance of its error, per frequency and instant. DMFA is a **linear** estimator of the envelope -- band selection, a diagonal weighting by the filter, and an inverse transform are all linear -- so the variance of its output is the covariance of a linear map applied to the measurement noise. That is the same route BLTVA takes, and it gives the expression of Chukwu et al. (2022) eq. (19)-(20): var(Re Z) = [ var_v + |Z|^2 * var_i ] / ( 2 * N' * |I_filtered|^2 ) N' = N / sum(|g|^2) with ``N`` the length of the whole record -- not of the extracted band -- and ``N'`` the usual equivalent noise bandwidth. The real and imaginary parts have the same variance, which is why the factor of two appears. Verified against the scatter of 200 noise realisations on a stationary cell: predicted and observed agree to better than 1%. Parameters ---------- variance_voltage, variance_current : float Variances (**not** standard deviations) of the noise on the two channels. They can be measured from the instrument, or -- better -- taken from bins the excitation never reaches, as :func:`deistools.processing.bltva.estimate_noise_variance` does, which also captures the noise colour. Returns ------- (impedance, variance) : ndarray, ndarray Both ``(n_frequencies, Npts_elab)``. ``variance`` is that of either the real or the imaginary part. Notes ----- This covers **noise only**. Nothing here knows about the band-limited model being wrong, which near the record edges it badly is; compare the prediction with the error you actually see, exactly as for BLTVA. """ _check_elaboration_range(indexes_multisine_freq, Npts_elab, ft_voltage.size) n_freq = len(indexes_multisine_freq) impedance = np.zeros((n_freq, Npts_elab), dtype="complex128") variance = np.zeros((n_freq, Npts_elab), dtype="float64") # N' uses the length of the record, which is what the noise was spread # over, not the width of the extracted band. N_prime = ft_voltage.size / np.sum(np.abs(filter) ** 2) for f in range(n_freq): if Npts_elab % 2 == 0: elaboration_rng = np.arange(indexes_multisine_freq[f] - Npts_elab // 2, indexes_multisine_freq[f] + Npts_elab // 2) else: elaboration_rng = np.arange(indexes_multisine_freq[f] - Npts_elab // 2, indexes_multisine_freq[f] + Npts_elab // 2 + 1) voltage_filtered = Npts_elab * ifft(ifftshift(ft_voltage[elaboration_rng] * filter)) current_filtered = Npts_elab * ifft(ifftshift(ft_current[elaboration_rng] * filter)) impedance[f] = voltage_filtered / current_filtered numerator = variance_voltage + np.abs(impedance[f]) ** 2 * variance_current variance[f] = numerator / (2 * N_prime * np.abs(current_filtered) ** 2) return impedance, variance
