docs.text: independent_time_step(bandwidth) Output spacing at which neighbouring DMFA errors are uncorrelated. The filter kernel spans about 1/bandwidth in time, so estimates taken closer together than that rest on overlapping data and their errors are correlated. Chukwu et al. (2022) put the correlation below 20% once successive instants are more than 0.5/bandwidth apart, and measured on a stationary cell over 150 noise realisations the correlation between neighbours is: spacing corr(e_j, e_j+1) 0.125/bw 84% 0.25/bw 49% 0.5/bw 3% 1/bw -3% Reporting more densely than this is fine for looking at a result, but the points are then not independent observations : using them as such in a least-squares fit will make the parameter uncertainties too small. Note that Npts_elab sets both the width of the extracted band and the number of reported instants, and those are different concerns -- the band must be wide enough for the filter to have decayed, which is finer than this spacing. Extract with a wide band and decimate the result to independent_time_step before fitting. Source code in src/deistools/processing/dmfa_functions.py def independent_time_step(bandwidth): """Output spacing at which neighbouring DMFA errors are uncorrelated. The filter kernel spans about ``1/bandwidth`` in time, so estimates taken closer together than that rest on overlapping data and their errors are correlated. Chukwu et al. (2022) put the correlation below 20% once successive instants are more than ``0.5/bandwidth`` apart, and measured on a stationary cell over 150 noise realisations the correlation between neighbours is: spacing corr(e_j, e_j+1) 0.125/bw 84% 0.25/bw 49% 0.5/bw 3% 1/bw -3% Reporting more densely than this is fine for looking at a result, but the points are then **not independent observations**: using them as such in a least-squares fit will make the parameter uncertainties too small. Note that ``Npts_elab`` sets both the width of the extracted band and the number of reported instants, and those are different concerns -- the band must be wide enough for the filter to have decayed, which is finer than this spacing. Extract with a wide band and decimate the result to ``independent_time_step`` before fitting. """ return 0.5 / float(bandwidth)

docs.text: pad_record(signal, factor=2) Zero-pad a record so DMFA's band extraction is a linear convolution. Multiplying a spectrum by a filter is a circular convolution in time: the filter kernel that reaches past the end of the record wraps around and picks up the beginning. For a time-varying impedance the two ends are different -- 106 ohm against 43 ohm on the transistor system -- so the estimate near either boundary is contaminated by the far one. That is where DMFA's edge oscillation comes from. Zero-padding before the transform makes the convolution linear, and the kernel then runs into zeros instead of into the other end of the record. Measured, with the band extracted 24 bandwidths wide and the output decimated to the independent spacing: =========== ============== ============== ============= system worst, plain worst, padded median =========== ============== ============== ============= transistor 7.5e-01 3.2e-02 unchanged legendre 8.8e-01 3.1e-02 unchanged =========== ============== ============== ============= A factor of 24 to 29 on the worst case, and the interior does not move at all (0.99x) -- as it must not, since the kernel never reaches that far. It works better than "assume the signal is zero outside" has any right to, and the reason is worth knowing: the padding attenuates the numerator and the denominator by the same factor . At the first instant the filtered current falls to 0.49 of its mid-record value, and the filtered voltage falls with it, so the ratio survives. Zero-padding tapers the estimate's signal-to-noise near the edges but not its accuracy. How much padding. Only as much as the kernel actually reaches, which is less than it sounds. Measured by sweeping the factor on the transistor record, where 1/bandwidth is 40 s against a 400 s record: ============ ================== ============== pad factor added / (1/bw) worst error ============ ================== ============== 1.00x 0 7.5e-01 1.10x 1.0 3.2e-02 1.50x 5.0 3.2e-02 2.00x 10.0 3.2e-02 ============ ================== ============== One kernel length already buys the whole benefit and more buys nothing. factor=2 is the convenient default -- it keeps the FFT size tidy and costs only arithmetic -- but 1 + 1/(bandwidth * duration) is enough. Note that this is not the mirroring suggested for non-periodic records in the DMFA literature. Mirroring a random-phase multisine destroys the carrier -- it scatters more energy off the excited bins than it leaves on them. See the implementation notes. Returns: ndarray – The record followed by (factor - 1) * len(signal) zeros. Source code in src/deistools/processing/dmfa_functions.py def pad_record(signal, factor=2): """Zero-pad a record so DMFA's band extraction is a *linear* convolution. That is where DMFA's edge oscillation comes from. Zero-padding before the transform makes the convolution linear, and the kernel then runs into zeros instead of into the other end of the record. Measured, with the band extracted 24 bandwidths wide and the output decimated to the independent spacing: =========== ============== ============== ============= system worst, plain worst, padded median =========== ============== ============== ============= transistor 7.5e-01 3.2e-02 unchanged legendre 8.8e-01 3.1e-02 unchanged =========== ============== ============== ============= A factor of 24 to 29 on the worst case, and the interior does not move at all (0.99x) -- as it must not, since the kernel never reaches that far. It works better than "assume the signal is zero outside" has any right to, and the reason is worth knowing: the padding attenuates the **numerator and the denominator by the same factor**. At the first instant the filtered current falls to 0.49 of its mid-record value, and the filtered voltage falls with it, so the ratio survives. Zero-padding tapers the estimate's signal-to-noise near the edges but not its accuracy. **How much padding.** Only as much as the kernel actually reaches, which is less than it sounds. Measured by sweeping the factor on the transistor record, where ``1/bandwidth`` is 40 s against a 400 s record: ============ ================== ============== pad factor added / (1/bw) worst error ============ ================== ============== 1.00x 0 7.5e-01 1.10x 1.0 3.2e-02 1.50x 5.0 3.2e-02 2.00x 10.0 3.2e-02 ============ ================== ============== One kernel length already buys the whole benefit and more buys nothing. ``factor=2`` is the convenient default -- it keeps the FFT size tidy and costs only arithmetic -- but ``1 + 1/(bandwidth * duration)`` is enough. """ signal = np.asarray(signal) extra = int(round((factor - 1) * signal.size)) if extra < 0: raise ValueError("factor must be at least 1") return np.concatenate([signal, np.zeros(extra, dtype=signal.dtype)])

docs.text: compute_freq_indexes(freq_axis, frequencies, sampling_time, tol=ON_BIN_TOLERANCE) Bin index of each excited frequency in a shifted spectrum. freq_axis must be fftshift(fftfreq(n, sampling_time)) built with the same n as the spectrum you are going to index , because the bin spacing 1/(n*sampling_time) is taken from its length. Mixing a full-record axis with a windowed spectrum, or the reverse, silently reads the wrong bins; that is the single easiest way to misuse this function. Uses round rather than ceil: the aim is the nearest bin. With ceil a frequency landing a hair above a bin centre is pushed to the next one. A multisine is designed so that every tone falls exactly on a bin -- that is what makes the DFT leakage-free. A tone further than tol bins from a centre therefore means the record length and the multisine period disagree, so it raises rather than rounding quietly. Pass tol=None to index an arbitrary frequency list, accepting the leakage that implies. Source code in src/deistools/processing/stft_functions.py def compute_freq_indexes( freq_axis, frequencies, sampling_time, tol=ON_BIN_TOLERANCE, ): """Bin index of each excited frequency in a shifted spectrum. ``freq_axis`` must be ``fftshift(fftfreq(n, sampling_time))`` built with the **same n as the spectrum you are going to index**, because the bin spacing ``1/(n*sampling_time)`` is taken from its length. Mixing a full-record axis with a windowed spectrum, or the reverse, silently reads the wrong bins; that is the single easiest way to misuse this function. Uses round rather than ceil: the aim is the *nearest* bin. With ceil a frequency landing a hair above a bin centre is pushed to the next one. A multisine is designed so that every tone falls exactly on a bin -- that is what makes the DFT leakage-free. A tone further than ``tol`` bins from a centre therefore means the record length and the multisine period disagree, so it raises rather than rounding quietly. Pass ``tol=None`` to index an arbitrary frequency list, accepting the leakage that implies. """ freq_axis = np.asarray(freq_axis) frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float) index_f0 = _zero_frequency_index(freq_axis) n = freq_axis.size offsets = frequencies * sampling_time * n rounded = np.round(offsets) if tol is not None: residual = np.abs(offsets - rounded) if residual.max() > tol: worst = int(np.argmax(residual)) df = 1.0 / (n * sampling_time) raise ValueError( f"{frequencies[worst]:g} Hz lies {residual[worst]:.3g} bins " f"from a bin centre (bin spacing {df:g} Hz). A multisine tone " "should land exactly on a bin; check that the record is a " "whole number of multisine periods and that freq_axis was " "built with the same n as the spectrum. Pass tol=None to " "index off-grid frequencies anyway.") nyquist = 0.5 / sampling_time if np.any(np.abs(frequencies) >= nyquist): raise ValueError( f"frequencies must lie below the Nyquist frequency {nyquist:g} Hz; " f"the highest requested is {np.abs(frequencies).max():g} Hz") return (rounded.astype(int) + index_f0).tolist(), index_f0
docs.title: compute_freq_indexes

docs.text: search_freq_indexes(spectrum, freq_axis, frequencies, sampling_time) Refine the computed bin indexes by finding the local spectral peak. spectrum must be a shifted spectrum , not a time series: the search indexes it with DFT bin numbers. Use this when the tones may not land exactly where asked -- a generator whose clock differs slightly from the acquisition card's, say. For a synthesised record :func: compute_freq_indexes is exact and this adds nothing. The window is bounded two ways: by half the distance to the nearer neighbouring excited frequency, and by the gap to the nearest neighbouring excited bin . Without the second bound the search can lock onto a neighbour, and when the two are equally strong argmax silently prefers the lower index. Adjacent excited bins leave no room to search at all, and the computed index stands. Source code in src/deistools/processing/stft_functions.py def search_freq_indexes( spectrum, freq_axis, frequencies, sampling_time ): """Refine the computed bin indexes by finding the local spectral peak. ``spectrum`` must be a *shifted spectrum*, not a time series: the search indexes it with DFT bin numbers. Use this when the tones may not land exactly where asked -- a generator whose clock differs slightly from the acquisition card's, say. For a synthesised record :func:`compute_freq_indexes` is exact and this adds nothing. The window is bounded two ways: by half the distance to the nearer neighbouring excited frequency, and by the gap to the nearest neighbouring excited *bin*. Without the second bound the search can lock onto a neighbour, and when the two are equally strong ``argmax`` silently prefers the lower index. Adjacent excited bins leave no room to search at all, and the computed index stands. """ frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float) spectrum = np.asarray(spectrum) if spectrum.size != np.asarray(freq_axis).size: raise ValueError( f"spectrum has {spectrum.size} bins but freq_axis has " f"{np.asarray(freq_axis).size}. They must describe the same " "transform -- mixing a windowed spectrum with a full-record " "axis, or the reverse, reads the wrong bins.") # tol=None: the whole point here is that the tones may be off-grid. guesses = np.asarray( compute_freq_indexes(freq_axis, frequencies, sampling_time, tol=None)[0], dtype=int) index_f0 = _zero_frequency_index(freq_axis) # Distance in Hz to the nearer neighbouring excited frequency. The # outermost tones have a neighbour on one side only; DC bounds the # first from below, and the last simply reuses its lower gap rather # than inventing a width for the side that has nothing on it. dist = np.empty(frequencies.size) if frequencies.size == 1: dist[0] = frequencies[0] else: dist[0] = min(frequencies[1] - frequencies[0], frequencies[0]) dist[-1] = frequencies[-1] - frequencies[-2] for f in range(1, frequencies.size - 1): dist[f] = min(frequencies[f] - frequencies[f - 1], frequencies[f + 1] - frequencies[f]) half_hz = np.floor(dist * sampling_time * np.asarray(freq_axis).size / 4).astype(int) # The window must never reach a neighbouring excited bin, or the search # can lock onto the neighbour -- and when the two are equally strong, # argmax silently prefers the lower index. Adjacent excited bins # therefore leave no room to search and the computed index stands. if guesses.size == 1: half_bins = half_hz else: gaps = np.diff(guesses) nearest = np.empty(guesses.size, dtype=int) nearest[0], nearest[-1] = gaps[0], gaps[-1] nearest[1:-1] = np.minimum(gaps[:-1], gaps[1:]) half_bins = np.minimum(half_hz, (nearest - 1) // 2) half_bins = np.maximum(half_bins, 0) index_multisine_freq = np.zeros(frequencies.size, dtype='int64') for f in range(frequencies.size): lo = max(0, guesses[f] - half_bins[f]) hi = min(spectrum.size, guesses[f] + half_bins[f] + 1) index_multisine_freq[f] = lo + int(np.argmax(np.abs(spectrum[lo:hi]))) return index_multisine_freq.tolist(), index_f0

docs.text: fft_eis(voltage, current, freq_indexes, index_f0) Impedance at the given bins, from one transform of the whole record. index_f0 is cross-checked against the record length. It is the only thing here that reveals which transform the indexes were computed for, so a mismatch means they describe a different-sized spectrum and would otherwise read neighbouring frequencies without complaint. Source code in src/deistools/processing/stft_functions.py def fft_eis(voltage, current, freq_indexes, index_f0): """Impedance at the given bins, from one transform of the whole record. ``index_f0`` is cross-checked against the record length. It is the only thing here that reveals which transform the indexes were computed for, so a mismatch means they describe a different-sized spectrum and would otherwise read neighbouring frequencies without complaint. """ if index_f0 != voltage.size // 2: raise ValueError( f"index_f0 = {index_f0} does not match a {voltage.size}-sample " f"record, whose zero-frequency bin is at {voltage.size // 2}. The " "indexes were computed for a different transform length.") ft_voltage = fftshift(fft(voltage)) /voltage.size ft_current = fftshift(fft(current)) / current.size impedance = (ft_voltage[freq_indexes]/ft_current[freq_indexes]) voltage_avg = abs(ft_voltage[index_f0]) current_avg = abs(ft_current[index_f0]) return impedance, voltage_avg, current_avg

docs.text: Digital lock-in amplifier for multi-frequency impedance. The classical instrument, implemented offline. For each excited frequency the record is multiplied ("mixed") with a cosine and a sine at that frequency and the product low-pass filtered, which leaves the slowly varying complex amplitude of that tone. The ratio of the voltage and current amplitudes is Z(f, t). Mathematics Write the response near the k -th tone as a carrier with a slowly varying phasor:: v(t) = A_v(t) * cos(w_k * t + phi_v(t)), w_k = 2*pi*f_k Mixing with the in-phase and quadrature references gives v(t) * cos(w_k t) = (A_v/2) * cos(phi_v) + (A_v/2) * cos(2 w_k t + phi_v) v(t) * sin(w_k t) = -(A_v/2) * sin(phi_v) + (A_v/2) * sin(2 w_k t + phi_v) so a low-pass filter that rejects 2*w_k and every other excited tone leaves X = (A_v/2) cos(phi_v) and Y = -(A_v/2) sin(phi_v) . Twice the complex combination is the phasor:: V(t) = 2 * (X - 1j*Y) = A_v(t) * exp(1j * phi_v(t)) The same is done for the current, and Z(f_k, t) = V(t) / I(t) Choosing the integrator The low-pass filter is the whole method, because it must reject the image at 2*f_k produced by the mixing, and every other tone of the multisine , which after mixing appears at the difference frequency |f_j - f_k| . The second requirement is the binding one. For a multisine whose tones are all harmonics of a base frequency f_b , a boxcar average over exactly an integer number of periods of f_b has spectral nulls at every multiple of f_b -- that is, at every difference frequency that can occur. It rejects all of them exactly. A Hann (or any tapered) window has its nulls in the same places but a mainlobe twice as wide, so with a one-period window the nearest harmonic sits inside the mainlobe and is not rejected. A Hann integrator therefore needs at least two base periods. :func: integrator_length enforces this, and :func: tone_rejection measures it. The integrator length is also the time resolution: a window of m periods of f_b cannot follow anything faster than m / f_b seconds, which is the same trade STFT makes with its window and DMFA with its bandwidth. Edges The output within half an integrator length of either end of the record is computed from a window that extends past the data. This module reflects the signal at the boundaries, which is exact for an envelope with zero slope there and good otherwise, and :func: valid_mask marks the affected samples so they can be excluded from a fit.

docs.text: integrator_length(sampling_time, base_frequency, n_periods=1, window='boxcar') Samples in the lock-in integrator, as a whole number of base periods. Parameters: sampling_time ( float ) – Seconds between samples. base_frequency ( float ) – The frequency every excited tone is a harmonic of, in Hz. For a multisine of period Tp this is 1/Tp , not the tone being demodulated. n_periods ( int , default: 1 ) – How many base periods the integrator spans. This sets the time resolution, n_periods / base_frequency seconds. window ( ( boxcar , hann ) , default: 'boxcar' ) – A tapered window has a mainlobe twice as wide as a boxcar, so it needs at least two base periods to put the nearest harmonic in a null. Returns: int – Exactly n_periods base periods in samples. The length is not rounded to an odd number: the nulls sit at multiples of 1/(samples*sampling_time) and only land on the harmonics if the window spans a whole number of base periods exactly. Forcing the length odd to centre the kernel on a sample detunes them -- it costs about 40 dB of rejection on a 20 000-sample period. The resulting half-sample group delay is common to voltage and current and cancels in their ratio. Source code in src/deistools/processing/lock_in_amp.py def integrator_length(sampling_time, base_frequency, n_periods=1, window="boxcar"): """Samples in the lock-in integrator, as a whole number of base periods. Parameters ---------- sampling_time : float Seconds between samples. base_frequency : float The frequency every excited tone is a harmonic of, in Hz. For a multisine of period ``Tp`` this is ``1/Tp``, *not* the tone being demodulated. n_periods : int How many base periods the integrator spans. This sets the time resolution, ``n_periods / base_frequency`` seconds. window : {'boxcar', 'hann'} A tapered window has a mainlobe twice as wide as a boxcar, so it needs at least two base periods to put the nearest harmonic in a null. Returns ------- int Exactly ``n_periods`` base periods in samples. The length is *not* rounded to an odd number: the nulls sit at multiples of ``1/(samples*sampling_time)`` and only land on the harmonics if the window spans a whole number of base periods exactly. Forcing the length odd to centre the kernel on a sample detunes them -- it costs about 40 dB of rejection on a 20 000-sample period. The resulting half-sample group delay is common to voltage and current and cancels in their ratio. """ if n_periods < 1: raise ValueError("n_periods must be at least 1") if window == "hann" and n_periods < 2: raise ValueError( "a Hann integrator needs n_periods >= 2: its mainlobe is twice as " "wide as a boxcar's, so over one base period the neighbouring " "harmonic falls inside it and is not rejected. Use " "window='boxcar' for a single period.") samples = n_periods / (base_frequency * sampling_time) if abs(samples - round(samples)) > 1e-6 * samples: raise ValueError( f"{n_periods} period(s) of {base_frequency} Hz is {samples:.4f} " "samples, not a whole number. The integrator cannot null the other " "tones unless it spans whole base periods; adjust the sampling " "rate or the base frequency.") return int(round(samples))
docs.title: integrator_length

docs.text: integrator_kernel(samples_window, window='boxcar') The normalised low-pass kernel, with unit DC gain. Source code in src/deistools/processing/lock_in_amp.py def integrator_kernel(samples_window, window="boxcar"): """The normalised low-pass kernel, with unit DC gain.""" if window == "hann": kernel = np.hanning(samples_window + 2)[1:-1] # periodic, no zeros elif window == "boxcar": kernel = np.ones(samples_window) else: raise ValueError("window must be 'boxcar' or 'hann'") return kernel / kernel.sum()

docs.text: tone_rejection(kernel, sampling_time, frequencies, f_k) How much the integrator suppresses each other tone, in dB. After mixing at f_k a tone at f_j lands at |f_j - f_k| ; this evaluates the kernel's frequency response there. Large positive numbers are good. A boxcar over whole base periods gives essentially infinite rejection (nulls), limited only by arithmetic. The returned array has one entry per frequency, including f_k itself , whose offset is zero and whose "rejection" is therefore 0 dB by construction. Drop that entry before taking a worst case over the others, or the answer is always 0 dB. Source code in src/deistools/processing/lock_in_amp.py def tone_rejection(kernel, sampling_time, frequencies, f_k): """How much the integrator suppresses each other tone, in dB. After mixing at ``f_k`` a tone at ``f_j`` lands at ``|f_j - f_k|``; this evaluates the kernel's frequency response there. Large positive numbers are good. A boxcar over whole base periods gives essentially infinite rejection (nulls), limited only by arithmetic. The returned array has one entry per frequency, **including ``f_k`` itself**, whose offset is zero and whose "rejection" is therefore 0 dB by construction. Drop that entry before taking a worst case over the others, or the answer is always 0 dB. """ offsets = np.abs(np.asarray(frequencies) - f_k) n = np.arange(kernel.size) response = np.array([np.abs(np.sum(kernel * np.exp(-2j * np.pi * df * n * sampling_time))) for df in offsets]) with np.errstate(divide="ignore"): return -20 * np.log10(np.maximum(response, 1e-300))
docs.title: tone_rejection

docs.text: valid_mask(n_samples, samples_window) False where the integrator window ran past the end of the record. Source code in src/deistools/processing/lock_in_amp.py def valid_mask(n_samples, samples_window): """False where the integrator window ran past the end of the record.""" mask = np.ones(n_samples, dtype=bool) half = samples_window // 2 mask[:half] = False mask[n_samples - half:] = False return mask

docs.text: lia_impedance_optim(t, v, i, dt, f0, samples_window, window='boxcar') Lock-in impedance at one frequency, by mixing and low-pass filtering. Parameters: t ( ndarray ) – Time, voltage and current, all the same length. v ( ndarray ) – Time, voltage and current, all the same length. i ( ndarray ) – Time, voltage and current, all the same length. dt ( float ) – Sampling time in seconds. f0 ( float ) – The frequency to demodulate, in Hz. samples_window ( int ) – Length of the integrator. Use :func: integrator_length to get a value that rejects the other tones. window ( ( boxcar , hann ) , default: 'boxcar' ) – Returns: ndarray – Complex Z(f0, t) , one value per input sample. Samples within half an integrator length of either end rest on reflected data; see :func: valid_mask . Source code in src/deistools/processing/lock_in_amp.py def lia_impedance_optim(t, v, i, dt, f0, samples_window, window="boxcar"): """Lock-in impedance at one frequency, by mixing and low-pass filtering. Parameters ---------- t, v, i : ndarray Time, voltage and current, all the same length. dt : float Sampling time in seconds. f0 : float The frequency to demodulate, in Hz. samples_window : int Length of the integrator. Use :func:`integrator_length` to get a value that rejects the other tones. window : {'boxcar', 'hann'} Returns ------- ndarray Complex ``Z(f0, t)``, one value per input sample. Samples within half an integrator length of either end rest on reflected data; see :func:`valid_mask`. """ omega = 2 * np.pi * f0 kernel = integrator_kernel(samples_window, window) ref_cos, ref_sin = np.cos(omega * t), np.sin(omega * t) # Factor 2 undoes the halving that mixing introduces, so that the complex # result is the phasor itself rather than half of it. It cancels in the # ratio below, but makes V and I meaningful on their own. V = 2 * (_lowpass(v * ref_cos, kernel) - 1j * _lowpass(v * ref_sin, kernel)) I = 2 * (_lowpass(i * ref_cos, kernel) - 1j * _lowpass(i * ref_sin, kernel)) return V / I

docs.text: local_ls(t, x, omega, idx, Nw) Fit cos, sin, an offset and a local slope in a window centred on idx . Returns the complex amplitude referenced to the centre of the window , not to t = 0. The reference cancels in V/I because both are fitted on the same window, which is why :func: lia_impedance_ls is correct; a caller using this function alone must undo the exp(-1j*omega*t0) itself. Source code in src/deistools/processing/lock_in_amp.py def local_ls(t, x, omega, idx, Nw): """Fit cos, sin, an offset and a local slope in a window centred on ``idx``. Returns the complex amplitude **referenced to the centre of the window**, not to t = 0. The reference cancels in ``V/I`` because both are fitted on the same window, which is why :func:`lia_impedance_ls` is correct; a caller using this function alone must undo the ``exp(-1j*omega*t0)`` itself. """ half = Nw // 2 sl = slice(max(0, idx - half), min(len(t), idx + half + 1)) tt, xx = t[sl], x[sl] tau = tt - tt.mean() design = np.column_stack([np.cos(omega * tau), np.sin(omega * tau), np.ones_like(tau), tau]) weight = np.sqrt(np.hanning(tau.size + 2)[1:-1]) theta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(design * weight[:, None], xx * weight, rcond=None) return theta[0] - 1j * theta[1]
docs.title: local_ls

docs.text: lia_impedance_ls(t, v, i, dt, f0, samples_window, stride=None) Lock-in impedance by local least squares instead of mixing. Fits a cosine, a sine, an offset and a linear slope in a sliding window. Carrying the offset and slope makes it insensitive to drift within the window, which plain mixing is not -- useful on a record with a trend. It is far more expensive: one least-squares solve per reported instant, against two FFT convolutions for the whole record. stride therefore evaluates every stride -th sample; the default keeps about 1000 instants, which is already finer than the integrator can resolve. Returns: (Z, t_out) : ndarray, ndarray – Unlike :func: lia_impedance_optim this returns its own time axis, because it reports on a decimated grid. Source code in src/deistools/processing/lock_in_amp.py def lia_impedance_ls(t, v, i, dt, f0, samples_window, stride=None): """Lock-in impedance by local least squares instead of mixing. Fits a cosine, a sine, an offset and a linear slope in a sliding window. Carrying the offset and slope makes it insensitive to drift *within* the window, which plain mixing is not -- useful on a record with a trend. It is far more expensive: one least-squares solve per reported instant, against two FFT convolutions for the whole record. ``stride`` therefore evaluates every ``stride``-th sample; the default keeps about 1000 instants, which is already finer than the integrator can resolve. Returns ------- (Z, t_out) : ndarray, ndarray Unlike :func:`lia_impedance_optim` this returns its own time axis, because it reports on a decimated grid. """ omega = 2 * np.pi * f0 if stride is None: stride = max(1, len(t) // 1000) idx = np.arange(0, len(t), stride) V = np.array([local_ls(t, v, omega, k, samples_window) for k in idx]) I = np.array([local_ls(t, i, omega, k, samples_window) for k in idx]) return V / I, t[idx]

docs.text: lia_eis(time, voltage, current, dt, frequencies, samples_window, impedance_calculation_fun=lia_impedance_optim, window='boxcar', decimate=None) Lock-in impedance at every excited frequency. Parameters: samples_window ( int ) – Integrator length, from :func: integrator_length . The same window is used at every frequency, which is what makes the spectra comparable: every point of a spectrum is then an average over the same interval. impedance_calculation_fun ( callable , default: lia_impedance_optim ) – :func: lia_impedance_optim (default) or :func: lia_impedance_ls . decimate ( int , default: None ) – Report every decimate -th sample. The output is smooth on the scale of the integrator, so nothing is lost by decimating to a few times len(time) * base_frequency / n_periods points, and the full-rate array is large: 13 frequencies over a million samples is 200 MB. Returns: (impedance, time_out) : ndarray, ndarray – impedance has shape (n_frequencies, n_instants) . Source code in src/deistools/processing/lock_in_amp.py def lia_eis(time, voltage, current, dt, frequencies, samples_window, impedance_calculation_fun=lia_impedance_optim, window="boxcar", decimate=None): """Lock-in impedance at every excited frequency. Parameters ---------- samples_window : int Integrator length, from :func:`integrator_length`. The same window is used at every frequency, which is what makes the spectra comparable: every point of a spectrum is then an average over the same interval. impedance_calculation_fun : callable :func:`lia_impedance_optim` (default) or :func:`lia_impedance_ls`. decimate : int, optional Report every ``decimate``-th sample. The output is smooth on the scale of the integrator, so nothing is lost by decimating to a few times ``len(time) * base_frequency / n_periods`` points, and the full-rate array is large: 13 frequencies over a million samples is 200 MB. Returns ------- (impedance, time_out) : ndarray, ndarray ``impedance`` has shape ``(n_frequencies, n_instants)``. """ frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float) if voltage.shape != current.shape or voltage.shape != time.shape: raise ValueError("time, voltage and current must have the same shape") columns = [] for f in frequencies: if impedance_calculation_fun is lia_impedance_ls: Z_f, t_out = lia_impedance_ls(time, voltage, current, dt, f, samples_window) else: Z_f = impedance_calculation_fun(time, voltage, current, dt, f, samples_window, window=window) t_out = time if decimate: Z_f, t_out = Z_f[::decimate], time[::decimate] columns.append(Z_f) return np.vstack(columns), t_out

docs.text: Goertzel filter for multi-frequency impedance. The Goertzel algorithm evaluates a single DFT bin with a second-order recurrence instead of a transform, costing O(N) per bin rather than O(N log N) for all of them. It is the standard way to detect a handful of known tones -- DTMF decoding is the textbook case -- and it is attractive here because a multisine measurement wants exactly a handful of known tones. Mathematics For a block of N samples and a bin k (the frequency in units of the block's own resolution, k = f * N * dt ), define w = 2*pi*k/N coeff = 2*cos(w) and run, from s1 = s2 = 0 , s[n] = x[n] + coeff*s[n-1] - s[n-2], n = 0 .. N-1 After the last sample the DFT value is recovered from the final two states:: X[k] = (exp(1j*w) * s[N-1] - s[N-2]) * exp(-1j*2*pi*k) That combination is asymmetric, and the symmetric-looking rearrangement is wrong:: X[k] = (s[N-1] - exp(-1j*w) * s[N-2]) * exp(-1j*2*pi*k) # WRONG It has the right magnitude and is out by exactly exp(-1j*w) in phase. The error cancels in any ratio -- including V/I -- so an impedance test will not catch it; only a comparison against the DFT itself will, which is what test_output_formula_is_not_the_tempting_rearrangement does. The correct form is what one further iteration with a zero input would give, s[N] - exp(-1j*w)*s[N-1] , written closed-form. The trailing factor is unity whenever k is an integer, which is the usual presentation. Keeping it is the generalised Goertzel of Sysel and Rajmic, and it makes the result correct for a non-integer k as well -- useful when a tone does not fall exactly on a bin of the block you chose. References Goertzel, Am. Math. Monthly 65 (1958) 34 -- the original recurrence. Sysel and Rajmic, EURASIP J. Adv. Signal Process. (2012) 56 -- the generalisation to non-integer bins, which is the form implemented here. Only two state variables are carried, so nothing but the recurrence has to be stored. That is what makes the filter usable on a stream, one sample at a time, with no buffer: see :class: GoertzelFilter . What it is, and is not, good for Offline, on the records this package deals with, Goertzel is slower than an FFT. The crossover is at roughly n_bins ~ log2(N) : below that Goertzel wins, above it the FFT does. A 13-tone multisine over a 20 000-sample block has log2(N) = 14.3 , so the two are a wash, and the FFT is better optimised. It is included because: it is a standard estimator and the package exists to collect them; it computes exactly the same quantity as a rectangular-window STFT, which makes it a useful independent check on that path; its per-sample recurrence is the natural route to online processing, where no FFT is possible because the record has not finished.

docs.text: One bin of a running DFT, updated a sample at a time. The offline functions above exist because this package analyses recorded files, but the recurrence itself needs no record: it carries two numbers. This class is the streaming form, for an acquisition that has not finished. filt = GoertzelFilter(frequency=0.05, sampling_time=1e-3, block=20000) for sample in stream: # doctest: +SKIP ... value = filt.push(sample) ... if value is not None: ... ... # one block completed push returns None until a block is complete, then the complex DFT value for that block, and resets itself for the next one. Source code in src/deistools/processing/goertzel.py class GoertzelFilter: """One bin of a running DFT, updated a sample at a time. The offline functions above exist because this package analyses recorded files, but the recurrence itself needs no record: it carries two numbers. This class is the streaming form, for an acquisition that has not finished. >>> filt = GoertzelFilter(frequency=0.05, sampling_time=1e-3, block=20000) >>> for sample in stream: # doctest: +SKIP ... value = filt.push(sample) ... if value is not None: ... ... # one block completed ``push`` returns ``None`` until a block is complete, then the complex DFT value for that block, and resets itself for the next one. """ def __init__(self, frequency, sampling_time, block): self.block = int(block) self.k = float(frequency) * self.block * float(sampling_time) self.omega = 2 * np.pi * self.k / self.block self.coeff = 2 * np.cos(self.omega) self.reset() def reset(self): self._s1 = 0.0 self._s2 = 0.0 self._n = 0 def push(self, sample): """Feed one sample; returns the block's DFT value when it completes.""" s = float(sample) + self.coeff * self._s1 - self._s2 self._s2, self._s1 = self._s1, s self._n += 1 if self._n < self.block: return None value = (np.exp(1j * self.omega) * self._s1 - self._s2) * \ np.exp(-1j * 2 * np.pi * self.k) self.reset() return value

docs.text: push(sample) Feed one sample; returns the block's DFT value when it completes. docs.text: goertzel_dft(block, bins) DFT values at the given bins, by recurrence rather than transform. Parameters: block ( ndarray ) – Either one block, shape (N,) , or several, shape (n_blocks, N) . bins ( array_like ) – Bin indices k = f * N * dt . May be non-integer; the generalised correction is always applied. Returns: ndarray – Complex, shape (n_bins,) or (n_blocks, n_bins) . Scaled like :func: numpy.fft.fft -- that is, not divided by N . Source code in src/deistools/processing/goertzel.py def goertzel_dft(block, bins): """DFT values at the given bins, by recurrence rather than transform. Parameters ---------- block : ndarray Either one block, shape ``(N,)``, or several, shape ``(n_blocks, N)``. bins : array_like Bin indices ``k = f * N * dt``. May be non-integer; the generalised correction is always applied. Returns ------- ndarray Complex, shape ``(n_bins,)`` or ``(n_blocks, n_bins)``. Scaled like :func:`numpy.fft.fft` -- that is, **not** divided by ``N``. """ block = np.asarray(block, dtype=float) single = block.ndim == 1 if single: block = block[None, :] if block.ndim != 2: raise ValueError("block must be 1-D or 2-D") n_blocks, n = block.shape k = np.asarray(bins, dtype=float) omega = 2 * np.pi * k / n coeff = 2 * np.cos(omega) s1 = np.zeros((n_blocks, k.size)) s2 = np.zeros((n_blocks, k.size)) for sample in range(n): s = block[:, sample][:, None] + coeff[None, :] * s1 - s2 s2, s1 = s1, s values = (np.exp(1j * omega)[None, :] * s1 - s2) * \ np.exp(-1j * 2 * np.pi * k)[None, :] return values[0] if single else values
docs.title: goertzel_dft

docs.text: goertzel_eis(voltage, current, frequencies, period, sampling_time) Impedance per block, computed with the Goertzel recurrence. The signature mirrors :func: deistools.processing.stft_functions.estimate_impedance , and so does the result: the record is cut into consecutive blocks of period seconds and one spectrum is produced per block, stamped at its midpoint. Only the excited bins are evaluated, which is the whole point of the algorithm. period must hold a whole number of periods of every tone, for the same reason a rectangular STFT window must: otherwise each bin picks up the others. Returns: (impedance, time) : ndarray, ndarray – impedance has shape (n_frequencies, n_blocks) . Source code in src/deistools/processing/goertzel.py def goertzel_eis(voltage, current, frequencies, period, sampling_time): """Impedance per block, computed with the Goertzel recurrence. The signature mirrors :func:`deistools.processing.stft_functions.estimate_impedance`, and so does the result: the record is cut into consecutive blocks of ``period`` seconds and one spectrum is produced per block, stamped at its midpoint. Only the excited bins are evaluated, which is the whole point of the algorithm. ``period`` must hold a whole number of periods of every tone, for the same reason a rectangular STFT window must: otherwise each bin picks up the others. Returns ------- (impedance, time) : ndarray, ndarray ``impedance`` has shape ``(n_frequencies, n_blocks)``. """ voltage = np.asarray(voltage, dtype=float) current = np.asarray(current, dtype=float) if voltage.shape != current.shape or voltage.ndim != 1: raise ValueError("voltage and current must be 1-D arrays of equal length") samples_window = int(round(period / sampling_time)) if samples_window < 2: raise ValueError("period is shorter than two samples") n_blocks = voltage.size // samples_window if n_blocks < 1: raise ValueError( f"the record holds {voltage.size} samples, less than one block of " f"{samples_window}") usable = n_blocks * samples_window v = voltage[:usable].reshape(n_blocks, samples_window) i = current[:usable].reshape(n_blocks, samples_window) bins = np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float) * period V = goertzel_dft(v, bins) I = goertzel_dft(i, bins) time = (np.arange(n_blocks) + 0.5) * period return (V / I).T, time
docs.title: goertzel_eis

docs.text: cost_ratio(n_bins, block) Goertzel cost divided by FFT cost, in multiply-accumulates. Goertzel is about n_bins * N operations for n_bins bins of an N -sample block; an FFT is about N * log2(N) for all of them. The ratio below one means Goertzel is the cheaper choice. This counts operations only. In practice a compiled FFT beats a recurrence at equal operation count by a wide margin, so the real crossover sits well below one. Source code in src/deistools/processing/goertzel.py def cost_ratio(n_bins, block): """Goertzel cost divided by FFT cost, in multiply-accumulates. Goertzel is about ``n_bins * N`` operations for ``n_bins`` bins of an ``N``-sample block; an FFT is about ``N * log2(N)`` for all of them. The ratio below one means Goertzel is the cheaper choice. This counts operations only. In practice a compiled FFT beats a recurrence at equal operation count by a wide margin, so the real crossover sits well below one. """ return n_bins / np.log2(block)

docs.text: create_fermi_dirac_fun(fr, fc, bw, n) Create a digital filter shaped as a symmetric Fermi-Dirac function. Y = cosh(n) / (cosh(n*X) + cosh(n)), X = (fr - fc) / bw Evaluated as 1 / (1 + cosh(n*X)/cosh(n)) with the ratio of hyperbolic cosines expanded in exponentials. Written literally, cosh(n*X) overflows for the far tails of a wide axis -- the answer is still right, since an infinite denominator correctly gives zero, but it warns on every call. The identity cosh(a)/cosh(b) = exp(|a| - b) * (1 + exp(-2|a|)) / (1 + exp(-2b)) is therefore taken in log space and finished with a numerically stable logistic, so no exponential of a large positive number is ever formed. Source code in src/deistools/processing/passband_filters.py def create_fermi_dirac_fun(fr, fc, bw, n): """ Create a digital filter shaped as a symmetric Fermi-Dirac function. Y = cosh(n) / (cosh(n*X) + cosh(n)), X = (fr - fc) / bw Evaluated as ``1 / (1 + cosh(n*X)/cosh(n))`` with the ratio of hyperbolic cosines expanded in exponentials. Written literally, ``cosh(n*X)`` overflows for the far tails of a wide axis -- the answer is still right, since an infinite denominator correctly gives zero, but it warns on every call. The identity cosh(a)/cosh(b) = exp(|a| - b) * (1 + exp(-2|a|)) / (1 + exp(-2b)) is therefore taken in log space and finished with a numerically stable logistic, so no exponential of a large positive number is ever formed. """ a = np.abs(n * np.asarray(fr - fc, dtype=float) / bw) b = abs(n) # log of cosh(n*X)/cosh(n); both exponentials have non-positive arguments log_ratio = (a - b) + np.log1p(np.exp(-2.0 * a)) - np.log1p(np.exp(-2.0 * b)) # 1/(1 + exp(log_ratio)), evaluated without overflow for either sign small = np.exp(-np.abs(log_ratio)) return np.where(log_ratio >= 0.0, small / (1.0 + small), 1.0 / (1.0 + small))
docs.title: create_fermi_dirac_fun

docs.text: create_raised_cosine_fun(fr, fc, bw, alpha=1.0) Raised-cosine (Tukey-in-frequency) passband, the usual DSP choice. Y = 1 |x| <= 1 - alpha = (1 + cos(pi*(|x| - 1 + alpha)/(2*alpha)))/2 1 - alpha < |x| < 1 + alpha = 0 |x| >= 1 + alpha with x = (fr - fc)/bw . Like :func: create_fermi_dirac_fun it is 1/2 at |x| = 1 , so bw means the same thing in both: the half-amplitude half-width. alpha is the roll-off, from a rectangle at 0 to a Hann-shaped bell at 1. It plays the same role as n in the Fermi-Dirac filter but inverted: small alpha is flat and rings, large alpha is smooth and does not. Offered beside the Fermi-Dirac because it is the shape most readers will recognise, and because it is compactly supported -- exactly zero beyond bw*(1 + alpha) -- so extracting a finite block of bins around a tone truncates nothing. The Fermi-Dirac has exponential tails and needs a block wide enough for them to have decayed. On the transistor system the Fermi-Dirac at n = 2 still measures best (worst-case 5.0e-04 against 7.4e-04 for alpha = 1 ), because on a band-limited extraction the dominant error is time-domain ringing and its time concentration is exceptional. See the method documentation. Source code in src/deistools/processing/passband_filters.py def create_raised_cosine_fun(fr, fc, bw, alpha=1.0): """Raised-cosine (Tukey-in-frequency) passband, the usual DSP choice. Y = 1 |x| <= 1 - alpha = (1 + cos(pi*(|x| - 1 + alpha)/(2*alpha)))/2 1 - alpha < |x| < 1 + alpha = 0 |x| >= 1 + alpha with ``x = (fr - fc)/bw``. Like :func:`create_fermi_dirac_fun` it is 1/2 at ``|x| = 1``, so ``bw`` means the same thing in both: the half-amplitude half-width. ``alpha`` is the roll-off, from a rectangle at 0 to a Hann-shaped bell at 1. It plays the same role as ``n`` in the Fermi-Dirac filter but inverted: small ``alpha`` is flat and rings, large ``alpha`` is smooth and does not. Offered beside the Fermi-Dirac because it is the shape most readers will recognise, and because it is **compactly supported** -- exactly zero beyond ``bw*(1 + alpha)`` -- so extracting a finite block of bins around a tone truncates nothing. The Fermi-Dirac has exponential tails and needs a block wide enough for them to have decayed. On the transistor system the Fermi-Dirac at ``n = 2`` still measures best (worst-case 5.0e-04 against 7.4e-04 for ``alpha = 1``), because on a band-limited extraction the dominant error is time-domain ringing and its time concentration is exceptional. See the method documentation. """ if not 0 < alpha <= 1: raise ValueError("alpha must be in (0, 1]") x = np.abs(np.asarray(fr, dtype=float) - fc) / bw out = np.zeros_like(x) out[x <= 1 - alpha] = 1.0 edge = (x > 1 - alpha) & (x < 1 + alpha) out[edge] = 0.5 * (1 + np.cos(np.pi * (x[edge] - 1 + alpha) / (2 * alpha))) return out

docs.text: create_window_filter(fr, fc, bw, window='blackman', beta=8.0) Passband built from a standard DSP window. All of these are scaled so that the response is 1/2 at |fr - fc| = bw , exactly as :func: create_fermi_dirac_fun and :func: create_raised_cosine_fun are, so bw means the same thing throughout and the families can be compared at equal bandwidth. Parameters: window ( str , default: 'blackman' ) – 'blackman' , 'blackman-harris' , 'nuttall' , 'hann' , 'kaiser' or 'gaussian' . beta ( float , default: 8.0 ) – Shape parameter, for 'kaiser' only. Notes These were added after a comparison against the Fermi-Dirac filter the DMFA papers specify, which it loses. Scored by worst-case relative error against known ground truth, with the band extracted wide and the output decimated to the independent spacing: ================ ============ ========== =============== filter transistor legendre block-oriented ================ ============ ========== =============== blackman 2.40e-04 5.21e-04 1.18e-01 kaiser, beta=8 2.92e-04 5.94e-04 1.18e-01 blackman-harris 2.96e-04 6.94e-04 1.18e-01 hann 4.71e-04 9.67e-04 1.17e-01 gaussian 3.05e-04 9.77e-04 1.18e-01 Fermi-Dirac n=2 4.98e-04 6.47e-04 1.27e-01 ================ ============ ========== =============== 'blackman' is the best of them on two of the three systems and never the worst; the block-oriented column is a tie because its error there is dominated by the branch filters' roll-off rather than by the extraction. A first Slepian sequence (DPSS, NW = 4) was also tried and lands within 1% of kaiser with beta=8 , which is the expected result since Kaiser is a closed-form approximation to it. It is not offered here because computing it needs an eigensolve for no measurable gain. Source code in src/deistools/processing/passband_filters.py def create_window_filter(fr, fc, bw, window="blackman", beta=8.0): """Passband built from a standard DSP window. All of these are scaled so that the response is **1/2 at** ``|fr - fc| = bw``, exactly as :func:`create_fermi_dirac_fun` and :func:`create_raised_cosine_fun` are, so ``bw`` means the same thing throughout and the families can be compared at equal bandwidth. Parameters ---------- window : str ``'blackman'``, ``'blackman-harris'``, ``'nuttall'``, ``'hann'``, ``'kaiser'`` or ``'gaussian'``. beta : float Shape parameter, for ``'kaiser'`` only. Notes ----- These were added after a comparison against the Fermi-Dirac filter the DMFA papers specify, which it loses. Scored by worst-case relative error against known ground truth, with the band extracted wide and the output decimated to the independent spacing: ================ ============ ========== =============== filter transistor legendre block-oriented ================ ============ ========== =============== blackman 2.40e-04 5.21e-04 1.18e-01 kaiser, beta=8 2.92e-04 5.94e-04 1.18e-01 blackman-harris 2.96e-04 6.94e-04 1.18e-01 hann 4.71e-04 9.67e-04 1.17e-01 gaussian 3.05e-04 9.77e-04 1.18e-01 Fermi-Dirac n=2 4.98e-04 6.47e-04 1.27e-01 ================ ============ ========== =============== ``'blackman'`` is the best of them on two of the three systems and never the worst; the block-oriented column is a tie because its error there is dominated by the branch filters' roll-off rather than by the extraction. A first Slepian sequence (DPSS, NW = 4) was also tried and lands within 1% of ``kaiser`` with ``beta=8``, which is the expected result since Kaiser is a closed-form approximation to it. It is not offered here because computing it needs an eigensolve for no measurable gain. """ x = np.abs(np.asarray(fr, dtype=float) - fc) / bw if window == "gaussian": return np.exp(-np.log(2.0) * x ** 2) scale = _half_point(window, beta) out = np.zeros_like(x) inside = x * scale <= 1.0 out[inside] = _window_profile(x[inside] * scale, window, beta) return out

docs.text: rejection_db(band_filter, band_axis, offset) How far the passband suppresses a disturbance at a given offset, in dB. band_axis is the band's local frequency axis, as :func: deistools.processing.dmfa_functions.elaboration_frequency_axis returns it, and offset is the distance in Hz from the band centre. Large positive numbers are good. The use this exists for is trends . A drift of the dc level lives at zero frequency, so for the tone at f_k it sits f_k away from the band centre; rejection_db(g, axis, f_k) is therefore how much of it survives into that tone's estimate. The lowest tone is the one at risk, because every other one is further from dc. This is DMFA's whole defence against a trend, and it is worth a great deal. Measured on a transistor record carrying a 5 V peak-to-peak order-3 trend against a 1.53 V signal, varying nothing but the filter: ================= ============== ===================== filter rejection error, lowest tone ================= ============== ===================== Fermi-Dirac n=2 18 dB 2.9e-01 Fermi-Dirac n=4 35 dB 3.6e-02 Fermi-Dirac n=8 69 dB 1.4e-03 Fermi-Dirac n=16 139 dB 2.1e-02 blackman 29 dB 6.8e-02 nuttall 27 dB 8.8e-02 ================= ============== ===================== Two things to take from that table. Rejection buys accuracy until the filter's own ringing takes over -- n = 16 has 70 dB more rejection than n = 8 and is 15x worse, because at that sharpness it rings. And a trend reverses the ranking of the filter families : the compactly supported windows win on a trend-free record but reach only about 30 dB here, where the Fermi-Dirac's exponential tail reaches 69 dB. Choose the filter against the trend you expect, not against a clean simulation. Source code in src/deistools/processing/passband_filters.py def rejection_db(band_filter, band_axis, offset): """How far the passband suppresses a disturbance at a given offset, in dB. ``band_axis`` is the band's local frequency axis, as :func:`deistools.processing.dmfa_functions.elaboration_frequency_axis` returns it, and ``offset`` is the distance in Hz from the band centre. Large positive numbers are good. The use this exists for is **trends**. A drift of the dc level lives at zero frequency, so for the tone at ``f_k`` it sits ``f_k`` away from the band centre; ``rejection_db(g, axis, f_k)`` is therefore how much of it survives into that tone's estimate. The lowest tone is the one at risk, because every other one is further from dc. This is DMFA's whole defence against a trend, and it is worth a great deal. Measured on a transistor record carrying a 5 V peak-to-peak order-3 trend against a 1.53 V signal, varying nothing but the filter: ================= ============== ===================== filter rejection error, lowest tone ================= ============== ===================== Fermi-Dirac n=2 18 dB 2.9e-01 Fermi-Dirac n=4 35 dB 3.6e-02 Fermi-Dirac n=8 69 dB 1.4e-03 Fermi-Dirac n=16 139 dB 2.1e-02 blackman 29 dB 6.8e-02 nuttall 27 dB 8.8e-02 ================= ============== ===================== Two things to take from that table. Rejection buys accuracy until the filter's own ringing takes over -- ``n = 16`` has 70 dB more rejection than ``n = 8`` and is 15x worse, because at that sharpness it rings. And **a trend reverses the ranking of the filter families**: the compactly supported windows win on a trend-free record but reach only about 30 dB here, where the Fermi-Dirac's exponential tail reaches 69 dB. Choose the filter against the trend you expect, not against a clean simulation. """ band_axis = np.asarray(band_axis, dtype=float) band_filter = np.asarray(band_filter, dtype=float) order = np.argsort(band_axis) gain = np.interp(abs(float(offset)), band_axis[order], band_filter[order], left=0.0, right=0.0) return -20.0 * np.log10(max(gain, 1e-300))

docs.text: Best linear approximation per burst, after Pintelon, Louarroudi and Lataire. The short-time Fourier estimator in :mod: ~deistools.processing.stft_functions reads the excited bins of each window and divides. That is enough to get an impedance and nothing else: a single window gives no way to say whether the number it produced is limited by measurement noise, by nonlinearity, or by the cell changing while the window was open. This module adds that. It keeps STFT's assumption -- the system is whatever it is inside one window, with no model of how it varies -- and uses the bins STFT throws away to classify the error. The one structural fact Cut a record into windows of P whole multisine periods. The DFT of a window has fundamental 1/(P*Tp) , so a tone at harmonic h of the multisine lands on bin P*h and only every P-th bin is a harmonic of the multisine at all . A nonlinear system of the PISPO class (period in, same period out) answers a periodic input with a periodic output, so its distortion is harmonically related to the input and can land only on those bins. That splits the spectrum of one burst into four classes: ======================== ==================================== bins what is there ======================== ==================================== ``k = P*h``, h excited signal (+ everything below) ``k = P*m``, m odd odd-order distortion + noise + drift ``k = P*m``, m even even-order distortion + noise + drift ``k`` not a multiple of P noise + drift ======================== ==================================== This requires P >= 2 . At P = 1 the window fundamental is the multisine fundamental, every bin is a harmonic, and the fourth class is empty. On the package's 13-tone grid, in band, :func: classify_bins counts === ======= ===== ====== ======== P noise odd even excited === ======= ===== ====== ======== 1 0 168 180 13 2 301 138 150 13 4 903 138 150 13 8 2107 138 150 13 === ======= ===== ====== ======== so the noise class appears only at P >= 2 and then grows with the burst, while the detection lines stay put. Since one period is exactly the window the plain STFT prefers, the uncertainty is bought with time resolution and there is no way around that. What the noise class actually contains On a time-varying cell the non-harmonic bins are not noise alone. The time variation convolves each excited line into its neighbours (Lataire 2012 eq. 48: a linear-in-time variation has B_1(k) ~ 1/k ), so every tone grows a skirt, and with a dozen tones the skirts cover the band. Measured on the transistor system, a 40 s burst cut from the usual 400 s record, as a ratio to the pure-noise floor at the same bins: ================ ======= distance to the ratio to nearest tone noise floor ================ ======= 1-2 bins 7656 6-10 bins 463 21-50 bins 71 51-100 bins 44 ================ ======= It decays, and it never arrives. So a noise level read off these bins is an upper bound , and on a strongly varying cell a loose one. That is not a defect of the implementation; separating the two needs a model of the variation, which is what :mod: ~deistools.processing.bltva is for and what this module deliberately does not assume. :func: ratio_noise_to_time_variation says which case you are in, so the bound can be read correctly rather than trusted blindly. References Lataire, Louarroudi and Pintelon, IEEE TIM 61 (2012) 2132 -- the best linear time-invariant approximation of a time-varying system, and the frequency-correlation test used here. Pintelon, Louarroudi and Lataire, IEEE TIM 61 (2012) 3387 -- the multiple-input time-invariant equivalent, and separating leakage from time variation. Pintelon, Louarroudi and Lataire, IEEE TIM 62 (2013) 3361 -- the periodic-excitation procedure this module follows: which bins carry what, and why two periods are the minimum. Pintelon and Schoukens, System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach , 2nd ed., Wiley-IEEE Press (2012) -- the underlying framework.

docs.text: What one burst says about itself. The three std_* attributes are measured levels, not a decomposition : each is what the bins of one class imply for the standard deviation of impedance , with nothing subtracted. They are reported that way on purpose. Subtracting one from another is how the distortion is normally quoted, and it is available from :meth: distortion_odd and :meth: distortion_even , but the subtraction has two failure modes that a stored, already-subtracted number would hide -- see those methods. Attributes: impedance ( (M,) complex ) – V/I at the excited bins -- the same number the STFT returns. std_noise ( (M,) float ) – Level at the non-harmonic bins. Noise alone on a time-invariant cell; noise plus the time-variation skirt otherwise, so an upper bound . :attr: r_ntv says which. std_odd_lines, std_even_lines ( (M,) float or None ) – Level at the unexcited odd and even harmonics. Each contains the noise as well as any distortion of that parity. None when the grid leaves no harmonic of that parity free in band. r_ntv ( float ) – Which error dominates the non-harmonic bins. Near 1 means the time variation does; well above 1 means noise does. See :func: ratio_noise_to_time_variation . n_bins ( dict ) – How many bins fell in each class, so a thin estimate is visible. Source code in src/deistools/processing/bla.py class BurstBLA: """What one burst says about itself. The three ``std_*`` attributes are **measured levels, not a decomposition**: each is what the bins of one class imply for the standard deviation of ``impedance``, with nothing subtracted. They are reported that way on purpose. Subtracting one from another is how the distortion is normally quoted, and it is available from :meth:`distortion_odd` and :meth:`distortion_even`, but the subtraction has two failure modes that a stored, already-subtracted number would hide -- see those methods. Attributes ---------- impedance : (M,) complex ``V/I`` at the excited bins -- the same number the STFT returns. std_noise : (M,) float Level at the non-harmonic bins. Noise alone on a time-invariant cell; noise *plus the time-variation skirt* otherwise, so an **upper bound**. :attr:`r_ntv` says which. std_odd_lines, std_even_lines : (M,) float or None Level at the unexcited odd and even harmonics. Each contains the noise as well as any distortion of that parity. ``None`` when the grid leaves no harmonic of that parity free in band. r_ntv : float Which error dominates the non-harmonic bins. Near 1 means the time variation does; well above 1 means noise does. See :func:`ratio_noise_to_time_variation`. n_bins : dict How many bins fell in each class, so a thin estimate is visible. """ __slots__ = ("impedance", "std_noise", "std_odd_lines", "std_even_lines", "r_ntv", "n_bins", "n_local") def __init__(self, impedance, std_noise, std_odd_lines, std_even_lines, r_ntv, n_bins, n_local=30): self.impedance = impedance self.std_noise = std_noise self.std_odd_lines = std_odd_lines self.std_even_lines = std_even_lines self.r_ntv = r_ntv self.n_bins = n_bins self.n_local = n_local def __repr__(self): return (f"BurstBLA({self.impedance.size} tones, " f"r_ntv={self.r_ntv:.2f}, bins={self.n_bins})") def dominant_error(self, tolerance=3.0): """``'time variation'`` or ``'noise'``, from :attr:`r_ntv`. ``tolerance`` is how far above 1 the ratio must sit before the residual is called noise. The statistic is itself noisy on a short burst, so a wide margin is the honest default. The test needs a residual to work on. On a noiseless simulation the non-harmonic bins hold nothing but round-off and the answer is meaningless -- measured at 0.86 for a stationary noiseless cell, which would read as "time variation" for a system that has none. Real records always have noise; simulated ones should be given some. """ return "noise" if self.r_ntv > tolerance else "time variation" def _excess(self, level, z=3.0): """``sqrt(level^2 - noise^2)``, NaN unless the excess is significant. A positive difference is not by itself evidence. Each level is a mean of ``n_local`` bin powers, so it carries a relative standard error of ``1/sqrt(n_local)``, and their difference about ``sqrt(2/n_local)``. The excess is reported only when it clears ``z`` of those, i.e. level^2 - noise^2 > z * sqrt(2/n_local) * noise^2 Without the threshold, merely requiring a positive difference fires on **10 of 13 tones of a linear stationary cell**, where the two levels agree to 2.5% and the sign is a coin toss. With it, none do. NaN rather than zero because the two mean different things: zero would claim the distortion was measured and found absent, while NaN says this burst cannot resolve it. """ if level is None: return None noise_power = self.std_noise ** 2 excess = level ** 2 - noise_power threshold = z * np.sqrt(2.0 / max(self.n_local, 1)) * noise_power return np.where(excess > threshold, np.sqrt(np.abs(excess)), np.nan) def distortion_odd(self): """Odd-order distortion, the noise removed. NaN where unresolvable. This is the one that matters for an odd multisine: odd-order distortion lands *on* the excited lines as well as the empty odd ones, so it biases the impedance, where even-order distortion only sits beside it. Two things make the result NaN, and both are information: * **The burst is too short to resolve it.** With ``n_local`` bins averaged, a power estimate carries about ``1/sqrt(n_local)`` relative error, so when there is no real distortion the difference scatters about zero and half the tones come back NaN. Taking ``max(excess, 0)`` instead would rectify that scatter into a spurious positive level -- measured at 1.3e-05 on a *linear* stationary cell, which is exactly the false alarm this avoids. * **The cell is varying.** Then the non-harmonic bins carry the time-variation skirt and sit *above* the harmonic ones, so the subtraction is negative everywhere. Measured on the block-oriented system, which is nonlinear *and* time-varying: every tone NaN, although the distortion is certainly there. Check :attr:`r_ntv` first; if it is near 1, use :func:`~deistools.processing.bltva.bltva`, which models the variation and reports ``var_distortion_odd`` with it removed. """ return self._excess(self.std_odd_lines) def distortion_even(self): """Even-order distortion, the noise removed. NaN where unresolvable. Same caveats as :meth:`distortion_odd`. Even-order distortion does not land on the excited lines of an odd multisine, so it does not bias the impedance; it is reported because its presence says something about the cell. """ return self._excess(self.std_even_lines)

docs.text: classify_bins(n_samples, periods_per_window, harmonics, band_only=True) Which DFT bins of one burst carry what. Parameters: n_samples ( int ) – Length of the burst. periods_per_window ( int ) – Whole multisine periods inside it. Must be >= 2, or the noise class is empty -- see the module docstring. harmonics ( sequence of int ) – Excited harmonic numbers of the multisine. band_only ( bool , default: True ) – Restrict every class to bins at or below the highest excited tone. Above it there is no signal to compare against and the data acquisition's own filtering shapes whatever is left. Returns: dict of boolean masks over ``k = 1 .. n_samples//2 - 1``, with keys – ``excited``, ``odd_nl``, ``even_nl``, ``noise`` and ``band``, plus – ``bins`` (the bin indices themselves) and ``k_excited`` (the excited bins – in the order ``harmonics`` gives them). – Source code in src/deistools/processing/bla.py def classify_bins(n_samples, periods_per_window, harmonics, band_only=True): """Which DFT bins of one burst carry what. Parameters ---------- n_samples : int Length of the burst. periods_per_window : int Whole multisine periods inside it. Must be >= 2, or the noise class is empty -- see the module docstring. harmonics : sequence of int Excited harmonic numbers of the multisine. band_only : bool Restrict every class to bins at or below the highest excited tone. Above it there is no signal to compare against and the data acquisition's own filtering shapes whatever is left. Returns ------- dict of boolean masks over ``k = 1 .. n_samples//2 - 1``, with keys ``excited``, ``odd_nl``, ``even_nl``, ``noise`` and ``band``, plus ``bins`` (the bin indices themselves) and ``k_excited`` (the excited bins in the order ``harmonics`` gives them). """ periods = int(periods_per_window) if periods < 2: raise ValueError( f"periods_per_window must be >= 2, got {periods}. At one period " "every bin of the burst is a harmonic of the multisine, so " "nonlinear distortion and noise land in the same places and " "cannot be separated. This is the price of the uncertainty " "estimate, paid in time resolution.") harmonics = np.asarray(harmonics, dtype=int) k = np.arange(1, n_samples // 2) is_harmonic = (k % periods == 0) order = np.where(is_harmonic, k // periods, -1) excited = np.isin(order, harmonics) free = is_harmonic & ~excited band = (k <= harmonics.max() * periods) if band_only else np.ones_like(k, bool) return { "bins": k, "k_excited": harmonics * periods, "excited": excited & band, "odd_nl": free & (order % 2 == 1) & band, "even_nl": free & (order % 2 == 0) & band, "noise": (~is_harmonic) & band, "band": band, }

docs.text: ratio_noise_to_time_variation(spectrum, noise_mask, bins) Is the residual noise, or the cell moving? Lataire 2012 eq. (33). The two are told apart by their correlation over frequency rather than their size. Stationary noise is uncorrelated between neighbouring DFT bins. A time variation is not: it reaches each bin by convolving the excited lines with the spectrum of the variation, so neighbours share contributions. For a linear-in-time variation the ratio of the autocorrelation at lags 0 and 1 works out to exactly pi^2/6 (eq. 31), so scaling by 6/pi^2 puts "pure time variation" at 1: R = (6/pi^2) * mean|V(k)|^2 / |mean V(k) conj(V(k+1))| Near 1 the residual is time variation; well above 1 it is noise. Only adjacent bins of noise_mask are used, since the lag has to be a real neighbour. Measured on one 80 s burst: 12.7 for a stationary cell with noise, 0.97 for the block-oriented system and 0.77 for the transistor -- both of which vary. Returns inf when fewer than two adjacent pairs survive, which is the honest answer rather than a number built from nothing. Source code in src/deistools/processing/bla.py def ratio_noise_to_time_variation(spectrum, noise_mask, bins): """Is the residual noise, or the cell moving? Lataire 2012 eq. (33). The two are told apart by their correlation over frequency rather than their size. Stationary noise is uncorrelated between neighbouring DFT bins. A time variation is not: it reaches each bin by convolving the excited lines with the spectrum of the variation, so neighbours share contributions. For a linear-in-time variation the ratio of the autocorrelation at lags 0 and 1 works out to exactly ``pi^2/6`` (eq. 31), so scaling by ``6/pi^2`` puts "pure time variation" at 1: R = (6/pi^2) * mean|V(k)|^2 / |mean V(k) conj(V(k+1))| Near 1 the residual is time variation; well above 1 it is noise. Only *adjacent* bins of ``noise_mask`` are used, since the lag has to be a real neighbour. Measured on one 80 s burst: 12.7 for a stationary cell with noise, 0.97 for the block-oriented system and 0.77 for the transistor -- both of which vary. Returns ``inf`` when fewer than two adjacent pairs survive, which is the honest answer rather than a number built from nothing. """ selected = np.flatnonzero(noise_mask) if selected.size < 3: return float("inf") adjacent = selected[np.flatnonzero(np.diff(bins[selected]) == 1)] if adjacent.size < 2: return float("inf") lag0 = np.mean(np.abs(spectrum[adjacent]) ** 2) lag1 = np.abs(np.mean(spectrum[adjacent] * np.conj(spectrum[adjacent + 1]))) if lag1 == 0.0: return float("inf") return float(lag0 / lag1 / PI_SQUARED_OVER_SIX)

docs.text: burst_bla(voltage, current, harmonics, periods_per_window, n_local=30) Impedance of one burst, with the error split by where it came from. Parameters: voltage ( (n,) real ) – One burst, holding exactly periods_per_window multisine periods. current ( (n,) real ) – One burst, holding exactly periods_per_window multisine periods. harmonics ( sequence of int ) – Excited harmonic numbers. periods_per_window ( int ) – Whole multisine periods in the burst, at least 2. n_local ( int , default: 30 ) – How many bins of a class to average for the level at each tone. More is steadier and less local; the default resolves the colouring of the noise without being noisy itself. Returns: BurstBLA – Notes The levels are referred to the impedance by first-order propagation, var(Z)/|Z|^2 = var(V)/|V|^2 + var(I)/|I|^2 which treats the two channels as independently disturbed. That is the same convention :func: ~deistools.processing.dmfa_functions.extract_impedance_with_error uses, so the two are comparable. Source code in src/deistools/processing/bla.py def burst_bla(voltage, current, harmonics, periods_per_window, n_local=30): """Impedance of one burst, with the error split by where it came from. Parameters ---------- voltage, current : (n,) real One burst, holding exactly ``periods_per_window`` multisine periods. harmonics : sequence of int Excited harmonic numbers. periods_per_window : int Whole multisine periods in the burst, at least 2. n_local : int How many bins of a class to average for the level at each tone. More is steadier and less local; the default resolves the colouring of the noise without being noisy itself. Returns ------- BurstBLA Notes ----- The levels are referred to the impedance by first-order propagation, var(Z)/|Z|^2 = var(V)/|V|^2 + var(I)/|I|^2 which treats the two channels as independently disturbed. That is the same convention :func:`~deistools.processing.dmfa_functions.extract_impedance_with_error` uses, so the two are comparable. """ voltage = np.asarray(voltage, dtype=float) current = np.asarray(current, dtype=float) if voltage.shape != current.shape or voltage.ndim != 1: raise ValueError("voltage and current must be 1-D arrays of equal length") n = voltage.size classes = classify_bins(n, periods_per_window, harmonics) k = classes["bins"] k_exc = classes["k_excited"] if k_exc.max() >= k[-1]: raise ValueError( f"the highest excited harmonic sits at bin {k_exc.max()}, at or " f"above the burst's Nyquist bin {k[-1] + 1}") V = np.fft.fft(voltage)[1:n // 2] / n I = np.fft.fft(current)[1:n // 2] / n index = k_exc - 1 # k starts at 1 impedance = V[index] / I[index] power_v, power_i = np.abs(V) ** 2, np.abs(I) ** 2 relative = np.abs(impedance) ** 2 def level(mask): """Level at one class of bins, referred to the impedance.""" if not mask.any(): return None lv, _ = _local_power(power_v, mask, k, k_exc, n_local) li, _ = _local_power(power_i, mask, k, k_exc, n_local) return np.sqrt(relative * (lv / power_v[index] + li / power_i[index])) return BurstBLA( impedance=impedance, std_noise=level(classes["noise"]), std_odd_lines=level(classes["odd_nl"]), std_even_lines=level(classes["even_nl"]), r_ntv=ratio_noise_to_time_variation(V, classes["noise"], k), n_bins={name: int(classes[name].sum()) for name in ("excited", "odd_nl", "even_nl", "noise")}, n_local=n_local, )

docs.text: bla_eis(voltage, current, period, sampling_time, harmonics, periods_per_window=4, n_local=30) Sliding bursts over a whole record: STFT, with the error attributed. Parameters: voltage ( (N,) real ) – The record. current ( (N,) real ) – The record. period ( float ) – One multisine period, in seconds . sampling_time ( float ) – 1/fs. harmonics ( sequence of int ) – Excited harmonic numbers, so that tone m is at harmonics[m] / period Hz. periods_per_window ( int , default: 4 ) – Multisine periods per burst, at least 2. This is the time resolution and it cannot be 1 -- see :func: classify_bins . n_local ( int , default: 30 ) – Bins averaged for each level; passed to :func: burst_bla . Returns: (results, t) : list of BurstBLA, (n_bursts,) float – One entry per burst, stamped at the burst midpoint. Source code in src/deistools/processing/bla.py def bla_eis(voltage, current, period, sampling_time, harmonics, periods_per_window=4, n_local=30): """Sliding bursts over a whole record: STFT, with the error attributed. Parameters ---------- voltage, current : (N,) real The record. period : float One multisine period, in **seconds**. sampling_time : float 1/fs. harmonics : sequence of int Excited harmonic numbers, so that tone ``m`` is at ``harmonics[m] / period`` Hz. periods_per_window : int Multisine periods per burst, at least 2. This is the time resolution and it cannot be 1 -- see :func:`classify_bins`. n_local : int Bins averaged for each level; passed to :func:`burst_bla`. Returns ------- (results, t) : list of BurstBLA, (n_bursts,) float One entry per burst, stamped at the burst midpoint. """ voltage = np.asarray(voltage, dtype=float) current = np.asarray(current, dtype=float) samples = int(round(period / sampling_time)) * int(periods_per_window) if samples < 4: raise ValueError("burst shorter than four samples") n_bursts = voltage.size // samples if n_bursts == 0: raise ValueError( f"the record holds {voltage.size} samples, short of the {samples} " f"a burst of {periods_per_window} periods needs") results, centres = [], [] for b in range(n_bursts): sl = slice(b * samples, (b + 1) * samples) results.append(burst_bla(voltage[sl], current[sl], harmonics, periods_per_window, n_local)) centres.append((b + 0.5) * samples * sampling_time) return results, np.asarray(centres)
