docs.text: Trend removal for BLTVA, following Hallemans et al., IEEE TIM 71 (2022) 6501711. Why this is not a preprocessing step A trend cannot simply be subtracted before estimation. Whatever filter removes it also shapes the signal of interest and the noise, and the estimator has to know about that shaping or it will report a biased transfer function with wrong uncertainties. Removing a trend therefore changes four things at once (2022 paper, eq. 18-27): every skirt regressor is multiplied by the filter response F(k) (eq. 21) the cost function is weighted by W = (F F^H)^-1 (eq. 26) the filter's boundary effects add their own regressors (eq. 21) the transient order Na shrinks by the order of the filter (eq. 22) A strategy here is consequently not "a function that returns a cleaned signal". It is the bundle of those four things, which is what the protocol below encodes. A strategy that cannot report its frequency_response cannot be used safely, because step 2 would be impossible. The weighting is what makes differencing free: it attenuates low frequencies and amplifies high ones, but it does the same to the signal and the noise, so the signal-to-noise ratio at every bin is unchanged (eq. 20). A naive low-pass-and-subtract has no such guarantee -- it would destroy exactly the low-frequency impedance information the measurement is for -- which is why frequency_response is mandatory rather than optional. Why only differencing works here Of the strategies in this module, only differencing may be passed to BLTVA . That is not an implementation gap; it follows from what the weighting does, and the reason is worth stating because it is easy to assume the opposite. (Differencing is also not usually the best option -- plain Nq , with no detrending at all, beats it unless eq. (49) caps Nq too low. See :class: Differencing .) A filter applied by circular convolution is diagonal in frequency: it multiplies bin k by F(k) and nothing else. Trend and signal that share a bin are scaled by the same number, so |T(k)| / |S(k)| is unchanged, for every k and every diagonal filter -- measured here as bit-identical before and after. The filter cannot separate them, because at a single bin there is nothing to separate them with. Step 2 then undoes even the attenuation: for a real, zero-phase response F/|F| = 1 , so the weighted system is identical to the one built from the raw record (verified to 5.6e-17 on the skirt regressors). What survives is only the damage: the trend block of eq. (58) has been deleted, the trend is still in the data, and nothing models it. Measured on the 2022 paper's own trend, with F(k) = 1 exactly -- a filter that does nothing at all, which the protocol happily accepts: ========================================== ========== configuration error at the lowest tone ========================================== ========== no trend, Nq = 5 2.2e-04 trend, Nq = 5, no detrending 1.6e-02 trend, ``F(k) = 1`` "detrending" 2.6e+00 ========================================== ========== A moving average does score well in that test (1.8e-04), which looks like a refutation until one varies the averaging length: L = 101 , 401 and 1601 all return 1.8e-04. An answer that does not depend on the averaging length is not coming from the averaging. It comes from the 1/|F(k)| weighting applied to the transient block, which eq. (21) does not multiply by F : since F ~ k^2 near DC for any boxcar, the weighting hands the transient polynomial a k^-2 envelope, and that reshaped basis absorbs the trend skirt. The trend removal is an accident of the reparametrisation, and a Butterworth low-pass -- same protocol, different 1/|F| shape -- scores 2.6e-02, worse than no detrending at all. Differencing escapes all of this because it is not diagonal. The zero-prepend of eq. (12) makes Delta^d annihilate a degree- d-1 polynomial identically in the time domain , which no multiplication in frequency can do, and leaves a boundary term that step 3 models exactly. Its F(k) = (1 - z_k^-1)^d is also complex, so F/|F| is a phase ramp that the magnitude weighting does not cancel. The non-circular route is closed for the others by eq. (49) rather than by principle: a causal length- L moving average with a zero-padded history would annihilate a constant exactly, but its boundary term needs L-1 regressors -- 400 columns for L = 401 , against the 2P-1 = 39 a band can support. So the other three strategies are provided for the estimators that have no weighting to undo, and for studying what naive detrending costs. They refuse to be used as a BLTVA weighting factor, and :func: check_response is the test that decides which category a new strategy falls into. Which strategy for which estimator Detrending is an argument to the BLTVA call rather than state on :class: ~deistools.processing.mfa.MultiFrequencyAnalysis , because only BLTVA can compensate for the shaping. The other estimators have no weighting at all, so for them whatever a filter removes is simply gone, and the choice inverts: ======================= ===================== ===================== strategy BLTVA DMFA / STFT ======================= ===================== ===================== :class:`Differencing` the only one that **destroys the works signal** :class:`MovingAverage` refused at best 1.7x, and not consistently :class:`LowPassRemoval` refused no help on an overlapping trend :class:`PolynomialFit` refused; use ``Nq`` the only one that reliably helps ======================= ===================== ===================== The two columns are exact complements, and one fact explains both. A diagonal filter cannot separate trend from signal inside a shared bin, so neither diagonal strategy helps anywhere. What remains is whether the estimator can undo an attenuation: BLTVA can, which is what lets differencing trade the whole low-frequency band away and get it back, so only differencing works there. DMFA and STFT cannot, so only the non-diagonal strategy -- the polynomial fit -- is any use, and it pays in distortion instead. Never pass differencing to DMFA or STFT. Differencing(1) attenuates the lowest excited bin of a 160000-sample record to |F| = 3e-04 ; the measured DMFA error at that tone is 1.00e+00, i.e. the tone is gone. In BLTVA the same attenuation costs nothing, because step 2 divides it back out. This is the single most dangerous thing in this module, and the reason frequency_response is mandatory: it is the only way to see the 3e-04 coming.

docs.text: Bases: Detrending d -th order differencing, 2022 paper Section III. y_d(n) = Delta^d y~(n), y~(n) = 0 for n < 0 Differencing suppresses a smooth trend without modelling it, which is the point of the 2022 paper: a trend that no finite polynomial captures well cannot be removed parametrically, and trying inflates the variance of the low-frequency estimates. What it buys is columns, not accuracy . The strategy to beat is no detrending at all with a generous Nq , and on the paper's own non-polynomial trend that usually wins -- relative error at the lowest excited tone: ====== ==================== ================= ============== Np Nq cap from eq. (49) best Nq Differencing(1) ====== ==================== ================= ============== 2 17 1.4e-04 (Nq=7) 8.2e-03 4 13 2.2e-04 (Nq=11) 5.5e-04 6 9 1.2e-04 (Nq=8) 7.1e-02 8 5 1.9e+00 (Nq=4) 4.6e-02 ====== ==================== ================= ============== The paper's comparison is the Nq = 2 case, where parametric removal does fail (1.35 against 7.8e-03). Raise Nq and it reverses, because a joint fit does not distort and a larger basis models the trend better. The last row is where differencing earns its place. Eq. (49), Nq + 3*Np + Na + 1 < 2P - 1 , means a high Np eats the budget: at Np = 8 the cap is Nq = 5 and the trend is then unmodellable (1.9e+00 at Nq = 4 , 5.4e+00 at Nq = 3 ), while differencing replaces the whole drift block with d-1 boundary columns -- 15 per band instead of 20 -- and reaches 4.6e-02. That configuration is not otherwise broken; on a trend-free record it gives 2.0e-04. So reach for Nq first, and for differencing when eq. (49) will not allow the trend order the record needs. Its response is a high-pass, eq. (12b):: F_d(k) = (1 - z_k^-1)^d, z_k = exp(j*2*pi*k/N) Because the samples at negative indices are replaced by zeros rather than their true values, differencing leaves a boundary term: a polynomial of degree d-1 in z_k^-1 (Theorem 2). Those are the extra regressors. The m = 0 term is omitted because a constant is already spanned by the transient polynomial, which is why eq. (21) sums from m = 1 . Source code in src/deistools/processing/detrending.py class Differencing(Detrending): """``d``-th order differencing, 2022 paper Section III. y_d(n) = Delta^d y~(n), y~(n) = 0 for n < 0 Differencing suppresses a smooth trend without modelling it, which is the point of the 2022 paper: a trend that no finite polynomial captures well cannot be removed parametrically, and trying inflates the variance of the low-frequency estimates. What it buys is **columns, not accuracy**. The strategy to beat is no detrending at all with a generous ``Nq``, and on the paper's own non-polynomial trend that usually wins -- relative error at the lowest excited tone: ====== ==================== ================= ============== Np Nq cap from eq. (49) best Nq Differencing(1) ====== ==================== ================= ============== 2 17 1.4e-04 (Nq=7) 8.2e-03 4 13 2.2e-04 (Nq=11) 5.5e-04 6 9 1.2e-04 (Nq=8) 7.1e-02 8 5 1.9e+00 (Nq=4) 4.6e-02 ====== ==================== ================= ============== The paper's comparison is the ``Nq = 2`` case, where parametric removal does fail (1.35 against 7.8e-03). Raise ``Nq`` and it reverses, because a joint fit does not distort and a larger basis models the trend better. The last row is where differencing earns its place. Eq. (49), ``Nq + 3*Np + Na + 1 < 2P - 1``, means a high ``Np`` eats the budget: at ``Np = 8`` the cap is ``Nq = 5`` and the trend is then unmodellable (1.9e+00 at ``Nq = 4``, 5.4e+00 at ``Nq = 3``), while differencing replaces the whole drift block with ``d-1`` boundary columns -- 15 per band instead of 20 -- and reaches 4.6e-02. That configuration is not otherwise broken; on a trend-free record it gives 2.0e-04. So reach for ``Nq`` first, and for differencing when eq. (49) will not allow the trend order the record needs. Its response is a high-pass, eq. (12b):: F_d(k) = (1 - z_k^-1)^d, z_k = exp(j*2*pi*k/N) Because the samples at negative indices are replaced by zeros rather than their true values, differencing leaves a boundary term: a polynomial of degree ``d-1`` in ``z_k^-1`` (Theorem 2). Those are the extra regressors. The ``m = 0`` term is omitted because a constant is already spanned by the transient polynomial, which is why eq. (21) sums from ``m = 1``. """ def __init__(self, order: int = 1): if order < 1: raise ValueError(f"differencing order must be >= 1, got {order}") self.order = int(order) def __repr__(self): return f"Differencing(order={self.order})" def apply(self, y): y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float) for _ in range(self.order): y = np.diff(y, prepend=0.0) return y def frequency_response(self, k, N): z_inv = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * np.asarray(k) / N) return (1.0 - z_inv) ** self.order def extra_regressors(self, k, N): k = np.asarray(k) m = np.arange(1, self.order) # eq. (21): m = 1..d-1 if m.size == 0: return np.zeros((k.size, 0), dtype=complex) return np.exp(-2j * np.pi * np.outer(k, m) / N) @property def n_extra_params(self): return max(self.order - 1, 0) def boundary_coefficients(self, y): """eq. (12c): the exact lambda_m, from the last ``d`` samples of ``y``. Not needed for estimation -- the gammas are fitted -- but it makes the boundary term checkable against theory. """ y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float) d = self.order return np.array([ sum((-1) ** (r + m + 1) * comb(d, r + m) * y[-r] for r in range(1, d - m + 1)) for m in range(d) ])

docs.text: Bases: Detrending Trend removal by a zero-phase response, applied by FFT. A subclass supplies :meth: frequency_response only; apply is then ifft(F * fft(y)) , which makes Y_d(k) = F(k) Y(k) hold exactly and contributes no boundary regressors. Two consequences follow from being diagonal, and both matter more than the convenience: the response must be symmetric, F(k) = F(N-k) , or the detrended record is not real. :func: check_response checks this. the record is treated as periodic. A trend makes y[N-1] differ sharply from y[0] , and the circular filter sees that jump as signal, so the lowest bins carry a residual the filter put there itself. There is no diagonal fix: a window would break step 1. Source code in src/deistools/processing/detrending.py class DiagonalDetrending(Detrending): """Trend removal by a zero-phase response, applied by FFT. A subclass supplies :meth:`frequency_response` only; ``apply`` is then ``ifft(F * fft(y))``, which makes ``Y_d(k) = F(k) Y(k)`` hold exactly and contributes no boundary regressors. Two consequences follow from being diagonal, and both matter more than the convenience: * the response must be symmetric, ``F(k) = F(N-k)``, or the detrended record is not real. :func:`check_response` checks this. * the record is treated as periodic. A trend makes ``y[N-1]`` differ sharply from ``y[0]``, and the circular filter sees that jump as signal, so the lowest bins carry a residual the filter put there itself. There is no diagonal fix: a window would break step 1. """ bltva_compatible = False def apply(self, y): y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float) N = y.size F = self.frequency_response(np.arange(N), N) return np.fft.ifft(F * np.fft.fft(y)).real def band_response(self, k_centre, half_width, N): """``|F|`` across the skirt an estimator actually uses around a tone. The response *at* a tone is not the diagnostic, and reporting it alone is actively misleading. DMFA reconstructs the time variation from the bins either side of each tone, so what biases the envelope is how much ``|F|`` *varies* over that band, not its value at the centre. Measured on ``MovingAverage(20001)`` with ``N = 160000``, a DMFA band of +-4 bins around bin 8: ``|F|`` at the tone is 1.0000, while across the band it runs from 0.363 to 1.214 -- a 3.3x ripple, and not even monotone, because the Dirichlet kernel overshoots. Nothing divides the estimate by this again, so all of it is uncorrected bias. For STFT, which uses only the centre bin, ``half_width = 0`` gives the relevant number. Parameters ---------- k_centre : int The tone's DFT bin, ``P * h`` for harmonic ``h``. half_width : int Half-width in bins of the band the estimator uses. For DMFA this is ``round(bandwidth * T)``. N : int Record length in samples. Returns ------- dict with ``centre``, ``minimum``, ``maximum`` and ``ripple`` (``maximum / minimum``, 1.0 for a perfectly flat band). """ k = np.arange(k_centre - half_width, k_centre + half_width + 1) F = np.abs(self.frequency_response(k, N)) lo = float(F.min()) return {"centre": float(abs(self.frequency_response( np.array([k_centre]), N)[0])), "minimum": lo, "maximum": float(F.max()), "ripple": float(F.max() / lo) if lo > 0 else float("inf")}

docs.text: Bases: DiagonalDetrending Subtract a centred moving average of length samples. y_d(n) = y(n) - (1/L) * sum_{m=-M}^{M} y(n-m), L = 2M+1 The response is one minus the Dirichlet kernel, which is real and symmetric because the window is centred:: F(k) = 1 - sin(pi k L / N) / (L sin(pi k / N)) length must be odd, so that the window has a true centre and the response carries no phase. Near DC F(k) ~ (L^2 - 1) (pi k / N)^2 / 6 : a double zero, so the constant bin is annihilated and everything else is merely attenuated. Choosing length : a boxcar is a poor filter and this is where it shows. Its response is the Dirichlet kernel, so F has sidelobes, overshoots above 1, and is not monotone. Checking |F| at the tone is therefore worthless -- MovingAverage(20001) on a 160000-sample record has |F| = 1.00005 at bin 8 and swings from 0.363 to 1.214 over the +-4 bins either side. Use :meth: band_response and judge by ripple . Measured cost on DMFA with that band, at the lowest tone, against a clean baseline of 4.1e-03: ==================== ========== ========== record no filter with it ==================== ========== ========== no trend 4.1e-03 1.9e-02 trended, L = 20001 8.7e-02 5.0e-02 trended, L = 40001 8.7e-02 9.7e-02 ==================== ========== ========== Read those three rows together before concluding anything. L = 20001 does improve the trended record, by 1.7x -- per-bin invariance does not forbid it, because a filter can still reweight which bins dominate a band fit even though it cannot change the ratio within any one of them. But L = 40001 makes it worse, so the direction is not even consistent across settings, and the win is bought by raising the trend-free floor 4.5x, from 4.1e-03 to 1.9e-02. Nothing is gained that :class: PolynomialFit does not gain better (7.9e-03 on the same record). The boxcar is here for completeness. :class: LowPassRemoval is strictly the better shape. Source code in src/deistools/processing/detrending.py class MovingAverage(DiagonalDetrending): """Subtract a centred moving average of ``length`` samples. y_d(n) = y(n) - (1/L) * sum_{m=-M}^{M} y(n-m), L = 2M+1 The response is one minus the Dirichlet kernel, which is real and symmetric because the window is centred:: F(k) = 1 - sin(pi k L / N) / (L sin(pi k / N)) ``length`` must be odd, so that the window has a true centre and the response carries no phase. Near DC ``F(k) ~ (L^2 - 1) (pi k / N)^2 / 6``: a double zero, so the constant bin is annihilated and everything else is merely attenuated. Choosing ``length``: a boxcar is a poor filter and this is where it shows. Its response is the Dirichlet kernel, so ``F`` has sidelobes, overshoots above 1, and is not monotone. Checking ``|F|`` at the tone is therefore worthless -- ``MovingAverage(20001)`` on a 160000-sample record has ``|F| = 1.00005`` at bin 8 and swings from 0.363 to 1.214 over the +-4 bins either side. Use :meth:`band_response` and judge by ``ripple``. Measured cost on DMFA with that band, at the lowest tone, against a clean baseline of 4.1e-03: ==================== ========== ========== record no filter with it ==================== ========== ========== no trend 4.1e-03 1.9e-02 trended, L = 20001 8.7e-02 5.0e-02 trended, L = 40001 8.7e-02 9.7e-02 ==================== ========== ========== Read those three rows together before concluding anything. ``L = 20001`` *does* improve the trended record, by 1.7x -- per-bin invariance does not forbid it, because a filter can still reweight which bins dominate a band fit even though it cannot change the ratio within any one of them. But ``L = 40001`` makes it worse, so the direction is not even consistent across settings, and the win is bought by raising the trend-free floor 4.5x, from 4.1e-03 to 1.9e-02. Nothing is gained that :class:`PolynomialFit` does not gain better (7.9e-03 on the same record). The boxcar is here for completeness. :class:`LowPassRemoval` is strictly the better shape. """ def __init__(self, length: int): length = int(length) if length < 3: raise ValueError(f"moving-average length must be >= 3, got {length}") if length % 2 == 0: raise ValueError( f"moving-average length must be odd so the window is centred " f"and the response has no phase, got {length}. Use " f"{length + 1}.") self.length = length self.order = 2 # double zero at DC def __repr__(self): return f"MovingAverage(length={self.length})" def frequency_response(self, k, N): x = np.pi * np.asarray(k, dtype=float) / N s = np.sin(x) at_dc = np.abs(s) < 1e-15 safe = np.where(at_dc, 1.0, s) dirichlet = np.where(at_dc, 1.0, np.sin(self.length * x) / (self.length * safe)) return (1.0 - dirichlet).astype(complex)

docs.text: Bases: DiagonalDetrending Subtract the low-pass content: high-pass with a Butterworth magnitude. F(k) = r^n / sqrt(1 + r^(2n)), r = |f_k| / f_c The filter is defined by this magnitude and applied as such, so it is zero-phase and has no startup transient -- unlike the same Butterworth run as a time-domain recursion, which would have both and would then need boundary regressors it cannot afford. The cutoff must stay well below the slowest excited bin, P * min(H_exc) ; :meth: band_response reports the cost there. Unlike a boxcar, the Butterworth magnitude is monotone and never exceeds 1, so a cutoff a few times below the slowest tone gives a genuinely flat band: measured at cutoff = 2 over +-4 bins around bin 8, ripple 1.03x and a DMFA error of 5.8e-03 on a trend-free record against a 4.1e-03 baseline. It still does not remove a trend that overlaps the tones -- 8.7e-02 before, 8.8e-02 after at cutoff = 2 , and 1.2e-01 at cutoff = 4, order = 6 -- for the reason in the module docstring. What it does well is remove a trend that is genuinely slower than everything excited, which is the case the cutoff describes. Whether a given trend is that case is an empirical question, and :meth: band_response answers it. Parameters: cutoff ( float ) – Half-power frequency in cycles per record , which is the DFT bin index: bin k is k / T Hz for a record of T seconds. Expressing it this way keeps the strategy independent of the sampling rate, and it is the only unit frequency_response(k, N) can resolve. A cutoff of 3 means "treat anything slower than three cycles over the whole record as trend". order ( int , default: 2 ) – Butterworth order n . F ~ r^n near DC, so a higher order rolls off more sharply and leaves more of the lowest tone intact. Source code in src/deistools/processing/detrending.py class LowPassRemoval(DiagonalDetrending): """Subtract the low-pass content: high-pass with a Butterworth magnitude. F(k) = r^n / sqrt(1 + r^(2n)), r = |f_k| / f_c The filter is defined by this magnitude and applied as such, so it is zero-phase and has no startup transient -- unlike the same Butterworth run as a time-domain recursion, which would have both and would then need boundary regressors it cannot afford. The cutoff must stay well below the slowest excited bin, ``P * min(H_exc)``; :meth:`band_response` reports the cost there. Unlike a boxcar, the Butterworth magnitude is monotone and never exceeds 1, so a cutoff a few times below the slowest tone gives a genuinely flat band: measured at ``cutoff = 2`` over +-4 bins around bin 8, ripple 1.03x and a DMFA error of 5.8e-03 on a trend-free record against a 4.1e-03 baseline. It still does not remove a trend that overlaps the tones -- 8.7e-02 before, 8.8e-02 after at ``cutoff = 2``, and 1.2e-01 at ``cutoff = 4, order = 6`` -- for the reason in the module docstring. What it does well is remove a trend that is genuinely *slower* than everything excited, which is the case the cutoff describes. Whether a given trend is that case is an empirical question, and :meth:`band_response` answers it. Parameters ---------- cutoff : float Half-power frequency in **cycles per record**, which is the DFT bin index: bin ``k`` is ``k / T`` Hz for a record of ``T`` seconds. Expressing it this way keeps the strategy independent of the sampling rate, and it is the only unit ``frequency_response(k, N)`` can resolve. A cutoff of 3 means "treat anything slower than three cycles over the whole record as trend". order : int Butterworth order ``n``. ``F ~ r^n`` near DC, so a higher order rolls off more sharply and leaves more of the lowest tone intact. """ def __init__(self, cutoff: float, order: int = 2): if cutoff <= 0: raise ValueError(f"cutoff must be positive, got {cutoff}") if order < 1: raise ValueError(f"Butterworth order must be >= 1, got {order}") self.cutoff = float(cutoff) self.order = int(order) def __repr__(self): return f"LowPassRemoval(cutoff={self.cutoff:g}, order={self.order})" def frequency_response(self, k, N): k = np.asarray(k, dtype=float) % N bins = np.minimum(k, N - k) # |f|, so F is symmetric r = bins / self.cutoff rn = r ** self.order return (rn / np.sqrt(1.0 + rn ** 2)).astype(complex)

docs.text: Bases: Detrending Fit a polynomial of degree order by least squares and subtract it. y_d = (I - b (b^T b)^-1 b^T) y with b the Legendre basis on the record, the same basis BLTVA uses for its trend block. Legendre rather than monomial because the monomial Vandermonde is hopeless beyond degree ~15 while Legendre stays usable. This is the one strategy with no frequency response at all , and not for want of deriving it. Subtracting a least-squares fit is an orthogonal projection: a rank- (order+1) operator whose frequency-domain kernel is sum_q B_q(k) B_q(k')* , dense in (k, k') . It mixes bins, so no F(k) exists, step 2 of the protocol cannot be carried out, and :meth: frequency_response raises. That is not a loss, because BLTVA already does polynomial trend removal and does it better. The Nq drift block of eq. (58) is this same Legendre basis, fitted jointly with the impedance instead of subtracted first , so the trend is separated from the signal using the whole band of data rather than removed from it by projection, and the distortion measured below does not arise. Use Nq , not this. Being non-diagonal is also what makes it the only strategy here that helps DMFA or STFT, which have no trend model of their own and no weighting either. On a trended record it takes the lowest tone from 8.7e-02 to 7.9e-03 where both diagonal filters leave it at 8.8e-02 or worse. The price is the distortion the user pays silently, measured by applying the same subtraction to a record with no trend , so that everything removed is signal. At the lowest tone, against a clean error of 4.1e-03: ====== ======== degree DMFA error at the lowest tone ====== ======== 1 4.9e-03 3 7.9e-03 8 4.0e-02 12 6.2e-02 ====== ======== The distortion grows with the degree and there is nothing to correct it with, which is both the reason the 2022 paper reaches for differencing and the reason BLTVA fits this basis instead of subtracting it. Keep the degree as low as the trend allows. Source code in src/deistools/processing/detrending.py class PolynomialFit(Detrending): """Fit a polynomial of degree ``order`` by least squares and subtract it. y_d = (I - b (b^T b)^-1 b^T) y with ``b`` the Legendre basis on the record, the same basis BLTVA uses for its trend block. Legendre rather than monomial because the monomial Vandermonde is hopeless beyond degree ~15 while Legendre stays usable. This is the one strategy with **no frequency response at all**, and not for want of deriving it. Subtracting a least-squares fit is an orthogonal projection: a rank-``(order+1)`` operator whose frequency-domain kernel is ``sum_q B_q(k) B_q(k')*``, dense in ``(k, k')``. It mixes bins, so no ``F(k)`` exists, step 2 of the protocol cannot be carried out, and :meth:`frequency_response` raises. That is not a loss, because BLTVA already does polynomial trend removal and does it better. The ``Nq`` drift block of eq. (58) is this same Legendre basis, *fitted jointly with the impedance instead of subtracted first*, so the trend is separated from the signal using the whole band of data rather than removed from it by projection, and the distortion measured below does not arise. Use ``Nq``, not this. Being non-diagonal is also what makes it the **only** strategy here that helps DMFA or STFT, which have no trend model of their own and no weighting either. On a trended record it takes the lowest tone from 8.7e-02 to 7.9e-03 where both diagonal filters leave it at 8.8e-02 or worse. The price is the distortion the user pays silently, measured by applying the same subtraction to a record with **no trend**, so that everything removed is signal. At the lowest tone, against a clean error of 4.1e-03: ====== ======== degree DMFA error at the lowest tone ====== ======== 1 4.9e-03 3 7.9e-03 8 4.0e-02 12 6.2e-02 ====== ======== The distortion grows with the degree and there is nothing to correct it with, which is both the reason the 2022 paper reaches for differencing and the reason BLTVA fits this basis instead of subtracting it. Keep the degree as low as the trend allows. """ bltva_compatible = False def __init__(self, order: int = 1): if order < 0: raise ValueError(f"polynomial order must be >= 0, got {order}") self.order = int(order) def __repr__(self): return f"PolynomialFit(order={self.order})" def basis(self, N): """The Legendre design matrix on the record, shape ``(N, order+1)``.""" xi = 2.0 * np.arange(N) / (N - 1) - 1.0 return legvander(xi, self.order) def trend(self, y): """The fitted trend itself, which ``apply`` subtracts.""" y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float) b = self.basis(y.size) coefficients, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(b, y, rcond=None) return b @ coefficients def apply(self, y): return np.asarray(y, dtype=float) - self.trend(y) def frequency_response(self, k, N): raise NotImplementedError( "PolynomialFit has no frequency response: subtracting a " "least-squares fit is a rank-deficient projection, not a " "convolution, so it mixes DFT bins and no F(k) exists. Inside " "BLTVA use the Nq drift block instead, which is the same " "Legendre basis fitted jointly rather than subtracted -- see the " "class docstring.")

docs.text: select_differencing_order(y, fs, f_max, max_order=5) Pick d by minimising the variance of the differenced series, eq. (11). d = argmin_{d >= 0} var(Delta^d y_bar(n)) y_bar is y subsampled by floor(fs / (2*f_max)) , which the paper requires so that the series looks random to the criterion rather than oversampled and smooth. Differencing too few times leaves trend; too many amplifies the high-frequency end and the variance rises again, so the minimum is the balance point. Returns 0 when no differencing helps, meaning the record carries no trend worth removing. Caveat: the criterion assumes the record is "a trend plus a random time series", which the paper justifies by the random phases of the multisine. A strongly low-pass response breaks that assumption -- its variance is dominated by the lowest excited frequencies, which differencing attenuates -- so the rule can return d >= 1 on a record with no trend at all. Treat the result as a starting point and check it against the spectrum rather than applying it blindly. Source code in src/deistools/processing/detrending.py def select_differencing_order(y, fs, f_max, max_order=5): """Pick ``d`` by minimising the variance of the differenced series, eq. (11). d = argmin_{d >= 0} var(Delta^d y_bar(n)) ``y_bar`` is ``y`` subsampled by ``floor(fs / (2*f_max))``, which the paper requires so that the series looks random to the criterion rather than oversampled and smooth. Differencing too few times leaves trend; too many amplifies the high-frequency end and the variance rises again, so the minimum is the balance point. Returns 0 when no differencing helps, meaning the record carries no trend worth removing. Caveat: the criterion assumes the record is "a trend plus a random time series", which the paper justifies by the random phases of the multisine. A strongly low-pass response breaks that assumption -- its variance is dominated by the lowest excited frequencies, which differencing attenuates -- so the rule can return ``d >= 1`` on a record with no trend at all. Treat the result as a starting point and check it against the spectrum rather than applying it blindly. """ y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float) q = max(1, int(np.floor(fs / (2.0 * f_max)))) series = y[::q] if series.size <= max_order + 1: raise ValueError( f"subsampling by {q} leaves only {series.size} samples, too few to " f"difference {max_order} times") variances = [] for d in range(max_order + 1): if d: series = np.diff(series, prepend=0.0) # the first d samples carry the zero-padding step, not signal variances.append(float(np.var(series[d:]))) return int(np.argmin(variances))

docs.text: check_response(strategy, N=4096, seed=0) Verify step 1 of the protocol: that apply is what F(k) claims. The contract a strategy must satisfy is eq. (12) of the 2022 paper, DFT(apply(y)) = F(k) * DFT(y) + (something in the span of ``extra_regressors``) for every y . This measures the part of the residual that the boundary regressors cannot absorb, relative to the signal, on a random record with a quadratic trend. A strategy that satisfies the contract returns ~1e-15; anything else is reporting a response that does not describe what it did, and an estimator built on it is biased with no warning. A constant column joins extra_regressors in the projection, because the estimator has one: eq. (21) omits the m = 0 boundary term on the grounds that the transient polynomial already spans a constant, and the first column of legvander is exactly that. Leaving it out would fail Differencing(1) -- whose entire boundary term is that constant -- at 7.8e-03, which is a gap in the check rather than in the class. Also reports whether the detrended record came back real, which requires F(k) = F(N-k) . Returns: dict with keys ``residual`` (the relative residual above), ``imaginary`` – (the largest imaginary part the response would have produced) and – ``exact`` (whether ``residual`` is at round-off). – Source code in src/deistools/processing/detrending.py def check_response(strategy, N=4096, seed=0): """Verify step 1 of the protocol: that ``apply`` is what ``F(k)`` claims. The contract a strategy must satisfy is eq. (12) of the 2022 paper, DFT(apply(y)) = F(k) * DFT(y) + (something in the span of ``extra_regressors``) for every ``y``. This measures the part of the residual that the boundary regressors cannot absorb, relative to the signal, on a random record with a quadratic trend. A strategy that satisfies the contract returns ~1e-15; anything else is reporting a response that does not describe what it did, and an estimator built on it is biased with no warning. A constant column joins ``extra_regressors`` in the projection, because the estimator has one: eq. (21) omits the ``m = 0`` boundary term on the grounds that the transient polynomial already spans a constant, and the first column of ``legvander`` is exactly that. Leaving it out would fail ``Differencing(1)`` -- whose entire boundary term is that constant -- at 7.8e-03, which is a gap in the check rather than in the class. Also reports whether the detrended record came back real, which requires ``F(k) = F(N-k)``. Returns ------- dict with keys ``residual`` (the relative residual above), ``imaginary`` (the largest imaginary part the response would have produced) and ``exact`` (whether ``residual`` is at round-off). """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) t = np.linspace(0.0, 1.0, N) y = rng.normal(size=N) + 3.0 * t ** 2 + 0.5 * t k = np.arange(N) F = strategy.frequency_response(k, N) target = F * np.fft.fft(y) residual = np.fft.fft(strategy.apply(y)) - target # what the estimator can legitimately absorb: the boundary block, plus the # constant that eq. (21) leaves to the transient polynomial absorbable = np.hstack([np.ones((N, 1), dtype=complex), strategy.extra_regressors(k, N)]) coefficients, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(absorbable, residual, rcond=None) residual = residual - absorbable @ coefficients scale = np.max(np.abs(target)) relative = float(np.max(np.abs(residual)) / scale) if scale else float("inf") imaginary = float(np.max(np.abs(np.fft.ifft(F * np.fft.fft(y)).imag))) return {"residual": relative, "imaginary": imaginary, "exact": relative < 1e-10}

The rejected strategies are not broken -- they satisfy the protocol -- but the eq. (26) weighting undoes them exactly, so passing one deletes the trend block of eq. (58) while leaving the trend in the data. The module docstring has the measurements. Source code in src/deistools/processing/detrending.py def require_bltva_compatible(strategy): """Raise unless ``strategy`` may be used as a BLTVA weighting factor. Called by the estimator. The rejected strategies are not broken -- they satisfy the protocol -- but the eq. (26) weighting undoes them exactly, so passing one deletes the trend block of eq. (58) while leaving the trend in the data. The module docstring has the measurements. """ if strategy is None or getattr(strategy, "bltva_compatible", True): return raise ValueError( f"{strategy!r} cannot be used as a BLTVA detrending strategy. It is " "diagonal in frequency, so the eq. (26) weighting 1/|F(k)| undoes it " "exactly: the trend-to-signal ratio at every bin is unchanged, while " "the trend block of eq. (58) has been removed. Measured on the 2022 " "paper's trend, the lowest tone goes from 1.6e-02 (no detrending, " "Nq=5) to 2.6e+00.
" " - for a polynomial trend, pass Nq instead: it is the same basis, " "fitted jointly rather than subtracted.
" " - for a trend no polynomial captures, pass Differencing(d), which " "cancels it in the time domain rather than by attenuation.
" " - to study what naive detrending costs, apply the strategy " "yourself and call bltva with detrend=None.")

docs.text: Does the record agree with the numbers that describe it? Every estimator here is handed a sampling time, a list of excited frequencies and -- for the windowed ones -- a multisine period, and every one of them assumes those numbers describe the record they were given. Four quantities are tied together by one equation, .. math:: N = P \, T_p \, f_s the samples in the record, the multisine periods it holds, the period and the sampling rate. Get one wrong and almost nothing refuses to run. The excited tones stop landing on DFT bin centres, the leakage that a periodic record was designed to avoid comes back, and every estimator in the package reports it as impedance: STFT sees a window that is not a whole number of periods and calls the leakage time variation, BLA's bin classes point at the wrong bins, BLTVA fits its Legendre polynomials to a record whose period it has wrong. The three error modes, and what separates them The arithmetic alone cannot say which number is wrong -- only that they disagree. The signal can, because a wrong fs or Tp moves the spectral lines while a wrong N only smears them: ========================= =========================================== what is wrong what the spectrum does ========================= =========================================== ``N`` (record truncated the lines stay where they are and the mid-period) *nominal* bin positions slide off the grid instead, in proportion to the harmonic number. Measured and nominal still agree with each other; each tone grows a leakage skirt because its bin is no longer a bin. ``fs`` (card clock, or a every line moves, by an amount typo) *proportional to its harmonic number*, away from a nominal position that is off the grid as well ``Tp`` (generator period the same as a wrong ``fs``: of the two only is not the one designed) the product ``T_p f_s`` is observable from one record, so the report gives both readings and you choose ``P`` (miscounted) nothing -- the record is what it is. The count is checked against the other three, and against how many whole periods the signal turns out to hold ========================= =========================================== So the measurement to make is the fractional bin position of each tone, :math: k_i , against its nominal position :math: h_i N T_s / T_p . Fitting .. math:: k_i^{\rm meas} = (1 + e) \, k_i^{\rm nom} gives one number, the relative timebase error :math: e , and the three readings of it are .. math:: f_s^{\rm true} = f_s / (1+e), \quad T_p^{\rm true} = T_p / (1+e), \quad P^{\rm true} = (1+e) P A record whose only fault is a truncated tail gives :math: e \ne 0 as well, and is told apart by :math: P^{\rm true} landing on a whole number while :math: f_s^{\rm true} comes out at an implausible value -- which is why the report prints all three and leaves the choice to the person who knows what the instrument was set to. :math: e is measured twice, by two routes that fail differently: from the whole-record spectrum, by sub-bin interpolation of each peak (Jacobsen's estimator). Precise, and blind to nothing except a tone buried in noise. from the phase of each tone period by period. If the period is right the phase is constant across periods; if it is off by a fraction of a sample the phase advances linearly, at a rate proportional to the harmonic number. This one also responds to the cell genuinely drifting -- but drift is not proportional to the harmonic number, and that is the discriminant. They agree on a timing error and part company on a drifting cell, so the pair says more than either alone. What else this looks at The same pass over the spectrum answers the neighbouring questions cheaply: whether every listed tone is actually present (a tone with no line above the local noise floor was not excited, or is not at the frequency it is listed at), whether anything not on the list is comparable to the tones (mains pickup, a forgotten harmonic, strong distortion), whether the harmonic numbers are integers at all -- :meth: ~deistools.processing.mfa.MultiFrequencyAnalysis.run_bla , run_bltva and run_lia all round f / f.min() and will quietly use the rounded value -- and whether the lowest listed tone really is the fundamental, which those same three functions assume. Nothing here raises on a bad record; reporting is the whole job. The one exception is a sampling time that is not a positive number, which leaves nothing to report on. References Jacobsen and Kootsookos, IEEE Signal Processing Magazine 24 (2007) 123 -- the sub-bin frequency estimator used for the peak positions. Pintelon and Schoukens, System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach , 2nd ed., Wiley-IEEE Press (2012), ch. 2 -- leakage, and why periodic excitation is measured over a whole number of periods.

Source code in src/deistools/processing/consistency.py @dataclass class ConsistencyReport: """Everything the check measured, and what it concluded. The headline is :attr:`worst` and :attr:`findings`; ``print(report)`` lays out the numbers in the order you need them to decide which of the four is wrong. The arrays are kept so that :func:`visualize_consistency` can draw them without measuring twice. """ # --- the metadata, as handed in and as implied ------------------------- n_samples: int sampling_time: float sampling_frequency: float duration: float period_claimed: float | None period: float #: the one the arithmetic below uses base_frequency: float samples_per_period: float periods_in_record: float n_periods_claimed: int | None frequencies: np.ndarray harmonics: np.ndarray #: ``frequencies * period``, unrounded subdivision: int #: 1 if the lowest tone is the fundamental # --- bin positions ---------------------------------------------------- bin_nominal: np.ndarray #: fractional, ``f * N * Ts`` bin_measured: np.ndarray #: fractional, from the spectrum bin_offset: np.ndarray #: measured minus nominal measured_on: np.ndarray #: 'V' or 'I', whichever tone was cleaner at_search_edge: np.ndarray #: peak hit the window edge: unreliable # --- the timebase error, both ways ------------------------------------ timebase_error: float #: e, from the whole-record spectrum timebase_scatter: float #: rms residual of that fit, in bins timebase_error_folded: float #: e, from the period-by-period phase phase_drift: np.ndarray #: (n_periods, n_tones) unwrapped, rad phase_slope: np.ndarray #: rad per period, per tone # --- levels ----------------------------------------------------------- amplitude_voltage: np.ndarray amplitude_current: np.ndarray snr_db_voltage: np.ndarray snr_db_current: np.ndarray stray_lines: list #: (frequency, amplitude, fraction, label) # --- for the figure --------------------------------------------------- bin_frequencies: np.ndarray = field(repr=False, default=None) magnitude_voltage: np.ndarray = field(repr=False, default=None) magnitude_current: np.ndarray = field(repr=False, default=None) voltage: np.ndarray = field(repr=False, default=None) current: np.ndarray = field(repr=False, default=None) findings: list = field(default_factory=list) # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- @property def worst(self) -> str: """The highest severity reached, ``'ok'`` if nothing was noticed.""" if not self.findings: return "ok" return max(self.findings, key=lambda f: LEVELS.index(f.level)).level @property def ok(self) -> bool: """True when nothing worse than ``info`` came up.""" return LEVELS.index(self.worst) <= LEVELS.index("info") def __getitem__(self, code): """The findings with a given code, as a list.""" return [f for f in self.findings if f.code == code] def worst_offset(self): """Largest measured-minus-nominal offset, over the trustworthy tones. A tone whose peak was found at the edge of its search window is left out: that line may not be the one it was looking for, and one mistyped frequency should not be allowed to set the headline number. """ trusted = np.isfinite(self.bin_offset) & ~self.at_search_edge if not np.any(trusted): return np.nan return float(np.max(np.abs(self.bin_offset[trusted]))) def implied(self): """The three readings of the measured timebase error. Returns ``(fs, period, n_periods)``: what each would have to be for the tones to sit where the spectrum says they do, on the assumption that the other two are right. """ scale = 1.0 + self.timebase_error return (self.sampling_frequency / scale, self.period / scale, self.periods_in_record * scale) def __str__(self): return self.summary() def summary(self): """The numbers, in the order you need them to place the blame.""" spp, P = self.samples_per_period, self.periods_in_record d_spp = spp - round(spp) if np.isfinite(spp) else np.nan d_P = P - round(P) if np.isfinite(P) else np.nan if self.period_claimed is None: claimed = " (from the tone list)" else: claimed = " (as given)" if self.n_periods_claimed is not None: P_int = self.n_periods_claimed elif np.isfinite(P): P_int = int(round(P)) else: P_int = 0 lines = [f"Multi-frequency record check -- {self.worst.upper()}", ""] lines += [ f" samples {self.n_samples}", f" sampling rate {self.sampling_frequency:.10g} Hz" f" (Ts = {self.sampling_time:.6g} s)", f" duration {self.duration:.10g} s", f" multisine period {self.period:.10g} s{claimed}", f" fundamental {self.base_frequency:.10g} Hz", f" samples per period {spp:.6f}" f" {_exactness(d_spp, 'sample')}", f" periods in record {P:.6f}" f" {_exactness(d_P, 'period')}", f" N = P x Tp x fs {self.n_samples} = {P_int}" f" x {self.period:.10g} s x {self.sampling_frequency:.10g} Hz" f" = {P_int * self.period * self.sampling_frequency:.10g}", "", f" tones {self.frequencies.size} from" f" {self.frequencies.min():.6g} to {self.frequencies.max():.6g} Hz", f" harmonic numbers {self.harmonics.min():.6g} ..", ] lines[-1] += (f" {self.harmonics.max():.6g}, integer to" f" {np.max(np.abs(self.harmonics - np.round(self.harmonics))):.2g}") residual = np.max(np.abs(self.bin_nominal - np.round(self.bin_nominal))) lines.append(f" nominal bins {np.min(self.bin_nominal):.6g} .." f" {np.max(self.bin_nominal):.6g}, on grid to" f" {residual:.2g} bins") lines += ["", " measured from the signals"] if np.isfinite(self.timebase_error): fs_i, Tp_i, P_i = self.implied() lines += [ f" timebase error {self.timebase_error:+.3e}" f" (scatter {self.timebase_scatter:.2g} bins," f" phase route {self.timebase_error_folded:+.3e})", f" reads as fs = {fs_i:.10g} Hz |" f" Tp = {Tp_i:.10g} s | P = {P_i:.6f}", f" worst tone moved {self.worst_offset():.3g} bins", ] else: lines.append(" timebase error not measurable") for name, snr in (("V", self.snr_db_voltage), ("I", self.snr_db_current)): finite = snr[np.isfinite(snr)] if finite.size: lines.append(f" tone SNR {name} {finite.min():.1f} .." f" {finite.max():.1f} dB, median" f" {np.median(finite):.1f} dB") else: lines.append(f" tone SNR {name} noiseless") if self.stray_lines: lines.append(f" stray lines {len(self.stray_lines)}:") for f_hz, amp, frac, label in self.stray_lines: lines.append(f" {f_hz:>12.6g} Hz" f" {100 * frac:6.1f}% of the tones {label}") else: lines.append(" stray lines none above" f" {100 * STRAY_FRACTION:g}% of the tones") lines.append("") if self.findings: # The verdict first, the evidence after: several of the findings # below offer alternatives that only the verdict chooses between. headline = [f for f in self.findings if f.code in ("diagnosis", "off_grid_scatter")] lines += [f" {f}" for f in headline] lines += [f" {f}" for f in self.findings if f not in headline] else: lines.append(" nothing to report") return "\n".join(lines)

A tone whose peak was found at the edge of its search window is left out: that line may not be the one it was looking for, and one mistyped frequency should not be allowed to set the headline number. Source code in src/deistools/processing/consistency.py def worst_offset(self): """Largest measured-minus-nominal offset, over the trustworthy tones. A tone whose peak was found at the edge of its search window is left out: that line may not be the one it was looking for, and one mistyped frequency should not be allowed to set the headline number. """ trusted = np.isfinite(self.bin_offset) & ~self.at_search_edge if not np.any(trusted): return np.nan return float(np.max(np.abs(self.bin_offset[trusted])))

docs.text: implied() The three readings of the measured timebase error. Returns (fs, period, n_periods) : what each would have to be for the tones to sit where the spectrum says they do, on the assumption that the other two are right. Source code in src/deistools/processing/consistency.py def implied(self): """The three readings of the measured timebase error. Returns ``(fs, period, n_periods)``: what each would have to be for the tones to sit where the spectrum says they do, on the assumption that the other two are right. """ scale = 1.0 + self.timebase_error return (self.sampling_frequency / scale, self.period / scale, self.periods_in_record * scale)

Source code in src/deistools/processing/consistency.py def summary(self): """The numbers, in the order you need them to place the blame.""" spp, P = self.samples_per_period, self.periods_in_record d_spp = spp - round(spp) if np.isfinite(spp) else np.nan d_P = P - round(P) if np.isfinite(P) else np.nan if self.period_claimed is None: claimed = " (from the tone list)" else: claimed = " (as given)" if self.n_periods_claimed is not None: P_int = self.n_periods_claimed elif np.isfinite(P): P_int = int(round(P)) else: P_int = 0 lines = [f"Multi-frequency record check -- {self.worst.upper()}", ""] lines += [ f" samples {self.n_samples}", f" sampling rate {self.sampling_frequency:.10g} Hz" f" (Ts = {self.sampling_time:.6g} s)", f" duration {self.duration:.10g} s", f" multisine period {self.period:.10g} s{claimed}", f" fundamental {self.base_frequency:.10g} Hz", f" samples per period {spp:.6f}" f" {_exactness(d_spp, 'sample')}", f" periods in record {P:.6f}" f" {_exactness(d_P, 'period')}", f" N = P x Tp x fs {self.n_samples} = {P_int}" f" x {self.period:.10g} s x {self.sampling_frequency:.10g} Hz" f" = {P_int * self.period * self.sampling_frequency:.10g}", "", f" tones {self.frequencies.size} from" f" {self.frequencies.min():.6g} to {self.frequencies.max():.6g} Hz", f" harmonic numbers {self.harmonics.min():.6g} ..", ] lines[-1] += (f" {self.harmonics.max():.6g}, integer to" f" {np.max(np.abs(self.harmonics - np.round(self.harmonics))):.2g}") residual = np.max(np.abs(self.bin_nominal - np.round(self.bin_nominal))) lines.append(f" nominal bins {np.min(self.bin_nominal):.6g} .." f" {np.max(self.bin_nominal):.6g}, on grid to" f" {residual:.2g} bins") lines += ["", " measured from the signals"] if np.isfinite(self.timebase_error): fs_i, Tp_i, P_i = self.implied() lines += [ f" timebase error {self.timebase_error:+.3e}" f" (scatter {self.timebase_scatter:.2g} bins," f" phase route {self.timebase_error_folded:+.3e})", f" reads as fs = {fs_i:.10g} Hz |" f" Tp = {Tp_i:.10g} s | P = {P_i:.6f}", f" worst tone moved {self.worst_offset():.3g} bins", ] else: lines.append(" timebase error not measurable") for name, snr in (("V", self.snr_db_voltage), ("I", self.snr_db_current)): finite = snr[np.isfinite(snr)] if finite.size: lines.append(f" tone SNR {name} {finite.min():.1f} .." f" {finite.max():.1f} dB, median" f" {np.median(finite):.1f} dB") else: lines.append(f" tone SNR {name} noiseless") if self.stray_lines: lines.append(f" stray lines {len(self.stray_lines)}:") for f_hz, amp, frac, label in self.stray_lines: lines.append(f" {f_hz:>12.6g} Hz" f" {100 * frac:6.1f}% of the tones {label}") else: lines.append(" stray lines none above" f" {100 * STRAY_FRACTION:g}% of the tones") lines.append("") if self.findings: # The verdict first, the evidence after: several of the findings # below offer alternatives that only the verdict chooses between. headline = [f for f in self.findings if f.code in ("diagnosis", "off_grid_scatter")] lines += [f" {f}" for f in headline] lines += [f" {f}" for f in self.findings if f not in headline] else: lines.append(" nothing to report") return "\n".join(lines)

docs.text: check_consistency(voltage, current, frequencies, sampling_time, *, period=None, n_periods=None, snr_warn_db=SNR_WARN_DB, stray_fraction=STRAY_FRACTION) Check a record against the metadata that is supposed to describe it. Parameters: voltage ( array_like ) – The measured record, as handed to the estimators. current ( array_like ) – The measured record, as handed to the estimators. frequencies ( array_like ) – The excited frequencies in Hz, as handed to the estimators. sampling_time ( float ) – Seconds between samples. period ( float , default: None ) – The multisine period in seconds -- the period argument of :meth: ~deistools.processing.mfa.MultiFrequencyAnalysis.run_stft_eis and the P of run_bltva . Pass it: it is one of the numbers being checked, and without it the fundamental has to be inferred from the tone list, which can only ever confirm the list is self-consistent. n_periods ( int , default: None ) – How many multisine periods you believe the record holds. Checked against the other three. snr_warn_db ( float , default: SNR_WARN_DB ) – Below this, a listed tone is reported as possibly not excited. stray_fraction ( float , default: STRAY_FRACTION ) – A line off the list is reported at this fraction of the median tone. Returns: class:`ConsistencyReport` – print(report) for the numbers, report.findings for the verdicts, report.ok for a single boolean, and :func: visualize_consistency for the figure. Notes Cheap enough to run before every estimation: two real FFTs of the record and one of each period. Source code in src/deistools/processing/consistency.py def check_consistency(voltage, current, frequencies, sampling_time, *, period=None, n_periods=None, snr_warn_db=SNR_WARN_DB, stray_fraction=STRAY_FRACTION): """Check a record against the metadata that is supposed to describe it. Parameters ---------- voltage, current : array_like The measured record, as handed to the estimators. frequencies : array_like The excited frequencies in Hz, as handed to the estimators. sampling_time : float Seconds between samples. period : float, optional The multisine period in seconds -- the ``period`` argument of :meth:`~deistools.processing.mfa.MultiFrequencyAnalysis.run_stft_eis` and the ``P`` of ``run_bltva``. Pass it: it is one of the numbers being checked, and without it the fundamental has to be inferred from the tone list, which can only ever confirm the list is self-consistent. n_periods : int, optional How many multisine periods you believe the record holds. Checked against the other three. snr_warn_db : float Below this, a listed tone is reported as possibly not excited. stray_fraction : float A line off the list is reported at this fraction of the median tone. Returns ------- :class:`ConsistencyReport` ``print(report)`` for the numbers, ``report.findings`` for the verdicts, ``report.ok`` for a single boolean, and :func:`visualize_consistency` for the figure. Notes ----- Cheap enough to run before every estimation: two real FFTs of the record and one of each period. """ findings = [] add = lambda level, code, message: findings.append(Finding(level, code, message)) sampling_time = float(sampling_time) if not np.isfinite(sampling_time) or sampling_time <= 0: raise ValueError(f"sampling_time must be a positive number, got " f"{sampling_time!r}; there is nothing to check " "a record against without it") voltage = np.asarray(voltage, dtype=float).ravel() current = np.asarray(current, dtype=float).ravel() frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float).ravel() # --- the arrays, before anything is measured from them ----------------- if voltage.size != current.size: shortest = min(voltage.size, current.size) add("fail", "arrays", f"voltage has {voltage.size} samples and current {current.size}. " f"They are two channels of one measurement and must have the same " f"length; the first {shortest} of each are checked below, but one " f"of the two files is not the one you think it is.") voltage, current = voltage[:shortest], current[:shortest] cleaned = [] for name, signal in (("voltage", voltage), ("current", current)): finite = np.isfinite(signal) bad = int(signal.size - np.count_nonzero(finite)) if bad: add("fail", "not_finite", f"{name} has {bad} non-finite samples ({100 * bad / signal.size:.2g}% " f"of the record). One NaN makes the whole DFT NaN, so every " f"estimator returns NaN at every frequency. For the checks " f"below they are replaced by the channel mean, in a copy -- " f"the array you passed is not touched.") signal = signal.copy() signal[~finite] = np.mean(signal[finite]) if np.any(finite) else 0.0 cleaned.append(signal) voltage, current = cleaned n_samples = int(voltage.size) sampling_frequency = 1.0 / sampling_time duration = n_samples * sampling_time if n_samples < 16: add("fail", "too_short", f"{n_samples} samples is too short to check anything.") if frequencies.size == 0 or np.any(frequencies <= 0): add("fail", "frequencies", "the frequency list must hold positive frequencies in Hz; " f"got {frequencies}") frequencies = frequencies[frequencies > 0] if frequencies.size else frequencies if frequencies.size and np.any(np.diff(frequencies) <= 0): add("warn", "frequency_order", "the frequency list is not strictly increasing. Every estimator " "returns its rows in the order of this list, so the impedance " "rows will be in that same scrambled order.") nyquist = 0.5 * sampling_frequency if frequencies.size and frequencies.max() >= nyquist: above = frequencies[frequencies >= nyquist] add("fail", "nyquist", f"{above.size} tone(s) at or above the Nyquist frequency " f"{nyquist:.6g} Hz (worst {above.max():.6g} Hz). These are " f"aliased: they appear at {sampling_frequency - above.max():.6g} Hz " f"and the impedance reported for them is another frequency's.") elif frequencies.size and frequencies.max() > 0.4 * sampling_frequency: add("info", "nyquist", f"the top tone {frequencies.max():.6g} Hz is at " f"{100 * frequencies.max() / nyquist:.0f}% of Nyquist, where an " f"anti-alias filter has amplitude and phase of its own. It divides " f"out of V/I only if both channels went through the same one.") # --- the fundamental: is the lowest tone harmonic 1? ------------------- if frequencies.size: base_inferred, subdivision = _infer_fundamental(frequencies) else: base_inferred, subdivision = np.nan, 1 if subdivision > 1: add("warn", "fundamental", f"the listed tones are harmonics of {base_inferred:.6g} Hz, not of " f"the lowest listed tone {frequencies.min():.6g} Hz: the lowest one " f"is harmonic {subdivision}, not 1. run_bla, run_bltva and run_lia " f"all take the harmonic numbers as round(f / f.min()) and will be " f"wrong about every one of them. Pass period={1 / base_inferred:.10g} " f"and treat their harmonic grids as suspect.") # --- the four numbers -------------------------------------------------- period_claimed = None if period is None else float(period) if period_claimed is not None: period_used = period_claimed if frequencies.size and np.isfinite(base_inferred): implied = 1.0 / base_inferred ratio = period_used / implied if abs(ratio - 1) > 1e-6 and abs(ratio - round(ratio)) > 1e-6: add("warn", "period_vs_tones", f"period={period_used:.10g} s, but the tone list is a " f"harmonic grid of {implied:.10g} s. The two disagree by a " f"factor {ratio:.6g}, which is not a whole number of " f"periods either way, so at least one of them is wrong.") elif frequencies.size and np.isfinite(base_inferred): period_used = 1.0 / base_inferred add("info", "period", f"no period given, so the tone list was used: it is a harmonic " f"grid of {period_used:.10g} s. That makes the period check " f"self-referential -- pass the period you set on the generator to " f"get a real one.") else: period_used = np.nan base_frequency = 1.0 / period_used if np.isfinite(period_used) else np.nan harmonics = frequencies * period_used samples_per_period = period_used / sampling_time periods_in_record = duration / period_used # --- the triangle N = P Tp fs ------------------------------------------ bin_nominal = frequencies * n_samples * sampling_time grid_residual = (float(np.max(np.abs(bin_nominal - np.round(bin_nominal)))) if frequencies.size else np.nan) if np.isfinite(samples_per_period): off = samples_per_period - round(samples_per_period) if abs(off) > 1e-9: spp_int = int(round(samples_per_period)) add("fail", "samples_per_period", f"one multisine period is {samples_per_period:.6f} samples, not " f"a whole number. Every windowed estimator turns the period " f"into int(round(period / sampling_time)) = {spp_int} samples, " f"so each window is {off:+.4g} samples wrong and the error " f"accumulates down the record. For a whole number, either " f"fs = {round(samples_per_period) / period_used:.10g} Hz at this " f"period, or period = {spp_int * sampling_time:.10g} s at this fs.") if np.isfinite(periods_in_record): whole = int(round(periods_in_record)) off = periods_in_record - whole if abs(off) > 1e-9 and whole >= 1: spp_int = max(int(round(samples_per_period)), 1) complete = int(np.floor(periods_in_record + 1e-9)) past = n_samples - complete * spp_int short = (complete + 1) * spp_int - n_samples add("fail", "whole_periods", f"the record holds {periods_in_record:.6f} multisine periods, " f"not a whole number: it runs {past} samples past {complete} " f"whole periods, and stops {short} samples short of " f"{complete + 1}. The DFT " f"of a record cut mid-period leaks, and the leakage is exactly " f"what STFT, DMFA and BLTVA report as time variation; " f"bltva() refuses the record outright (N % P). Three ways out, " f"and only you know which number is the wrong one: keep the " f"first {complete * spp_int} samples of {n_samples}, which is " f"{complete} whole periods (cut_signal_tail); or fs is really " f"{n_samples / (whole * period_used):.10g} Hz; or the period is " f"really {n_samples / (whole * sampling_frequency):.10g} s. The " f"measured timebase error below says which.") if n_periods is not None and np.isfinite(periods_in_record): if abs(periods_in_record - n_periods) > 1e-6: add("fail", "n_periods", f"you say the record holds {n_periods} periods; N, period and fs " f"say {periods_in_record:.6f}. BLTVA reads the excited tones at " f"bins P*h and treats every bin with k % P == 0 as a multisine " f"harmonic, so a wrong P does not degrade the estimate, it reads " f"a different set of bins. run_bla's periods_per_window is " f"affected the same way.") if frequencies.size and np.isfinite(grid_residual): if grid_residual > ON_BIN_TOLERANCE: worst = int(np.argmax(np.abs(bin_nominal - np.round(bin_nominal)))) add("fail", "on_grid", f"{frequencies[worst]:.6g} Hz sits {grid_residual:.4g} bins from " f"a bin centre (bin spacing {1 / duration:.6g} Hz). " f"compute_freq_indexes raises on anything past " f"{ON_BIN_TOLERANCE} bins, so run_fft_eis and run_dmfa will not " f"start; what a tone off a bin centre costs is leakage into its " f"neighbours, which is the same error the windowed methods make " f"silently.") elif grid_residual > 1e-6: add("info", "on_grid", f"the tones are within {grid_residual:.2g} bins of a centre -- " f"close enough for compute_freq_indexes, far enough to leak a " f"little. Exact is reachable: it needs f * N * sampling_time to " f"be whole for every tone.") if frequencies.size > 1: rounded = np.round(bin_nominal).astype(int) gaps = np.diff(rounded) if np.any(gaps == 0): share = frequencies[:-1][gaps == 0] add("fail", "bin_collision", f"{share.size} pair(s) of tones land on the same DFT bin " f"(first at {share[0]:.6g} Hz). The impedance reported for both " f"is the same number; the record is too short to separate them, " f"and needs {1 / np.min(np.diff(frequencies)):.6g} s to do so.") elif np.any(gaps == 1): add("warn", "bin_collision", f"{int(np.count_nonzero(gaps == 1))} pair(s) of tones land on " f"adjacent DFT bins. Nothing can be read about either one's " f"neighbourhood -- no leakage check, no local noise floor, and " f"search_freq_indexes has no room to search.") harmonic_residual = (float(np.max(np.abs(harmonics - np.round(harmonics)))) if frequencies.size and np.isfinite(period_used) else np.nan) if np.isfinite(harmonic_residual) and harmonic_residual > HARMONIC_TOLERANCE: worst = int(np.argmax(np.abs(harmonics - np.round(harmonics)))) add("warn", "harmonics", f"harmonic number {harmonics[worst]:.6g} at {frequencies[worst]:.6g} Hz " f"is not an integer ({harmonic_residual:.3g} off). run_bla, " f"run_bltva and run_lia round it to {round(harmonics[worst])}, and " f"then work at a frequency you did not excite.") # --- what the signals themselves say ----------------------------------- spectrum_voltage = np.fft.rfft(voltage) / n_samples spectrum_current = np.fft.rfft(current) / n_samples magnitude_voltage = np.abs(spectrum_voltage) magnitude_current = np.abs(spectrum_current) bin_frequencies = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, sampling_time) n_bins = bin_frequencies.size tiny = np.finfo(float).tiny floor_voltage_all = max(float(np.median(magnitude_voltage[1:])), tiny) floor_current_all = max(float(np.median(magnitude_current[1:])), tiny) if frequencies.size and n_bins > 4: centres = np.clip(np.round(bin_nominal).astype(int), 1, n_bins - 2) # Which channel shows each tone more clearly. Volts and amps cannot be # compared, so the comparison is each channel's line against its own # broadband level, which is a ratio and has no units. clarity_voltage = magnitude_voltage[centres] / floor_voltage_all clarity_current = magnitude_current[centres] / floor_current_all use_voltage = clarity_voltage > clarity_current halfwidth = _search_halfwidth(centres, n_bins) position_voltage, edge_voltage = _measure_peaks( spectrum_voltage, centres, halfwidth) position_current, edge_current = _measure_peaks( spectrum_current, centres, halfwidth) bin_measured = np.where(use_voltage, position_voltage, position_current) at_search_edge = np.where(use_voltage, edge_voltage, edge_current) measured_on = np.where(use_voltage, "V", "I") weight = np.clip(np.where(use_voltage, clarity_voltage, clarity_current), 0.0, 1e4) timebase_error, timebase_scatter = _fit_timebase( bin_nominal, bin_measured, np.where(at_search_edge, 0.0, weight)) # A large error means the first pass was searching off-centre. Recentre # on what it found and measure again, narrowly: a wide window around # the right place is how a neighbouring line gets picked up instead. if (np.isfinite(timebase_error) and abs(timebase_error) * np.max(bin_nominal) > 1.0): moved_centres = np.clip( np.round(bin_nominal * (1.0 + timebase_error)).astype(int), 1, n_bins - 2) narrow = np.clip(_search_halfwidth(moved_centres, n_bins), 1, 4) position_voltage, edge_voltage = _measure_peaks( spectrum_voltage, moved_centres, narrow) position_current, edge_current = _measure_peaks( spectrum_current, moved_centres, narrow) bin_measured = np.where(use_voltage, position_voltage, position_current) at_search_edge = np.where(use_voltage, edge_voltage, edge_current) timebase_error, timebase_scatter = _fit_timebase( bin_nominal, bin_measured, np.where(at_search_edge, 0.0, weight)) peak_voltage = np.clip(np.round(position_voltage).astype(int), 0, n_bins - 1) peak_current = np.clip(np.round(position_current).astype(int), 0, n_bins - 1) excited = np.zeros(n_bins, dtype=bool) excited[:3] = True for k in np.round(bin_measured).astype(int): excited[max(int(k) - 3, 0):int(k) + 4] = True floor_voltage = _noise_floor(magnitude_voltage, peak_voltage, excited) floor_current = _noise_floor(magnitude_current, peak_current, excited) amplitude_voltage = 2.0 * magnitude_voltage[peak_voltage] amplitude_current = 2.0 * magnitude_current[peak_current] snr_db_voltage = _snr_db(magnitude_voltage[peak_voltage], floor_voltage) snr_db_current = _snr_db(magnitude_current[peak_current], floor_current) stray_lines = [] for tag, magnitude, peaks in (("in the voltage", magnitude_voltage, peak_voltage), ("in the current", magnitude_current, peak_current)): reference = float(np.median(magnitude[peaks])) if reference <= 0: continue for f_hz, amp, frac, label in _stray_lines( magnitude, bin_frequencies, excited, reference, base_frequency, fraction=stray_fraction, limit=4): stray_lines.append((f_hz, amp, frac, f"{label}, {tag}")) stray_lines.sort() else: bin_measured = np.full(frequencies.shape, np.nan) at_search_edge = np.zeros(frequencies.shape, dtype=bool) measured_on = np.full(frequencies.shape, "-", dtype="<U1") timebase_error = timebase_scatter = np.nan amplitude_voltage = np.full(frequencies.shape, np.nan) amplitude_current = np.full(frequencies.shape, np.nan) snr_db_voltage = np.full(frequencies.shape, np.nan) snr_db_current = np.full(frequencies.shape, np.nan) stray_lines = [] use_voltage = np.zeros(frequencies.shape, dtype=bool) bin_offset = bin_measured - bin_nominal # --- the same error, measured again period by period -------------------- # On the current, because the current is the excitation (every estimator # here is called with the voltage as the response). Its phase moves with # the timebase and with nothing else, while the voltage's also moves when # the cell drifts -- which is why the two routes below can disagree. phase_drift = np.zeros((0, frequencies.size)) phase_slope = np.full(frequencies.shape, np.nan) timebase_error_folded = np.nan if (frequencies.size and np.isfinite(samples_per_period) and samples_per_period >= 8 and periods_in_record >= 3): complete = int(np.floor(periods_in_record + 1e-9)) phase_drift, phase_slope = _folded_phase( current, samples_per_period, complete, harmonics) whole_harmonics = np.round(harmonics) with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"): per_tone = phase_slope / (2.0 * np.pi * whole_harmonics) # A step of more than pi per period is aliased by the unwrap, so those # tones are dropped rather than believed. usable = (np.isfinite(per_tone) & (np.abs(phase_slope) < np.pi) & (whole_harmonics >= 1)) if np.any(usable): timebase_error_folded = float(np.median(per_tone[usable])) # --- the verdict -------------------------------------------------------- whole_record = (np.isfinite(periods_in_record) and abs(periods_in_record - round(periods_in_record)) < 1e-6) # Only the tones the fit was allowed to use. A line found at the edge of # its search window may be a different line altogether, and letting one # of those set the headline number is how a single mistyped frequency # comes to look like a broken clock. trusted = np.isfinite(bin_offset) & ~at_search_edge moved = float(np.max(np.abs(bin_offset[trusted]))) if np.any(trusted) else np.nan if np.isfinite(timebase_error): implied_fs = sampling_frequency / (1.0 + timebase_error) implied_period = period_used / (1.0 + timebase_error) implied_periods = periods_in_record * (1.0 + timebase_error) implied_whole = (np.isfinite(implied_periods) and abs(implied_periods - round(implied_periods)) < 2e-3) significant = np.isfinite(moved) and moved > ON_BIN_TOLERANCE common_scale = timebase_scatter <= max(0.05, 0.3 * moved) readings = (f"fs = {implied_fs:.10g} Hz, or the period = " f"{implied_period:.10g} s, or the record holding " f"{implied_periods:.6f} periods") if significant and not common_scale: add("fail", "off_grid_scatter", f"the tones are off their bins by up to {moved:.3g} bins, and " f"not by a common factor: the scatter around the best " f"proportional fit is {timebase_scatter:.3g} bins against a fit " f"of {abs(timebase_error) * np.max(bin_nominal):.3g}. No " f"sampling rate, period or record length does that. The tone " f"list itself is wrong, or the generator is not producing a " f"harmonic multisine. search_freq_indexes will find the lines; " f"nothing will make them leakage-free.") elif significant and implied_whole and not whole_record: add("fail", "diagnosis", f"the record length is right and the sampling rate or the " f"period is wrong. The tones sit {timebase_error:+.4g} of their " f"frequency away from where the metadata puts them, and at that " f"correction the record holds {round(implied_periods)} whole " f"periods exactly. So: {readings}. Which of the two it is, one " f"record cannot say -- only the product Tp*fs is observable -- " f"so take it from whichever of the generator and the card you " f"trust less.") elif significant: add("fail", "diagnosis", f"the tones are {timebase_error:+.4g} of their frequency away " f"from where the metadata puts them (up to {moved:.3g} bins at " f"the top tone), which reads as {readings}. That corrected count " f"is not a whole number either, so the record length is wrong as " f"well as the rate or the period.") elif not whole_record: add("fail", "diagnosis", f"the sampling rate and the period are right and the record " f"length is wrong. Every tone is within {moved:.2g} bins of " f"where fs and the period put it (timebase error " f"{timebase_error:+.2g}, far too small to explain " f"{periods_in_record:.6f} periods), so nothing is wrong with the " f"timebase: the record simply does not end on a period boundary. " f"Trim it.") elif grid_residual > ON_BIN_TOLERANCE: add("warn", "diagnosis", f"N, P, Tp and fs agree with each other and with the signals -- " f"{periods_in_record:.0f} whole periods, timebase error " f"{timebase_error:+.2g} -- and it is the frequency list that " f"does not fit the grid those four define, by up to " f"{grid_residual:.3g} bins. The tones named above are the ones " f"to correct; the metadata is not the problem.") else: add("ok", "diagnosis", f"N, P, Tp and fs agree with each other and with the signals: " f"{periods_in_record:.0f} whole periods, every tone on a bin " f"centre to {grid_residual:.1g} bins, and the measured timebase " f"error is {timebase_error:+.2g} ({abs(timebase_error) * np.max(bin_nominal):.2g} " f"bins at the top tone).") if (np.isfinite(timebase_error_folded) and abs(timebase_error_folded - timebase_error) > max(5e-6, 3 * abs(timebase_error))): add("info", "phase_drift", f"the two measurements of the timebase error disagree: " f"{timebase_error:+.3g} from the whole-record spectrum, " f"{timebase_error_folded:+.3g} from the phase walk period to " f"period. They are sensitive to different things, which is why " f"both are here: the first compares the lines against the " f"frequency list and is blind to the period, the second cuts " f"the record into periods and so feels the period as well. " f"Three things separate them -- a period that is wrong while " f"the frequency list is right, a cell that is drifting (whose " f"phase also walks, but not in proportion to the harmonic " f"number), or an actual clock error. The last panel of " f"visualize_consistency tells them apart: a slope proportional " f"to h is timing.") # --- is every listed tone actually there? ------------------------------- for name, snr in (("voltage", snr_db_voltage), ("current", snr_db_current)): weak = np.isfinite(snr) & (snr < snr_warn_db) if np.any(weak): worst = int(np.argmin(np.where(weak, snr, np.inf))) add("warn", "tone_missing", f"{int(np.count_nonzero(weak))} of {frequencies.size} tones are " f"less than {snr_warn_db:g} dB above the local noise floor in " f"the {name} (worst {frequencies[worst]:.6g} Hz at " f"{snr[worst]:.1f} dB). Either the tone was not excited, or it " f"is not at the frequency it is listed at; the impedance " f"reported there is a ratio of two noise samples, and it will " f"look like a wildly time-varying cell.") if np.any(at_search_edge): add("info", "search_edge", f"{int(np.count_nonzero(at_search_edge))} tone(s) peaked at the edge " f"of their search window, so the line found may not be the right " f"one and those positions are excluded from the timebase fit.") if stray_lines: biggest = max(stray_lines, key=lambda row: row[2]) add("warn" if biggest[2] > 0.2 else "info", "stray_line", f"{len(stray_lines)} line(s) that are not on the tone list reach " f"{100 * biggest[2]:.0f}% of the median tone ({biggest[0]:.6g} Hz, " f"{biggest[3]}). A harmonic of the fundamental is distortion or a " f"tone left off the list; anything else is pickup, and it biases " f"the bins it lands near.") # --- the two faults that make all of the above meaningless -------------- for name, signal in (("voltage", voltage), ("current", current)): span = float(np.ptp(signal)) if span <= 0: add("fail", "constant", f"the {name} does not change over the whole record.") continue at_rail = (np.count_nonzero(np.abs(signal - signal.max()) <= 1e-9 * span) + np.count_nonzero(np.abs(signal - signal.min()) <= 1e-9 * span)) if at_rail > max(8, 0.001 * n_samples): add("warn", "clipping", f"{at_rail} samples of the {name} ({100 * at_rail / n_samples:.2g}%) " f"sit exactly at the extreme value: the channel is clipping, or " f"the range was set too small. Clipping is a nonlinearity, so " f"the harmonics it generates appear as distortion and, on an " f"odd-harmonic grid, partly on the excited bins themselves.") if np.any(np.isfinite(amplitude_voltage)) and n_samples > 2: index = np.arange(n_samples, dtype=float) slope = np.polyfit(index, voltage, 1)[0] trend_span = abs(slope) * (n_samples - 1) # The median tone, not the sum: a trend this size leaks into the # lowest bins and inflates the tones there, so a sum would partly # measure the drift it is being compared against. typical = float(np.nanmedian(amplitude_voltage)) periods = periods_in_record if np.isfinite(periods_in_record) else 1.0 per_period = trend_span / max(periods, 1.0) if typical > 0 and per_period > typical: add("info", "drift", f"the voltage trends {trend_span:.4g} V across the record, " f"{per_period:.4g} V within one multisine period, against a " f"typical tone amplitude of {typical:.4g} V -- a factor " f"{per_period / typical:.3g}. That is the cell doing something " f"besides answering the excitation, which is what this package " f"is for; it is reported because a one-period window sees that " f"trend as leakage into the lowest tones. See " f"deistools.processing.detrending, and prefer run_bltva, which " f"models the trend, over run_stft_eis, which does not.") return ConsistencyReport( n_samples=n_samples, sampling_time=sampling_time, sampling_frequency=sampling_frequency, duration=duration, period_claimed=period_claimed, period=period_used, base_frequency=base_frequency, samples_per_period=samples_per_period, periods_in_record=periods_in_record, n_periods_claimed=None if n_periods is None else int(n_periods), frequencies=frequencies, harmonics=harmonics, subdivision=subdivision, bin_nominal=bin_nominal, bin_measured=bin_measured, bin_offset=bin_offset, measured_on=measured_on, at_search_edge=at_search_edge, timebase_error=timebase_error, timebase_scatter=timebase_scatter, timebase_error_folded=timebase_error_folded, phase_drift=phase_drift, phase_slope=phase_slope, amplitude_voltage=amplitude_voltage, amplitude_current=amplitude_current, snr_db_voltage=snr_db_voltage, snr_db_current=snr_db_current, stray_lines=stray_lines, bin_frequencies=bin_frequencies, magnitude_voltage=magnitude_voltage, magnitude_current=magnitude_current, voltage=voltage, current=current, findings=findings, )
