docs.text: visualize_consistency(report, max_points=4000, n_shown=3) Six panels of a :class: ConsistencyReport , in the order you read them. =========================== ========================================= panel what a fault looks like =========================== ========================================= the record, with the period the shaded tail is the part of the record boundaries drawn that is not a whole period the two spectra, the listed a marker beside a line instead of on it, tones marked or a line with no marker at all bin offsets against measured minus nominal rising along the harmonic number dashed fit: the rate or the period is wrong. Nominal off its bin centre rising instead: the record length is. Scatter with no slope: the tone list is. signal to noise per tone a tone near or below the dotted line is not reliably in the record at all the periods, overlaid a fan instead of one curve: the period is not the one the record was measured with phase, period by period sloping lines mean the period is wrong, and the slope is then proportional to the harmonic number. Sloping but not in proportion: the cell is drifting, which is a result and not a fault. =========================== ========================================= Returns (fig, axs) . Source code in src/deistools/processing/consistency.py def visualize_consistency(report, max_points=4000, n_shown=3): """Six panels of a :class:`ConsistencyReport`, in the order you read them. =========================== ========================================= panel what a fault looks like =========================== ========================================= the record, with the period the shaded tail is the part of the record boundaries drawn that is not a whole period the two spectra, the listed a marker beside a line instead of on it, tones marked or a line with no marker at all bin offsets against *measured minus nominal* rising along the harmonic number dashed fit: the rate or the period is wrong. *Nominal off its bin centre* rising instead: the record length is. Scatter with no slope: the tone list is. signal to noise per tone a tone near or below the dotted line is not reliably in the record at all the periods, overlaid a fan instead of one curve: the period is not the one the record was measured with phase, period by period sloping lines mean the period is wrong, and the slope is then proportional to the harmonic number. Sloping but not in proportion: the cell is drifting, which is a result and not a fault. =========================== ========================================= Returns ``(fig, axs)``. """ fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(16.5, 9)) fig.suptitle(f"record against its metadata -- {report.worst.upper()}" f" (N = {report.n_samples}, fs = " f"{report.sampling_frequency:.10g} Hz, Tp = " f"{report.period:.10g} s, P = {report.periods_in_record:.6f})") frequencies = report.frequencies if frequencies.size: harmonics = np.round(report.harmonics).astype(int) else: harmonics = np.array([], dtype=int) # --- the record -------------------------------------------------------- ax = axs[0, 0] step = max(1, report.n_samples // max_points) time = np.arange(0, report.n_samples, step) * report.sampling_time ax.plot(time, report.voltage[::step], lw=0.7, color="C0", label="voltage") twin = ax.twinx() twin.plot(time, report.current[::step], lw=0.7, color="C1", alpha=0.55) if np.isfinite(report.periods_in_record): complete = int(np.floor(report.periods_in_record + 1e-9)) else: complete = 0 if 1 <= complete <= 60: for p in range(complete + 1): ax.axvline(p * report.period, color="0.6", lw=0.6, ls=":") if (np.isfinite(report.periods_in_record) and report.periods_in_record > complete + 1e-9): ax.axvspan(complete * report.period, report.duration, color="C3", alpha=0.18, label="incomplete period") ax.set(xlabel="time / s", ylabel="voltage / V", title=f"the record: {report.periods_in_record:.4f} periods of " f"{report.period:.6g} s") twin.set_ylabel("current / A") ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper left") # --- the spectra ------------------------------------------------------- ax = axs[0, 1] keep = report.bin_frequencies > 0 ax.loglog(report.bin_frequencies[keep], report.magnitude_voltage[keep], lw=0.6, color="C0", alpha=0.8, label="voltage") ax.loglog(report.bin_frequencies[keep], report.magnitude_current[keep], lw=0.6, color="C1", alpha=0.8, label="current") if frequencies.size: ax.loglog(frequencies, report.amplitude_voltage / 2, "v", ms=6, color="C0", mfc="none", label="listed tones") ax.loglog(frequencies, report.amplitude_current / 2, "v", ms=6, color="C1", mfc="none") for row in report.stray_lines: ax.axvline(row[0], color="C3", lw=0.8, ls="--") ax.set(xlabel="frequency / Hz", ylabel="DFT magnitude", title="spectra, with the listed tones marked") ax.legend(fontsize=7) ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.2) # --- the two discriminants --------------------------------------------- ax = axs[0, 2] if frequencies.size: nominal_off_bin = report.bin_nominal - np.round(report.bin_nominal) ax.plot(harmonics, nominal_off_bin, "s", ms=5, color="C2", mfc="none", label="nominal bin off its centre (blames N)") ax.plot(harmonics, report.bin_offset, "o", ms=5, color="C3", label="measured minus nominal (blames fs or Tp)") if np.isfinite(report.timebase_error) and harmonics.size: bins_per_harmonic = report.bin_nominal[-1] / max(harmonics[-1], 1) grid = np.linspace(0, harmonics.max() * 1.05, 32) ax.plot(grid, report.timebase_error * grid * bins_per_harmonic, "--", color="C3", lw=1, label=f"fit e = {report.timebase_error:+.3g}") ax.axhline(0, color="0.5", lw=0.6) for sign in (-1, 1): ax.axhline(sign * ON_BIN_TOLERANCE, color="0.7", lw=0.6, ls=":") ax.set(xlabel="harmonic number", ylabel="bins", title="where the tones are, against where they should be") ax.legend(fontsize=7) # --- signal to noise --------------------------------------------------- ax = axs[1, 0] if frequencies.size: finite_voltage = np.isfinite(report.snr_db_voltage) finite_current = np.isfinite(report.snr_db_current) ax.semilogx(frequencies[finite_voltage], report.snr_db_voltage[finite_voltage], "o-", ms=4, color="C0", label="voltage") ax.semilogx(frequencies[finite_current], report.snr_db_current[finite_current], "o-", ms=4, color="C1", label="current") if not np.any(finite_voltage) and not np.any(finite_current): ax.text(0.5, 0.5, "noiseless record", ha="center", transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=9, color="0.4") ax.axhline(SNR_WARN_DB, color="C3", lw=0.8, ls=":", label=f"{SNR_WARN_DB:g} dB") ax.set(xlabel="frequency / Hz", ylabel="tone over local floor / dB", title="is every listed tone really there?") ax.legend(fontsize=7) ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.2) # --- the periods, overlaid --------------------------------------------- ax = axs[1, 1] if np.isfinite(report.samples_per_period): spp = int(round(report.samples_per_period)) else: spp = 0 if spp >= 8 and complete >= 2 and complete * spp <= report.current.size: segments = report.current[:complete * spp].reshape(complete, spp) inner = max(1, spp // 2000) position = np.arange(0, spp, inner) / spp colours = plt.cm.viridis(np.linspace(0, 1, complete)) for p in range(complete): ax.plot(position, segments[p, ::inner], lw=0.6, color=colours[p], alpha=0.8) ax.set(xlabel="position within the period", ylabel="current / A", title=f"{complete} periods overlaid, dark to light in time") else: ax.text(0.5, 0.5, "too few whole periods to overlay", ha="center", transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=9, color="0.4") ax.set(title="the periods, overlaid") # --- the phase, period by period --------------------------------------- ax = axs[1, 2] if report.phase_drift.size: usable = np.flatnonzero(np.isfinite(report.phase_slope)) if usable.size: pick = np.unique(np.linspace(0, usable.size - 1, min(n_shown, usable.size)).astype(int)) index = np.arange(report.phase_drift.shape[0]) for i, colour in zip(usable[pick], ("C0", "C1", "C2", "C4", "C5")): curve = report.phase_drift[:, i] - report.phase_drift[0, i] implied = report.phase_slope[i] / (2 * np.pi * max(harmonics[i], 1)) ax.plot(index, curve, "o-", ms=4, color=colour, label=f"h = {harmonics[i]} ({implied:+.2g})") ax.legend(fontsize=7, title="tone (implied e)", title_fontsize=7) else: ax.text(0.5, 0.5, "fewer than three whole periods", ha="center", transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=9, color="0.4") ax.axhline(0, color="0.5", lw=0.6) ax.set(xlabel="period index", ylabel="phase, relative to the first / rad", title="phase walk: a slope proportional to h means timing") fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0, 1, 0.96)) plt.show() return fig, axs

docs.text: Source code in src/deistools/processing/mfa.py class MultiFrequencyAnalysis: def __init__(self, frequencies: np.array, voltage: np.array, current: np.array, sampling_time:float, freq_indexes = None, impedance = None): self.frequencies = frequencies self.voltage = voltage self.current = current self.sampling_time = sampling_time self.freq_indexes = freq_indexes def compute_freq_axis(self): self.freq_axis = fftshift(fftfreq(self.voltage.size, self.sampling_time)) def compute_fft(self): self.ft_voltage = fftshift(fft(self.voltage)) / self.voltage.size self.ft_current = fftshift(fft(self.current)) / self.current.size def check_consistency(self, period=None, n_periods=None, plot=True, **kwargs): """Check the record against the metadata, before estimating anything. The first thing to run on a new dataset, and the thing to run when an estimate comes back looking like a cell that cannot exist. It answers one question -- do ``N``, ``P``, ``T_p`` and ``f_s`` agree with each other and with the signals? -- and when they do not, it says which of them the signals disagree with. See :mod:`deistools.processing.consistency` for how. Parameters ---------- period : float, optional The multisine period in seconds: the ``period`` of :meth:`run_stft_eis` and the ``P`` of :meth:`run_bltva`. Pass it. Without it the fundamental is inferred from ``self.frequencies``, which can only show that the tone list is self-consistent. n_periods : int, optional How many periods you believe the record holds. plot : bool Draw :func:`~deistools.processing.consistency.visualize_consistency`. Returns ------- :class:`~deistools.processing.consistency.ConsistencyReport` ``print`` it for the numbers, ``.ok`` for one boolean, ``.findings`` for the verdicts. Notes ----- Deliberately independent of the rest of the object: it builds its own spectra and takes the period as an argument, so it works on a freshly constructed instance and before :meth:`compute_freq_indexes`, which is itself one of the things that raises when the metadata is wrong. """ report = check_consistency( self.voltage, self.current, self.frequencies, self.sampling_time, period=period, n_periods=n_periods, **kwargs) if plot: visualize_consistency(report) return report def run_fft_eis(self): return self.ft_voltage[self.freq_indexes] / self.ft_current[self.freq_indexes] def run_stft_eis(self, period): impedance, voltage, current, time = stft_eis( self.voltage, self.current, self.frequencies, period, self.sampling_time ) return impedance, voltage, current, time def run_dmfa(self, filter, time_resolution, Npts_elab ): voltage, current, time = extract_zero_frequency( self.ft_voltage, self.ft_current, self.freq_axis, filter, Npts_elab, time_resolution, ) impedance = extract_impedance( self.ft_voltage, self.ft_current, self.freq_indexes, filter, Npts_elab ) return impedance, voltage, current, time def visualize_dmfa_filtering( self, filter, ): visualize_dmfa_filtering( filter, self.ft_voltage, self.ft_current, self.freq_axis, self.frequencies, self.freq_indexes, ) def run_dmfa_with_error( self, filter, time_resolution, Npts_elab, voltage_variance, current_variance ): voltage, current, time = extract_zero_frequency( self.ft_voltage, self.ft_current, self.freq_axis, filter, Npts_elab, time_resolution, ) impedance, variance = extract_impedance_with_error( self.ft_voltage, self.ft_current, voltage_variance, current_variance, self.freq_indexes, filter, Npts_elab ) return impedance, variance, voltage, current, time def run_bla(self, period, *, periods_per_window=4, n_local=30): """Per-burst impedance with the error attributed to its source. The short-time Fourier estimate, plus what the bins it discards say about *why* it is wrong: measurement noise, nonlinear distortion, or the cell changing while the burst was open. Parameters ---------- period : float One multisine period in seconds. periods_per_window : int Multisine periods per burst. **At least 2**: at one period every bin of the burst is a harmonic of the multisine, so noise and distortion land in the same places. The uncertainty is paid for in time resolution. n_local : int Bins averaged for each level at each tone. Returns ------- (results, t) : list of :class:`~deistools.processing.bla.BurstBLA`, ndarray One entry per burst, stamped at the burst midpoint. Notes ----- Check ``r_ntv`` before reading the levels. On a cell that varies, the non-harmonic bins carry the time-variation skirt as well as the noise, so ``std_noise`` is an upper bound and the distortion cannot be resolved at all. :meth:`run_bltva` is the estimator that models the variation and separates them. """ harmonics = np.round( self.frequencies / self.frequencies.min()).astype(int) return bla_eis(self.voltage, self.current, period, self.sampling_time, harmonics, periods_per_window=periods_per_window, n_local=n_local) def run_goertzel(self, period): """Impedance per block, evaluated with the Goertzel recurrence. Computes the same quantity as :meth:`run_stft_eis` -- the record cut into blocks of ``period`` seconds, one spectrum each -- but evaluates only the excited bins, by a second-order recurrence instead of a transform. The two agree to about 1e-10. On a record of this size it is the slower of the two, because an FFT gives every bin for ``N*log2(N)`` operations while Goertzel costs ``N`` per bin: :func:`goertzel_cost_ratio` reports the crossover. It earns its place as an independent check on the STFT path, and because its recurrence is the one that also runs on a live stream. Returns ------- (impedance, time) : ndarray, ndarray """ return goertzel_eis(self.voltage, self.current, self.frequencies, period, self.sampling_time) def goertzel_cost_ratio(self, period): """Goertzel operations divided by FFT operations; below 1 favours Goertzel.""" return cost_ratio(np.size(self.frequencies), int(round(period / self.sampling_time))) def run_lia(self, n_periods=1, *, base_frequency=None, window="boxcar", method="mix", decimate=None, stride=None): """Digital lock-in estimate of Z(f,t) at every excited frequency. Each tone is mixed down with a cosine and a sine at its own frequency and the product low-pass filtered, leaving that tone's slowly varying phasor. The ratio of the voltage and current phasors is Z(f,t). Parameters ---------- n_periods : int Integrator length, in periods of ``base_frequency``. This is the time resolution: ``n_periods / base_frequency`` seconds. base_frequency : float, optional The frequency every tone is a harmonic of, in Hz. Defaults to the lowest excited frequency, which is correct for a multisine built on harmonics of ``1/Tp``. The integrator has to span whole periods of *this* frequency, not of the tone being demodulated, because that is what puts the other tones in its nulls. window : {'boxcar', 'hann'} ``'boxcar'`` nulls every harmonic exactly and is the default. ``'hann'`` rolls off faster but needs ``n_periods >= 2``. method : {'mix', 'ls'} ``'mix'`` demodulates and filters. ``'ls'`` fits a cosine, a sine, an offset and a local slope in a sliding window instead, which is insensitive to drift within the window but far slower. decimate : int, optional Report every n-th sample (``'mix'`` only). The result is smooth on the scale of the integrator, and the full-rate array is large. stride : int, optional Spacing of the reported instants for ``method='ls'``. Returns ------- (impedance, time) : ndarray, ndarray ``impedance`` has shape ``(n_frequencies, n_instants)``. Notes ----- A boxcar integrator spanning exactly one base period makes this identical to :meth:`run_stft_eis` with a one-period window -- verified to 1e-13 -- evaluated at every sample instead of once per window. Use :meth:`lia_valid_mask` to drop the instants whose window ran past the end of the record. """ if base_frequency is None: base_frequency = float(np.min(self.frequencies)) samples_window = integrator_length( self.sampling_time, base_frequency, n_periods, window) self.lia_samples_window = samples_window time = np.arange(self.voltage.size) * self.sampling_time fun = lia_impedance_ls if method == "ls" else lia_impedance_optim if method == "ls": columns, t_out = [], None for f in np.asarray(self.frequencies, dtype=float): Z_f, t_out = lia_impedance_ls( time, self.voltage, self.current, self.sampling_time, f, samples_window, stride=stride) columns.append(Z_f) return np.vstack(columns), t_out return lia_eis(time, self.voltage, self.current, self.sampling_time, self.frequencies, samples_window, impedance_calculation_fun=fun, window=window, decimate=decimate) def lia_tone_rejection(self, n_periods=1, *, base_frequency=None, window="boxcar"): """How far the lock-in integrator suppresses each other tone, in dB. After mixing at one frequency, every other tone of the multisine lands at the difference frequency. This reports the integrator's response there -- one row per demodulated tone. A boxcar over whole base periods nulls them all, so the numbers are limited only by arithmetic. """ if base_frequency is None: base_frequency = float(np.min(self.frequencies)) samples_window = integrator_length( self.sampling_time, base_frequency, n_periods, window) kernel = integrator_kernel(samples_window, window) return np.vstack([ tone_rejection(kernel, self.sampling_time, self.frequencies, f) for f in self.frequencies]) def lia_valid_mask(self, samples_window=None): """False where the lock-in integrator ran past the end of the record.""" if samples_window is None: samples_window = getattr(self, "lia_samples_window", None) if samples_window is None: raise ValueError("run_lia has not been called yet; pass " "samples_window explicitly") return valid_mask(self.voltage.size, samples_window) def run_bltva(self, P, *, Np=6, Nq=5, Na=None, harmonics="all_nl", band_halfwidth=None, rcond=None, noise=None, prune=True, detrend=None): """Estimate the time-varying transfer function (TIM 2021/2022). ``detrend`` takes a strategy from :mod:`deistools.processing.detrending`, in practice ``Differencing(d)``: it is the only one whose attenuation the eq. (26) weighting can undo, and the estimator refuses the rest with an explanation. It is an argument here rather than state on the object on purpose. The other estimators cannot compensate for the shaping a detrending filter applies, so a detrended signal must never reach ``run_stft_eis`` or ``run_dmfa`` -- differencing in particular would annihilate the lowest tones there rather than cost nothing.""" fs = 1.0 / self.sampling_time H_exc = np.round(self.frequencies / self.frequencies.min()).astype(int) return bltva( self.voltage, self.current, fs, P, H_exc, Np=Np, Nq=Nq, Na=Na, harmonics=harmonics, band_halfwidth=band_halfwidth, rcond=rcond, noise=noise, prune=prune, detrend=detrend, ) def visualize_bltva_fit(self, P, *, Np=6, Nq=5, Na=None, harmonics="all_nl", band_halfwidth=None, rcond=None, noise=None, prune=True, detrend=None): fs = 1.0 / self.sampling_time H_exc = np.round(self.frequencies / self.frequencies.min()).astype(int) return visualize_bltva_fit( self.voltage, self.current, fs, P, H_exc, Np=Np, Nq=Nq, Na=Na, harmonics=harmonics, band_halfwidth=band_halfwidth, rcond=rcond, noise=noise, prune=prune, detrend=detrend, ) def estimate_noise_variance(self, P, *, Np=6, Nq=5, Na=None, dof=5, safety=10.0, k_max=None, step=None, detrend=None): """Noise variance spectrum of the response (TIM 2021, Algorithm 1). Returns a ``NoiseEstimate``; ``.at(k)`` interpolates it onto arbitrary DFT bins. The variance is that of the 1/N-scaled DFT, so white output noise of standard deviation ``s`` gives ``s**2 / N``. docs.text: check_consistency(period=None, n_periods=None, plot=True, **kwargs) Check the record against the metadata, before estimating anything. The first thing to run on a new dataset, and the thing to run when an estimate comes back looking like a cell that cannot exist. It answers one question -- do N , P , T_p and f_s agree with each other and with the signals? -- and when they do not, it says which of them the signals disagree with. See :mod: deistools.processing.consistency for how. Parameters: period ( float , default: None ) – The multisine period in seconds: the period of :meth: run_stft_eis and the P of :meth: run_bltva . Pass it. Without it the fundamental is inferred from self.frequencies , which can only show that the tone list is self-consistent. n_periods ( int , default: None ) – How many periods you believe the record holds. plot ( bool , default: True ) – Draw :func: ~deistools.processing.consistency.visualize_consistency . Returns: class:`~deistools.processing.consistency.ConsistencyReport` – print it for the numbers, .ok for one boolean, .findings for the verdicts. Notes Deliberately independent of the rest of the object: it builds its own spectra and takes the period as an argument, so it works on a freshly constructed instance and before :meth: compute_freq_indexes , which is itself one of the things that raises when the metadata is wrong. Source code in src/deistools/processing/mfa.py def check_consistency(self, period=None, n_periods=None, plot=True, **kwargs): """Check the record against the metadata, before estimating anything. The first thing to run on a new dataset, and the thing to run when an estimate comes back looking like a cell that cannot exist. It answers one question -- do ``N``, ``P``, ``T_p`` and ``f_s`` agree with each other and with the signals? -- and when they do not, it says which of them the signals disagree with. See :mod:`deistools.processing.consistency` for how. Parameters ---------- period : float, optional The multisine period in seconds: the ``period`` of :meth:`run_stft_eis` and the ``P`` of :meth:`run_bltva`. Pass it. Without it the fundamental is inferred from ``self.frequencies``, which can only show that the tone list is self-consistent. n_periods : int, optional How many periods you believe the record holds. plot : bool Draw :func:`~deistools.processing.consistency.visualize_consistency`. Returns ------- :class:`~deistools.processing.consistency.ConsistencyReport` ``print`` it for the numbers, ``.ok`` for one boolean, ``.findings`` for the verdicts. Notes ----- Deliberately independent of the rest of the object: it builds its own spectra and takes the period as an argument, so it works on a freshly constructed instance and before :meth:`compute_freq_indexes`, which is itself one of the things that raises when the metadata is wrong. """ report = check_consistency( self.voltage, self.current, self.frequencies, self.sampling_time, period=period, n_periods=n_periods, **kwargs) if plot: visualize_consistency(report) return report

docs.text: run_bla(period, *, periods_per_window=4, n_local=30) Per-burst impedance with the error attributed to its source. The short-time Fourier estimate, plus what the bins it discards say about why it is wrong: measurement noise, nonlinear distortion, or the cell changing while the burst was open. Parameters: period ( float ) – One multisine period in seconds. periods_per_window ( int , default: 4 ) – Multisine periods per burst. At least 2 : at one period every bin of the burst is a harmonic of the multisine, so noise and distortion land in the same places. The uncertainty is paid for in time resolution. n_local ( int , default: 30 ) – Bins averaged for each level at each tone. On a cell that varies, the non-harmonic bins carry the time-variation skirt as well as the noise, so std_noise is an upper bound and the distortion cannot be resolved at all. :meth: run_bltva is the estimator that models the variation and separates them. docs.text: run_goertzel(period) Impedance per block, evaluated with the Goertzel recurrence. Computes the same quantity as :meth: run_stft_eis -- the record cut into blocks of period seconds, one spectrum each -- but evaluates only the excited bins, by a second-order recurrence instead of a transform. The two agree to about 1e-10. On a record of this size it is the slower of the two, because an FFT gives every bin for N*log2(N) operations while Goertzel costs N per bin: :func: goertzel_cost_ratio reports the crossover. It earns its place as an independent check on the STFT path, and because its recurrence is the one that also runs on a live stream. Returns: (impedance, time) : ndarray, ndarray – Source code in src/deistools/processing/mfa.py def run_goertzel(self, period): """Impedance per block, evaluated with the Goertzel recurrence. Computes the same quantity as :meth:`run_stft_eis` -- the record cut into blocks of ``period`` seconds, one spectrum each -- but evaluates only the excited bins, by a second-order recurrence instead of a transform. The two agree to about 1e-10. On a record of this size it is the slower of the two, because an FFT gives every bin for ``N*log2(N)`` operations while Goertzel costs ``N`` per bin: :func:`goertzel_cost_ratio` reports the crossover. It earns its place as an independent check on the STFT path, and because its recurrence is the one that also runs on a live stream. docs.text: run_lia(n_periods=1, *, base_frequency=None, window='boxcar', method='mix', decimate=None, stride=None) Digital lock-in estimate of Z(f,t) at every excited frequency. Each tone is mixed down with a cosine and a sine at its own frequency and the product low-pass filtered, leaving that tone's slowly varying phasor. The ratio of the voltage and current phasors is Z(f,t). Parameters: n_periods ( int , default: 1 ) – Integrator length, in periods of base_frequency . This is the time resolution: n_periods / base_frequency seconds. base_frequency ( float , default: None ) – The frequency every tone is a harmonic of, in Hz. Defaults to the lowest excited frequency, which is correct for a multisine built on harmonics of 1/Tp . The integrator has to span whole periods of this frequency, not of the tone being demodulated, because that is what puts the other tones in its nulls. window ( ( boxcar , hann ) , default: 'boxcar' ) – 'boxcar' nulls every harmonic exactly and is the default. 'hann' rolls off faster but needs n_periods >= 2 . method ( ( mix , ls ) , default: 'mix' ) – 'mix' demodulates and filters. 'ls' fits a cosine, a sine, an offset and a local slope in a sliding window instead, which is insensitive to drift within the window but far slower. decimate ( int , default: None ) – Report every n-th sample ( 'mix' only). The result is smooth on the scale of the integrator, and the full-rate array is large. stride ( int , default: None ) – Spacing of the reported instants for method='ls' . Returns: (impedance, time) : ndarray, ndarray – impedance has shape (n_frequencies, n_instants) . Notes A boxcar integrator spanning exactly one base period makes this identical to :meth: run_stft_eis with a one-period window -- verified to 1e-13 -- evaluated at every sample instead of once per window. Use :meth: lia_valid_mask to drop the instants whose window ran past the end of the record. Source code in src/deistools/processing/mfa.py def run_lia(self, n_periods=1, *, base_frequency=None, window="boxcar", method="mix", decimate=None, stride=None): """Digital lock-in estimate of Z(f,t) at every excited frequency. Each tone is mixed down with a cosine and a sine at its own frequency and the product low-pass filtered, leaving that tone's slowly varying phasor. The ratio of the voltage and current phasors is Z(f,t). Parameters ---------- n_periods : int Integrator length, in periods of ``base_frequency``. This is the time resolution: ``n_periods / base_frequency`` seconds. base_frequency : float, optional The frequency every tone is a harmonic of, in Hz. Defaults to the lowest excited frequency, which is correct for a multisine built on harmonics of ``1/Tp``. The integrator has to span whole periods of *this* frequency, not of the tone being demodulated, because that is what puts the other tones in its nulls. window : {'boxcar', 'hann'} ``'boxcar'`` nulls every harmonic exactly and is the default. ``'hann'`` rolls off faster but needs ``n_periods >= 2``. method : {'mix', 'ls'} ``'mix'`` demodulates and filters. ``'ls'`` fits a cosine, a sine, an offset and a local slope in a sliding window instead, which is insensitive to drift within the window but far slower. decimate : int, optional Report every n-th sample (``'mix'`` only). The result is smooth on the scale of the integrator, and the full-rate array is large. stride : int, optional Spacing of the reported instants for ``method='ls'``. Returns ------- (impedance, time) : ndarray, ndarray ``impedance`` has shape ``(n_frequencies, n_instants)``. Notes ----- A boxcar integrator spanning exactly one base period makes this identical to :meth:`run_stft_eis` with a one-period window -- verified to 1e-13 -- evaluated at every sample instead of once per window. Use :meth:`lia_valid_mask` to drop the instants whose window ran past the end of the record. """ if base_frequency is None: base_frequency = float(np.min(self.frequencies)) samples_window = integrator_length( self.sampling_time, base_frequency, n_periods, window) self.lia_samples_window = samples_window time = np.arange(self.voltage.size) * self.sampling_time fun = lia_impedance_ls if method == "ls" else lia_impedance_optim if method == "ls": columns, t_out = [], None for f in np.asarray(self.frequencies, dtype=float): Z_f, t_out = lia_impedance_ls( time, self.voltage, self.current, self.sampling_time, f, samples_window, stride=stride) columns.append(Z_f) return np.vstack(columns), t_out return lia_eis(time, self.voltage, self.current, self.sampling_time, self.frequencies, samples_window, impedance_calculation_fun=fun, window=window, decimate=decimate)

docs.text: deistools.simulation ¶ Synthetic measurements with known ground truth, for testing and benchmarking estimators. Each model gives a different kind of ground truth — see the concepts pages for what that means in practice. Engine ¶ engine ¶ simulate ¶ simulate(duration_s, sampling_time_s, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, impedance_fn, noise_std_V=0.0, noise_std_A=0.0, seed=None) Simulate a multisine-excited electrochemical cell. impedance_fn(f, t) must return a (n_freq, N) complex array giving the frozen-time impedance at each excitation frequency and each sample time. Returns a dict with time_s, voltage_V, current_A, Z_true, frequencies_Hz. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/engine.py def simulate(duration_s, sampling_time_s, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, impedance_fn, noise_std_V=0.0, noise_std_A=0.0, seed=None): """ Simulate a multisine-excited electrochemical cell. impedance_fn(f, t) must return a (n_freq, N) complex array giving the frozen-time impedance at each excitation frequency and each sample time. Returns a dict with time_s, voltage_V, current_A, Z_true, frequencies_Hz. """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) N = int(round(duration_s / sampling_time_s)) t = np.arange(N) * sampling_time_s frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies) amplitudes = np.asarray(amplitudes) phases = np.asarray(phases) Z = impedance_fn(frequencies, t) current_A = generate_multisine(t, frequencies, amplitudes, phases) voltage_V = synthesize_voltage(t, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, Z) if noise_std_V > 0: voltage_V += rng.normal(0.0, noise_std_V, N) if noise_std_A > 0: current_A += rng.normal(0.0, noise_std_A, N) return { 'time_s': t, 'voltage_V': voltage_V, 'current_A': current_A, 'Z_true': Z, 'frequencies_Hz': frequencies, } Stationary R + (R‖C) ¶ r_rc ¶ Stationary R + RC circuit (series resistance plus a parallel RC element). Z(f) = R_s + R_p / (1 + j * 2*pi*f * R_p * C) All parameters are scalars (time-invariant). Use this as a stationary reference baseline when benchmarking time-varying estimation algorithms. Transistor-gated R + (R_ct(t)‖C) ¶ r_rc_transistor ¶ Non-stationary R + (R_ct(t) || C) circuit, solved as a true time-varying ODE. A transistor T is placed in series with R_p inside the parallel branch: R_s ---+--- R_p --- T ---+ | | +------- C -------+ The transistor is modelled as a voltage-controlled resistance R_T(V_gate): V_gate >= V_on : R_T = 0 (fully conducting, short circuit) V_off < V_gate < V_on : R_T varies linearly from R_T_max to 0 V_gate <= V_off : R_T = R_T_max (fully blocking) Driving V_gate with a linear ramp makes the effective charge-transfer resistance R_ct(t) = R_p + R_T(V_gate(t)) change continuously, producing a physically motivated non-stationary system. This is the circuit of Breugelmans et al., Electrochim. Acta 76 (2012) 375, Fig. 7 -- the only model in this package that can be built on the bench as well as simulated. Frozen-time impedance versus true response The frozen-time (quasi-static) impedance Z(f, t) = R_s + R_ct(t) / (1 + j*2*pi*f * R_ct(t) * C) is the ground truth an estimator is supposed to recover, and it is returned as Z_true . It is not , however, the response the circuit actually produces. Because Z depends nonlinearly on R_ct(t), the quasi-static response is only an approximation of the governing equation, valid when R_ct varies slowly compared with the local time constant tau = R_ct*C. At realistic gate-ramp rates the two differ by on the order of 1% rms -- far above the numerical precision of the estimators under test, so the distinction matters. The voltage returned here is therefore obtained by integrating the circuit equation. Under galvanostatic excitation, with v_C the voltage across the parallel branch: i(t) = v_C/R_ct(t) + C * dv_C/dt => dv_C/dt = (i(t) - v_C/R_ct(t)) / C v(t) = R_s*i(t) + v_C(t) a scalar linear ODE with a time-varying coefficient, integrated with fixed-step RK4. voltage_quasistatic_V carries the frozen-time synthesis alongside it so the modelling error is directly observable. Contrast with legendre.py : there the frozen-time synthesis is algebraically exact , because the basis functions are real and the impedance is linear in them. Here it is not, which is precisely what makes this model useful for testing estimators against a system that does not satisfy their assumptions. impedance ¶ impedance(f, R_s, R_ct_t, C) Frozen-time impedance, shape (n_freq, N) when R_ct_t is an array. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/r_rc_transistor.py def impedance(f, R_s, R_ct_t, C): """Frozen-time impedance, shape (n_freq, N) when R_ct_t is an array.""" f = np.atleast_1d(f)[:, None] Z = R_s + R_ct_t / (1 + 1j * 2 * np.pi * f * R_ct_t * C) return Z simulate_r_rc_transistor ¶ simulate_r_rc_transistor(duration_s, sampling_time_s, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, R_s, R_p, C, V_gate_start, V_gate_rate, R_T_max, V_off=V_OFF_DEFAULT, V_on=V_ON_DEFAULT, noise_std_V=0.0, noise_std_A=0.0, seed=None) Simulate the transistor-gated circuit by integrating its ODE. Returns a dict with the usual time_s , voltage_V , current_A , Z_true and frequencies_Hz , plus: voltage_quasistatic_V The frozen-time synthesis, for comparison. voltage_V minus this is the error incurred by assuming quasi-static behaviour. R_ct_t , V_gate_t The time-varying charge-transfer resistance and the gate ramp driving it. Z_true is the frozen-time impedance at each excited frequency and each sample, which is the quantity an estimator should recover. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/r_rc_transistor.py def simulate_r_rc_transistor(duration_s, sampling_time_s, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, R_s, R_p, C, V_gate_start, V_gate_rate, R_T_max, V_off=V_OFF_DEFAULT, V_on=V_ON_DEFAULT, noise_std_V=0.0, noise_std_A=0.0, seed=None): """Simulate the transistor-gated circuit by integrating its ODE. Returns a dict with the usual ``time_s``, ``voltage_V``, ``current_A``, ``Z_true`` and ``frequencies_Hz``, plus: ``voltage_quasistatic_V`` The frozen-time synthesis, for comparison. ``voltage_V`` minus this is the error incurred by assuming quasi-static behaviour. ``R_ct_t``, ``V_gate_t`` The time-varying charge-transfer resistance and the gate ramp driving it. ``Z_true`` is the frozen-time impedance at each excited frequency and each sample, which is the quantity an estimator should recover. """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) N = int(round(duration_s / sampling_time_s)) dt = sampling_time_s t = np.arange(N) * dt frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies) amplitudes = np.asarray(amplitudes) phases = np.asarray(phases) def gate(tq): return V_gate_start + V_gate_rate * tq def r_ct(tq): return transistor_r_ct(gate(tq), R_p, R_T_max, V_off, V_on) V_gate_t = gate(t) R_ct_t = r_ct(t) tau_min = float(np.min(R_ct_t) * C) if dt > 0.1 * tau_min: warnings.warn( f"sampling_time_s={dt:.3g} is not small against the fastest circuit " f"time constant tau={tau_min:.3g}; the RK4 integration may be " "inaccurate. Reduce sampling_time_s.") # Noise-free current drives the circuit; measurement noise is added after. current_A = generate_multisine(t, frequencies, amplitudes, phases) current_half = generate_multisine(t + 0.5 * dt, frequencies, amplitudes, phases) R_ct_half = r_ct(t + 0.5 * dt) # Start from the quasi-static state, i.e. as if the circuit had already # been running. Starting from v_C = 0 would add a ~5*tau startup transient # that has nothing to do with the time variation under study. Zp0 = _parallel_impedance(frequencies, R_ct_t[0], C) v_C0 = float(np.sum(amplitudes * np.real(Zp0 * np.exp(1j * phases)))) v_C = _integrate_parallel_branch(dt, current_A, R_ct_t, current_half, R_ct_half, C, v_C0) voltage_V = R_s * current_A + v_C Z_true = impedance(frequencies, R_s, R_ct_t, C) voltage_quasistatic_V = synthesize_voltage(t, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, Z_true) if noise_std_V > 0: voltage_V = voltage_V + rng.normal(0.0, noise_std_V, N) if noise_std_A > 0: current_A = current_A + rng.normal(0.0, noise_std_A, N) return { 'time_s': t, 'voltage_V': voltage_V, 'current_A': current_A, 'Z_true': Z_true, 'frequencies_Hz': frequencies, 'voltage_quasistatic_V': voltage_quasistatic_V, 'R_s': R_s, 'R_p': R_p, 'C': C, 'V_gate_t': V_gate_t, 'R_ct_t': R_ct_t, } Prescribed Legendre expansion ¶ legendre ¶ Legendre polynomial oracle model for non-stationary transfer function estimation. The transfer function at each excited frequency f_k is parameterised as a sum of Legendre polynomials in time up to order P: H(f_k, t) = sum_{p=0}^{P} a_p(f_k) * L_p(2*t/T - 1) where T is the total window length and L_p is the p-th Legendre polynomial. An additive voltage drift is modelled separately as its own Legendre expansion: v_drift(t) = sum_{q=0}^{Q} b_q * L_q(2*t/T - 1) This is exactly the signal model that BLTVA assumes, so the algorithm should recover the coefficients a_p and b_q exactly (up to noise). Use this model as an oracle test: if BLTVA fails to recover known coefficients, there is a bug. The voltage response is: v(t) = v_drift(t) + sum_k |H(f_k,t)| * A_k * cos(2*pi*f_k*t + phi_k + angle(H(f_k,t))) Specifying coefficients impedance_coefficients : array_like, shape (n_freq, P+1), complex a[k, p] is the coefficient of L_p for frequency f_k. a[k, 0] sets the mean impedance at f_k over the window. a[k, 1] sets a linear variation, a[k, 2] a quadratic one. drift_coefficients : array_like, shape (Q+1,), real, optional b[q] is the coefficient of L_q for the additive drift. Set to None for no drift (default). Block-oriented nonlinear system ¶ block_oriented ¶ Block-oriented nonlinear time-varying systems, Hallemans TIM 2021 Section II. This is the system class the BLTVA is actually derived for: parallel branches, each a nonlinear time-invariant block followed by a time-varying gain (Fig. 2):: y(t) = sum_p NL_p{u(t)} * b_p(t) with each branch a Wiener-Hammerstein structure (Fig. 7):: y_p(t) = f2_p( L^-1{ H_p(s) L{ f1_p(u(t)) } } ) a static nonlinearity, an LTI filter, then another static nonlinearity. Choosing which of the two nonlinearities is the identity gives a Hammerstein branch, a Wiener branch, or a purely linear one. Why this model and not the frozen-time one legendre.py and r_rc_transistor.py both prescribe an impedance and synthesise a response from it. Neither can produce nonlinear distortion , so neither can exercise Section V, and neither has a ground truth for the best linear approximation beyond "the impedance we prescribed". Here the ground truth has to be computed, because the BLA of a nonlinear block is not its linear part. The static nonlinearities move it. The paper obtains it by averaging Y(k)/U(k) over many random phase realisations of the input, which is what :func: best_linear_approximation does. That gives a genuine target for H_p and, from the residuals, for the distortion variances. Filtering without an ODE solver f1_p(u) is a static function of a periodic multisine, so it is periodic with the same period, and so is the filter's steady-state response. Filtering in the DFT domain is therefore exact for the periodic steady state, needs no integrator, and no scipy:: Y(k) = H(j*2*pi*f_k) * X(k) The one thing it omits is the startup transient, which the paper models separately with the alpha_r polynomial rather than treating as signal. Use r_rc_transistor when the transient itself is the object of study. SecondOrderLowpass dataclass ¶ H(s) = dc_gain * wn**2 / (s**2 + 2*zeta*wn*s + wn**2) . wn is in rad/s . The paper quotes its natural frequencies in Hz ("wn,0 = 0.7 Hz") while naming them wn , which is ambiguous; use :meth: from_hz to be explicit about which you mean. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py @dataclass class SecondOrderLowpass: """``H(s) = dc_gain * wn**2 / (s**2 + 2*zeta*wn*s + wn**2)``. ``wn`` is in **rad/s**. The paper quotes its natural frequencies in Hz ("wn,0 = 0.7 Hz") while naming them ``wn``, which is ambiguous; use :meth:`from_hz` to be explicit about which you mean. """ wn: float zeta: float dc_gain: float = 1.0 @classmethod def from_hz(cls, f_n, zeta, dc_gain=1.0): return cls(2 * np.pi * f_n, zeta, dc_gain) def response(self, f): """``H(j*2*pi*f)``, conjugate-symmetric in ``f`` so the filtered signal comes back real.""" s = 2j * np.pi * np.asarray(f, dtype=float) return self.dc_gain * self.wn ** 2 / (s ** 2 + 2 * self.zeta * self.wn * s + self.wn ** 2) response ¶ response(f) H(j*2*pi*f) , conjugate-symmetric in f so the filtered signal comes back real. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py def response(self, f): """``H(j*2*pi*f)``, conjugate-symmetric in ``f`` so the filtered signal comes back real.""" s = 2j * np.pi * np.asarray(f, dtype=float) return self.dc_gain * self.wn ** 2 / (s ** 2 + 2 * self.zeta * self.wn * s + self.wn ** 2) Branch dataclass ¶ One parallel branch: f2( filter( f1(u) ) ) , scaled by b_p(t) . f1 and f2 default to the identity, so a branch is linear unless you say otherwise. name is only for reporting. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py @dataclass class Branch: """One parallel branch: ``f2( filter( f1(u) ) )``, scaled by ``b_p(t)``. ``f1`` and ``f2`` default to the identity, so a branch is linear unless you say otherwise. ``name`` is only for reporting. """ filter: SecondOrderLowpass f1: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] = field(default=lambda x: x) f2: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] = field(default=lambda x: x) name: str = "" @property def is_linear(self): probe = np.linspace(-2.0, 2.0, 41) return (np.allclose(self.f1(probe), probe) and np.allclose(self.f2(probe), probe)) def apply(self, u, fs): """Branch output before the time-varying gain.""" x = np.asarray(self.f1(np.asarray(u, dtype=float)), dtype=float) f = np.fft.fftfreq(x.size, 1.0 / fs) filtered = np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(x) * self.filter.response(f)).real return np.asarray(self.f2(filtered), dtype=float) apply ¶ apply(u, fs) Branch output before the time-varying gain. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py def apply(self, u, fs): """Branch output before the time-varying gain.""" x = np.asarray(self.f1(np.asarray(u, dtype=float)), dtype=float) f = np.fft.fftfreq(x.size, 1.0 / fs) filtered = np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(x) * self.filter.response(f)).real return np.asarray(self.f2(filtered), dtype=float) hallemans_2021_system ¶ hallemans_2021_system() The three branches of the simulation in Section VII, eq. (91d)-(91g). NL_0 is Wiener-Hammerstein (nonlinear either side of the filter), NL_1 Hammerstein (nonlinear before), NL_2 Wiener (nonlinear after). The distortion of each is weak -- the paper reports the variances at least 20 dB below the linear part -- which is the regime where a linear approximation is worth making at all. Natural frequencies are read as Hz, as printed. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py def hallemans_2021_system(): """The three branches of the simulation in Section VII, eq. (91d)-(91g). ``NL_0`` is Wiener-Hammerstein (nonlinear either side of the filter), ``NL_1`` Hammerstein (nonlinear before), ``NL_2`` Wiener (nonlinear after). The distortion of each is weak -- the paper reports the variances at least 20 dB below the linear part -- which is the regime where a linear approximation is worth making at all. Natural frequencies are read as Hz, as printed. """ return [ Branch(SecondOrderLowpass.from_hz(0.7, 0.15, 1.0), f1=lambda x: x + 0.02 * np.tanh(x - 2), f2=lambda x: x + 0.03 * np.tanh(x - 1), name="NL_0 Wiener-Hammerstein"), Branch(SecondOrderLowpass.from_hz(1.0, 0.10, 0.2), f1=lambda x: x + 0.08 * x ** 2, name="NL_1 Hammerstein"), Branch(SecondOrderLowpass.from_hz(1.5, 0.15, 0.2), f2=lambda x: x + 0.15 * x ** 3, name="NL_2 Wiener"), ] simulate_block_oriented ¶ simulate_block_oriented(duration_s, sampling_time_s, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, branches, trend_coefficients=None, noise_std_V=0.0, noise_std_A=0.0, seed=None) Simulate y(t) = y_trend(t) + sum_p NL_p{u(t)} b_p(t) + v(t) . Mirrors eq. (90)-(91). Branch p is multiplied by the p -th Legendre basis function, so the branch list defines Np implicitly. Returns the usual time_s / voltage_V / current_A / frequencies_Hz plus H_linear -- the branch filters evaluated at the excited frequencies, shape (n_freq, n_branches) . That is the linear part , which equals the BLA only for a linear system; use :func: best_linear_approximation for the true target. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py def simulate_block_oriented(duration_s, sampling_time_s, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, branches, trend_coefficients=None, noise_std_V=0.0, noise_std_A=0.0, seed=None): """Simulate ``y(t) = y_trend(t) + sum_p NL_p{u(t)} b_p(t) + v(t)``. Mirrors eq. (90)-(91). Branch ``p`` is multiplied by the ``p``-th Legendre basis function, so the branch list defines ``Np`` implicitly. Returns the usual ``time_s``/``voltage_V``/``current_A``/``frequencies_Hz`` plus ``H_linear`` -- the branch filters evaluated at the excited frequencies, shape ``(n_freq, n_branches)``. That is the *linear part*, which equals the BLA only for a linear system; use :func:`best_linear_approximation` for the true target. """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) N = int(round(duration_s / sampling_time_s)) fs = 1.0 / sampling_time_s t = np.arange(N) * sampling_time_s frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float) current_A = generate_multisine(t, frequencies, np.asarray(amplitudes), np.asarray(phases)) b = legendre_basis(N, max(len(branches) - 1, 0)) voltage_V = np.zeros(N) for p, branch in enumerate(branches): voltage_V += branch.apply(current_A, fs) * b[:, p] drift_V = np.zeros(N) if trend_coefficients is not None: q = np.asarray(trend_coefficients, dtype=float) drift_V = legendre_basis(N, q.size - 1) @ q voltage_V = voltage_V + drift_V if noise_std_V > 0: voltage_V = voltage_V + rng.normal(0.0, noise_std_V, N) if noise_std_A > 0: current_A = current_A + rng.normal(0.0, noise_std_A, N) H_linear = np.stack([br.filter.response(frequencies) for br in branches], axis=1) return { 'time_s': t, 'voltage_V': voltage_V, 'current_A': current_A, 'frequencies_Hz': frequencies, 'H_linear': H_linear, 'drift_V': drift_V, 'branches': branches, } best_linear_approximation ¶ best_linear_approximation(branches, frequencies, amplitudes, sampling_time_s, duration_s, n_realisations=100, seed=None) Monte Carlo BLA of each branch, as the paper computes its ground truth. For every random phase realisation of the multisine, each branch is driven on its own and Y_p(k)/U(k) taken at the excited bins; the mean over realisations is G_p . Random phases are what make this converge: the distortion is uncorrelated with the input and averages away, while the linear part does not. Returns (G, scatter) , each (n_freq, n_branches) -- the BLA and the standard error of its mean, so a caller can see whether n_realisations was enough. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py def best_linear_approximation(branches, frequencies, amplitudes, sampling_time_s, duration_s, n_realisations=100, seed=None): """Monte Carlo BLA of each branch, as the paper computes its ground truth. For every random phase realisation of the multisine, each branch is driven on its own and ``Y_p(k)/U(k)`` taken at the excited bins; the mean over realisations is ``G_p``. Random phases are what make this converge: the distortion is uncorrelated with the input and averages away, while the linear part does not. Returns ``(G, scatter)``, each ``(n_freq, n_branches)`` -- the BLA and the standard error of its mean, so a caller can see whether ``n_realisations`` was enough. """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) N = int(round(duration_s / sampling_time_s)) fs = 1.0 / sampling_time_s t = np.arange(N) * sampling_time_s frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float) amplitudes = np.asarray(amplitudes, dtype=float) bins = np.round(frequencies * duration_s).astype(int) ratios = np.empty((n_realisations, frequencies.size, len(branches)), dtype=complex) for r in range(n_realisations): phases = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, frequencies.size) u = generate_multisine(t, frequencies, amplitudes, phases) U = np.fft.fft(u)[bins] for p, branch in enumerate(branches): ratios[r, :, p] = np.fft.fft(branch.apply(u, fs))[bins] / U G = ratios.mean(axis=0) scatter = ratios.std(axis=0, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n_realisations) return G, scatter frozen_impedance ¶ frozen_impedance(G, N) Z(f, t) = sum_p G_p(f) b_p(t) , shape (n_freq, N) . The time-varying transfer function a BLTVA of this system should return. Identical in form to the Legendre model, which is the point: a linear block-oriented system is exactly that model with a_p(f) = H_p(j2*pi*f) . Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py def frozen_impedance(G, N): """``Z(f, t) = sum_p G_p(f) b_p(t)``, shape ``(n_freq, N)``. The time-varying transfer function a BLTVA of this system should return. Identical in form to the Legendre model, which is the point: a *linear* block-oriented system is exactly that model with ``a_p(f) = H_p(j2*pi*f)``. """ G = np.atleast_2d(G) return G @ legendre_basis(N, G.shape[1] - 1).T

docs.text: Non-stationary R + (R_ct(t) || C) circuit, solved as a true time-varying ODE. A transistor T is placed in series with R_p inside the parallel branch: R_s ---+--- R_p --- T ---+ | | +------- C -------+ The transistor is modelled as a voltage-controlled resistance R_T(V_gate): V_gate >= V_on : R_T = 0 (fully conducting, short circuit) V_off < V_gate < V_on : R_T varies linearly from R_T_max to 0 V_gate <= V_off : R_T = R_T_max (fully blocking) Driving V_gate with a linear ramp makes the effective charge-transfer resistance R_ct(t) = R_p + R_T(V_gate(t)) change continuously, producing a physically motivated non-stationary system. This is the circuit of Breugelmans et al., Electrochim. Acta 76 (2012) 375, Fig. 7 -- the only model in this package that can be built on the bench as well as simulated. Frozen-time impedance versus true response The frozen-time (quasi-static) impedance Z(f, t) = R_s + R_ct(t) / (1 + j*2*pi*f * R_ct(t) * C) is the ground truth an estimator is supposed to recover, and it is returned as Z_true . It is not , however, the response the circuit actually produces. Because Z depends nonlinearly on R_ct(t), the quasi-static response is only an approximation of the governing equation, valid when R_ct varies slowly compared with the local time constant tau = R_ct*C. At realistic gate-ramp rates the two differ by on the order of 1% rms -- far above the numerical precision of the estimators under test, so the distinction matters. The voltage returned here is therefore obtained by integrating the circuit equation. Under galvanostatic excitation, with v_C the voltage across the parallel branch: i(t) = v_C/R_ct(t) + C * dv_C/dt => dv_C/dt = (i(t) - v_C/R_ct(t)) / C v(t) = R_s*i(t) + v_C(t) a scalar linear ODE with a time-varying coefficient, integrated with fixed-step RK4. voltage_quasistatic_V carries the frozen-time synthesis alongside it so the modelling error is directly observable. Contrast with legendre.py : there the frozen-time synthesis is algebraically exact , because the basis functions are real and the impedance is linear in them. Here it is not, which is precisely what makes this model useful for testing estimators against a system that does not satisfy their assumptions.

""" rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) N = int(round(duration_s / sampling_time_s)) dt = sampling_time_s t = np.arange(N) * dt frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies) amplitudes = np.asarray(amplitudes) phases = np.asarray(phases) def gate(tq): return V_gate_start + V_gate_rate * tq def r_ct(tq): return transistor_r_ct(gate(tq), R_p, R_T_max, V_off, V_on) V_gate_t = gate(t) R_ct_t = r_ct(t) tau_min = float(np.min(R_ct_t) * C) if dt > 0.1 * tau_min: warnings.warn( f"sampling_time_s={dt:.3g} is not small against the fastest circuit " f"time constant tau={tau_min:.3g}; the RK4 integration may be " "inaccurate. Reduce sampling_time_s.") # Noise-free current drives the circuit; measurement noise is added after. current_A = generate_multisine(t, frequencies, amplitudes, phases) current_half = generate_multisine(t + 0.5 * dt, frequencies, amplitudes, phases) R_ct_half = r_ct(t + 0.5 * dt) # Start from the quasi-static state, i.e. as if the circuit had already # been running. Starting from v_C = 0 would add a ~5*tau startup transient # that has nothing to do with the time variation under study. Zp0 = _parallel_impedance(frequencies, R_ct_t[0], C) v_C0 = float(np.sum(amplitudes * np.real(Zp0 * np.exp(1j * phases)))) v_C = _integrate_parallel_branch(dt, current_A, R_ct_t, current_half, R_ct_half, C, v_C0) voltage_V = R_s * current_A + v_C Z_true = impedance(frequencies, R_s, R_ct_t, C) voltage_quasistatic_V = synthesize_voltage(t, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, Z_true) if noise_std_V > 0: voltage_V = voltage_V + rng.normal(0.0, noise_std_V, N) if noise_std_A > 0: current_A = current_A + rng.normal(0.0, noise_std_A, N) return { 'time_s': t, 'voltage_V': voltage_V, 'current_A': current_A, 'Z_true': Z_true, 'frequencies_Hz': frequencies, 'voltage_quasistatic_V': voltage_quasistatic_V, 'R_s': R_s, 'R_p': R_p, 'C': C, 'V_gate_t': V_gate_t, 'R_ct_t': R_ct_t, }

docs.text: Legendre polynomial oracle model for non-stationary transfer function estimation. The transfer function at each excited frequency f_k is parameterised as a sum of Legendre polynomials in time up to order P: H(f_k, t) = sum_{p=0}^{P} a_p(f_k) * L_p(2*t/T - 1) where T is the total window length and L_p is the p-th Legendre polynomial. An additive voltage drift is modelled separately as its own Legendre expansion: v_drift(t) = sum_{q=0}^{Q} b_q * L_q(2*t/T - 1) This is exactly the signal model that BLTVA assumes, so the algorithm should recover the coefficients a_p and b_q exactly (up to noise). Use this model as an oracle test: if BLTVA fails to recover known coefficients, there is a bug. The voltage response is: v(t) = v_drift(t) + sum_k |H(f_k,t)| * A_k * cos(2*pi*f_k*t + phi_k + angle(H(f_k,t))) Specifying coefficients impedance_coefficients : array_like, shape (n_freq, P+1), complex a[k, p] is the coefficient of L_p for frequency f_k. a[k, 0] sets the mean impedance at f_k over the window. a[k, 1] sets a linear variation, a[k, 2] a quadratic one. drift_coefficients : array_like, shape (Q+1,), real, optional b[q] is the coefficient of L_q for the additive drift. Set to None for no drift (default).

docs.text: Block-oriented nonlinear time-varying systems, Hallemans TIM 2021 Section II. This is the system class the BLTVA is actually derived for: parallel branches, each a nonlinear time-invariant block followed by a time-varying gain (Fig. 2):: y(t) = sum_p NL_p{u(t)} * b_p(t) with each branch a Wiener-Hammerstein structure (Fig. 7):: y_p(t) = f2_p( L^-1{ H_p(s) L{ f1_p(u(t)) } } ) a static nonlinearity, an LTI filter, then another static nonlinearity. Choosing which of the two nonlinearities is the identity gives a Hammerstein branch, a Wiener branch, or a purely linear one. Why this model and not the frozen-time one legendre.py and r_rc_transistor.py both prescribe an impedance and synthesise a response from it. Neither can produce nonlinear distortion , so neither can exercise Section V, and neither has a ground truth for the best linear approximation beyond "the impedance we prescribed". Here the ground truth has to be computed, because the BLA of a nonlinear block is not its linear part. The static nonlinearities move it. The paper obtains it by averaging Y(k)/U(k) over many random phase realisations of the input, which is what :func: best_linear_approximation does. That gives a genuine target for H_p and, from the residuals, for the distortion variances. Filtering without an ODE solver f1_p(u) is a static function of a periodic multisine, so it is periodic with the same period, and so is the filter's steady-state response. Filtering in the DFT domain is therefore exact for the periodic steady state, needs no integrator, and no scipy:: Y(k) = H(j*2*pi*f_k) * X(k) The one thing it omits is the startup transient, which the paper models separately with the alpha_r polynomial rather than treating as signal. Use r_rc_transistor when the transient itself is the object of study.

docs.text: H(s) = dc_gain * wn**2 / (s**2 + 2*zeta*wn*s + wn**2) . wn is in rad/s . The paper quotes its natural frequencies in Hz ("wn,0 = 0.7 Hz") while naming them wn , which is ambiguous; use :meth: from_hz to be explicit about which you mean. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py @dataclass class SecondOrderLowpass: """``H(s) = dc_gain * wn**2 / (s**2 + 2*zeta*wn*s + wn**2)``. ``wn`` is in **rad/s**. The paper quotes its natural frequencies in Hz ("wn,0 = 0.7 Hz") while naming them ``wn``, which is ambiguous; use :meth:`from_hz` to be explicit about which you mean. """ wn: float zeta: float dc_gain: float = 1.0 @classmethod def from_hz(cls, f_n, zeta, dc_gain=1.0): return cls(2 * np.pi * f_n, zeta, dc_gain) def response(self, f): """``H(j*2*pi*f)``, conjugate-symmetric in ``f`` so the filtered signal comes back real.""" s = 2j * np.pi * np.asarray(f, dtype=float) return self.dc_gain * self.wn ** 2 / (s ** 2 + 2 * self.zeta * self.wn * s + self.wn ** 2)

docs.text: One parallel branch: f2( filter( f1(u) ) ) , scaled by b_p(t) . f1 and f2 default to the identity, so a branch is linear unless you say otherwise. name is only for reporting. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py @dataclass class Branch: """One parallel branch: ``f2( filter( f1(u) ) )``, scaled by ``b_p(t)``. ``f1`` and ``f2`` default to the identity, so a branch is linear unless you say otherwise. ``name`` is only for reporting. """ filter: SecondOrderLowpass f1: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] = field(default=lambda x: x) f2: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] = field(default=lambda x: x) name: str = "" @property def is_linear(self): probe = np.linspace(-2.0, 2.0, 41) return (np.allclose(self.f1(probe), probe) and np.allclose(self.f2(probe), probe)) def apply(self, u, fs): """Branch output before the time-varying gain.""" x = np.asarray(self.f1(np.asarray(u, dtype=float)), dtype=float) f = np.fft.fftfreq(x.size, 1.0 / fs) filtered = np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(x) * self.filter.response(f)).real return np.asarray(self.f2(filtered), dtype=float)

docs.text: hallemans_2021_system() The three branches of the simulation in Section VII, eq. (91d)-(91g). NL_0 is Wiener-Hammerstein (nonlinear either side of the filter), NL_1 Hammerstein (nonlinear before), NL_2 Wiener (nonlinear after). The distortion of each is weak -- the paper reports the variances at least 20 dB below the linear part -- which is the regime where a linear approximation is worth making at all. Natural frequencies are read as Hz, as printed. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py def hallemans_2021_system(): """The three branches of the simulation in Section VII, eq. (91d)-(91g). ``NL_0`` is Wiener-Hammerstein (nonlinear either side of the filter), ``NL_1`` Hammerstein (nonlinear before), ``NL_2`` Wiener (nonlinear after). The distortion of each is weak -- the paper reports the variances at least 20 dB below the linear part -- which is the regime where a linear approximation is worth making at all. Natural frequencies are read as Hz, as printed. """ return [ Branch(SecondOrderLowpass.from_hz(0.7, 0.15, 1.0), f1=lambda x: x + 0.02 * np.tanh(x - 2), f2=lambda x: x + 0.03 * np.tanh(x - 1), name="NL_0 Wiener-Hammerstein"), Branch(SecondOrderLowpass.from_hz(1.0, 0.10, 0.2), f1=lambda x: x + 0.08 * x ** 2, name="NL_1 Hammerstein"), Branch(SecondOrderLowpass.from_hz(1.5, 0.15, 0.2), f2=lambda x: x + 0.15 * x ** 3, name="NL_2 Wiener"), ]

docs.text: simulate_block_oriented(duration_s, sampling_time_s, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, branches, trend_coefficients=None, noise_std_V=0.0, noise_std_A=0.0, seed=None) Simulate y(t) = y_trend(t) + sum_p NL_p{u(t)} b_p(t) + v(t) . Mirrors eq. (90)-(91). Branch p is multiplied by the p -th Legendre basis function, so the branch list defines Np implicitly. Returns the usual time_s / voltage_V / current_A / frequencies_Hz plus H_linear -- the branch filters evaluated at the excited frequencies, shape (n_freq, n_branches) . That is the linear part , which equals the BLA only for a linear system; use :func: best_linear_approximation for the true target. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py def simulate_block_oriented(duration_s, sampling_time_s, frequencies, amplitudes, phases, branches, trend_coefficients=None, noise_std_V=0.0, noise_std_A=0.0, seed=None): """Simulate ``y(t) = y_trend(t) + sum_p NL_p{u(t)} b_p(t) + v(t)``. Mirrors eq. (90)-(91). Branch ``p`` is multiplied by the ``p``-th Legendre basis function, so the branch list defines ``Np`` implicitly. Returns the usual ``time_s``/``voltage_V``/``current_A``/``frequencies_Hz`` plus ``H_linear`` -- the branch filters evaluated at the excited frequencies, shape ``(n_freq, n_branches)``. That is the *linear part*, which equals the BLA only for a linear system; use :func:`best_linear_approximation` for the true target. """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) N = int(round(duration_s / sampling_time_s)) fs = 1.0 / sampling_time_s t = np.arange(N) * sampling_time_s frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float) current_A = generate_multisine(t, frequencies, np.asarray(amplitudes), np.asarray(phases)) b = legendre_basis(N, max(len(branches) - 1, 0)) voltage_V = np.zeros(N) for p, branch in enumerate(branches): voltage_V += branch.apply(current_A, fs) * b[:, p] drift_V = np.zeros(N) if trend_coefficients is not None: q = np.asarray(trend_coefficients, dtype=float) drift_V = legendre_basis(N, q.size - 1) @ q voltage_V = voltage_V + drift_V if noise_std_V > 0: voltage_V = voltage_V + rng.normal(0.0, noise_std_V, N) if noise_std_A > 0: current_A = current_A + rng.normal(0.0, noise_std_A, N) H_linear = np.stack([br.filter.response(frequencies) for br in branches], axis=1) return { 'time_s': t, 'voltage_V': voltage_V, 'current_A': current_A, 'frequencies_Hz': frequencies, 'H_linear': H_linear, 'drift_V': drift_V, 'branches': branches, }

docs.text: best_linear_approximation(branches, frequencies, amplitudes, sampling_time_s, duration_s, n_realisations=100, seed=None) Monte Carlo BLA of each branch, as the paper computes its ground truth. For every random phase realisation of the multisine, each branch is driven on its own and Y_p(k)/U(k) taken at the excited bins; the mean over realisations is G_p . Random phases are what make this converge: the distortion is uncorrelated with the input and averages away, while the linear part does not. Returns (G, scatter) , each (n_freq, n_branches) -- the BLA and the standard error of its mean, so a caller can see whether n_realisations was enough. Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py def best_linear_approximation(branches, frequencies, amplitudes, sampling_time_s, duration_s, n_realisations=100, seed=None): """Monte Carlo BLA of each branch, as the paper computes its ground truth. For every random phase realisation of the multisine, each branch is driven on its own and ``Y_p(k)/U(k)`` taken at the excited bins; the mean over realisations is ``G_p``. Random phases are what make this converge: the distortion is uncorrelated with the input and averages away, while the linear part does not. Returns ``(G, scatter)``, each ``(n_freq, n_branches)`` -- the BLA and the standard error of its mean, so a caller can see whether ``n_realisations`` was enough. """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) N = int(round(duration_s / sampling_time_s)) fs = 1.0 / sampling_time_s t = np.arange(N) * sampling_time_s frequencies = np.asarray(frequencies, dtype=float) amplitudes = np.asarray(amplitudes, dtype=float) bins = np.round(frequencies * duration_s).astype(int) ratios = np.empty((n_realisations, frequencies.size, len(branches)), dtype=complex) for r in range(n_realisations): phases = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, frequencies.size) u = generate_multisine(t, frequencies, amplitudes, phases) U = np.fft.fft(u)[bins] for p, branch in enumerate(branches): ratios[r, :, p] = np.fft.fft(branch.apply(u, fs))[bins] / U G = ratios.mean(axis=0) scatter = ratios.std(axis=0, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n_realisations) return G, scatter
docs.title: best_linear_approximation

docs.text: frozen_impedance(G, N) Z(f, t) = sum_p G_p(f) b_p(t) , shape (n_freq, N) . The time-varying transfer function a BLTVA of this system should return. Identical in form to the Legendre model, which is the point: a linear block-oriented system is exactly that model with a_p(f) = H_p(j2*pi*f) . Source code in src/deistools/simulation/models/block_oriented.py def frozen_impedance(G, N): """``Z(f, t) = sum_p G_p(f) b_p(t)``, shape ``(n_freq, N)``. The time-varying transfer function a BLTVA of this system should return. Identical in form to the Legendre model, which is the point: a *linear* block-oriented system is exactly that model with ``a_p(f) = H_p(j2*pi*f)``. """ G = np.atleast_2d(G) return G @ legendre_basis(N, G.shape[1] - 1).T

docs.text: Designing the excitation ¶ Most of what limits a time-varying impedance measurement is decided before any data exists. This page collects those decisions. Odd harmonics, with gaps ¶ The excitation used throughout this package is a multisine on odd harmonics of \(1/T_p\) , on a quasi-logarithmic grid : harmonics = np.array([1, 3, 5, 9, 13, 17, 27, 39, 59, 89, 133, 201, 301]) frequencies = harmonics / Tp # 0.05 ... 15.05 Hz for Tp = 20 s Three separate choices are bundled there. Logarithmic spacing , because that is how electrochemical features are distributed — a cell has decades of relevant behaviour, not a linear sweep of it. Fifteen tones over three decades is roughly what one acquisition can practically deliver. Odd harmonics , because even-order distortion then lands on even bins, which no tone occupies. You can measure it instead of guessing at it. This is exact, not approximate: in the block-oriented example, the branch whose nonlinearity is \(x + 0.08x^2\) — an even function — shifts the best linear approximation by \(10^{-16}\) , machine zero, at every drive amplitude. An even nonlinearity driven by odd harmonics simply cannot reach an excited bin. Gaps , because odd-order distortion lands on the odd harmonics you skipped. With a sparse grid, most harmonic bins are free, and their level is a direct measurement of how far from linear the cell is. Where the distortion goes In example 03, of the harmonic bins up to \(1.5 \times h_{\max}\) : 13 are excited, 212 are unexcited odd, 225 unexcited even. The unexcited bins sit about \(10^{-4}\) of the excited level, which is the distortion floor of that system. Left: the voltage spectrum, with excited tones, unexcited odd bins and unexcited even bins marked separately. The gaps in the grid are what make the distortion measurable. Whole periods ¶ The record must hold an integer number of multisine periods . A fractional period leaks each spectral line into its neighbours, and that leakage is mathematically the same shape as the skirt produced by genuine time variation. No method can separate them. bltva refuses a non-integer record. STFT and DMFA will not complain, so trim the record yourself. How many periods, \(P\) ¶ This is the decision that sets everything else for BLTVA, because the model orders share a budget fixed by \(P\) : \[ N_q + 3N_p + N_a + 1 \;<\; 2P - 1 \] with \(N_a\) itself determined by \(P\) and \(N_p\) . Substituting one into the other leaves \(N_p < 0.625P - 4\) at fixed \(N_q\) , so the number of periods caps the model order, and the model order caps how fast a variation can be followed. Measuring longer helps, but with diminishing returns: the record grows linearly in \(P\) while the affordable \(N_p\) grows more slowly, so the ratio converges. eq. (49) is necessary, not sufficient A configuration can satisfy the inequality and still be refused, because Algorithm 1 estimates the noise from a sliding band that needs strictly more equations than regressors. On a 6-period record, \(N_p = 2\) with \(N_q = 2\) passes eq. (49) and is then rejected with exactly 10 regressors for 10 equations. See implementation notes . Amplitude ¶ Two effects pull in opposite directions: Too small and the response is noise-limited, particularly at the top of the grid where \(|Z|\) is smallest. Too large and the cell distorts, which moves the best linear approximation — the target itself — as shown in when is \(Z(f,t)\) meaningful . There is therefore a minimum total error at a finite amplitude, neither the smallest nor the largest you can apply. If you use BLTVA with harmonics="all_nl" , its SNDR tells you which side of that minimum you are on. Choosing the frequency range ¶ Put the grid where the cell responds. Two checks: Bracket the feature you care about. For an \(R\|C\) arc the apex sits at \(f = 1/(2\pi R_{ct}C)\) ; a grid that stops below it gives a fragment of a semicircle that an equivalent-circuit fit will happily misinterpret. Do not extend past where the response has rolled off. In the block-oriented example the branch filters roll off near 1 Hz, so by 15 Hz \(|G_0|\) has fallen by a factor of 1484 and the relative error there is measuring the signal-to-noise ratio, not the estimator. Raising the lowest frequency is also the only way to shorten the time-resolution floor in seconds, so the grid and the tracking speed are the same decision.

docs.text: The signal model ¶ This package sits between two fields that use different words for the same things. Electrochemistry speaks of impedance, cells and spectra; system theory speaks of transfer functions, plants and frequency responses. The code and the source papers use the system-theory vocabulary, so this page gives the translation first. Notation ¶ symbol meaning notes \(u(t)\) , \(y(t)\) excitation and response here current and voltage, so \(Z = Y/U\) \(Z(f,t)\) the time-varying impedance the quantity every estimator tries to recover \(f_k\) the \(k\) -th excited frequency Hz \(T_p\) period of the multisine s; \(f_{\min} = 1/T_p\) \(P\) number of periods in the record the single most consequential choice \(N\) samples in the record \(N = P \cdot f_s T_p\) \(T\) record duration \(T = N/f_s = P \cdot T_p\) \(f_s\) sampling rate Hz \(k\) DFT bin index bins are \(1/T\) apart \(h\) harmonic number tone \(h\) sits at bin \(h \cdot P\) \(b_p(t)\) the \(p\) -th Legendre basis function \(b_p(t) = L_p(2t/T - 1)\) \(H_p(f)\) the \(p\) -th coefficient of \(Z(f,t)\) what BLTVA estimates \(N_p\) order of the Legendre expansion how much time structure the model can express \(N_q\) order of the trend polynomial at DC how much drift it can absorb \(N_a\) order of the transient polynomial per band chosen automatically A note on \(h\) versus \(k\) that causes real confusion: bltva takes harmonic numbers , not frequencies and not bin indices. Harmonic \(h\) of a \(P\) -period record occupies DFT bin \(h \cdot P\) . So \(f_{\min}\) , one harmonic, is \(P\) bins wide in the spectrum — a fact that matters when choosing bandwidths and band widths. The model ¶ A time-invariant system has one transfer function. A time-varying one does not, and the model this package uses expands it in time: \[ Z(f, t) \;=\; \sum_{p=0}^{N_p} H_p(f)\, b_p(t) \] with \(b_p\) the Legendre polynomials on the record, rescaled so that \(b_p(t) = L_p(2t/T - 1)\) . Two properties make this a convenient basis rather than an arbitrary one: \(b_0 \equiv 1\) , and every higher order has zero mean . So \(H_0(f)\) is the time-averaged impedance — the best stationary approximation of a cell that was not stationary — and every higher coefficient describes only change. The basis functions are real . That is what makes the frozen-time synthesis exact for a linear time-varying system: because \(b_p(t)\) is real, the sum over \(p\) and the sum over excited tones commute, so evaluating the stationary formula at each instant gives the same answer as the full time-varying convolution. This is why simulate_legendre can produce an exactly-known time-varying ground truth without integrating anything. The convention has to be shared The simulator and the estimator import the same legendre_basis from deistools.processing.bltva . If they used different mean-removal conventions, a comparison between them would measure the convention and not the estimator. See conventions . Skirts ¶ This is the idea everything in the frequency domain rests on. For a stationary system, a periodic excitation produces a response concentrated entirely on the excited DFT bins. Nothing lands in between. For a time-varying system, the response at each tone is modulated by \(Z(f_k, t)\) . Middle: each voltage tone has grown skirts, while the current tones have none. Right: the impedance at a series of instants, blue to red. Band width sets the time resolution BLTVA frequency fits a model of the skirts, band by band, and returns the coefficients \(H_p\) The three differ in what they assume, which is the subject of the Methods pages.

docs.text: This package sits between two fields that use different words for the same things. Electrochemistry speaks of impedance, cells and spectra; system theory speaks of transfer functions, plants and frequency responses. The code and the source papers use the system-theory vocabulary, so this page gives the translation first.

docs.title: Notation

docs.text: A time-invariant system has one transfer function. A time-varying one does not, and the model this package uses expands it in time: \[ Z(f, t) \;=\; \sum_{p=0}^{N_p} H_p(f)\, b_p(t) \] with \(b_p\) the Legendre polynomials on the record, rescaled so that \(b_p(t) = L_p(2t/T - 1)\) . Two properties make this a convenient basis rather than an arbitrary one: \(b_0 \equiv 1\) , and every higher order has zero mean . So \(H_0(f)\) is the time-averaged impedance — the best stationary approximation of a cell that was not stationary — and every higher coefficient describes only change. The basis functions are real . That is what makes the frozen-time synthesis exact for a linear time-varying system: because \(b_p(t)\) is real, the sum over \(p\) and the sum over excited tones commute, so evaluating the stationary formula at each instant gives the same answer as the full time-varying convolution. This is why simulate_legendre can produce an exactly-known time-varying ground truth without integrating anything. The convention has to be shared The simulator and the estimator import the same legendre_basis from deistools.processing.bltva . If they used different mean-removal conventions, a comparison between them would measure the convention and not the estimator. See conventions .
