docs.text: When is \(Z(f,t)\) meaningful? ¶ Before asking which estimator to use, it is worth asking whether the quantity they all estimate exists for your system. Two conditions have to hold, and both can be checked. 1. The system must change slowly compared with its own dynamics ¶ "The impedance at time \(t\) " means: the impedance the cell would have if it were frozen in the state it is in at time \(t\) . This is the frozen-time or quasi-static impedance, and it is an approximation to what a time-varying system actually does. The approximation is good when the system changes little during one of its own time constants. For an \(R_s + (R_{ct}\|C)\) cell the useful dimensionless measure is \[ \frac{\Delta R_{ct}}{R_{ct}} \quad\text{per time constant } \tau = R_{ct}C \] In the transistor example the gate ramp changes \(R_{ct}\) by 0.016 % of itself per time constant, and the frozen-time synthesis then differs from the true ODE solution by 0.014 % rms — the two agree, as they should. The practical consequence: if your cell changes appreciably within one \(RC\) time, no estimator here is wrong so much as answering a question that does not have an answer. The output will still look reasonable. You can check this on your own system simulate_r_rc_transistor returns both voltage_V (the integrated ODE) and voltage_quasistatic_V (the frozen-time synthesis). The rms difference between them is the size of the approximation at your ramp rate. Example 01 does exactly this. Left: the two responses over the first two periods, indistinguishable at this scale. Right: their difference, 0.014 % rms. 2. The system must be close enough to linear ¶ A nonlinear system has no transfer function at all. What an estimator returns is then a best linear approximation (BLA): the transfer function a linear model converges to under that particular excitation , at that particular amplitude. This is not a technicality. In the block-oriented example, doubling the drive moves the ground truth by \(3.2\times10^{-5}\) relative, against a best estimator error of \(9.4\times10^{-5}\) — a factor of three apart. At four times the drive the shift overtakes the estimator error, because it grows with amplitude while the estimator error does not. So: An impedance reported without its excitation amplitude is incomplete whenever the cell is not strictly linear. Results are comparable only at fixed drive. BLTVA can measure how much of its residual is distortion rather than noise. See distortion . The time-resolution floor ¶ Even when both conditions hold, there is a limit on how finely time can be resolved, and it differs by method: method finest resolution set by STFT one multisine period the lowest tone must fit in the window DMFA \(\approx 1/\mathrm{bandwidth}\) capped by the spacing of your tones BLTVA no fixed instant grid the model order affordable at your \(P\) STFT's floor is hard: nothing recovers detail finer than one period of the lowest tone. DMFA's is set by how wide a band the filter can take before it reaches the neighbouring tone, which is a property of your frequency grid rather than of the method. BLTVA returns a continuous function of time, so its limit is the finest feature a polynomial of the affordable order can describe. All three therefore push in the same direction: if you need fine time resolution, raise your lowest frequency. A 10 mHz tone fixes STFT's resolution at 100 s whatever else you do. The bottom decade is always the worst ¶ In every comparison in this package, on every system, the largest relative errors sit at the lowest frequencies. The cause is shared, even though the mechanism differs by method. What matters is how many cycles of a tone fit inside the time the cell takes to change. In the transistor example the 0.05 Hz tone completes 20 cycles over the whole variation while the 15 Hz tone completes 6020. The low tone is being asked to measure an impedance that changes noticeably within a single period of itself. If you fit an equivalent circuit to a time-varying spectrum, weight the bottom decade accordingly.

docs.text: Implementation notes ¶ The papers this package implements leave some things ambiguous, and in a few places this code makes a choice they do not dictate. Those choices change the numbers, so they are recorded here with the evidence rather than left in the source for a reader to reverse-engineer. This section exists because the package crosses electrochemistry and system theory, where a reader is likely to be expert in one and not the other. If you are going to cite a result from DEIStools, these are the pages to read first. What is on these pages ¶ BLTVA — the ambiguous reading of the rank threshold, why the solver deliberately does not equilibrate, the Legendre basis convention, why eq. (49) is necessary but not sufficient, and why \(N_p\) and the band width compete. DMFA — the local filter axis, the edge artefact, and the current verification status. BLA — where the frequency derivatives of eq. (15) come from, and why the central differences of step 3 cannot be transcribed onto a quasi-logarithmic grid: 156× on the first derivative, and a second-difference formula that diverges under refinement. Includes the replacement. How to read a claim here ¶ Every entry states what was tested and what the number was. Where a choice was made between two readings of a paper, both were implemented and measured; the one that is used is the one that was unbiased, not the one that looked plausible. Where something is not verified, it says so. The DMFA page is mostly such a statement at present, and the BLA page is a design note for work not yet done rather than a record of work finished -- it says so at the end. A general convention ¶ Where a paper gives a rule and this package also allows a manual override, the rule is the default and the override exists because real frequency grids are not always what the papers assumed. Two cases: quantity paper rule override why the override exists \(N_a\) eq. (22) of the 2022 paper Na= none needed in practice; the rule beat a hand-picked value by 19× band width eq. (55) of the 2021 paper band_halfwidth= the rule produces enormous bands at the top of a sparse quasi-log grid The papers use linearly spaced odd harmonics. Electrochemistry uses logarithmic grids with fifteen tones over three decades. Several rules that are natural on the first are impractical on the second, and where that is the case it is noted on the method's page. The sharpest instance is on the BLA page : a numerical differentiation that is second-order accurate on an equispaced grid is not merely less accurate on a logarithmic one but, for the second derivative, inconsistent -- its error grows as the grid is refined. The grid this package uses throughout is 1 3 5 9 13 17 27 39 59 89 133 201 301 whose gaps between neighbouring tones span a factor of 50.

docs.text: BLA implementation notes ¶ Why step 3 of Pintelon 2013 is not transcribed ¶ The per-burst estimator on the BLA page stops short of the full three-step procedure of Pintelon, Louarroudi and Lataire ( IEEE TIM 62 (2013) 3361, §V-B). Steps 1 and 2 transcribe directly. Step 3 does not, and the obstruction is this package's frequency grid rather than anything about the method. This page records why, with the numbers, because it decides how roadmap item 2b has to be built. Where the derivatives come from ¶ The time variation is carried by polynomial basis functions, \(G(s,t) = \sum_p G_p(s) f_p(t)\) with \(f_p\) of degree \(p\) . Theorem 2 of the 2012 companion paper rewrites that single-input time- varying system as a multiple-input time- invariant one whose inputs are \(u(t) f_p(t)\) . The bridge is the Laplace duality \[ \mathcal{L}\{t\,x(t)\} = -X'(s) \] Multiplying by \(t\) in the time domain is differentiating with respect to \(s\) in the Laplace domain. So trading the \(f_p(t)\) factors for extra inputs turns powers of \(t\) into \(s\) -derivatives, and they survive into the relation between the BLTI approximation and the branch transfer functions (eq. 15): \[ G_\text{BLTI}(s) = H_0(s) + \frac{2}{T}\sum_{p} H^{(1)}_{2p+1}(s) + \frac{4}{T^2}\sum_{p} \beta_{2p} H^{(2)}_{2p}(s) + O(T^{-3}) \] Those are derivatives along the frequency axis , of quantities known only as samples, so they have to be computed numerically. Eq. (27) does it with central differences between neighbouring excited harmonics — and that is the step that carries Assumption 3's requirement that the excited harmonics be equispaced. Two separate things go wrong without it ¶ This package's grid is 1, 3, 5, 9, 13, 17, 27, 39, 59, 89, 133, 201, 301, so the gaps between neighbouring excited harmonics are 2 2 4 4 4 10 12 20 30 44 68 100 a 50× spread . Both failure modes below are measured on an R+RC impedance standing in for \(H_p\) , whose derivatives are analytic. The step size ¶ A central difference carries \(O(h^2)\) truncation error. Symmetric stencil, widened: half-span relative error ±2 harmonics 1.18e-04 ±4 4.74e-04 ±10 2.97e-03 ±30 2.69e-02 ±100 3.14e-01 2661× over a 50× span, which is \(h^2\) to within the fit. The top of a quasi-log grid sits in the last row. The asymmetry ¶ The \(O(h^2)\) accuracy exists because the odd-order Taylor terms cancel, and that cancellation needs equal distance either side. Unequal spacing puts a term in \(f'\) back. For the first derivative this costs an order of accuracy. For the second derivative — which the \(O(T^{-2})\) term of eq. (15) needs — the three-point formula written for a symmetric stencil is not merely less accurate, it is inconsistent . Fixed 1:2 asymmetry, stencil halved each row: \(a\) \(b\) formula as written proper unequal-spacing weights 40 80 1.07 1.31e-01 20 40 2.01 8.37e-02 10 20 4.02 4.77e-02 5 10 8.09 2.55e-02 2.5 5 1.62e+01 1.32e-02 1.25 2.5 3.26e+01 6.69e-03 The error doubles every time the stencil is refined . The leading term is \((b-a)f'/h^2 \sim f'/h\) , so it diverges as \(h \to 0\) : refining the grid makes it worse. The proper weights converge at \(O(h)\) , as they should. At the gap ratios this package's grid actually has: left right formula as written proper weights 30 30 2.69e-02 2.69e-02 30 44 9.59e-01 4.74e-02 44 68 7.53e-01 7.20e-02 68 100 5.18e-01 1.08e-01 Equal spacing is the only row where the two agree, which is the point. A 30/44 ratio — the gap pattern around harmonic 89 — already gives a 96% error. What it costs here ¶ First derivative, over the whole grid: grid median error worst quasi-log (this package) 5.5e-02 8.1e-02 at \(h = 133\) equispaced, same tone count 3.5e-04 3.6e-04 equispaced, denser 3.1e-04 3.6e-04 156× on the median. Per harmonic: harmonic stencil span relative error 3 4 3.6e-04 5 6 1.9e-02 9 8 1.4e-03 17 14 5.5e-02 39 32 6.4e-02 89 74 7.2e-02 133 112 8.1e-02 201 168 6.3e-02 It is not monotone, and that is worse than if it were Harmonic 5 (span 6) is 13× worse than harmonic 9 (span 8), despite the narrower stencil. The step-size error and the asymmetry error have independent signs and partially cancel at some tones. So the damage is unpredictable per tone rather than simply growing with the gap, which rules out correcting it with a rule of thumb. Since the correction is itself the \(O(T^{-1})\) term, computing it to 5–8% still beats using \(H_0\) alone — but it does not deliver the \(O(T^{-2})\) the construction promises, and the \(O(T^{-2})\) term is unusable outright. The route that does work ¶ Do not difference at all. The local polynomial method already fits a polynomial in the frequency index over a band of consecutive DFT bins, \[ H(k+r) = \sum_{s=0}^{R} g_s\, r^s \] and those \(g_s\) are Taylor coefficients. With \(\Delta\omega\) the spacing of one DFT bin, \[ H' = \frac{g_1}{\Delta\omega}, \qquad H'' = \frac{2 g_2}{\Delta\omega^2} \] The fit runs over consecutive bins , which are equispaced by construction whatever the tones do, so the grid stops mattering. The \(H_p\) for \(p \ge 1\) are estimated at the non-excited bins in step 1 anyway, so the dense samples are already there. Recovered from a noiseless fit: band half-width order \(R\) \(dH/ds\) \(d^2H/ds^2\) 5 2 8.6e-05 1.2e-04 5 3 4.5e-09 1.2e-04 5 4 4.5e-09 8.1e-09 10 3 6.6e-08 4.5e-04 10 4 6.6e-08 1.2e-07 20 4 9.8e-07 1.9e-06 Note the parity: \(R = 3\) fixes the first derivative and leaves the second where \(R = 2\) had it; the second needs \(R = 4\) . Adding an odd-order term removes the next even remainder and vice versa. Pintelon 2012 already requires \(R \ge 2\) for this correction, so raising it to 4 is a small change. That table is noiseless It isolates the approximation error. With noise, a narrow band and a high order inflate the variance — the usual LPM bias/variance trade, which the LPM's own residuals quantify. The orders above are therefore a starting point, not a recommendation. This is also why "use adjacent DFT bins in the difference instead" is not the fix it looks like. Adjacent LPM estimates share most of their data, so the difference between them is dominated by correlated estimation error rather than by the derivative. Reading the fitted coefficients avoids that; differencing the fitted outputs does not. Status ¶ Nothing on this page is implemented. It is the design note for roadmap item 2b, recorded now because the measurements were made while deciding whether step 3 could be transcribed as published. It cannot, on this grid, and the replacement is specific enough to build from. The numbers here are properties of the numerical scheme and the grid, not of package code, so unlike the rest of these notes they are not pinned by tests — there is nothing yet to pin. They are reproducible from the published formulas and the grid in the general convention .

A 30/44 ratio — the gap pattern around harmonic 89 — already gives a 96% error.
docs.title: The asymmetry

docs.text: First derivative, over the whole grid: grid median error worst quasi-log (this package) 5.5e-02 8.1e-02 at \(h = 133\) equispaced, same tone count 3.5e-04 3.6e-04 equispaced, denser 3.1e-04 3.6e-04 156× on the median. Per harmonic: harmonic stencil span relative error 3 4 3.6e-04 5 6 1.9e-02 9 8 1.4e-03 17 14 5.5e-02 39 32 6.4e-02 89 74 7.2e-02 133 112 8.1e-02 201 168 6.3e-02 It is not monotone, and that is worse than if it were Harmonic 5 (span 6) is 13× worse than harmonic 9 (span 8), despite the narrower stencil. The step-size error and the asymmetry error have independent signs and partially cancel at some tones. So the damage is unpredictable per tone rather than simply growing with the gap, which rules out correcting it with a rule of thumb. Since the correction is itself the \(O(T^{-1})\) term, computing it to 5–8% still beats using \(H_0\) alone — but it does not deliver the \(O(T^{-2})\) the construction promises, and the \(O(T^{-2})\) term is unusable outright.
docs.title: What it costs here

docs.text: Do not difference at all. The local polynomial method already fits a polynomial in the frequency index over a band of consecutive DFT bins, \[ H(k+r) = \sum_{s=0}^{R} g_s\, r^s \] and those \(g_s\) are Taylor coefficients. With \(\Delta\omega\) the spacing of one DFT bin, \[ H' = \frac{g_1}{\Delta\omega}, \qquad H'' = \frac{2 g_2}{\Delta\omega^2} \] The fit runs over consecutive bins , which are equispaced by construction whatever the tones do, so the grid stops mattering. The \(H_p\) for \(p \ge 1\) are estimated at the non-excited bins in step 1 anyway, so the dense samples are already there. Recovered from a noiseless fit: band half-width order \(R\) \(dH/ds\) \(d^2H/ds^2\) 5 2 8.6e-05 1.2e-04 5 3 4.5e-09 1.2e-04 5 4 4.5e-09 8.1e-09 10 3 6.6e-08 4.5e-04 10 4 6.6e-08 1.2e-07 20 4 9.8e-07 1.9e-06 Note the parity: \(R = 3\) fixes the first derivative and leaves the second where \(R = 2\) had it; the second needs \(R = 4\) . Adding an odd-order term removes the next even remainder and vice versa. Pintelon 2012 already requires \(R \ge 2\) for this correction, so raising it to 4 is a small change. That table is noiseless It isolates the approximation error. With noise, a narrow band and a high order inflate the variance — the usual LPM bias/variance trade, which the LPM's own residuals quantify. The orders above are therefore a starting point, not a recommendation. This is also why "use adjacent DFT bins in the difference instead" is not the fix it looks like. Adjacent LPM estimates share most of their data, so the difference between them is dominated by correlated estimation error rather than by the derivative. Reading the fitted coefficients avoids that; differencing the fitted outputs does not.

docs.text: BLTVA implementation notes ¶ The rank threshold in eq. (53) is ambiguous ¶ Algorithm 1 truncates the residual used for the noise-variance estimate at a rank determined by a threshold. The paper prints the threshold in a form that reads as \(a \cdot \mathrm{snr}\) , which always truncates at \(m = 1\) — the threshold is met immediately and nothing is retained. Both readings were implemented and tested against a known noise level: reading estimated / true noise variance \(a \cdot \mathrm{snr}\) 1.86 – 5.81 \(1 / (a \cdot \mathrm{snr})\) 0.97 – 0.98 The reciprocal reading is unbiased, so that is what the code uses. The choice is pinned by test_rank_threshold_is_unbiased , so a future change that reverts it will fail the test suite rather than silently shift every noise estimate. The band solver deliberately does not equilibrate ¶ Column equilibration is the obvious conditioning improvement for a least-squares problem whose regressors have wildly different scales, and an earlier version of this code did it. It is wrong here, and subtly so. Algorithm 2 step 6 prunes coefficients whose magnitude falls below the noise floor. With equilibration, collinear columns that cancel against one another produce coefficients of order \(10^{10}\) — which are never below any threshold, so pruning never fires . The fit then keeps every regressor it was given, including the ones the data does not support. Using the plain minimum-norm solution instead gives \(|\theta| \approx 10^{-10}\) for the same columns, and all five spurious drift columns are pruned, with an identical residual. So _solve_band uses np.linalg.lstsq without equilibration, on purpose. The pruning behaviour described in BLTVA § pruning depends on it. The Legendre basis convention ¶ legendre_basis mean-removes every column of order \(p \ge 1\) , as the 2021 paper prescribes after eq. (26). That is what makes \(H_0\) the time-averaged impedance. The simulators import the same function from deistools.processing.bltva rather than building their own basis. This is not tidiness: when simulate_legendre used a raw legvander while the estimator mean-removed, the apparent error floor of an exact-recovery test sat at \(2\times10^{-5}\) — entirely a convention mismatch. Sharing the function moved it to \(10^{-7}\) . If you write a new simulator, import that basis. eq. (49) is necessary, not sufficient ¶ The identifiability bound \[ N_q + 3N_p + N_a + 1 \;<\; 2P - 1 \] counts the parameters a band must support. check_identifiability enforces it. But Algorithm 1 estimates the noise variance from a sliding band , and that band needs strictly more equations than regressors. On a short record it can fail first. On a 6-period record, \(N_p = 2\) with \(N_q = 2\) satisfies eq. (49) and is then refused: ValueError: noise band at bin 6: 10 equations for 10 regressors. The practical ceiling on 6 periods is \(N_p = 1\) with \(N_q \le 1\) . If BLTVA refuses a configuration the inequality admits, this is usually why. Lower \(N_q\) before lowering \(N_p\) . \(N_p\) and the band width compete for \(N_a\) ¶ The interaction documented on the BLTVA page has a specific cause, and it is not the one that first suggests itself. It is not ill-conditioning. Measured across the band width at \(N_p = 8\) , the per-band condition number improves as the band widens — 148 at halfwidth 50 down to 25 at halfwidth 400 — while the error gets worse. The diagnostics say what is actually happening: band bins skirt centres parameters pruned residual 50 70 1 29 7 2.20e-06 100 120 2 38 6 3.03e-06 200 220 3 47 3 1.73e-05 400 420 5 65 0 5.71e-05 Two things happen together. More skirt centres fall inside a wider band, each bringing its own block of \(N_p + 1\) regressors. And the residual rises by 26× — the model fits the band worse despite having more than twice the parameters, which means it is mis-specified rather than over-fitted. The culprit is \(N_a\) . eq. (22) sets \[ N_a = \left\lfloor 3P/4 \right\rfloor - N_p - d + 1 \] so the budget spent on \(N_p\) comes straight out of the transient polynomial: \(N_a = 13\) at \(N_p = 3\) , but only \(8\) at \(N_p = 8\) . That polynomial has to describe the smooth out-of-band background across the whole band. Over 70 bins an order-8 polynomial is ample; over 420 bins it is stretched far too thin. Hence: raise \(N_p\) and you must narrow the band. Why band_halfwidth exists at all ¶ The eq. (55) rule builds a band spanning three consecutive excited frequencies, which is right and well-motivated: it parameterises both immediate neighbours explicitly, so the nearest unmodelled skirt sits two spacings away and is flat enough for the transient polynomial to absorb honestly. On a linearly spaced odd grid, as the papers use, those bands are modest. On a quasi-logarithmic grid with 13 tones over 2.5 decades, the spacing at the top is enormous and the rule produces a band of about 5360 bins — roughly 268 harmonics. The package warns when that happens. band_halfwidth overrides the rule with a fixed number of bins. It is also more robust where the grid spacing changes abruptly. A correction to an earlier claim An earlier draft of this analysis stated that the neighbour rule degrades by 100× on logarithmic grids. That was wrong — it was an artefact of a buggy test helper that emitted adjacent harmonics. The real failure mode is an abrupt change in spacing, which is what test_neighbour_rule_degrades_on_abrupt_spacing_change pins.

docs.text: DMFA implementation notes ¶ Verification status The definition and the filter have now been checked line by line against Battistel et al. (2016), Koster et al. (2017) and Battistel and La Mantia (2019), and both match — see below. What is still open is an end-to-end comparison against an independent implementation on the same data. One finding from that check is a caveat the papers do not state: the mirroring they recommend for non-periodic records must not be applied to a random-phase multisine . See below . Which definition is implemented ¶ Three definitions appear in this literature, and they are not equivalent. Battistel 2016, eq. (11) writes the dynamic impedance as the stationary ratio times a correction, \[ Z_k(t) = \frac{V_k}{I_k}\left\{1 - \sum_{l=1}^{bw} \left[\frac{I_{k,l}}{I_k}e^{\,2\pi \mathrm{j} l \Delta f t} + \frac{I_{k,l}}{I_k}e^{-2\pi \mathrm{j} l \Delta f t}\right]\right\} \] This is a first-order expansion , valid only while the skirt is small against its carrier. The odd look of it — a series that has to be truncated, with the truncation doubling as the bandwidth — is real, and it is why the later papers replaced it. Koster 2017, eq. (9) is the clean statement: the ratio of two filtered inverse transforms, with no expansion and no smallness assumption. This is what DEIStools implements , and it is the current definition. Battistel 2019, eq. (4) goes further and gives the physical definition via a Volterra series, against which both heuristics can be judged. It is a reference point rather than an algorithm; the paper finds DMFA within about 1% of it at the lowest frequency and below 0.1% at the highest. So: the calculation that looked odd was the 2016 one, and it is not the one in this package. The filter matches the published one up to a constant ¶ create_fermi_dirac_fun evaluates \[ \tilde g = \frac{\cosh n}{\cosh n + \cosh (n x)}, \qquad x = \frac{f - f_c}{bw} \] while Battistel 2019 eq. (12) and Chukwu 2022 eq. (3) specify the product of two Fermi-Dirac functions, which simplifies exactly to \[ \tilde g_{\text{paper}} = \frac{\cosh n + 1}{\cosh n + \cosh (n x)} \] Checked numerically: the two agree in shape to 1e-14, and their ratio is the frequency-independent constant \[ \frac{\tilde g_{\text{DEIStools}}}{\tilde g_{\text{paper}}} = \frac{\cosh n}{\cosh n + 1} = 0.999329524658 \quad (n = 8) \] Since DMFA divides voltage by current through the same filter, the constant cancels exactly and the impedance is unaffected. The only consequence is that the DEIStools filter has gain 0.99933 at the centre rather than 1, which matters if you use the filter for anything that is not a ratio. Both conventions put \(\tilde g = 1/2\) at \(x = \pm 1\) , so bw means the same thing in both: the half-amplitude half-width. The one-sided extraction is correct ¶ The papers stress that \(\tilde g\) is a quadrature filter, defined only for positive frequencies, because that is what makes the inverse transform the analytic signal — the complex envelope — rather than a real band-limited signal. extract_impedance takes a block of bins around \(+f_k\) only and never the mirror at \(-f_k\) , so the output is inherently one-sided. That is correct and deliberate. The resulting factor of \(1/2\) (a real cosine carries half its energy on each side) cancels in the ratio, as does the Npts_elab scaling. Block extraction is a controlled approximation ¶ Here DEIStools departs from the papers' procedure, for cost. The papers filter the whole spectrum and inverse-transform at full length; extract_impedance takes only Npts_elab bins around each tone and inverse-transforms those. That is equivalent to filtering the full spectrum with a filter forced to zero outside the block, so the two agree only to the extent that the filter has already decayed at the block edge. Measured on the transistor record at bw = 0.5 f_min , n = 2 : block width filter value at the edge difference from full-spectrum filtering (median / worst) 4 bandwidths 1.2e-01 1.1e-03 / 2.3e-02 8 bandwidths 2.5e-03 1.5e-05 / 2.6e-03 16 bandwidths 8.5e-07 4.5e-09 / 9.2e-07 The error tracks the edge value almost exactly, as it should. Use at least 16 bandwidths The examples size the block at 8 bandwidths, which with a soft filter ( n = 2 ) leaves a worst-case 2.6e-03 — the same order as the method's own error. Sixteen costs nothing but arithmetic and puts the truncation at 1e-09. A sharper filter needs a narrower block; the rule is to extend the block until the filter has fallen below about 1e-06. Mirroring must not be used with a random-phase multisine ¶ Battistel 2019 §3.1 recommends mirroring a non-periodic record about its last point, doubling its length, to suppress the Gibbs skirt. Applied to a random-phase multisine it is destructive , and badly so. Mirroring reflects the record in time. For a tone \(\cos(\omega t + \varphi)\) occupying a whole number of periods, the reflection is \(\cos(\omega t - \varphi)\) : the cosine part is even and survives, but the sine part is folded into \(\sin(\omega|t|)\) , which has a derivative kink at the seam and therefore a broadband spectrum. The scattered energy lands in every extraction band. Measured on the standard 13-tone grid: record off-bin / on-bin energy original 1.1e-24 mirrored, phases all zero 6.2e-04 mirrored, random phases 1.5e+00 With random phases the multisine scatters more energy off its bins than it leaves on them. The end-to-end effect on the impedance is what you would expect: worst error, edges included plain 4.1e-01 mirrored 7.5e+00 The paper's own case is different: their multisine was periodic and it was the cyclic voltammetry that was not, so mirroring fixed the dc skirt without touching the tones. The technique is sound there and wrong here. Conclusion: discard the edges. It is the robust answer, it costs a fixed fraction of the record, and it is what the examples do. If you need the edges, the lock-in filters in the time domain, where the boundary can be reflected on the smooth baseband envelope instead of being wrapped around by a circular DFT. Is the Fermi-Dirac filter the right choice? No. ¶ The Fermi-Dirac distribution comes from statistical physics, not from signal processing, and the natural question is whether a standard DSP window does better. It does. Scored against known ground truth, the published filter comes last of seven , and the best standard window is about twice as good on the worst case. This corrects an earlier conclusion on this page A first comparison here tested only the raised-cosine (Tukey) family and reported that the Fermi-Dirac won. That comparison was incomplete: the cosine-sum windows — Blackman, Blackman-Harris, Nuttall — and Kaiser were not in it, and they are the ones that beat it. The table below supersedes it. What the filter actually does to the result ¶ In a galvanostatic measurement the current is the excitation: exactly periodic, so its envelope is constant and the filter merely scales it. All the time variation sits in the voltage. The consequence is that \[ Z_{\text{measured}}(f_k, t) \;\approx\; \frac{\big(\tilde g * Z\big)(f_k, t)}{\tilde g(0)} \] — the reported impedance is the true \(Z(f_k,t)\) convolved with the filter's time-domain kernel . So the filter's frequency response is, directly, the transfer function applied to the time variation, and its time-domain sidelobes are the ringing: at the record edges, and wherever the variation turns. That is precisely the quantity the classical window designs optimise, which is why they win. The measurement ¶ Every candidate scaled to 1/2 at \(|f - f_c| = bw\) so that the bandwidth means the same thing in each, every bandwidth swept, the band extracted 24 bandwidths wide and the output decimated to the independent spacing. Scored by worst-case relative error over the usable part of the record: filter transistor legendre block-oriented mean rank blackman 2.40e-04 5.21e-04 1.18e-01 2.7 kaiser, β = 8 2.92e-04 5.94e-04 1.18e-01 3.0 blackman-harris 2.96e-04 6.94e-04 1.18e-01 3.7 DPSS, NW = 4 2.97e-04 7.09e-04 1.18e-01 4.0 hann (= raised cosine α=1) 4.71e-04 9.67e-04 1.17e-01 4.3 gaussian 3.05e-04 9.77e-04 1.18e-01 4.7 Fermi-Dirac, n = 2 4.98e-04 6.47e-04 1.27e-01 5.7 Three systems, and the ordering is stable on the two that discriminate. The block-oriented column is effectively a tie because its error there is dominated by the branch filters' roll-off rather than by the extraction — see example 23 . Two details worth noting: DPSS lands on top of Kaiser , within 1%, which is the expected result: Kaiser is a closed-form approximation to the first Slepian sequence. Since time concentration is what decides this problem, the provably optimal concentration was the obvious thing to try, and it confirms that Kaiser is already at that limit. It is not offered in the package because it needs an eigensolve for no measurable gain. A rectangular filter — eq. (13) of the paper — is catastrophic , at 3.8e-02. The smooth filter of eq. (12) was a large improvement over it; it simply was not taken as far as the window literature already had. What n actually controls ¶ A second correction. At n = 8 the Fermi-Dirac is a flat top with a steep roll-off. At n = 2 — the value the bandwidth/sharpness sweep selects — it is not flat at all , but a smooth bell. Calling n a sharpness parameter is misleading: it trades passband flatness against time concentration, and on this problem concentration is what pays. That is also why the two least flat-topped candidates came out ahead of the flatter ones. A metric that did not survive scrutiny An earlier version of this page quoted a "time concentration" figure — the fraction of kernel energy beyond \(5/bw\) — and drew conclusions from it. That number turned out to depend on the frequency grid it was evaluated on, moving by orders of magnitude between two reasonable choices, and the ranking it implied did not match the end-to-end result. It has been removed. The error against ground truth is the measure that decides. What this package does about it ¶ The Fermi-Dirac remains the default , because it is what the DMFA papers specify and this package's job is to implement the published methods faithfully. But create_window_filter makes every alternative a one-line change: from deistools.processing.passband_filters import create_window_filter band_filter = create_window_filter(band_axis, 0, bandwidth, "blackman") and create_raised_cosine_fun covers the Tukey family. Example 12 runs the comparison, so the ranking can be re-checked on your own system rather than taken on trust — which is the point, since the block-oriented column already shows a case where the filter choice does not matter at all. DMFA as linear algebra: it is BLTVA in a different basis ¶ DMFA looks like a filtering operation and BLTVA looks like a least-squares fit, which makes them seem like different kinds of thing. They are not. DMFA is already a linear-algebra estimator; it just happens to use a basis in which the solve is trivial. The implicit model ¶ Filtering a band of width \(bw\) around a tone and transforming back assumes the envelope is band-limited to \(|f| < bw\) . That is a model, and on a record of length \(T\) it is this one: \[ V_k(t) \;=\; \sum_{m=-M}^{M} c_m \, e^{\,\mathrm{j}2\pi m t / T}, \qquad M = bw\,T \] — the envelope is a trigonometric polynomial of degree \(bw\,T\) , with \(2M+1\) complex coefficients. Compare BLTVA, whose model is \[ Z(f,t) \;=\; \sum_{p=0}^{N_p} H_p(f)\, b_p(t) \] with \(b_p\) the Legendre polynomials and \(N_p+1\) coefficients. Same structure, different basis. Fitting it gives exactly DMFA ¶ Build the design matrix in the time domain — one column pair per mode, \(\cos\) and \(-\sin\) of \((\omega_k + 2\pi m/T)\,t\) — and solve the ordinary least-squares problem. The result is the band extraction, to machine precision: max |DMFA − least squares| / max = 1.3e-15 design-matrix condition number = 1.000000 That condition number is the whole explanation. The columns are distinct Fourier harmonics, so they are orthogonal on the record ; the normal equations \(K^{\mathrm{H}}K\,\hat\theta = K^{\mathrm{H}}y\) have a diagonal matrix on the left, and the solve degenerates into reading off the DFT bins. There is nothing to invert. BLTVA's Legendre columns are not orthogonal in the band, which is why it has a solve, a condition number worth reporting, and a pruning step. A smooth filter is ridge regularisation ¶ Multiplying coefficient \(m\) by the filter gain \(g_m\) is exactly diagonal Tikhonov shrinkage. Minimising \(\|y - Kc\|^2 + \sum_m \lambda_m |c_m|^2\) gives \(\hat c_m = y_m/(1+\lambda_m)\) , so \[ g_m \;=\; \frac{1}{1+\lambda_m} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \lambda_m \;=\; \frac{1}{g_m} - 1 \] Verified to 1.2e-15. So the choice between a rectangular and a Fermi-Dirac filter is not a choice between "no filter" and "a filter" — it is a choice between hard model-order truncation and a ridge prior , with the penalty rising smoothly towards the band edge. The filter is the regulariser. Three things this explains ¶ It gives DMFA an uncertainty. A linear estimator \(\hat c = Ay\) has covariance \(A\Sigma A^{\mathrm{H}}\) , which is the route BLTVA already takes. Working it through reproduces Chukwu eq. (19)–(20) exactly — their error propagation is this covariance — and extract_impedance_with_error now computes it, agreeing with the scatter over 200 noise realisations to better than 1%. It explains the independent spacing. The model has \(2\,bw\,T\) free coefficients over a record of length \(T\) , so there is one degree of freedom per \(T/(2\,bw\,T) = 1/(2\,bw)\) seconds. That is precisely the \(0.5/bw\) at which neighbouring errors stop being correlated — the rule is just "do not report more points than the model has parameters". It explains the edges, and points at a better basis. The Fourier basis is periodic by construction . Band-limitedness does not require periodicity; the basis imposes it, and a non-periodic envelope then produces Gibbs oscillation. BLTVA's polynomial basis carries no such constraint, which is why it has no edge problem at all. The natural basis for band-limited on a finite interval is the Slepian (DPSS) basis, not the Fourier one. Fitting the same band with the same number of coefficients: basis at \(t=0\) interior at \(t=T\) Fourier (periodic) 26.8% 1.5% 3.2% Slepian (not periodic) 5.0% 1.6% 2.4% Five times better at the leading edge, for nothing — same bandwidth, same degrees of freedom, same data. The interior is unchanged, as it must be. Not implemented A Slepian-basis DMFA is a genuine improvement over zero-padding rather than an alternative to it: padding removes the wrap-around, a non-periodic basis removes the reason the wrap hurt. It needs an eigensolve per bandwidth and a different code path from extract_impedance , so it is on the roadmap rather than in the package. The same DPSS appeared in the filter comparison above, for the same underlying reason. Variance: propagation, or measured in-band? ¶ Chukwu et al. (2022) derive the expected variance of the error on the admittance by propagating the measurement noise through the DMFA chain: \[ \sigma^2_{Y_{l,k_0}} \;=\; \frac{\sigma_i^2 + \big|Y_{l,k_0}\big|^2\,\sigma_v^2} {2\,N'\,\big|\tilde v_{l,k_0}\big|^2}, \qquad N' = \frac{N}{\sum_{k=-N/2}^{N/2}\big|\tilde g(k-k_0)\big|^2} \tag{19, 20} \] The derivation is sound — \(N'\) is the usual equivalent-noise-bandwidth factor, and the assumptions (noise of constant variance, uncorrelated between samples, Parseval for the filter norm) are stated rather than hidden. The weakness is not the algebra; it is where \(\sigma_i\) and \(\sigma_v\) come from . The paper obtains them from a separate calibration: zero volts across resistors, histogrammed. That assumes the noise is white and that it has not changed between the calibration and the measurement. The BLTVA route is available and is better ¶ BLTVA already estimates the noise variance from the measurement itself , using bins the excitation never reaches (Algorithm 1 of Hallemans TIM 2021, exposed here as estimate_noise_variance ). On an odd-harmonic grid with gaps those bins are plentiful, and the estimate: needs no separate instrument calibration; captures the noise colour , not just its level; reflects the noise as it was during that measurement; can be separated from nonlinear distortion by the parity of the bins. The two are complementary rather than rival. Keep eq. (19) — it is the correct propagation through the filter — and feed it a \(\sigma^2(f)\) measured from the unexcited bins instead of from a resistor. That removes the assumption the formula rests on while keeping its structure. The section above shows that eq. (19) is nothing more than the covariance of a linear estimator, which is also why BLTVA can report one. extract_impedance_with_error now computes it correctly. Three bugs had survived in that function, unnoticed because it had no test coverage: it returned the reciprocal of the variance (a half-finished edit was still commented out on its last line), it squared arguments already named variance_* , and its N' used the width of the extracted band where eq. (20) calls for the length of the record. Corrected, it agrees with the scatter over 200 noise realisations to 0.3%. Passing it a data-driven noise variance from the unexcited bins, rather than a resistor calibration, is left to the caller and is the remaining improvement. A testable hypothesis about the paper's own residual Chukwu et al. report that below 100 Hz their measured standard deviations run up to four times the predicted value, and state the reason could not be ascertained. A noise floor rising towards low frequency — \(1/f\) noise, which is ubiquitous in electrochemical cells — would produce exactly that signature, and a white-noise calibration cannot see it. A data-driven estimate from the unexcited bins would. This has not been tested here and is offered as a hypothesis, not a result. Do not treat successive instants as independent ¶ Neighbouring estimates rest on overlapping filter kernels, so their errors are correlated. Chukwu et al. put the correlation below 20% once successive instants are more than \(0.5/bw\) apart. Measured here on a stationary cell — where the impedance never moves, so the whole spread of the estimate is noise — over 150 noise realisations: output spacing instants over the record corr( \(e_j\) , \(e_{j+1}\) ) corr( \(e_j\) , \(e_{j+2}\) ) 0.125/bw 80 84% 50% 0.25/bw 40 49% 4% 0.5/bw 20 3% 0% 1/bw 10 −3% −3% 2/bw 4 −9% −1% The rule is confirmed, and the earlier examples sat at 0.125/bw — four times too dense, with 84% correlated neighbours. Reporting densely is fine for looking at a result; using every point as an independent observation in a least-squares fit is not, and will make the parameter uncertainties too small. independent_time_step(bandwidth) returns \(0.5/bw\) . Note that Npts_elab sets the band width and the reporting rate together, and they are different concerns — the band must be wide enough for the filter to decay, which is finer than this spacing. Extract wide, then decimate , which is what the examples now do. The time resolution is not free after all At the bandwidth that measures best here, \(bw = 0.5 f_{\min}\) , the independent spacing works out to \(0.5/bw\) = one multisine period — exactly STFT's window. DMFA's resolution is adjustable where STFT's is fixed, which is a real advantage, but the claim that it is simply finer was an artefact of reporting more densely than the data supports. Buying genuinely finer resolution means widening the band, and example 12 shows what that costs. The record edges are a property of the method ¶ The band-limited inverse transform rings at the record boundaries. Measured on the four simulated systems: system worst, edges removed worst, edges kept stationary 1.35e-05 1.35e-05 transistor 1.39e-03 4.13e-01 legendre 1.33e-03 8.85e-01 block-oriented 1.71e-01 4.26e-01 The stationary row is the diagnostic one: identical with and without the edges. A constant impedance occupies a single bin, so truncating the band removes nothing and there is nothing to ring. That establishes the cause. The artefact is not "the record ended" — it is the cost of representing a changing quantity with a finite band, under a DFT that treats the record as periodic when the envelope is not. No parameter setting removes it. This package discards the first and last tenth throughout. The filter belongs on the band's local axis ¶ elaboration_frequency_axis(n_points, T) returns the frequency axis of an extracted band: n_points bins of width \(1/T\) , centred on zero — about 0.2 Hz in the worked example. The full spectrum axis spans \(f_s\) , 1000 Hz there. Build the passband on the wrong axis and its bandwidth is scaled wrongly by \(f_s T / n_{\text{points}}\) , a factor of 2500. The result is not an error, just a filter that does something entirely different from what was asked. This is the easiest mistake to make with the method and the reason elaboration_frequency_axis exists as a named function rather than being inlined. Display fixes in visualize_dmfa_filtering ¶ Three defects were corrected in the slider view. They were display-only — no estimation path was affected — but they had survived because the function had no test coverage: the voltage panel drew its "Original data" trace with the filter applied , making it identical to the filtered trace until the slider was first moved; the initial title hard-coded the first frequency rather than the selected one; a stray parenthesis in the updated title ( Fouri(er ). The parameter name frequenies is still misspelled in the public signature, so pass that argument positionally.
docs.title: DMFA implementation notes

docs.text: Verification status The definition and the filter have now been checked line by line against Battistel et al. (2016), Koster et al. (2017) and Battistel and La Mantia (2019), and both match — see below. What is still open is an end-to-end comparison against an independent implementation on the same data. One finding from that check is a caveat the papers do not state: the mirroring they recommend for non-periodic records must not be applied to a random-phase multisine . See below .
docs.title: DMFA implementation notes

docs.text: Three definitions appear in this literature, and they are not equivalent. Battistel 2016, eq. (11) writes the dynamic impedance as the stationary ratio times a correction, \[ Z_k(t) = \frac{V_k}{I_k}\left\{1 - \sum_{l=1}^{bw} \left[\frac{I_{k,l}}{I_k}e^{\,2\pi \mathrm{j} l \Delta f t} + \frac{I_{k,l}}{I_k}e^{-2\pi \mathrm{j} l \Delta f t}\right]\right\} \] This is a first-order expansion , valid only while the skirt is small against its carrier. The odd look of it — a series that has to be truncated, with the truncation doubling as the bandwidth — is real, and it is why the later papers replaced it. Koster 2017, eq. (9) is the clean statement: the ratio of two filtered inverse transforms, with no expansion and no smallness assumption. This is what DEIStools implements , and it is the current definition. Battistel 2019, eq. (4) goes further and gives the physical definition via a Volterra series, against which both heuristics can be judged. It is a reference point rather than an algorithm; the paper finds DMFA within about 1% of it at the lowest frequency and below 0.1% at the highest. So: the calculation that looked odd was the 2016 one, and it is not the one in this package.
docs.title: Which definition is implemented

docs.text: create_fermi_dirac_fun evaluates \[ \tilde g = \frac{\cosh n}{\cosh n + \cosh (n x)}, \qquad x = \frac{f - f_c}{bw} \] while Battistel 2019 eq. (12) and Chukwu 2022 eq. (3) specify the product of two Fermi-Dirac functions, which simplifies exactly to \[ \tilde g_{\text{paper}} = \frac{\cosh n + 1}{\cosh n + \cosh (n x)} \] Checked numerically: the two agree in shape to 1e-14, and their ratio is the frequency-independent constant \[ \frac{\tilde g_{\text{DEIStools}}}{\tilde g_{\text{paper}}} = \frac{\cosh n}{\cosh n + 1} = 0.999329524658 \quad (n = 8) \] Since DMFA divides voltage by current through the same filter, the constant cancels exactly and the impedance is unaffected. The only consequence is that the DEIStools filter has gain 0.99933 at the centre rather than 1, which matters if you use the filter for anything that is not a ratio. Both conventions put \(\tilde g = 1/2\) at \(x = \pm 1\) , so bw means the same thing in both: the half-amplitude half-width.
docs.title: The filter matches the published one up to a constant

docs.text: The papers stress that \(\tilde g\) is a quadrature filter, defined only for positive frequencies, because that is what makes the inverse transform the analytic signal — the complex envelope — rather than a real band-limited signal. extract_impedance takes a block of bins around \(+f_k\) only and never the mirror at \(-f_k\) , so the output is inherently one-sided. That is correct and deliberate. The resulting factor of \(1/2\) (a real cosine carries half its energy on each side) cancels in the ratio, as does the Npts_elab scaling.
docs.title: The one-sided extraction is correct

docs.text: Here DEIStools departs from the papers' procedure, for cost. The papers filter the whole spectrum and inverse-transform at full length; extract_impedance takes only Npts_elab bins around each tone and inverse-transforms those. That is equivalent to filtering the full spectrum with a filter forced to zero outside the block, so the two agree only to the extent that the filter has already decayed at the block edge. Measured on the transistor record at bw = 0.5 f_min , n = 2 : block width filter value at the edge difference from full-spectrum filtering (median / worst) 4 bandwidths 1.2e-01 1.1e-03 / 2.3e-02 8 bandwidths 2.5e-03 1.5e-05 / 2.6e-03 16 bandwidths 8.5e-07 4.5e-09 / 9.2e-07 The error tracks the edge value almost exactly, as it should. Use at least 16 bandwidths The examples size the block at 8 bandwidths, which with a soft filter ( n = 2 ) leaves a worst-case 2.6e-03 — the same order as the method's own error. Sixteen costs nothing but arithmetic and puts the truncation at 1e-09. A sharper filter needs a narrower block; the rule is to extend the block until the filter has fallen below about 1e-06.
docs.title: Block extraction is a controlled approximation

docs.text: Battistel 2019 §3.1 recommends mirroring a non-periodic record about its last point, doubling its length, to suppress the Gibbs skirt. Applied to a random-phase multisine it is destructive , and badly so. Mirroring reflects the record in time. For a tone \(\cos(\omega t + \varphi)\) occupying a whole number of periods, the reflection is \(\cos(\omega t - \varphi)\) : the cosine part is even and survives, but the sine part is folded into \(\sin(\omega|t|)\) , which has a derivative kink at the seam and therefore a broadband spectrum. The scattered energy lands in every extraction band. Measured on the standard 13-tone grid: record off-bin / on-bin energy original 1.1e-24 mirrored, phases all zero 6.2e-04 mirrored, random phases 1.5e+00 With random phases the multisine scatters more energy off its bins than it leaves on them. The end-to-end effect on the impedance is what you would expect: worst error, edges included plain 4.1e-01 mirrored 7.5e+00 The paper's own case is different: their multisine was periodic and it was the cyclic voltammetry that was not, so mirroring fixed the dc skirt without touching the tones. The technique is sound there and wrong here. Conclusion: discard the edges. It is the robust answer, it costs a fixed fraction of the record, and it is what the examples do. If you need the edges, the lock-in filters in the time domain, where the boundary can be reflected on the smooth baseband envelope instead of being wrapped around by a circular DFT.
docs.title: Mirroring must not be used with a random-phase multisine

docs.text: The Fermi-Dirac distribution comes from statistical physics, not from signal processing, and the natural question is whether a standard DSP window does better. It does. Scored against known ground truth, the published filter comes last of seven , and the best standard window is about twice as good on the worst case. This corrects an earlier conclusion on this page A first comparison here tested only the raised-cosine (Tukey) family and reported that the Fermi-Dirac won. That comparison was incomplete: the cosine-sum windows — Blackman, Blackman-Harris, Nuttall — and Kaiser were not in it, and they are the ones that beat it. The table below supersedes it.
docs.title: Is the Fermi-Dirac filter the right choice? No.

docs.text: In a galvanostatic measurement the current is the excitation: exactly periodic, so its envelope is constant and the filter merely scales it. All the time variation sits in the voltage. The consequence is that \[ Z_{\text{measured}}(f_k, t) \;\approx\; \frac{\big(\tilde g * Z\big)(f_k, t)}{\tilde g(0)} \] — the reported impedance is the true \(Z(f_k,t)\) convolved with the filter's time-domain kernel . So the filter's frequency response is, directly, the transfer function applied to the time variation, and its time-domain sidelobes are the ringing: at the record edges, and wherever the variation turns. That is precisely the quantity the classical window designs optimise, which is why they win.
docs.title: What the filter actually does to the result

docs.text: Every candidate scaled to 1/2 at \(|f - f_c| = bw\) so that the bandwidth means the same thing in each, every bandwidth swept, the band extracted 24 bandwidths wide and the output decimated to the independent spacing. Scored by worst-case relative error over the usable part of the record: filter transistor legendre block-oriented mean rank blackman 2.40e-04 5.21e-04 1.18e-01 2.7 kaiser, β = 8 2.92e-04 5.94e-04 1.18e-01 3.0 blackman-harris 2.96e-04 6.94e-04 1.18e-01 3.7 DPSS, NW = 4 2.97e-04 7.09e-04 1.18e-01 4.0 hann (= raised cosine α=1) 4.71e-04 9.67e-04 1.17e-01 4.3 gaussian 3.05e-04 9.77e-04 1.18e-01 4.7 Fermi-Dirac, n = 2 4.98e-04 6.47e-04 1.27e-01 5.7 Three systems, and the ordering is stable on the two that discriminate. The block-oriented column is effectively a tie because its error there is dominated by the branch filters' roll-off rather than by the extraction — see example 23 . Two details worth noting: DPSS lands on top of Kaiser , within 1%, which is the expected result: Kaiser is a closed-form approximation to the first Slepian sequence. Since time concentration is what decides this problem, the provably optimal concentration was the obvious thing to try, and it confirms that Kaiser is already at that limit. It is not offered in the package because it needs an eigensolve for no measurable gain. A rectangular filter — eq. (13) of the paper — is catastrophic , at 3.8e-02. The smooth filter of eq. (12) was a large improvement over it; it simply was not taken as far as the window literature already had.
docs.title: The measurement

docs.text: A second correction. At n = 8 the Fermi-Dirac is a flat top with a steep roll-off. At n = 2 — the value the bandwidth/sharpness sweep selects — it is not flat at all , but a smooth bell. Calling n a sharpness parameter is misleading: it trades passband flatness against time concentration, and on this problem concentration is what pays. That is also why the two least flat-topped candidates came out ahead of the flatter ones. A metric that did not survive scrutiny An earlier version of this page quoted a "time concentration" figure — the fraction of kernel energy beyond \(5/bw\) — and drew conclusions from it. That number turned out to depend on the frequency grid it was evaluated on, moving by orders of magnitude between two reasonable choices, and the ranking it implied did not match the end-to-end result. It has been removed. The error against ground truth is the measure that decides.
docs.title: What n actually controls

docs.text: The Fermi-Dirac remains the default , because it is what the DMFA papers specify and this package's job is to implement the published methods faithfully. But create_window_filter makes every alternative a one-line change: from deistools.processing.passband_filters import create_window_filter band_filter = create_window_filter(band_axis, 0, bandwidth, "blackman") and create_raised_cosine_fun covers the Tukey family. Example 12 runs the comparison, so the ranking can be re-checked on your own system rather than taken on trust — which is the point, since the block-oriented column already shows a case where the filter choice does not matter at all.
docs.title: What this package does about it

docs.text: DMFA looks like a filtering operation and BLTVA looks like a least-squares fit, which makes them seem like different kinds of thing. They are not. DMFA is already a linear-algebra estimator; it just happens to use a basis in which the solve is trivial.
docs.title: DMFA as linear algebra: it is BLTVA in a different basis

docs.text: Filtering a band of width \(bw\) around a tone and transforming back assumes the envelope is band-limited to \(|f| < bw\) . That is a model, and on a record of length \(T\) it is this one: \[ V_k(t) \;=\; \sum_{m=-M}^{M} c_m \, e^{\,\mathrm{j}2\pi m t / T}, \qquad M = bw\,T \] — the envelope is a trigonometric polynomial of degree \(bw\,T\) , with \(2M+1\) complex coefficients. Compare BLTVA, whose model is \[ Z(f,t) \;=\; \sum_{p=0}^{N_p} H_p(f)\, b_p(t) \] with \(b_p\) the Legendre polynomials and \(N_p+1\) coefficients. Same structure, different basis.
docs.title: The implicit model

docs.text: Build the design matrix in the time domain — one column pair per mode, \(\cos\) and \(-\sin\) of \((\omega_k + 2\pi m/T)\,t\) — and solve the ordinary least-squares problem. The result is the band extraction, to machine precision: max |DMFA − least squares| / max = 1.3e-15 design-matrix condition number = 1.000000 That condition number is the whole explanation. The columns are distinct Fourier harmonics, so they are orthogonal on the record ; the normal equations \(K^{\mathrm{H}}K\,\hat\theta = K^{\mathrm{H}}y\) have a diagonal matrix on the left, and the solve degenerates into reading off the DFT bins. There is nothing to invert. BLTVA's Legendre columns are not orthogonal in the band, which is why it has a solve, a condition number worth reporting, and a pruning step.
docs.title: Fitting it gives exactly DMFA

docs.text: Multiplying coefficient \(m\) by the filter gain \(g_m\) is exactly diagonal Tikhonov shrinkage. Minimising \(\|y - Kc\|^2 + \sum_m \lambda_m |c_m|^2\) gives \(\hat c_m = y_m/(1+\lambda_m)\) , so \[ g_m \;=\; \frac{1}{1+\lambda_m} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \lambda_m \;=\; \frac{1}{g_m} - 1 \] Verified to 1.2e-15. So the choice between a rectangular and a Fermi-Dirac filter is not a choice between "no filter" and "a filter" — it is a choice between hard model-order truncation and a ridge prior , with the penalty rising smoothly towards the band edge. The filter is the regulariser.
docs.title: A smooth filter is ridge regularisation

docs.text: It gives DMFA an uncertainty. A linear estimator \(\hat c = Ay\) has covariance \(A\Sigma A^{\mathrm{H}}\) , which is the route BLTVA already takes. Working it through reproduces Chukwu eq. (19)–(20) exactly — their error propagation is this covariance — and extract_impedance_with_error now computes it, agreeing with the scatter over 200 noise realisations to better than 1%. It explains the independent spacing. The model has \(2\,bw\,T\) free coefficients over a record of length \(T\) , so there is one degree of freedom per \(T/(2\,bw\,T) = 1/(2\,bw)\) seconds. That is precisely the \(0.5/bw\) at which neighbouring errors stop being correlated — the rule is just "do not report more points than the model has parameters". It explains the edges, and points at a better basis. The Fourier basis is periodic by construction . Band-limitedness does not require periodicity; the basis imposes it, and a non-periodic envelope then produces Gibbs oscillation. BLTVA's polynomial basis carries no such constraint, which is why it has no edge problem at all. The natural basis for band-limited on a finite interval is the Slepian (DPSS) basis, not the Fourier one. Fitting the same band with the same number of coefficients: basis at \(t=0\) interior at \(t=T\) Fourier (periodic) 26.8% 1.5% 3.2% Slepian (not periodic) 5.0% 1.6% 2.4% Five times better at the leading edge, for nothing — same bandwidth, same degrees of freedom, same data. The interior is unchanged, as it must be. Not implemented A Slepian-basis DMFA is a genuine improvement over zero-padding rather than an alternative to it: padding removes the wrap-around, a non-periodic basis removes the reason the wrap hurt. It needs an eigensolve per bandwidth and a different code path from extract_impedance , so it is on the roadmap rather than in the package. The same DPSS appeared in the filter comparison above, for the same underlying reason.
docs.title: Three things this explains

docs.text: Best linear approximation per burst ¶ STFT reads the excited bins of each window and divides. That gives an impedance and nothing else — a single window offers no way to say whether the number it produced is limited by measurement noise, by nonlinearity, or by the cell changing while the window was open. This page is about recovering that. It keeps STFT's assumption — the system is whatever it is inside one window, with no model of how it varies — and uses the bins STFT throws away. The one structural fact ¶ Cut the record into windows of \(P\) whole multisine periods. The DFT of a window has fundamental \(1/(PT_p)\) , so a tone at harmonic \(h\) lands on bin \(Ph\) and only every \(P\) -th bin is a harmonic of the multisine at all . A nonlinear system of the PISPO class (period in, same period out) answers a periodic input with a periodic output, so its distortion is harmonically related to the input and can land only on those bins. That splits one burst into four classes: bins what is there \(k = Ph\) , \(h\) excited signal, plus everything below \(k = Pm\) , \(m\) odd, unexcited odd-order distortion + noise + drift \(k = Pm\) , \(m\) even, unexcited even-order distortion + noise + drift \(k\) not a multiple of \(P\) noise + drift This needs \(P \ge 2\) , and that is the whole price At \(P = 1\) the window fundamental is the multisine fundamental, every bin is a harmonic, and the fourth class is empty. On the package's 13-tone grid, in band: \(P\) noise odd even excited 1 0 168 180 13 2 301 138 150 13 4 903 138 150 13 8 2107 138 150 13 One period is exactly the window plain STFT prefers on a strongly excited cell. So the uncertainty is bought with time resolution, and there is no way around it. classify_bins raises rather than returning an empty class. docs.text: STFT reads the excited bins of each window and divides. That gives an impedance and nothing else — a single window offers no way to say whether the number it produced is limited by measurement noise, by nonlinearity, or by the cell changing while the window was open. This page is about recovering that. It keeps STFT's assumption — the system is whatever it is inside one window, with no model of how it varies — and uses the bins STFT throws away.
docs.title: Best linear approximation per burst

docs.text: Cut the record into windows of \(P\) whole multisine periods. The DFT of a window has fundamental \(1/(PT_p)\) , so a tone at harmonic \(h\) lands on bin \(Ph\) and only every \(P\) -th bin is a harmonic of the multisine at all . A nonlinear system of the PISPO class (period in, same period out) answers a periodic input with a periodic output, so its distortion is harmonically related to the input and can land only on those bins. That splits one burst into four classes: bins what is there \(k = Ph\) , \(h\) excited signal, plus everything below \(k = Pm\) , \(m\) odd, unexcited odd-order distortion + noise + drift \(k = Pm\) , \(m\) even, unexcited even-order distortion + noise + drift \(k\) not a multiple of \(P\) noise + drift This needs \(P \ge 2\) , and that is the whole price At \(P = 1\) the window fundamental is the multisine fundamental, every bin is a harmonic, and the fourth class is empty. On the package's 13-tone grid, in band: \(P\) noise odd even excited 1 0 168 180 13 2 301 138 150 13 4 903 138 150 13 8 2107 138 150 13 One period is exactly the window plain STFT prefers on a strongly excited cell. So the uncertainty is bought with time resolution, and there is no way around it. classify_bins raises rather than returning an empty class.

docs.text: BLTVA ¶ Best linear time-varying approximation. BLTVA assumes a form for the variation, \[ Z(f, t) \;=\; \sum_{p=0}^{N_p} H_p(f)\, b_p(t) \] and fits the coefficients \(H_p\) directly in the frequency domain, band by band. Instead of cutting the record or filtering a band it uses the skirts as its data. It is the most accurate of the three when its assumption holds, and the only one that reports an uncertainty. Calling it ¶ from deistools.processing.bltva import bltva, legendre_basis result = bltva( voltage, current, fs, P, harmonics, # excited HARMONIC NUMBERS, not frequencies Np=8, # order of the Legendre expansion of Z(f,t) Nq=2, # order of the trend polynomial at DC Na=None, # transient order: chosen automatically harmonics="excited", # or "all_nl" to keep the unexcited harmonic bins band_halfwidth=50, # DFT bins either side of each tone ) Harmonic numbers, not frequencies bltva works in DFT bins throughout, so it takes integers. Harmonic \(h\) of a \(P\) -period record occupies bin \(h \cdot P\) . What comes back ¶ BLTVAResult holds coefficients, not an impedance per instant: field shape meaning H_p (n_freq, Np+1) the coefficients. H_p[:, 0] is the time average f_exc (n_freq,) the excited frequencies std_H_p (n_freq, Np+1) uncertainty on each coefficient diagnostics list one entry per band fitted var_distortion_even/odd (n_freq, Np+1) only with harmonics="all_nl" To get an impedance, evaluate the model wherever you want it: Z = result.H_p @ legendre_basis(N, Np).T # (n_freq, N) It is a smooth polynomial, so 200 instants carry the same information as all 400 000 samples. Left: the time average with its uncertainty. Middle: the orders that describe the change, each falling about an order of magnitude below the last. Right: the basis functions they multiply. The parameters ¶ \(N_p\) — the order of the expansion ¶ The one that matters. Under-specify and the error hits a floor that no amount of signal quality moves; over-specify and almost nothing happens, because coefficients the data does not support are pruned away. \(N_p\) median worst 1 1.04e-02 1.11e-01 2 1.20e-03 2.66e-02 4 1.29e-04 1.88e-03 8 1.02e-04 2.91e-04 (transistor system, example 14) Err high. The two mistakes are not symmetric. \(N_q\) — the trend order ¶ Insurance against drift, and it does nothing if there is none. On the transistor circuit — which changes its impedance but not its DC level — \(N_q\) makes no difference at all. Add an order-3 voltage trend of 5 V peak-to-peak, and it does: \(N_q\) median worst 0 1.33e-04 9.28e-01 1 1.33e-04 1.36e-01 2 1.32e-04 1.02e-02 3 1.29e-04 1.88e-03 It matters in the worst case , not the median, because a trend is a disturbance near DC that corrupts the lowest tones and leaves the rest alone. It saturates exactly at the order of the trend present. Detrending is specific to BLTVA, and differencing is specific to it twice over Nq and the differencing of deistools.processing.detrending exist because BLTVA models the trend and differencing reduces the number of coefficients that takes. Differencing works here precisely because step 2 divides its attenuation back out — and that is why it must never be handed to DMFA or STFT, which have no such step. Differencing(1) leaves \(|F| = 3\times10^{-4}\) at the lowest excited bin of a 160 000-sample record; the measured DMFA error at that tone is 1.00, i.e. the tone is gone. Of the four strategies in the module, only differencing may be passed as detrend ; the estimator refuses the rest with an explanation. See Detrending for which one to use where, and DMFA and trends . band_halfwidth — and why it is not independent of \(N_p\) ¶ Bands are meant to overlap: the default rule spans three consecutive excited frequencies deliberately. A skirt whose centre lies inside the band gets its own block of regressors and is fitted explicitly; one outside contributes only a tail, which is nearly collinear with the transient polynomial and cannot be separated from it. But the two parameters interact, and the sign of the effect flips: band 50 band 100 band 200 band 400 \(N_p = 3\) 8.70e-03 7.13e-03 6.33e-03 5.92e-03 \(N_p = 4\) 2.48e-03 1.88e-03 1.58e-03 1.43e-03 \(N_p = 6\) 7.70e-04 6.33e-04 2.65e-04 3.76e-04 \(N_p = 8\) 1.45e-04 2.91e-04 8.51e-04 4.26e-03 (worst relative error; example 14) Tuning them separately picks \(N_p = 8\) , band 400 — 29× worse than the joint optimum. The cause is explained in the implementation notes . Raise \(N_p\) and you must narrow the band. \(N_a\) — leave it at None ¶ Chosen by a closed-form rule from \(P\) , \(N_p\) and the detrending order. A hand-picked value was 19× worse in testing, and the curve is monotone, so there is no optimum to hunt for. The uncertainty is a model-error detector ¶ BLTVA estimates the noise from bins the excitation never touched and propagates it to the coefficients. That gives a predicted \(\sigma\) which covers noise only — so comparing it with the error you actually see tells you which of the two is limiting you: system actual median predicted noise ratio stationary 1.11e-06 1.51e-06 0.7 legendre 1.30e-06 9.31e-07 1.4 block-oriented 1.71e-04 9.01e-05 1.9 transistor 1.06e-04 5.56e-07 190 Three of the four sit near one, because those systems have no model error to have — nothing varies, or the Legendre model is exactly right, or the excess is genuine distortion. The transistor is the outlier because its \(Z(f,t)\) is a rational function of time, not a polynomial, so a Legendre series approximates it and leaves a residue. Practical use: compare the reported \(\sigma\) with your own repeatability. If your error is far larger, more averaging will not help — raise \(N_p\) or change method. Solid: the error actually made. Dashed: what noise alone predicts. They coincide except on the transistor, where the model is the limit. Pruning: it can say "stationary" ¶ Coefficients the data does not support are removed from the fit rather than left to absorb noise. On a stationary cell, BLTVA's time-varying coefficient comes back as exactly zero at every tone — not small, absent. On the transistor record the same coefficient is 0.37 of \(|H_0|\) . That is a different kind of answer from "the variation I measured was small", and it is worth having. The true impedance is constant, so every wobble here is invented. BLTVA's panel is flat at machine precision because the coefficient was pruned away. Distortion and SNDR ¶ With harmonics="all_nl" the fit keeps the unexcited harmonic bins, and the parity of those bins separates even-order from odd-order distortion. The result then offers var_distortion_even , var_distortion_odd and sndr_db() — the signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio, i.e. how far the linear part stands above everything that is not it. On the block-oriented system SNDR runs 24 to 76 dB across the grid, falling where the branch filters have rolled off. It is the number to check before trusting an impedance from a cell driven hard enough to distort, and neither STFT nor DMFA computes it. harmonics="all_nl" also improved the estimate there, from 1.7e-04 to 9.5e-05, because the nonlinear harmonics are modelled instead of being left to disturb the bands they fall in. On a linear system there is nothing there to model and nothing to gain. Inspecting a fit ¶ from deistools.processing.bltva import visualize_bltva_fit visualize_bltva_fit(voltage, current, fs, P, harmonics, Np=8, Nq=2, harmonics="excited", band_halfwidth=50) Takes the same arguments as bltva , so you can point it at the call you actually ran. For each tone it shows the band data against the fitted model, and the coefficients that become \(H_p\) . A healthy fit has the low orders dominant and the high ones falling away. Coefficients that are all the same size, or that grow with order, mean the band is being fitted by cancellation between large terms — the fingerprint of an ill-conditioned or over-specified problem. When not to use it ¶ When the variation is not smooth. A kink is the one shape a polynomial basis is worst at, and no affordable order fixes it. If raising \(N_p\) stops helping and the uncertainty ratio stays large, the model is wrong and STFT is the honest answer.
