The transistor is the outlier because its \(Z(f,t)\) is a rational function of time, not a polynomial, so a Legendre series approximates it and leaves a residue. Practical use: compare the reported \(\sigma\) with your own repeatability. If your error is far larger, more averaging will not help — raise \(N_p\) or change method. Solid: the error actually made. Dashed: what noise alone predicts. They coincide except on the transistor, where the model is the limit.
docs.title: The uncertainty is a model-error detector

docs.text: Coefficients the data does not support are removed from the fit rather than left to absorb noise. On a stationary cell, BLTVA's time-varying coefficient comes back as exactly zero at every tone — not small, absent. On the transistor record the same coefficient is 0.37 of \(|H_0|\) . That is a different kind of answer from "the variation I measured was small", and it is worth having. The true impedance is constant, so every wobble here is invented. BLTVA's panel is flat at machine precision because the coefficient was pruned away.
docs.title: Pruning: it can say "stationary"

docs.text: With harmonics="all_nl" the fit keeps the unexcited harmonic bins, and the parity of those bins separates even-order from odd-order distortion. The result then offers var_distortion_even , var_distortion_odd and sndr_db() — the signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio, i.e. how far the linear part stands above everything that is not it. On the block-oriented system SNDR runs 24 to 76 dB across the grid, falling where the branch filters have rolled off. It is the number to check before trusting an impedance from a cell driven hard enough to distort, and neither STFT nor DMFA computes it. harmonics="all_nl" also improved the estimate there, from 1.7e-04 to 9.5e-05, because the nonlinear harmonics are modelled instead of being left to disturb the bands they fall in. On a linear system there is nothing there to model and nothing to gain.
docs.title: Distortion and SNDR

docs.text: from deistools.processing.bltva import visualize_bltva_fit visualize_bltva_fit(voltage, current, fs, P, harmonics, Np=8, Nq=2, harmonics="excited", band_halfwidth=50) Takes the same arguments as bltva , so you can point it at the call you actually ran. For each tone it shows the band data against the fitted model, and the coefficients that become \(H_p\) . A healthy fit has the low orders dominant and the high ones falling away. Coefficients that are all the same size, or that grow with order, mean the band is being fitted by cancellation between large terms — the fingerprint of an ill-conditioned or over-specified problem.
docs.title: Inspecting a fit

docs.text: When the variation is not smooth. A kink is the one shape a polynomial basis is worst at, and no affordable order fixes it. If raising \(N_p\) stops helping and the uncertainty ratio stays large, the model is wrong and STFT is the honest answer.
docs.title: When not to use it

docs.text: Detrending ¶ A measured cell drifts. Its open-circuit voltage wanders, its temperature moves, a reference electrode ages — and the resulting slow excursion can be tens of volts peak-to-peak on a signal of one volt. That drift is not what the measurement is for, so the instinct is to filter it out first and estimate afterwards. The instinct is wrong, and this page is mostly about why. Four strategies are implemented. Each one is useless or harmful with three of the four estimators , and the pattern is not arbitrary: it falls out of one fact about what a filter can do. The one fact ¶ A filter applied by convolution is diagonal in frequency . It multiplies bin \(k\) by \(F(k)\) and does nothing else. So if a trend and the signal both have content at bin \(k\) , they are scaled by the same number: \[ \frac{|T(k)|}{|S(k)|} \quad\text{is unchanged, for every } k \text{ and every diagonal filter} \] Measured here as bit-identical before and after, for both a boxcar and a Butterworth. A filter cannot separate a trend from the signal where the two overlap, because at a single bin there is nothing to separate them with. It can only reject a disturbance that lives somewhere else in frequency. Whether a trend overlaps is not a matter of taste. A trend that takes the whole record to unfold has its energy in the lowest few bins — exactly where the slowest excited tones sit. For a typical multisine, the lowest three to five tones are inside the drift's skirt. For those tones, no filter helps. A projection is not gentler than a filter It is tempting to think a polynomial fit leaves the excited bins alone, because a polynomial is "slow" and the tones are not. It does not. A degree- \(q\) Legendre polynomial on a finite record is not band-limited : its spectrum reaches every bin, decaying only as a power law. So the projection removes signal at the excited bins, and measurably more than a filter does. Measured on the stationary cell of example 00, whose impedance does not move, so every change at an excited bin is signal destroyed: strategy lowest tone top tone MovingAverage(20001) 5.0e-05 5.0e-05 LowPassRemoval(2, 2) 1.9e-03 2.4e-13 PolynomialFit(1) 6.5e-03 5.3e-05 PolynomialFit(3) 2.1e-02 1.8e-04 PolynomialFit(8) 8.8e-02 5.0e-04 PolynomialFit(12) 1.4e-01 2.7e-04 (example 09) The damage falls off as \(1/h\) with harmonic number — 6.5e-03, 2.2e-03, 1.3e-03, 7.3e-04 at \(h = 1, 3, 5, 9\) , whose product with \(h\) is constant to two figures — which is the spectrum of a ramp. So it is worst at the lowest tones: exactly the ones the detrending was for. Two things can work: Annihilate the trend in the time domain. \(\Delta^d\) applied to a polynomial of degree \(d-1\) gives exactly zero, pointwise. No multiplication in frequency can do that, and differencing achieves it by not being diagonal — the zero-padded history is what buys the extra power. Model the trend and fit it jointly. Put trend regressors in the design matrix alongside the signal model and let least squares apportion the shared bins. This is what BLTVA's \(N_q\) block does. Everything below is a consequence. Which strategy, which estimator ¶ strategy BLTVA DMFA / STFT Differencing the only one that works — though plain \(N_q\) usually beats it destroys the signal (error 1.00) MovingAverage refused at best 1.7×, and not consistently LowPassRemoval refused no help on an overlapping trend PolynomialFit refused — use \(N_q\) the only one that reliably helps The two columns are exact complements, and one question decides both: can the estimator undo an attenuation? BLTVA can. Its cost function is weighted by \(W = (FF^H)^{-1}\) , so whatever the filter took out is divided back in. That is what lets differencing trade away the entire low-frequency band and still get the answer. DMFA and STFT have no such step, so for them whatever a filter removes is simply gone — and differencing, which removes almost everything near DC, is catastrophic rather than free. Never pass Differencing to DMFA or STFT Differencing(1) attenuates the lowest excited bin of a 160 000-sample record to \(|F| = 3\times10^{-4}\) . The measured DMFA error at that tone is 1.00 — the tone is gone. In BLTVA the same attenuation costs nothing. This is the most dangerous thing in the module, and the reason frequency_response is a mandatory part of the protocol: it is the only way to see the \(3\times10^{-4}\) coming. Detrending for BLTVA is not a preprocessing step ¶ Removing a trend before a BLTVA fit changes four things at once (2022 paper, eq. 18–27): every skirt regressor is multiplied by \(F(k)\) — eq. (21) the cost function is weighted by \(W = (FF^H)^{-1}\) — eq. (26) the filter's boundary effects add their own regressors — eq. (21) the transient order \(N_a\) shrinks by the filter order — eq. (22) So a strategy is not "a function returning a cleaned signal". It is the bundle of those four things, which is what the Detrending protocol encodes. A strategy that cannot report its frequency_response cannot be used, because step 2 would be impossible. Why the weighting rules out three of the four ¶ Step 2 is also what disqualifies them. For a real, zero-phase response \(F/|F| = 1\) , so the weighted system is identical to the one built from the raw record — verified to \(5.6\times10^{-17}\) on the skirt regressors. Nothing about the trend was removed. What did change is that the trend block of eq. (58) is gone, replaced by nothing. Measured on the 2022 paper's own trend, with \(F(k) = 1\) exactly — a filter that does nothing at all, which the protocol happily accepts: configuration error at the lowest tone no trend, \(N_q = 5\) 2.2e-04 trend, \(N_q = 5\) , no detrending 1.6e-02 trend, \(F(k) = 1\) "detrending" 2.6e+00 A moving average scores well in the same test (1.8e-04), which looks like a refutation until the averaging length is varied: length error at the lowest tone 101 1.83e-04 401 1.82e-04 1601 1.68e-04 An answer that does not depend on the averaging length is not coming from the averaging. It comes from the \(1/|F(k)|\) weighting applied to the transient block, which eq. (21) does not multiply by \(F\) : since \(F \sim k^2\) near DC for any boxcar, the weighting hands the transient polynomial a \(k^{-2}\) envelope, and that reshaped basis happens to absorb the trend skirt. The trend removal is an accident of the reparametrisation — and a Butterworth low-pass, same protocol but a different \(1/|F|\) shape, scores 2.6e-02, worse than no detrending at all. So BLTVA refuses them, with an error naming the alternative. The strategies ¶ Differencing ¶ \[ y_d(n) = \Delta^d \tilde y(n), \qquad \tilde y(n) = 0 \text{ for } n < 0 \] High-pass, eq. (12b): \(F_d(k) = (1 - z_k^{-1})^d\) with \(z_k = e^{j2\pi k/N}\) . The published strategy, and the only one BLTVA accepts. It suppresses a smooth trend without modelling it , which is the point of the 2022 paper: a trend that no finite polynomial captures cannot be removed parametrically, and trying inflates the variance of the low-frequency estimates. Two properties make it work where the others fail. It annihilates a degree- \((d-1)\) polynomial identically in the time domain, which no diagonal filter can. And its \(F\) is complex, so \(F/|F|\) is a phase ramp the magnitude weighting does not cancel. The price is the boundary term — the zero-padded history leaves a polynomial of degree \(d-1\) in \(z_k^{-1}\) (Theorem 2), which becomes the extra regressors of step 3. select_differencing_order picks \(d\) by eq. (11), with a documented caveat: the criterion assumes "trend plus random series", and a strongly low-pass response breaks that, so it can recommend differencing a record with no trend at all. Treat it as a starting point. What it buys is columns, not accuracy ¶ The strategy to beat is no detrending at all, with a generous \(N_q\) — and on accuracy differencing usually loses to it, including on the non-polynomial trend the 2022 paper chose precisely to motivate differencing: \(N_p\) \(N_q\) cap from eq. (49) best \(N_q\) Differencing(1) 2 17 1.4e-04 ( \(N_q=7\) ) 8.2e-03 \(N_q\) wins 60× 4 13 2.2e-04 ( \(N_q=11\) ) 5.5e-04 \(N_q\) wins 2.5× 6 9 1.2e-04 ( \(N_q=8\) ) 7.1e-02 \(N_q\) wins 588× 8 5 1.9e+00 ( \(N_q=4\) ) 4.6e-02 differencing wins 42× (relative error at the lowest excited tone; the paper's trend, 92 V p-p) The paper's own comparison is the \(N_q = 2\) column of this picture: at that order parametric removal does fail, by 1.35 against differencing's 7.8e-03. Raise \(N_q\) and the conclusion reverses, because a joint fit does not distort and a larger basis simply models the trend better. What flips the table at \(N_p = 8\) is eq. (49), \(N_q + 3N_p + N_a + 1 < 2P - 1\) . A high \(N_p\) — fine time resolution — eats the budget, capping \(N_q\) at 5, and at that order the trend is unmodellable: \(N_q = 4\) gives 1.9e+00, \(N_q = 3\) gives 5.4e+00. Differencing replaces the whole \(N_q\) block with \(d-1\) boundary columns — 15 columns per band instead of 20, for \(N_p=2, N_q=5, N_a=8\) — and those freed columns are the entire point. The \(N_p = 8\) configuration is not otherwise broken: on a trend-free record it reaches 2.0e-04. So: reach for a generous \(N_q\) first. Use differencing when eq. (49) will not let you afford the trend order you need, which in practice means when you want fine time resolution. MovingAverage ¶ Subtract a centred boxcar average of \(L\) samples. The response is one minus the Dirichlet kernel: \[ F(k) = 1 - \frac{\sin(\pi k L/N)}{L \sin(\pi k /N)} \] \(L\) must be odd, so the window has a true centre and \(F\) carries no phase. A boxcar is a poor filter and this is where it shows. \(F\) has sidelobes, overshoots above 1, and is not monotone — so checking \(|F|\) at a tone is worthless. MovingAverage(20001) on a 160 000-sample record has \(|F| = 1.00005\) at bin 8 and swings from 0.363 to 1.214 over the \(\pm 4\) bins either side, a 3.3× ripple. That band is exactly what DMFA reconstructs the time variation from, so the ripple is an uncorrected envelope distortion. Use band_response and judge by ripple , never by the centre value. Measured on DMFA at the lowest tone, against a clean baseline of 4.1e-03: record no filter with it no trend 4.1e-03 1.9e-02 trended, \(L = 20001\) 8.7e-02 5.0e-02 trended, \(L = 40001\) 8.7e-02 9.7e-02 Those three rows have to be read together. \(L = 20001\) does improve the trended record, by 1.7× — per-bin invariance does not forbid that, because a filter can still reweight which bins dominate a band fit even though it cannot change the ratio within any one of them. But \(L = 40001\) makes it worse, so the direction is not consistent across settings, and the win is paid for by raising the trend-free floor 4.5×. Nothing is gained here that PolynomialFit does not gain better, and more predictably, on the same record. Present for completeness; LowPassRemoval is strictly the better shape. LowPassRemoval ¶ Subtract the low-pass content, with a Butterworth magnitude: \[ F(k) = \frac{r^n}{\sqrt{1 + r^{2n}}}, \qquad r = |f_k| / f_c \] Defined by this magnitude and applied as such, so it is zero-phase and has no startup transient — unlike the same Butterworth run as a time-domain recursion, which would have both and would then need boundary regressors it cannot afford. The cutoff is in cycles per record , which is the DFT bin index: bin \(k\) is \(k/T\) Hz. That keeps the strategy independent of the sampling rate, and it is the only unit frequency_response(k, N) can resolve. A cutoff of 3 means "treat anything slower than three cycles over the whole record as trend". Unlike the boxcar it is monotone and never exceeds 1, so a cutoff a few times below the slowest tone gives a genuinely flat band: at cutoff = 2 over \(\pm 4\) bins around bin 8, ripple 1.03× and a DMFA error of 5.8e-03 on a trend-free record against the 4.1e-03 baseline. It still does not remove a trend that overlaps the tones — 8.7e-02 before, 8.8e-02 after at cutoff = 2 , and 1.2e-01 at cutoff = 4, order = 6 . What it does well is remove a trend genuinely slower than everything excited, which is the case the cutoff describes. Whether your trend is that case is an empirical question; band_response answers it. PolynomialFit ¶ \[ y_d = \left(I - b (b^Tb)^{-1} b^T\right) y \] with \(b\) the Legendre basis on the record — the same basis BLTVA uses for its trend block. Legendre rather than monomial because the monomial Vandermonde is hopeless beyond degree ~15. This is the one strategy with no frequency response at all , and not for want of deriving it. Subtracting a least-squares fit is an orthogonal projection: a rank- \((q+1)\) operator whose frequency-domain kernel is \(\sum_q B_q(k) B_q(k')^*\) , dense in \((k,k')\) . It mixes bins, so no \(F(k)\) exists, step 2 cannot be carried out, and frequency_response raises. Being non-diagonal is also exactly what makes it the only strategy that helps DMFA or STFT. On a trended record it takes the lowest tone from 8.7e-02 to 7.9e-03 , where both diagonal filters leave it at 8.8e-02 or worse. The price is paid silently, and it is the thing to understand before using it. Applying the same subtraction to a record with no trend — so that everything removed is signal — gives, at the lowest tone against a clean error of 4.1e-03: degree DMFA error at the lowest tone 1 4.9e-03 3 7.9e-03 8 4.0e-02 12 6.2e-02 The distortion grows with the degree and there is nothing to correct it with . That is both why the 2022 paper reaches for differencing and why BLTVA fits this basis instead of subtracting it. Keep the degree as low as the trend allows, and read the result as a trade rather than a cleanup. Inside BLTVA, use Nq instead The \(N_q\) drift block of eq. (58) is this same Legendre basis, fitted jointly with the impedance rather than subtracted first . The trend is then separated from the signal using the whole band of data, and the distortion above does not arise at all. PolynomialFit exists for the estimators that have no such block, and for measuring what its absence costs. Worked example ¶ examples/09_detrending.py runs all four strategies on one drifting record and plots what the user usually wants to see first: the original and detrended signals, and the effect on the DFT spectrum. It also reproduces the three tables on this page — the trend-to-signal ratio per bin, the damage to the excited bins, and the DMFA error before and after — and shows BLTVA accepting exactly one of the four. The record there has 8 periods rather than the 20 used elsewhere, which puts the lowest tone at bin 8 instead of bin 20 and so much closer to the drift's skirt. That is the situation detrending exists for, and it is where the numbers on this page come from. Checking a strategy ¶ check_response verifies step 1 of the protocol — that apply is what frequency_response claims: \[ \mathrm{DFT}(\texttt{apply}(y)) = F(k)\,\mathrm{DFT}(y) + \big(\text{something in the span of } \texttt{extra\_regressors}\big) \] It returns the part of the residual the boundary regressors cannot absorb. All four implemented strategies return \(\sim 10^{-15}\) : strategy residual Differencing(1) 2.9e-15 Differencing(4) 9.6e-16 MovingAverage(401) 6.8e-13 LowPassRemoval(3, 2) 4.2e-16 Anything larger means the strategy is reporting a response that does not describe what it did, and an estimator built on it is biased with no warning. A constant column joins the projection, because the estimator has one: eq. (21) omits the \(m=0\) boundary term on the grounds that the transient polynomial already spans a constant. This is the test that decides which category a new strategy falls into, and it is worth running on anything added later. In practice ¶ A polynomial trend, with BLTVA. Use Nq . Nothing else, no detrending. A trend no polynomial captures, with BLTVA. Still try \(N_q\) first, as generously as eq. (49) allows — it beat Differencing(1) by 60× on the 2022 paper's own trend. Reach for Differencing(d) when \(N_p\) has eaten the budget and the \(N_q\) cap is below what the trend needs, with \(d\) from select_differencing_order as a starting point, checked against the spectrum. See what it buys . Any trend, with DMFA or STFT. PolynomialFit at the lowest degree that works, accepting the distortion in the table above — or, for the tones the drift actually overlaps, use BLTVA instead. The DMFA page has the measurements and the joint-solve alternative. To study what naive detrending costs , apply the strategy yourself and call bltva with detrend=None . That is the honest way to reproduce what a user who filters first would get, and it needs no escape hatch.

Raise \(N_q\) and the conclusion reverses, because a joint fit does not distort and a larger basis simply models the trend better. What flips the table at \(N_p = 8\) is eq. (49), \(N_q + 3N_p + N_a + 1 < 2P - 1\) . A high \(N_p\) — fine time resolution — eats the budget, capping \(N_q\) at 5, and at that order the trend is unmodellable: \(N_q = 4\) gives 1.9e+00, \(N_q = 3\) gives 5.4e+00. Differencing replaces the whole \(N_q\) block with \(d-1\) boundary columns — 15 columns per band instead of 20, for \(N_p=2, N_q=5, N_a=8\) — and those freed columns are the entire point. The \(N_p = 8\) configuration is not otherwise broken: on a trend-free record it reaches 2.0e-04. So: reach for a generous \(N_q\) first. Use differencing when eq. (49) will not let you afford the trend order you need, which in practice means when you want fine time resolution.
docs.title: What it buys is columns, not accuracy

docs.text: Subtract a centred boxcar average of \(L\) samples. The response is one minus the Dirichlet kernel: \[ F(k) = 1 - \frac{\sin(\pi k L/N)}{L \sin(\pi k /N)} \] \(L\) must be odd, so the window has a true centre and \(F\) carries no phase. A boxcar is a poor filter and this is where it shows. \(F\) has sidelobes, overshoots above 1, and is not monotone — so checking \(|F|\) at a tone is worthless. MovingAverage(20001) on a 160 000-sample record has \(|F| = 1.00005\) at bin 8 and swings from 0.363 to 1.214 over the \(\pm 4\) bins either side, a 3.3× ripple. That band is exactly what DMFA reconstructs the time variation from, so the ripple is an uncorrected envelope distortion. Use band_response and judge by ripple , never by the centre value. Measured on DMFA at the lowest tone, against a clean baseline of 4.1e-03: record no filter with it no trend 4.1e-03 1.9e-02 trended, \(L = 20001\) 8.7e-02 5.0e-02 trended, \(L = 40001\) 8.7e-02 9.7e-02 Those three rows have to be read together. \(L = 20001\) does improve the trended record, by 1.7× — per-bin invariance does not forbid that, because a filter can still reweight which bins dominate a band fit even though it cannot change the ratio within any one of them. But \(L = 40001\) makes it worse, so the direction is not consistent across settings, and the win is paid for by raising the trend-free floor 4.5×. Nothing is gained here that PolynomialFit does not gain better, and more predictably, on the same record. Present for completeness; LowPassRemoval is strictly the better shape.
docs.title: MovingAverage

docs.text: Subtract the low-pass content, with a Butterworth magnitude: \[ F(k) = \frac{r^n}{\sqrt{1 + r^{2n}}}, \qquad r = |f_k| / f_c \] Defined by this magnitude and applied as such, so it is zero-phase and has no startup transient — unlike the same Butterworth run as a time-domain recursion, which would have both and would then need boundary regressors it cannot afford. The cutoff is in cycles per record , which is the DFT bin index: bin \(k\) is \(k/T\) Hz. That keeps the strategy independent of the sampling rate, and it is the only unit frequency_response(k, N) can resolve. A cutoff of 3 means "treat anything slower than three cycles over the whole record as trend". Unlike the boxcar it is monotone and never exceeds 1, so a cutoff a few times below the slowest tone gives a genuinely flat band: at cutoff = 2 over \(\pm 4\) bins around bin 8, ripple 1.03× and a DMFA error of 5.8e-03 on a trend-free record against the 4.1e-03 baseline. It still does not remove a trend that overlaps the tones — 8.7e-02 before, 8.8e-02 after at cutoff = 2 , and 1.2e-01 at cutoff = 4, order = 6 . What it does well is remove a trend genuinely slower than everything excited, which is the case the cutoff describes. Whether your trend is that case is an empirical question; band_response answers it.
docs.title: LowPassRemoval

docs.text: \[ y_d = \left(I - b (b^Tb)^{-1} b^T\right) y \] with \(b\) the Legendre basis on the record — the same basis BLTVA uses for its trend block. Legendre rather than monomial because the monomial Vandermonde is hopeless beyond degree ~15. This is the one strategy with no frequency response at all , and not for want of deriving it. Subtracting a least-squares fit is an orthogonal projection: a rank- \((q+1)\) operator whose frequency-domain kernel is \(\sum_q B_q(k) B_q(k')^*\) , dense in \((k,k')\) . It mixes bins, so no \(F(k)\) exists, step 2 cannot be carried out, and frequency_response raises. Being non-diagonal is also exactly what makes it the only strategy that helps DMFA or STFT. On a trended record it takes the lowest tone from 8.7e-02 to 7.9e-03 , where both diagonal filters leave it at 8.8e-02 or worse. The price is paid silently, and it is the thing to understand before using it. Applying the same subtraction to a record with no trend — so that everything removed is signal — gives, at the lowest tone against a clean error of 4.1e-03: degree DMFA error at the lowest tone 1 4.9e-03 3 7.9e-03 8 4.0e-02 12 6.2e-02 The distortion grows with the degree and there is nothing to correct it with . That is both why the 2022 paper reaches for differencing and why BLTVA fits this basis instead of subtracting it. Keep the degree as low as the trend allows, and read the result as a trade rather than a cleanup. Inside BLTVA, use Nq instead The \(N_q\) drift block of eq. (58) is this same Legendre basis, fitted jointly with the impedance rather than subtracted first . The trend is then separated from the signal using the whole band of data, and the distortion above does not arise at all. PolynomialFit exists for the estimators that have no such block, and for measuring what its absence costs.
docs.title: PolynomialFit

docs.text: examples/09_detrending.py runs all four strategies on one drifting record and plots what the user usually wants to see first: the original and detrended signals, and the effect on the DFT spectrum. It also reproduces the three tables on this page — the trend-to-signal ratio per bin, the damage to the excited bins, and the DMFA error before and after — and shows BLTVA accepting exactly one of the four. The record there has 8 periods rather than the 20 used elsewhere, which puts the lowest tone at bin 8 instead of bin 20 and so much closer to the drift's skirt. That is the situation detrending exists for, and it is where the numbers on this page come from.
docs.title: Worked example

docs.text: check_response verifies step 1 of the protocol — that apply is what frequency_response claims: \[ \mathrm{DFT}(\texttt{apply}(y)) = F(k)\,\mathrm{DFT}(y) + \big(\text{something in the span of } \texttt{extra\_regressors}\big) \] It returns the part of the residual the boundary regressors cannot absorb. All four implemented strategies return \(\sim 10^{-15}\) : strategy residual Differencing(1) 2.9e-15 Differencing(4) 9.6e-16 MovingAverage(401) 6.8e-13 LowPassRemoval(3, 2) 4.2e-16 Anything larger means the strategy is reporting a response that does not describe what it did, and an estimator built on it is biased with no warning. A constant column joins the projection, because the estimator has one: eq. (21) omits the \(m=0\) boundary term on the grounds that the transient polynomial already spans a constant. This is the test that decides which category a new strategy falls into, and it is worth running on anything added later.
docs.title: Checking a strategy

docs.text: A polynomial trend, with BLTVA. Use Nq . Nothing else, no detrending. A trend no polynomial captures, with BLTVA. Still try \(N_q\) first, as generously as eq. (49) allows — it beat Differencing(1) by 60× on the 2022 paper's own trend. Reach for Differencing(d) when \(N_p\) has eaten the budget and the \(N_q\) cap is below what the trend needs, with \(d\) from select_differencing_order as a starting point, checked against the spectrum. See what it buys . Any trend, with DMFA or STFT. PolynomialFit at the lowest degree that works, accepting the distortion in the table above — or, for the tones the drift actually overlaps, use BLTVA instead. The DMFA page has the measurements and the joint-solve alternative. To study what naive detrending costs , apply the strategy yourself and call bltva with detrend=None . That is the honest way to reproduce what a user who filters first would get, and it needs no escape hatch.
docs.title: In practice

docs.text: DMFA ¶ Demodulated multi-frequency analysis. Transform the whole record once; around each excited tone, cut out a band with a passband filter; transform that band back. What comes out is that tone's complex amplitude as a function of time, and voltage over current is \(Z(f,t)\) . Nothing is windowed, so the time resolution is not tied to the multisine period — it is set by the filter bandwidth instead. Provisional This implementation reproduces the behaviour one expects of the method, but it has not been checked against the original description in the literature. Verifying it is an open item on the roadmap . Treat DMFA results as provisional and cross-check them against STFT. The mathematics ¶ Definition ¶ For a stationary system the impedance is simply the ratio of the transforms, \[ Z(\omega) \;=\; \frac{\mathcal{F}[\Delta u](\omega)}{\mathcal{F}[i](\omega)} \] which has no time dependence at all. Koster et al. (2017) rewrite this with an apparent time dependence by filtering and transforming back, \[ Z(\omega) \;=\; \lim_{bw \to 0} \frac{\mathcal{F}^{-1}\big[\Delta\tilde{u}(\omega')\, \tilde{g}(\omega'-\omega,\,bw)\big]} {\mathcal{F}^{-1}\big[\tilde{I}(\omega')\, \tilde{g}(\omega'-\omega,\,bw)\big]} \tag{8} \] where \(\tilde g\) is a filter centred on \(\omega\) with bandwidth \(bw\) . As \(bw \to 0\) the result is constant in time and equals the stationary impedance. Dynamic impedance is what you get by keeping the bandwidth finite: \[ Z'(\omega, t) \;=\; \frac{\mathcal{F}^{-1}\big[\Delta\tilde{u}(\omega')\, \tilde{g}(\omega'-\omega,\,bw)\big]} {\mathcal{F}^{-1}\big[\tilde{I}(\omega')\, \tilde{g}(\omega'-\omega,\,bw)\big]} \tag{9} \] This is the definition DEIStools implements. The bandwidth is the only thing that creates the time dependence: it decides how much of each tone's skirt is admitted, and the skirt is the time variation. Relation to STFT ¶ The short-time Fourier transform is \[ \mathrm{STFT}[x](\omega, t) = \int_{t-\Delta t/2}^{\,t+\Delta t/2} w(t'-t)\,x(t')\,e^{-\mathrm{j}\omega t'}\,\mathrm{d}t' \tag{10} \] and the older definition of dynamic impedance is the ratio of two of these, \[ Z'(\omega, t) \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{STFT}[\Delta u](\omega, t)}{\mathrm{STFT}[i](\omega, t)} \tag{11} \] Equations (9) and (11) are the same thing whenever the filter \(\tilde g\) is the Fourier transform of the window \(w\) . DMFA and STFT are therefore not rival methods but the same operation with the roles of windowing and filtering exchanged — and, as Battistel and La Mantia (2019) put it, differing only in the order the operations are performed: STFT / FFT-EIS DMFA 1 split the record into windows transform the whole record 2 window each one split the spectrum into bands 3 transform each one filter each band 4 one spectrum per window transform each band back Filters have more freedom of shape than window functions do, which is the practical argument for (9) over (11). Quadrature filters ¶ \(\tilde g\) is a quadrature filter: it is defined only for positive frequencies. Taking one side of the spectrum makes the inverse transform the analytic signal — a complex envelope — rather than a real band-limited signal, which is exactly what is wanted, since the envelope's magnitude and phase are the amplitude and phase of the tone. The simplest is rectangular, \[ \tilde g(\omega'-\omega,\,bw) = \begin{cases} 0 & \omega' < \omega - bw\\ 1 & \omega - bw \le \omega' \le \omega + bw\\ 0 & \omega' > \omega + bw \end{cases} \tag{13} \] but a hard edge rings badly in time. DEIStools uses the smooth version of Battistel and La Mantia (2019), a product of two Fermi-Dirac functions normalised to unit gain at the centre: \[ \tilde g(\omega'-\omega,\,bw) \;=\; \frac{\big[1+e^{-n}\big]^{2}} {\Big[1+e^{-n\frac{\omega'-\omega+bw}{bw}}\Big] \Big[1+e^{\;n\frac{\omega'-\omega-bw}{bw}}\Big]} \tag{12} \] which simplifies to the form the code evaluates, \[ \tilde g \;=\; \frac{\cosh n + 1}{\cosh n + \cosh\!\big(n\,x\big)}, \qquad x = \frac{\omega'-\omega}{bw} \] a flat top with a logistic roll-off, equal to \(1/2\) at \(x = \pm 1\) . So bw is the half-amplitude half-width , and n sets how sharply the filter falls — the parameter swept in example 12. The bandwidth ceiling ¶ bw cannot be chosen freely. It must be small enough that the band around \(\omega_k\) is not reached by the neighbouring tone \(\omega_{k\pm1}\) , nor by an intermodulation \(\omega_i \pm \omega_j\) . Koster et al. give the limit in terms of the minimum spacing \(d\) designed into the multisine (in units of the base frequency \(f_b\) ): \[ bw \;\le\; 2\pi f_b \frac{(d+1)}{2} \] A multisine designed with no minimum spacing, \(d = 0\) , allows only \(bw \le \pi f_b\) — which is why the frequency grid and the achievable time resolution are the same decision. Their recommendation, from both simulation and experiment, is \(d = 7\) . The Gabor limit ¶ Underneath all of this is the uncertainty relation between time and frequency resolution, \[ \sigma_t \, \sigma_f \;\ge\; \frac{1}{4\pi} \tag{1} \] No method escapes it. STFT, DMFA, the lock-in and BLTVA simply offer different ways to spend the same budget. Calling it ¶ DMFA is assembled from four functions rather than called as one. import numpy as np from numpy.fft import fft, fftshift, fftfreq from deistools.processing.dmfa_functions import ( extract_impedance, max_elaboration_points, elaboration_frequency_axis, elaboration_time_axis) from deistools.processing.passband_filters import create_fermi_dirac_fun # 1. transform the whole record, zero frequency in the middle ft_voltage = fftshift(fft(voltage)) / N ft_current = fftshift(fft(current)) / N spectrum_axis = fftshift(fftfreq(N, 1.0 / fs)) # 2. the bin of each excited tone index_f0 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(spectrum_axis))) indexes = (np.round(frequencies * T).astype(int) + index_f0).tolist() # 3. the passband, on the band's LOCAL frequency axis bandwidth = 0.5 * frequencies.min() n_points = min(int(round(8 * bandwidth * T)), max_elaboration_points(indexes, N)) band_axis = elaboration_frequency_axis(n_points, T) band_filter = create_fermi_dirac_fun(band_axis, 0, bandwidth, 2) # 4. extract and divide Z = extract_impedance(ft_voltage, ft_current, indexes, band_filter, n_points) t = elaboration_time_axis(n_points, T) Build the filter on the local axis elaboration_frequency_axis(n_points, T) spans n_points bins of width \(1/T\) — about 0.2 Hz in the example above. The full spectrum axis spans \(f_s\) , which is 1000 Hz. Build the filter on the wrong one and its bandwidth is wrong by a factor of \(f_s T / n_{\text{points}}\) — 2500 here. This is the easiest mistake to make with this method. The two parameters ¶ Bandwidth ¶ Wider bands give finer time resolution and admit more of the neighbouring tone. The useful unit is \(f_{\min}\) , because in DFT bins \(f_{\min}\) is exactly \(P\) bins, and the closest pair of tones on a quasi-log odd grid sits \(2f_{\min}\) apart. So a passband of \(2f_{\min}\) is already reaching its neighbour. bandwidth instants median worst (edges removed) 0.5 \(f_{\min}\) 80 1.35e-04 2.20e-02 1.0 \(f_{\min}\) 160 1.01e-04 2.66e-03 2.0 \(f_{\min}\) 320 9.31e-05 2.19e-01 4.0 \(f_{\min}\) 640 1.04e-04 3.39e-01 (transistor system, sharpness \(n = 8\) ; example 12) The median barely moves while the worst case moves by two orders of magnitude. Judge DMFA settings by the worst case, not the median — the leakage shows up as a large error at a few instants, not a small error everywhere. Selecting on the median here would pick \(2f_{\min}\) , whose worst case is 158× poorer than the best setting. Sharpness ¶ n is the Fermi-Dirac exponent; large n approaches a brick wall. It has to be matched to the bandwidth, because there are two opposite failure modes: Wide band, gentle filter — the passband reaches the neighbouring tone and leakage dominates. Narrow band, sharp filter — the band is truncated abruptly, so its inverse transform rings in time. At \(0.5f_{\min}\) the worst case grows from 1.4e-03 at \(n=2\) to 4.5e-02 at \(n=16\) , with no neighbouring tone anywhere near the passband to blame. An ideal passband is the \(n \to \infty\) corner, and that corner is a bad place to be. This is why the filter is parameterised with an adjustable n . A standard DSP window does better than the published filter The Fermi-Dirac comes from statistical physics. Scored against known ground truth on three systems it ranks last of seven candidates, with Blackman about twice as good on the worst case. It remains the default because it is what the papers specify; create_window_filter switches to any of blackman , blackman-harris , nuttall , hann , kaiser or gaussian in one line. The measurement is in the implementation notes and example 12 re-runs it. Left: the Fermi-Dirac passband at four sharpnesses, with the nearest tone marked. Right: worst relative error over the grid — the best settings lie on a diagonal, not at a corner. The record edges are unusable ¶ The band-limited inverse transform rings at the record boundaries. Discard the first and last tenth of every DMFA result. This is not optional and no setting removes it: worst, edges removed worst, edges kept transistor 1.39e-03 4.13e-01 legendre 1.33e-03 8.85e-01 This is now fixable The edge damage is circular wrap-around, and zero-padding the record before the transform removes 24-29x of it at no cost to the interior. See another way to apply the filter . The stationary system shows no difference at all , which is the proof of what causes the rings: a constant impedance occupies a single bin, so truncating the band removes nothing and there is nothing to ring. The artefact is the cost of representing a changing quantity with a finite band, not an artefact of the record ending. Right: error against position in the record. The three time-varying systems show the same U shape; the stationary one is flat to both ends. Is the operation safe? The division, and the truncation ¶ Two separate worries, with two different answers. The division is safe, and it is not where the ringing comes from ¶ The concern is natural: \(Z = \mathcal{F}^{-1}[\tilde V \tilde g] \big/ \mathcal{F}^{-1}[\tilde I \tilde g]\) divides one reconstructed signal by another, and if the denominator ever approaches zero the result explodes. It does not, and the reason is structural. In a galvanostatic measurement the current is the excitation: exactly periodic, so its spectrum near \(f_k\) is a single line with no skirt . Filtering a single line gives a constant. The denominator is therefore constant by construction, not merely small-varying: measured variation of \(\|I_{\text{filtered}}\|\) over the record 4.5e-03 \(\min\|I_f\| / \mathrm{mean}\|I_f\|\) 0.9936 same, with 1e-4 A of current noise added 0.9934 Replacing \(I_f(t)\) by the single constant \(I_f(T/2)\) changes the error nowhere by more than 1e-2 absolute — at the edges, where the error is 0.26 anyway. The ringing is entirely in the numerator : it is the band-limited reconstruction of the voltage envelope, and the division neither creates nor amplifies it. This is why Chukwu et al. compute the admittance Their measurements are potentiostatic, so for them the voltage is the clean excitation and the current carries the skirt. Taking \(Y = I/V\) rather than \(Z = V/I\) keeps the clean signal in the denominator. The rule is general: put the excitation in the denominator , then invert at the end if you want the other quantity. Most of the spectrum is discarded, and that is the point ¶ Also true that almost everything is zeroed: on the standard grid the extracted bands are 0.78% of the bins . But they hold about a third of the record's total energy — more than half of the positive-frequency half — because the bins that are kept are exactly where the signal is. The rest is the other tones, the harmonics, the trend near DC and the noise floor. Zeroing them is selection, not loss. The excited line plus its skirt is the entire information about that tone's time-varying amplitude. What is unsafe is the wrap-around ¶ The genuine problem is neither of those. Multiplying a spectrum by a filter is a circular convolution in time. The kernel that reaches past the end of the record wraps around and picks up the beginning — and on a time-varying system the two ends are different. On the transistor record, \(|Z|\) at the lowest tone runs from 106 Ω at \(t=0\) to 43 Ω at \(t=T\) , so the estimate near either boundary is contaminated by a value 2.4× away. That, and not the division, is the edge oscillation. Another way to apply the filter ¶ Three alternatives were tried against known ground truth. Zero-padding — works, and is the recommended fix ¶ Padding the record before the transform makes the convolution linear: the kernel then runs into zeros instead of into the far end. system worst, plain worst, padded median transistor 7.5e-01 3.2e-02 unchanged (0.99×) legendre 8.8e-01 3.1e-02 unchanged (0.99×) 24× to 29× on the worst case, with the interior untouched — as it must be, since the kernel never reaches that far. It works better than "assume the signal is zero outside" has any right to, and the reason is the structure above: the padding attenuates the numerator and the denominator by the same factor . At the first instant the filtered current falls to 0.49 of its mid-record value and the filtered voltage falls with it, so the ratio survives. Zero-padding costs signal-to-noise near the edges, not accuracy. pad_record does it: from deistools.processing.dmfa_functions import pad_record ft_voltage = fftshift(fft(pad_record(voltage))) / n_padded The padding must be at least the kernel length, \(\approx 1/bw\) ; doubling the record is ample. Time-domain filtering — better at the edges, worse in the middle ¶ The lock-in demodulates first and filters in the time domain, where the boundary can be handled explicitly by reflecting the smooth baseband envelope. No circularity arises at all. Matched to the same 20 s resolution: position in record DMFA (circular) lock-in (time domain) 0% 2.6e-01 4.4e-03 25% 9.8e-05 7.2e-04 50% 1.2e-04 9.3e-04 100% 3.9e-01 1.6e-02 worst overall 7.5e-01 6.0e-02 A clean trade: the lock-in is 25–60× better at the boundaries, DMFA about 7× better in the interior, because a boxcar integrator has poorer frequency selectivity than a smooth filter of the same bandwidth. There is a reason you cannot simply reflect the record and get the lock-in's behaviour out of DMFA: reflecting a random-phase multisine destroys the carrier (see mirroring ). A carrier-preserving reflection has to act on the baseband envelope, which means demodulating first — and once you have demodulated, you are running a lock-in. The two facts are the same fact. Envelope detrending — tried, and it does not work ¶ The idea: the envelope is non-periodic, so subtract the linear ramp that makes it periodic, filter, then add the ramp back. Measured, it is far worse — median 1.3e-04 → 1.2e-01, with 97% of the record above 1e-02 instead of 6%. The reason is instructive. The ramp's own spectrum is not band-limited; it is a broad skirt. Subtracting it in the time domain removes all of it, but the band extraction only puts back the part inside the band, so adding the full analytic ramp back over-corrects. Adding back the filtered ramp instead makes the whole procedure an identity. The approach is circular, and no arrangement of it escapes that. In short ¶ Use zero-padding . It is one line, it costs nothing in the interior, and it removes the mechanism rather than compensating for it. Reach for the lock-in when the first or last few percent of the record is what you actually care about. Trends: why BLTVA's detrending does not transfer ¶ BLTVA handles a trend by differencing : the filter \(F_d(k) = (1-z_k^{-1})^d\) is applied to the data, the regressors are filtered with it too , the rows are reweighted by \(1/|F|\) to undo the colouring it imposes on the noise, and boundary regressors absorb the startup transient. Four coupled pieces. None of them has a counterpart in DMFA, because DMFA has no model to filter and no weighting to restore . It does not estimate the trend; it rejects it. And since it forms a ratio of two filtered signals, any filter applied to both channels largely cancels: differencing order, applied to both channels median error 0 1.315e-04 1 1.308e-04 2 3.229e-04 3 5.263e-04 The median barely moves at \(d=1\) — the common factor divides out — and degrades beyond it. The reason it is not exactly a no-op is that \(F(k)\) varies across the band, so it reshapes the passband rather than scaling it. Near dc that variation is steep, which is why the lowest tone is the one it disturbs: differencing costs it 6.7e-03 even with no trend present . What a trend actually does ¶ Only one tone is at risk. With a 5 V peak-to-peak order-3 trend on a 1.53 V signal: lowest tone median over all tones no trend 2.1e-04 1.315e-04 with trend 2.9e-01 1.319e-04 A factor of 1400 on the lowest tone and nothing anywhere else. A trend lives at dc, so it reaches the band around \(f_k\) only through the filter's stopband, and every tone above the first is further away. DMFA's actual knob: stopband rejection at dc ¶ For the tone at \(f_k\) the trend sits \(f_k\) from the band centre, so what matters is the filter's gain there. Varying nothing else: filter rejection at \(f_{\min}\) error, lowest tone Fermi-Dirac n = 2 18 dB 2.9e-01 Fermi-Dirac n = 4 35 dB 3.6e-02 Fermi-Dirac n = 8 69 dB 1.4e-03 Fermi-Dirac n = 16 139 dB 2.1e-02 blackman 29 dB 6.8e-02 nuttall 27 dB 8.8e-02 A 211× improvement from changing one parameter. rejection_db reports the number. Two things in that table are worth dwelling on. Rejection buys accuracy only until the filter's own ringing takes over: n = 16 has 70 dB more than n = 8 and is 15× worse, because at that sharpness it rings. There is an optimum, and it is not at the extreme. And a trend reverses the filter ranking . The compactly supported windows won the trend-free comparison , but they reach only about 30 dB at \(f_{\min}\) , where the Fermi-Dirac's exponential tail reaches 69. Blackman is the better filter on a clean record and 48× worse on this one. Choose against the trend you expect, not against a clean simulation. The full ladder ¶ approach lowest tone vs doing nothing nothing (n = 2) 2.9e-01 — differencing, d = 1 1.0e-02 28× subtract an order-3 polynomial first 4.7e-03 61× filter n = 8 1.4e-03 211× n = 8 + subtract the polynomial 1.6e-04 1800× no trend at all, n = 8 1.5e-04 (the floor) The combination reaches the trend-free floor exactly. Note the ordering: differencing is the weakest of the three , which is the opposite of its standing in BLTVA — there it reduces the number of trend parameters, and here there are none to reduce. When the dc skirt reaches several tones ¶ The single-tone case above is the easy one. In a real measurement the trend is large and the record is short, and then the skirt swallows the bottom of the grid. With a 48 V peak-to-peak drift on a 1.53 V signal over 8 periods: tone f / Hz trend/signal at that bin error, no trend error, with trend 0 0.05 2.6 4.3e-03 8.3e-01 (193×) 1 0.15 0.86 5.5e-03 1.8e-01 (33×) 2 0.25 0.51 5.7e-03 1.1e-01 (19×) 3 0.45 0.29 4.9e-03 5.2e-02 (11×) 4 0.65 0.21 4.5e-03 4.4e-02 (10×) 5 0.85 0.16 4.7e-03 3.0e-02 (6×) Six tones compromised, not one. Raising the filter's stopband rejection no longer saves you, because the trend is not leaking in through the skirt of the filter — it is sitting in the same bins as the signal . Why no filter can fix this ¶ A filter is diagonal in frequency: it multiplies bin \(k\) by \(g_k\) . The trend's contribution \(T(k)\) and the signal's \(S(k)\) are both in bin \(k\) , so any filter scales them together and the ratio \(T(k)/S(k)\) is untouched. That is a property of the operation, not of the particular filter, and it is why differencing measured as the weakest option: differencing is also diagonal. Subtracting a polynomial in the time domain is not diagonal and does help — but it removes signal along with the trend, and DMFA has no way to know how much. Measured by applying the same subtraction to a record with no trend , so that everything removed is signal: trend-model order distortion at tone 0 at tone 1 at tone 2 1 2.1e-03 4.5e-04 2.4e-04 3 5.9e-03 1.4e-03 7.3e-04 8 3.7e-02 3.3e-03 1.5e-03 12 6.3e-02 6.1e-03 2.2e-03 Against a clean error of 4.3e-03 at tone 0, an order-3 subtraction already costs more than the measurement is worth, and an awkward trend needing order 8 or 12 costs an order of magnitude more. This is the real limitation : the detrending distorts, the distortion grows with the trend order, and the filter formulation offers nothing to correct it with. The fix: estimate the trend and the envelope together ¶ DMFA is least squares in a Fourier basis . Once that is seen, the fix is the obvious one and the same one BLTVA uses: put the trend in the design matrix and solve for it alongside the envelope coefficients. \[ v(t) \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{j=0}^{q} a_j\,b_j(t)}_{\text{trend}} \;+\; \sum_k \mathrm{Re}\Big\{ \underbrace{\textstyle\sum_m c_{k,m} e^{\mathrm{j}2\pi m t/T}}_{\text{envelope}} e^{\mathrm{j}\omega_k t}\Big\} \;+\; \text{noise} \] The trend columns and the band columns are not orthogonal — that non-orthogonality is the overlap problem — and a joint solve handles it exactly, paying the usual price of collinearity in variance rather than in bias. The filter is not lost: it reappears as a ridge penalty \(\lambda_m = 1/g_m - 1\) on the band columns and none on the trend columns. Measured on the same six-tone case: tone no trend trend, plain DMFA trend, subtract first trend, joint ridge 0 4.27e-03 8.26e-01 8.04e-03 4.73e-03 1 5.50e-03 1.81e-01 6.28e-03 5.46e-03 2 5.72e-03 1.06e-01 5.61e-03 5.63e-03 3 4.86e-03 5.20e-02 4.91e-03 4.88e-03 4 4.45e-03 4.42e-02 4.47e-03 4.46e-03 5 4.72e-03 2.96e-02 4.67e-03 4.68e-03 The joint fit returns every tone to its trend-free value. Subtraction leaves a residual distortion at the lowest tone — 8.0e-03 against a floor of 4.3e-03 — and the joint fit does not. Where this leaves the two methods The fix for DMFA's trend problem is to use its least-squares form with trend regressors — at which point it differs from BLTVA only in the basis chosen for the envelope, Fourier against Legendre. That is not a coincidence or a defeat; it is the same observation from the other side. A filter can reject a disturbance that lives somewhere else in frequency. Separating two things that occupy the same bins needs a model , and adding one is what turns a filter bank into an estimator. Not implemented. A dense solve does not scale -- 13 tones on a 400 s record is a 400000 x 2110 design matrix -- but the structure is friendly: the tone blocks are mutually orthogonal and couple only to the trend block, so the normal equations are block-arrow and can be formed by FFT. It is on the roadmap . Until then, on a record whose trend reaches the bottom of the grid, use BLTVA for the lowest few tones . It already solves this problem, and Nq is the parameter that does it. In practice ¶ Pick the filter for the rejection you need. rejection_db(g, axis, f_min) tells you what you have. On this record 69 dB was enough and 18 dB was not. Subtract a smooth trend before the transform if one is visible. This is safe in a way it is not for BLTVA: a smooth polynomial has energy only near dc, so removing it does not touch the bands. Match the order to the trend — order 3 scored 4.7e-03 here, and going to 5 or 8 was slightly worse , since the extra freedom starts removing signal. Or raise the lowest excited frequency , which moves the first band further from dc and costs nothing but time resolution. Check whether the skirt has reached the bottom of your grid at all. Compare the trend's magnitude at each excited bin with the signal's. If the ratio exceeds a few tenths at more than the lowest tone, none of the above is enough and the section above applies: use BLTVA for those tones, or wait for the joint solve. What you should not do is reach for differencing because BLTVA uses it. The two methods are solving different problems with the same word. Inspecting a fit ¶ from deistools.processing.dmfa_functions import visualize_dmfa_filtering visualize_dmfa_filtering(band_filter, ft_voltage, ft_current, spectrum_axis, list(frequencies), indexes) A slider pages through the excited tones, showing the raw band, the filtered band and the filter itself, for voltage and for current. It is the first thing to open when a DMFA result looks wrong: a band that is visibly clipped, or one with a neighbouring tone inside the passband, explains more than any residual number. When to use it ¶ You want time resolution decoupled from the multisine period. DMFA's is set by the bandwidth, so it is adjustable — but see the caveat below: at the bandwidth that measures best here, the independent spacing works out the same as STFT's one-period window. Finer costs accuracy. You want a method that, like STFT, assumes nothing about the form of the variation. As a cross-check on BLTVA, whose accuracy depends on an assumption DMFA does not make. Given the provisional status above, do not use DMFA alone for a result you intend to publish.
docs.title: DMFA

docs.text: Demodulated multi-frequency analysis. Transform the whole record once; around each excited tone, cut out a band with a passband filter; transform that band back. What comes out is that tone's complex amplitude as a function of time, and voltage over current is \(Z(f,t)\) . Nothing is windowed, so the time resolution is not tied to the multisine period — it is set by the filter bandwidth instead. Provisional This implementation reproduces the behaviour one expects of the method, but it has not been checked against the original description in the literature. Verifying it is an open item on the roadmap . Treat DMFA results as provisional and cross-check them against STFT.
docs.title: DMFA

docs.text: For a stationary system the impedance is simply the ratio of the transforms, \[ Z(\omega) \;=\; \frac{\mathcal{F}[\Delta u](\omega)}{\mathcal{F}[i](\omega)} \] which has no time dependence at all. Koster et al. (2017) rewrite this with an apparent time dependence by filtering and transforming back, \[ Z(\omega) \;=\; \lim_{bw \to 0} \frac{\mathcal{F}^{-1}\big[\Delta\tilde{u}(\omega')\, \tilde{g}(\omega'-\omega,\,bw)\big]} {\mathcal{F}^{-1}\big[\tilde{I}(\omega')\, \tilde{g}(\omega'-\omega,\,bw)\big]} \tag{8} \] where \(\tilde g\) is a filter centred on \(\omega\) with bandwidth \(bw\) . As \(bw \to 0\) the result is constant in time and equals the stationary impedance. Dynamic impedance is what you get by keeping the bandwidth finite: \[ Z'(\omega, t) \;=\; \frac{\mathcal{F}^{-1}\big[\Delta\tilde{u}(\omega')\, \tilde{g}(\omega'-\omega,\,bw)\big]} {\mathcal{F}^{-1}\big[\tilde{I}(\omega')\, \tilde{g}(\omega'-\omega,\,bw)\big]} \tag{9} \] This is the definition DEIStools implements. The bandwidth is the only thing that creates the time dependence: it decides how much of each tone's skirt is admitted, and the skirt is the time variation.
docs.title: Definition

docs.text: The short-time Fourier transform is \[ \mathrm{STFT}[x](\omega, t) = \int_{t-\Delta t/2}^{\,t+\Delta t/2} w(t'-t)\,x(t')\,e^{-\mathrm{j}\omega t'}\,\mathrm{d}t' \tag{10} \] and the older definition of dynamic impedance is the ratio of two of these, \[ Z'(\omega, t) \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{STFT}[\Delta u](\omega, t)}{\mathrm{STFT}[i](\omega, t)} \tag{11} \] Equations (9) and (11) are the same thing whenever the filter \(\tilde g\) is the Fourier transform of the window \(w\) . DMFA and STFT are therefore not rival methods but the same operation with the roles of windowing and filtering exchanged — and, as Battistel and La Mantia (2019) put it, differing only in the order the operations are performed: STFT / FFT-EIS DMFA 1 split the record into windows transform the whole record 2 window each one split the spectrum into bands 3 transform each one filter each band 4 one spectrum per window transform each band back Filters have more freedom of shape than window functions do, which is the practical argument for (9) over (11).
docs.title: Relation to STFT

docs.text: \(\tilde g\) is a quadrature filter: it is defined only for positive frequencies. Taking one side of the spectrum makes the inverse transform the analytic signal — a complex envelope — rather than a real band-limited signal, which is exactly what is wanted, since the envelope's magnitude and phase are the amplitude and phase of the tone. The simplest is rectangular, \[ \tilde g(\omega'-\omega,\,bw) = \begin{cases} 0 & \omega' < \omega - bw\\ 1 & \omega - bw \le \omega' \le \omega + bw\\ 0 & \omega' > \omega + bw \end{cases} \tag{13} \] but a hard edge rings badly in time. DEIStools uses the smooth version of Battistel and La Mantia (2019), a product of two Fermi-Dirac functions normalised to unit gain at the centre: \[ \tilde g(\omega'-\omega,\,bw) \;=\; \frac{\big[1+e^{-n}\big]^{2}} {\Big[1+e^{-n\frac{\omega'-\omega+bw}{bw}}\Big] \Big[1+e^{\;n\frac{\omega'-\omega-bw}{bw}}\Big]} \tag{12} \] which simplifies to the form the code evaluates, \[ \tilde g \;=\; \frac{\cosh n + 1}{\cosh n + \cosh\!\big(n\,x\big)}, \qquad x = \frac{\omega'-\omega}{bw} \] a flat top with a logistic roll-off, equal to \(1/2\) at \(x = \pm 1\) . So bw is the half-amplitude half-width , and n sets how sharply the filter falls — the parameter swept in example 12.
docs.title: Quadrature filters

docs.text: bw cannot be chosen freely. It must be small enough that the band around \(\omega_k\) is not reached by the neighbouring tone \(\omega_{k\pm1}\) , nor by an intermodulation \(\omega_i \pm \omega_j\) . Koster et al. give the limit in terms of the minimum spacing \(d\) designed into the multisine (in units of the base frequency \(f_b\) ): \[ bw \;\le\; 2\pi f_b \frac{(d+1)}{2} \] A multisine designed with no minimum spacing, \(d = 0\) , allows only \(bw \le \pi f_b\) — which is why the frequency grid and the achievable time resolution are the same decision. Their recommendation, from both simulation and experiment, is \(d = 7\) .
docs.title: The bandwidth ceiling

docs.text: Underneath all of this is the uncertainty relation between time and frequency resolution, \[ \sigma_t \, \sigma_f \;\ge\; \frac{1}{4\pi} \tag{1} \] No method escapes it. STFT, DMFA, the lock-in and BLTVA simply offer different ways to spend the same budget.
docs.title: The Gabor limit

docs.text: DMFA is assembled from four functions rather than called as one. import numpy as np from numpy.fft import fft, fftshift, fftfreq from deistools.processing.dmfa_functions import ( extract_impedance, max_elaboration_points, elaboration_frequency_axis, elaboration_time_axis) from deistools.processing.passband_filters import create_fermi_dirac_fun # 1. transform the whole record, zero frequency in the middle ft_voltage = fftshift(fft(voltage)) / N ft_current = fftshift(fft(current)) / N spectrum_axis = fftshift(fftfreq(N, 1.0 / fs)) # 2. the bin of each excited tone index_f0 = int(np.argmin(np.abs(spectrum_axis))) indexes = (np.round(frequencies * T).astype(int) + index_f0).tolist() # 3. the passband, on the band's LOCAL frequency axis bandwidth = 0.5 * frequencies.min() n_points = min(int(round(8 * bandwidth * T)), max_elaboration_points(indexes, N)) band_axis = elaboration_frequency_axis(n_points, T) band_filter = create_fermi_dirac_fun(band_axis, 0, bandwidth, 2) # 4. extract and divide Z = extract_impedance(ft_voltage, ft_current, indexes, band_filter, n_points) t = elaboration_time_axis(n_points, T) Build the filter on the local axis elaboration_frequency_axis(n_points, T) spans n_points bins of width \(1/T\) — about 0.2 Hz in the example above. The full spectrum axis spans \(f_s\) , which is 1000 Hz. Build the filter on the wrong one and its bandwidth is wrong by a factor of \(f_s T / n_{\text{points}}\) — 2500 here. This is the easiest mistake to make with this method.
docs.title: Calling it

docs.text: Wider bands give finer time resolution and admit more of the neighbouring tone. The useful unit is \(f_{\min}\) , because in DFT bins \(f_{\min}\) is exactly \(P\) bins, and the closest pair of tones on a quasi-log odd grid sits \(2f_{\min}\) apart. So a passband of \(2f_{\min}\) is already reaching its neighbour. bandwidth instants median worst (edges removed) 0.5 \(f_{\min}\) 80 1.35e-04 2.20e-02 1.0 \(f_{\min}\) 160 1.01e-04 2.66e-03 2.0 \(f_{\min}\) 320 9.31e-05 2.19e-01 4.0 \(f_{\min}\) 640 1.04e-04 3.39e-01 (transistor system, sharpness \(n = 8\) ; example 12) The median barely moves while the worst case moves by two orders of magnitude. Judge DMFA settings by the worst case, not the median — the leakage shows up as a large error at a few instants, not a small error everywhere. Selecting on the median here would pick \(2f_{\min}\) , whose worst case is 158× poorer than the best setting.
docs.title: Bandwidth

docs.text: n is the Fermi-Dirac exponent; large n approaches a brick wall. It has to be matched to the bandwidth, because there are two opposite failure modes: Wide band, gentle filter — the passband reaches the neighbouring tone and leakage dominates. Narrow band, sharp filter — the band is truncated abruptly, so its inverse transform rings in time. At \(0.5f_{\min}\) the worst case grows from 1.4e-03 at \(n=2\) to 4.5e-02 at \(n=16\) , with no neighbouring tone anywhere near the passband to blame. An ideal passband is the \(n \to \infty\) corner, and that corner is a bad place to be. This is why the filter is parameterised with an adjustable n . A standard DSP window does better than the published filter The Fermi-Dirac comes from statistical physics. Scored against known ground truth on three systems it ranks last of seven candidates, with Blackman about twice as good on the worst case. It remains the default because it is what the papers specify; create_window_filter switches to any of blackman , blackman-harris , nuttall , hann , kaiser or gaussian in one line. The measurement is in the implementation notes and example 12 re-runs it. Left: the Fermi-Dirac passband at four sharpnesses, with the nearest tone marked. Right: worst relative error over the grid — the best settings lie on a diagonal, not at a corner.
docs.title: Sharpness

docs.text: The band-limited inverse transform rings at the record boundaries. Discard the first and last tenth of every DMFA result. This is not optional and no setting removes it: worst, edges removed worst, edges kept transistor 1.39e-03 4.13e-01 legendre 1.33e-03 8.85e-01 This is now fixable The edge damage is circular wrap-around, and zero-padding the record before the transform removes 24-29x of it at no cost to the interior. See another way to apply the filter . The stationary system shows no difference at all , which is the proof of what causes the rings: a constant impedance occupies a single bin, so truncating the band removes nothing and there is nothing to ring. The artefact is the cost of representing a changing quantity with a finite band, not an artefact of the record ending. Right: error against position in the record. The three time-varying systems show the same U shape; the stationary one is flat to both ends.
docs.title: The record edges are unusable

docs.text: Two separate worries, with two different answers.
docs.title: Is the operation safe? The division, and the truncation

docs.text: The concern is natural: \(Z = \mathcal{F}^{-1}[\tilde V \tilde g] \big/ \mathcal{F}^{-1}[\tilde I \tilde g]\) divides one reconstructed signal by another, and if the denominator ever approaches zero the result explodes. It does not, and the reason is structural. In a galvanostatic measurement the current is the excitation: exactly periodic, so its spectrum near \(f_k\) is a single line with no skirt . Filtering a single line gives a constant. The denominator is therefore constant by construction, not merely small-varying: measured variation of \(\|I_{\text{filtered}}\|\) over the record 4.5e-03 \(\min\|I_f\| / \mathrm{mean}\|I_f\|\) 0.9936 same, with 1e-4 A of current noise added 0.9934 Replacing \(I_f(t)\) by the single constant \(I_f(T/2)\) changes the error nowhere by more than 1e-2 absolute — at the edges, where the error is 0.26 anyway. The ringing is entirely in the numerator : it is the band-limited reconstruction of the voltage envelope, and the division neither creates nor amplifies it. This is why Chukwu et al. compute the admittance Their measurements are potentiostatic, so for them the voltage is the clean excitation and the current carries the skirt. Taking \(Y = I/V\) rather than \(Z = V/I\) keeps the clean signal in the denominator. The rule is general: put the excitation in the denominator , then invert at the end if you want the other quantity.
docs.title: The division is safe, and it is not where the ringing comes from

docs.text: Also true that almost everything is zeroed: on the standard grid the extracted bands are 0.78% of the bins . But they hold about a third of the record's total energy — more than half of the positive-frequency half — because the bins that are kept are exactly where the signal is. The rest is the other tones, the harmonics, the trend near DC and the noise floor. Zeroing them is selection, not loss. The excited line plus its skirt is the entire information about that tone's time-varying amplitude.
docs.title: Most of the spectrum is discarded, and that is the point

docs.text: The genuine problem is neither of those. Multiplying a spectrum by a filter is a circular convolution in time. The kernel that reaches past the end of the record wraps around and picks up the beginning — and on a time-varying system the two ends are different. On the transistor record, \(|Z|\) at the lowest tone runs from 106 Ω at \(t=0\) to 43 Ω at \(t=T\) , so the estimate near either boundary is contaminated by a value 2.4× away. That, and not the division, is the edge oscillation.
docs.title: What is unsafe is the wrap-around

docs.text: Three alternatives were tried against known ground truth.
docs.title: Another way to apply the filter

docs.text: Padding the record before the transform makes the convolution linear: the kernel then runs into zeros instead of into the far end. system worst, plain worst, padded median transistor 7.5e-01 3.2e-02 unchanged (0.99×) legendre 8.8e-01 3.1e-02 unchanged (0.99×) 24× to 29× on the worst case, with the interior untouched — as it must be, since the kernel never reaches that far. It works better than "assume the signal is zero outside" has any right to, and the reason is the structure above: the padding attenuates the numerator and the denominator by the same factor . At the first instant the filtered current falls to 0.49 of its mid-record value and the filtered voltage falls with it, so the ratio survives. Zero-padding costs signal-to-noise near the edges, not accuracy. pad_record does it: from deistools.processing.dmfa_functions import pad_record ft_voltage = fftshift(fft(pad_record(voltage))) / n_padded The padding must be at least the kernel length, \(\approx 1/bw\) ; doubling the record is ample.
docs.title: Zero-padding — works, and is the recommended fix

docs.text: The lock-in demodulates first and filters in the time domain, where the boundary can be handled explicitly by reflecting the smooth baseband envelope. No circularity arises at all. Matched to the same 20 s resolution: position in record DMFA (circular) lock-in (time domain) 0% 2.6e-01 4.4e-03 25% 9.8e-05 7.2e-04 50% 1.2e-04 9.3e-04 100% 3.9e-01 1.6e-02 worst overall 7.5e-01 6.0e-02 A clean trade: the lock-in is 25–60× better at the boundaries, DMFA about 7× better in the interior, because a boxcar integrator has poorer frequency selectivity than a smooth filter of the same bandwidth. There is a reason you cannot simply reflect the record and get the lock-in's behaviour out of DMFA: reflecting a random-phase multisine destroys the carrier (see mirroring ). A carrier-preserving reflection has to act on the baseband envelope, which means demodulating first — and once you have demodulated, you are running a lock-in. The two facts are the same fact.
docs.title: Time-domain filtering — better at the edges, worse in the middle

docs.text: The idea: the envelope is non-periodic, so subtract the linear ramp that makes it periodic, filter, then add the ramp back. Measured, it is far worse — median 1.3e-04 → 1.2e-01, with 97% of the record above 1e-02 instead of 6%. The reason is instructive. The ramp's own spectrum is not band-limited; it is a broad skirt. Subtracting it in the time domain removes all of it, but the band extraction only puts back the part inside the band, so adding the full analytic ramp back over-corrects. Adding back the filtered ramp instead makes the whole procedure an identity. The approach is circular, and no arrangement of it escapes that.
docs.title: Envelope detrending — tried, and it does not work

docs.text: Use zero-padding . It is one line, it costs nothing in the interior, and it removes the mechanism rather than compensating for it. Reach for the lock-in when the first or last few percent of the record is what you actually care about.
docs.title: In short

docs.text: BLTVA handles a trend by differencing : the filter \(F_d(k) = (1-z_k^{-1})^d\) is applied to the data, the regressors are filtered with it too , the rows are reweighted by \(1/|F|\) to undo the colouring it imposes on the noise, and boundary regressors absorb the startup transient. Four coupled pieces. None of them has a counterpart in DMFA, because DMFA has no model to filter and no weighting to restore . It does not estimate the trend; it rejects it. And since it forms a ratio of two filtered signals, any filter applied to both channels largely cancels: differencing order, applied to both channels median error 0 1.315e-04 1 1.308e-04 2 3.229e-04 3 5.263e-04 The median barely moves at \(d=1\) — the common factor divides out — and degrades beyond it. The reason it is not exactly a no-op is that \(F(k)\) varies across the band, so it reshapes the passband rather than scaling it. Near dc that variation is steep, which is why the lowest tone is the one it disturbs: differencing costs it 6.7e-03 even with no trend present .
docs.title: Trends: why BLTVA's detrending does not transfer

docs.text: Only one tone is at risk. With a 5 V peak-to-peak order-3 trend on a 1.53 V signal: lowest tone median over all tones no trend 2.1e-04 1.315e-04 with trend 2.9e-01 1.319e-04 A factor of 1400 on the lowest tone and nothing anywhere else. A trend lives at dc, so it reaches the band around \(f_k\) only through the filter's stopband, and every tone above the first is further away.
docs.title: What a trend actually does

docs.text: For the tone at \(f_k\) the trend sits \(f_k\) from the band centre, so what matters is the filter's gain there. Varying nothing else: filter rejection at \(f_{\min}\) error, lowest tone Fermi-Dirac n = 2 18 dB 2.9e-01 Fermi-Dirac n = 4 35 dB 3.6e-02 Fermi-Dirac n = 8 69 dB 1.4e-03 Fermi-Dirac n = 16 139 dB 2.1e-02 blackman 29 dB 6.8e-02 nuttall 27 dB 8.8e-02 A 211× improvement from changing one parameter. rejection_db reports the number. Two things in that table are worth dwelling on. Rejection buys accuracy only until the filter's own ringing takes over: n = 16 has 70 dB more than n = 8 and is 15× worse, because at that sharpness it rings. There is an optimum, and it is not at the extreme. And a trend reverses the filter ranking . The compactly supported windows won the trend-free comparison , but they reach only about 30 dB at \(f_{\min}\) , where the Fermi-Dirac's exponential tail reaches 69. Blackman is the better filter on a clean record and 48× worse on this one. Choose against the trend you expect, not against a clean simulation.
docs.title: DMFA's actual knob: stopband rejection at dc

docs.text: approach lowest tone vs doing nothing nothing (n = 2) 2.9e-01 — differencing, d = 1 1.0e-02 28× subtract an order-3 polynomial first 4.7e-03 61× filter n = 8 1.4e-03 211× n = 8 + subtract the polynomial 1.6e-04 1800× no trend at all, n = 8 1.5e-04 (the floor) The combination reaches the trend-free floor exactly. Note the ordering: differencing is the weakest of the three , which is the opposite of its standing in BLTVA — there it reduces the number of trend parameters, and here there are none to reduce.
docs.title: The full ladder

docs.text: The single-tone case above is the easy one. In a real measurement the trend is large and the record is short, and then the skirt swallows the bottom of the grid. With a 48 V peak-to-peak drift on a 1.53 V signal over 8 periods: tone f / Hz trend/signal at that bin error, no trend error, with trend 0 0.05 2.6 4.3e-03 8.3e-01 (193×) 1 0.15 0.86 5.5e-03 1.8e-01 (33×) 2 0.25 0.51 5.7e-03 1.1e-01 (19×) 3 0.45 0.29 4.9e-03 5.2e-02 (11×) 4 0.65 0.21 4.5e-03 4.4e-02 (10×) 5 0.85 0.16 4.7e-03 3.0e-02 (6×) Six tones compromised, not one. Raising the filter's stopband rejection no longer saves you, because the trend is not leaking in through the skirt of the filter — it is sitting in the same bins as the signal .
docs.title: When the dc skirt reaches several tones

docs.text: A filter is diagonal in frequency: it multiplies bin \(k\) by \(g_k\) . The trend's contribution \(T(k)\) and the signal's \(S(k)\) are both in bin \(k\) , so any filter scales them together and the ratio \(T(k)/S(k)\) is untouched. That is a property of the operation, not of the particular filter, and it is why differencing measured as the weakest option: differencing is also diagonal. Subtracting a polynomial in the time domain is not diagonal and does help — but it removes signal along with the trend, and DMFA has no way to know how much. Measured by applying the same subtraction to a record with no trend , so that everything removed is signal: trend-model order distortion at tone 0 at tone 1 at tone 2 1 2.1e-03 4.5e-04 2.4e-04 3 5.9e-03 1.4e-03 7.3e-04 8 3.7e-02 3.3e-03 1.5e-03 12 6.3e-02 6.1e-03 2.2e-03 Against a clean error of 4.3e-03 at tone 0, an order-3 subtraction already costs more than the measurement is worth, and an awkward trend needing order 8 or 12 costs an order of magnitude more. This is the real limitation : the detrending distorts, the distortion grows with the trend order, and the filter formulation offers nothing to correct it with.
docs.title: Why no filter can fix this

docs.text: DMFA is least squares in a Fourier basis . Once that is seen, the fix is the obvious one and the same one BLTVA uses: put the trend in the design matrix and solve for it alongside the envelope coefficients. \[ v(t) \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{j=0}^{q} a_j\,b_j(t)}_{\text{trend}} \;+\; \sum_k \mathrm{Re}\Big\{ \underbrace{\textstyle\sum_m c_{k,m} e^{\mathrm{j}2\pi m t/T}}_{\text{envelope}} e^{\mathrm{j}\omega_k t}\Big\} \;+\; \text{noise} \] The trend columns and the band columns are not orthogonal — that non-orthogonality is the overlap problem — and a joint solve handles it exactly, paying the usual price of collinearity in variance rather than in bias. The filter is not lost: it reappears as a ridge penalty \(\lambda_m = 1/g_m - 1\) on the band columns and none on the trend columns. Measured on the same six-tone case: tone no trend trend, plain DMFA trend, subtract first trend, joint ridge 0 4.27e-03 8.26e-01 8.04e-03 4.73e-03 1 5.50e-03 1.81e-01 6.28e-03 5.46e-03 2 5.72e-03 1.06e-01 5.61e-03 5.63e-03 3 4.86e-03 5.20e-02 4.91e-03 4.88e-03 4 4.45e-03 4.42e-02 4.47e-03 4.46e-03 5 4.72e-03 2.96e-02 4.67e-03 4.68e-03 The joint fit returns every tone to its trend-free value. Subtraction leaves a residual distortion at the lowest tone — 8.0e-03 against a floor of 4.3e-03 — and the joint fit does not. Where this leaves the two methods The fix for DMFA's trend problem is to use its least-squares form with trend regressors — at which point it differs from BLTVA only in the basis chosen for the envelope, Fourier against Legendre. That is not a coincidence or a defeat; it is the same observation from the other side. A filter can reject a disturbance that lives somewhere else in frequency. Separating two things that occupy the same bins needs a model , and adding one is what turns a filter bank into an estimator. Not implemented. A dense solve does not scale -- 13 tones on a 400 s record is a 400000 x 2110 design matrix -- but the structure is friendly: the tone blocks are mutually orthogonal and couple only to the trend block, so the normal equations are block-arrow and can be formed by FFT. It is on the roadmap . Until then, on a record whose trend reaches the bottom of the grid, use BLTVA for the lowest few tones . It already solves this problem, and Nq is the parameter that does it.
docs.title: The fix: estimate the trend and the envelope together

docs.text: Pick the filter for the rejection you need. rejection_db(g, axis, f_min) tells you what you have. On this record 69 dB was enough and 18 dB was not. Subtract a smooth trend before the transform if one is visible. This is safe in a way it is not for BLTVA: a smooth polynomial has energy only near dc, so removing it does not touch the bands. Match the order to the trend — order 3 scored 4.7e-03 here, and going to 5 or 8 was slightly worse , since the extra freedom starts removing signal. Or raise the lowest excited frequency , which moves the first band further from dc and costs nothing but time resolution. Check whether the skirt has reached the bottom of your grid at all. Compare the trend's magnitude at each excited bin with the signal's. If the ratio exceeds a few tenths at more than the lowest tone, none of the above is enough and the section above applies: use BLTVA for those tones, or wait for the joint solve. What you should not do is reach for differencing because BLTVA uses it. The two methods are solving different problems with the same word.

docs.text: You want time resolution decoupled from the multisine period. DMFA's is set by the bandwidth, so it is adjustable — but see the caveat below: at the bandwidth that measures best here, the independent spacing works out the same as STFT's one-period window. Finer costs accuracy. You want a method that, like STFT, assumes nothing about the form of the variation. As a cross-check on BLTVA, whose accuracy depends on an assumption DMFA does not make.
