docs.text: Goertzel filter ¶ The Goertzel algorithm evaluates a single DFT bin with a second-order recurrence instead of a transform. A multisine measurement wants exactly a handful of known bins, which is the case the algorithm was made for. It computes the same quantity as a rectangular-window STFT , by different arithmetic — verified here to 1e-10 — so it is best understood as an independent route to that estimator rather than as a fourth method. The mathematics ¶ For a block of \(N\) samples and a bin \(k\) — the frequency in units of the block's own resolution, \(k = f N \Delta t\) — define \[ \omega = \frac{2\pi k}{N}, \qquad \text{coeff} = 2\cos\omega \] and run, from \(s_{-1} = s_{-2} = 0\) , \[ s[n] \;=\; x[n] + \text{coeff}\cdot s[n-1] - s[n-2], \qquad n = 0 \ldots N-1 \] Only the final two states are needed: \[ X[k] \;=\; \Big(e^{\mathrm{j}\omega}\,s[N-1] - s[N-2]\Big)\,e^{-\mathrm{j}2\pi k} \] The output formula is asymmetric, and the tempting form is wrong \(s[N-1] - e^{-\mathrm{j}\omega}s[N-2]\) looks like the natural rearrangement and appears in some write-ups. It has the right magnitude and is wrong by exactly \(e^{-\mathrm{j}\omega}\) in phase. That error cancels in any ratio — including \(V/I\) — so an impedance test will not catch it. Only a comparison against the DFT itself will, which is what test_output_formula_is_not_the_tempting_rearrangement does. The correct combination is what you get by running one further step with a zero input and forming \(s[N] - e^{-\mathrm{j}\omega}s[N-1]\) ; writing it closed-form avoids the extra iteration. The trailing \(e^{-\mathrm{j}2\pi k}\) is unity whenever \(k\) is an integer, which is why most presentations omit it. Keeping it is the generalised Goertzel of Sysel and Rajmic ( EURASIP J. Adv. Signal Process. 2012, 56), and it makes the result correct for a non-integer \(k\) — a tone that does not land exactly on a bin of the block you chose, which is the ordinary case rather than an exotic one. Calling it ¶ from deistools.processing import MultiFrequencyAnalysis mfa = MultiFrequencyAnalysis(frequencies, voltage, current, sampling_time) Z, t = mfa.run_goertzel(period=Tp) # one spectrum per block Or directly: from deistools.processing.goertzel import goertzel_dft, goertzel_eis Z, t = goertzel_eis(voltage, current, frequencies, period, sampling_time) # or one block, one set of bins, with no transform anywhere values = goertzel_dft(block, bins=frequencies * period) period must hold a whole number of periods of every tone, for the same reason a rectangular STFT window must: otherwise each bin picks up the others. On a stream ¶ The recurrence carries two numbers. Nothing is buffered, so it runs during an acquisition rather than after it — which is the one thing none of the other estimators in this package can do. from deistools.processing.goertzel import GoertzelFilter filt = GoertzelFilter(frequency=0.05, sampling_time=1e-3, block=20000) for sample in stream: value = filt.push(sample) if value is not None: ... # one block completed; the filter has reset itself push returns None until a block is complete, then that block's complex DFT value. Cost: it is slower here, and that is expected ¶ Goertzel costs about \(N\) operations per bin; an FFT costs about \(N\log_2 N\) for every bin at once. The crossover is at roughly \(n_{\text{bins}} \approx \log_2 N\) : \[ \text{ratio} = \frac{n_{\text{bins}}}{\log_2 N} \] For 13 tones in a 20 000-sample block that is 0.91 — nominally a wash, and in practice a loss, because a compiled FFT beats a Python recurrence at equal operation count by a wide margin. Measured: 0.17 s against 0.05 s . cost_ratio(n_bins, block) reports the number. Below one favours Goertzel on operations alone; the real crossover sits well below that. So it is not here for speed on recorded files. It is here because it is a standard estimator, because it checks the STFT path independently, and because its recurrence is the one that also runs live. Accuracy ¶ Identical to STFT, necessarily — same estimator. On the transistor system with a one-period block: median relative error worst Goertzel 7.13e-04 8.96e-03 STFT 7.13e-04 8.96e-03 Its limits are STFT's limits: time resolution is the block length, with a floor of one multisine period; the skirts are not used; no uncertainty is reported. See STFT . Sources ¶ Goertzel, Am. Math. Monthly 65 (1958) 34 — the original recurrence. Sysel and Rajmic, EURASIP J. Adv. Signal Process. (2012) 56 — the generalisation to non-integer bins, which is the form implemented here. Worked example ¶ examples/07_goertzel_first_run.py checks the recurrence against np.fft , reproduces the STFT estimate, times both, and feeds the streaming GoertzelFilter sample by sample. When to use it ¶ Live processing , where no FFT is possible because the record has not finished. Very few bins out of very many — a handful of tones in a long block, where \(n_{\text{bins}} \ll \log_2 N\) . As a cross-check. Agreement to 1e-10 with a completely different arithmetic path is a meaningful check on an FFT-based implementation, including on the bin indexing that is easy to get subtly wrong.

docs.text: Lock-in amplifier ¶ The classical instrument, implemented offline. For each excited tone the record is multiplied by a cosine and a sine at that frequency, and the products are low-pass filtered. What survives is that tone's slowly varying complex amplitude, and the ratio of the voltage and current amplitudes is \(Z(f,t)\) . It is the most familiar of the four methods to an experimentalist, and — as shown below — it turns out to be the continuous-time generalisation of STFT rather than a separate idea. The mathematics ¶ Write the response near the \(k\) -th tone as a carrier with a slowly varying phasor: \[ v(t) \;=\; A_v(t)\,\cos\!\big(\omega_k t + \varphi_v(t)\big), \qquad \omega_k = 2\pi f_k \] Mixing with the in-phase and quadrature references gives \[ \begin{aligned} v(t)\cos(\omega_k t) &= \tfrac{A_v}{2}\cos\varphi_v \;+\; \tfrac{A_v}{2}\cos(2\omega_k t + \varphi_v) \\ v(t)\sin(\omega_k t) &= -\tfrac{A_v}{2}\sin\varphi_v \;+\; \tfrac{A_v}{2}\sin(2\omega_k t + \varphi_v) \end{aligned} \] Each product has a baseband term carrying the information and an image at \(2\omega_k\) . A low-pass filter \(h\) that rejects the image leaves \[ X = \tfrac{A_v}{2}\cos\varphi_v, \qquad Y = -\tfrac{A_v}{2}\sin\varphi_v \] and twice the complex combination is the phasor itself: \[ V(t) \;=\; 2\big(X - \mathrm{j}Y\big) \;=\; A_v(t)\,e^{\mathrm{j}\varphi_v(t)} \] The same is done for the current, and \[ Z(f_k, t) \;=\; \frac{V(t)}{I(t)} \] The factor of two and the one-sided convention both cancel in that ratio, so they matter only if you want \(V\) and \(I\) to be meaningful on their own. Choosing the integrator — the whole method ¶ The low-pass filter has two jobs. Rejecting the image at \(2f_k\) is easy. The binding requirement is the other one: every other tone of the multisine , after mixing at \(f_k\) , lands at the difference frequency \(|f_j - f_k|\) , and must be rejected too. For a multisine whose tones are all harmonics of a base frequency \(f_b\) , every such difference is a multiple of \(f_b\) . A boxcar average over exactly an integer number of periods of \(f_b\) has spectral nulls at every multiple of \(1/(N_w \Delta t)\) — that is, at every one of those difference frequencies. It rejects them all, exactly. integrator worst rejection of the other 12 tones boxcar, 1 base period 307 dB (arithmetic limit) boxcar, 2 base periods 311 dB Hann, 2 base periods 116 dB Hann, 4 base periods 134 dB (example 08; the boxcar rows are round-off, not a real finite rejection) tone_rejection includes the tone you demodulated Each row it returns has one entry per frequency, and the entry for \(f_k\) itself has zero offset and therefore 0 dB. Drop it before taking a worst case, or the answer is always 0 dB. The window must span whole base periods of \(f_b\) , not of \(f_k\) The nulls sit at multiples of \(1/(N_w\Delta t)\) and only land on the harmonics if \(N_w \Delta t\) is a whole number of base periods. Rounding \(N_w\) to an odd number to centre the kernel on a sample detunes them: on a 20 000-sample period that one extra sample costs about 230 dB of rejection. integrator_length therefore returns the exact length and refuses a non-integer one. The resulting half-sample group delay is common to voltage and current and cancels in their ratio. A Hann window has its nulls in the same places but a mainlobe twice as wide, so over a single base period the nearest harmonic falls inside the mainlobe and is not rejected at all. integrator_length refuses window='hann' with n_periods=1 for that reason. The integrator length is also the time resolution : a window of \(m\) base periods cannot follow anything faster than \(m/f_b\) seconds. That is the same trade STFT makes with its window and DMFA with its bandwidth. Two demodulators ¶ Mixing ( method='mix' ) ¶ The textbook route described above. Two FFT convolutions per frequency, so the whole record at every sample costs a couple of seconds. Local least squares ( method='ls' ) ¶ Instead of mixing, fit \[ x(t) \approx a\cos\omega_k\tau + b\sin\omega_k\tau + c + d\,\tau, \qquad \tau = t - t_0 \] in a sliding window, and take \(a - \mathrm{j}b\) as the phasor. Carrying the offset \(c\) and the local slope \(d\) is the point: the fit tracks drift within the window instead of averaging over it. That matters more than it sounds. On the transistor system: demodulator median relative error mixing, 1-period boxcar 1.16e-03 local least squares, same window 1.05e-04 (valid instants only; example 08) An order of magnitude, from the same data and the same window, because the within-window averaging bias is what limits the mixing route on a drifting system. The cost is one least-squares solve per reported instant, so it must be evaluated on a decimated grid. The phasor is referenced to the window centre local_ls centres \(\tau\) on the window, so the phase it returns is relative to \(t_0\) , not to \(t=0\) . The reference cancels in \(V/I\) because both are fitted on the same window — which is why lia_impedance_ls is correct — but a caller using local_ls on its own must undo the \(e^{-\mathrm{j}\omega t_0}\) itself. Calling it ¶ from deistools.processing import MultiFrequencyAnalysis mfa = MultiFrequencyAnalysis(frequencies, voltage, current, sampling_time) Z, t = mfa.run_lia(n_periods=1, decimate=200) # mixing Z, t = mfa.run_lia(n_periods=1, method="ls", stride=20000) # local LS mfa.lia_tone_rejection(1) # dB, one row per demodulated tone mfa.lia_valid_mask() # False where the window ran past the record Or directly: from deistools.processing.lock_in_amp import integrator_length, lia_eis samples_window = integrator_length(sampling_time, base_frequency=1/Tp, n_periods=1, window="boxcar") Z, t = lia_eis(time, voltage, current, sampling_time, frequencies, samples_window, decimate=200) Edges ¶ The output within half an integrator length of either end rests on a window that extends past the data. This implementation reflects the signal at the boundaries, which is exact for an envelope with zero slope there and good otherwise, and valid_mask marks the affected samples so a fit can exclude them. This is the lock-in's version of DMFA's edge problem , but it is milder and explicitly controllable, because the filtering happens in the time domain where the boundary can be handled directly instead of being wrapped around by a circular DFT. Worked example ¶ examples/08_lock_in_first_run.py runs all of the above on the transistor system: designing the integrator, the rejection table, the estimate, the edges, the agreement with STFT, and the two demodulators side by side. It is STFT, evaluated everywhere ¶ A boxcar lock-in over exactly one base period and a rectangular STFT over the same window are the same estimator . Verified on the transistor record: max |Z_lia − Z_stft| / |Z_stft| = 9e-14 (at the STFT window centres) STFT is that estimator decimated to one point per window; the lock-in reports at every sample. So the lock-in buys no accuracy over STFT at the instants STFT reports — its median error over all instants is higher (1.2e-03 against 7.1e-04) precisely because it also reports between the centres, where the within-window bias is larger. What it buys is a continuous output, an explicit and adjustable integrator, and — through method='ls' — a way to remove the within-window bias that neither STFT nor plain mixing can. When to use it ¶ You want the familiar instrument. This is what a hardware lock-in does, so the parameters mean what an experimentalist expects them to mean. You want a continuous \(Z(f,t)\) rather than one value per window. Your system drifts within a window — use method='ls' , which is the only estimator here that removes that bias without assuming a global model the way BLTVA does. You are heading towards online processing. The mixing route is the one that becomes a streaming filter, though a causal integrator would replace the zero-phase one used here. Limits ¶ Time resolution is the integrator length, with the same floor as STFT: one base period. No uncertainty is reported, as with STFT and DMFA. Cost grows linearly with the number of tones, since each is demodulated separately. DMFA transforms once for all of them.

docs.text: Time resolution is the integrator length, with the same floor as STFT: one base period. No uncertainty is reported, as with STFT and DMFA. Cost grows linearly with the number of tones, since each is demodulated separately. DMFA transforms once for all of them.
docs.title: Limits

docs.text: STFT ¶ Short-time Fourier estimation. Cut the record into consecutive windows, take the DFT of each, divide voltage by current at the excited bins. Each window gives one spectrum, stamped at its own midpoint. It is the method with nothing to assume and almost nothing to tune, which makes it the right first thing to try and the right fallback when the others fail. Calling it ¶ from deistools.processing.stft_functions import estimate_impedance Z, voltage_avg, current_avg, t = estimate_impedance( voltage, # measured response current, # measured excitation frequencies, # the excited frequencies [Hz] period, # window length in SECONDS sampling_time, # 1/fs window_fun="rectangular", ) returned shape meaning Z (n_freq, n_windows) the impedance in each window voltage_avg (n_windows,) mean voltage in each window current_avg (n_windows,) mean current in each window t (n_windows,) midpoint of each window, in seconds voltage_avg and current_avg carry no impedance information, but a drifting voltage_avg is a direct warning that the cell is doing something besides responding to your excitation. period is in seconds Not samples, and not multisine periods. It must hold a whole number of periods of every tone, or the rectangular window leaks. The one parameter ¶ The window length fixes three things at once: the time resolution (one estimate per window), how much noise is averaged away, and how much the impedance is smeared by varying within a window. Shorter windows track better and average less. Which wins depends on the noise: noise 1 × \(T_p\) 2 × \(T_p\) 4 × \(T_p\) best \(10^{-4}\) V 7.1e-04 9.5e-04 1.7e-03 1 × \(T_p\) \(10^{-2}\) V 1.1e-03 1.1e-03 1.7e-03 2 × \(T_p\) \(3\times10^{-2}\) V 1.7e-03 1.5e-03 1.8e-03 2 × \(T_p\) (median relative error on the transistor system; example 10) With a strong excitation the shortest window wins. On a real cell with a small excitation the optimum moves out, and the choice becomes a real decision rather than "use the shortest". On a stationary system the bias term is identically zero, so the trade has only one side: the whole record in one window is best. If a window sweep picks the longest window, that is itself a useful signal about your cell. Limits ¶ Time resolution cannot go below one multisine period. The lowest tone would not fit in a shorter window. This is a hard floor. The skirts are not used. All the information about how the system changed between windows is discarded. No uncertainty from the excited bins alone. A window of two or more multisine periods does carry it, in the bins this estimator discards — see BLA per burst , which reads the noise and nonlinear distortion off them. The catch is in the window length: at one period every bin is a harmonic of the multisine and the separation is impossible, so the error bars cost at least half the time resolution. When to use it ¶ Your variation is not smooth — a step, a kink, anything a low-order polynomial cannot follow. STFT will track it; BLTVA will not. You want a result that depends on as few assumptions as possible. As a cross-check on the others. In example 20 all three agree to within a factor of three on a stationary cell; a disagreement there would point at a problem with the setup, not the physics. Failure mode ¶ The error concentrates at the lowest tones, where a window holds only one or two cycles and whatever the cell did during that window is baked into them. If a result is worst at the bottom of the grid and improves monotonically upward, that is the within-window bias and a shorter window is the remedy — if the noise allows it.
